And: [Manu 2.153] "One should address a king's paternal uncle as 'Sir' (*bhavat*); a king's maternal uncle should be addressed as 'Sir' (*bhavat*). And: [Manu 2.154] "One should address a king's brother as 'Sir' (*bhavat*); a king's sister's husband should be addressed as 'Sir' (*bhavat*). And: [Manu 2.155] "One should address a king's daughter's husband as 'Sir' (*bhavat*); a king's son's wife should be addressed as 'Madam' (*bhagavatī*). And: [Manu 2.156] "One should address a king's daughter as 'Princess' (*kumārī*); a king's wife should be addressed as 'Madam' (*bhagavatī*). And: [Manu 2.157] "One should address a king's sister as 'Madam' (*bhagavatī*); a king's mother-in-law should be addressed as 'Madam' (*bhagavatī*). And: [Manu 2.158] "One should address a king's maternal aunt as 'Madam' (*bhagavatī*); a king's paternal aunt should be addressed as 'Madam'
When greeting a Brahmin, one should say, "May you be long-lived, O gentle one.
Furthermore, the letter *a* at the end of his name should be pronounced with a protracted (pluta) vowel, preceded by its preceding syllable.

The application is as follows: “O gentle Devadatta, may you be long-lived! (āyuṣmān bhava saumya devadattā3a). In the case of names such as Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and Pinākapāṇi, when the *guṇa* substitution has been applied in the vocative, this rule also applies: “In place of *e* and *o* that are not *pragṛhya*, when used in calling from a distance, there are *i* and *u* in place of the latter half of the preceding vowel and the first half of the following vowel. At the end, the letter *a* becomes *y* or *v* according to Pāṇini 8.2.108 (*tayor yvāv aci saṃhitāyām*). Thus: *śambhā3va*, *viṣṇā3va*, *pinākapāṇā3ya*. Regarding the word *ca* (“and”) in the sūtra “*pratyabhivādane ca*,” we do not see its purpose. Another says: “There is prolation (*plāvana*) both in greeting (*abhivādana*) and in responding to a greeting (*pratyabhivādana*). Even in this view, because the two are expressed by a copulative compound (*dvandva*), the word *ca* is indeed redundant. Furthermore, in no other treatise is prolation prescribed for the act of greeting; therefore, the word *ca* is truly redundant. And particles (*nipāta*) are frequently employed even when they are redundant. || 1.5.17 ||
But when the sun has risen, he should meet his teacher and perform the formal salutation.
But when the sun has risen, having come together with his teacher for the purpose of study, he should perform the formal salutation according to the procedure to be described. 1.5.18.
One should always offer a respectful salutation. 1.5.19.
At other times, at all times, there is only salutation in the manner previously described; this, however, is a restatement intended for what follows. 1.5.19.
Some say that after having received him [as a pupil], he is called an *ācārya*. 1.5.20.
Some maintain that, on the occasion of a salutation, one should always clasp [the teacher's feet], thinking, "He is my teacher. 1.5.20.
What is this "clasping"? To that he says: having touched the right foot from below with his right hand, he should clasp it including the ankle. 1.5.21.

With his own right hand, having touched the teacher’s right foot from below—the word *adhi* here signifying the sense of "above"—he should grasp it, touching both the top and the bottom, including the toes and the ankle; others say "including the thumb" (*sāṅguṣṭham*). He should perform this salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*), that is, he should do this. 1.5.21.
Some say that both [the teacher and the student] should press both [hands] together and clasp them. 1.5.22.

Some authorities maintain that both feet of the teacher must be grasped by the student with both hands while pressing them. In the expression "abhipīḍayataḥ," the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent, according to the rule *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā* (Pāṇini 2.3.71). On this point, Manu says:
"The grasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands;
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right. (1.5.22)
Being well-prepared throughout the entire day, he should study immediately after his recitation. 1.5.23.

“*Sarvāhṇam*” means that entire day. By the rules *Pāṇini* 5.4.91 (*rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac*) and 5.4.88 (*ahnohṇa etebhyaḥ*), the substitution of *ahn* for *ahaḥ* occurs; by 8.4.7 (*ahnodantāt*), the change to *ṇ* is applied. The accusative case is used here to denote continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). “*Sarvāhṇaṃ suyuktaḥ*” means well-engaged, well-composed, and with a mind focused on nothing else. “*Anantaraḥ*” means immediately following the study; it does not allow an interval (*na antaram karoti*). Thus, he should be such that he does not create an interval for himself from his study, nor does he interrupt his study. “*Adhyāye*” refers to the time of Vedic recitation. The term “*adhyāya*” here is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because of the specific injunction in Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.5.25: “and mentally during the non-periods of study (*anadhyāya*)”; for that reason, most read “*adhyāyet*. In that case, the letter *t* is either a scribal error (*apapāṭha*) or a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). 1.5.23.
Likewise, in the case of weighty duties. || 1.5.24 ||
And likewise in weighty tasks, he should be well-prepared and immediate in his action. || 1.5.24 ||
And one should not recite mentally during a time unfit for study.

And during times when formal recitation is not permitted, he should engage in mental study; thus, he should remain uninterrupted. He should examine with his mind those points where doubt arises and direct his reflection solely toward the subject matter of his studies. (1.5.25)
And he should study when summoned. 1.5.26.
Being summoned by the teacher, he should study; he should not initiate himself into teaching. 1.5.26.
Thus ends the fifth section:
One should always put the teacher to bed at night, having washed his feet and massaged them. 1.6.1.

Every day, when the night has passed and the evening twilight has ended, he should lay his teacher to rest. How? By washing the feet of that teacher and by massaging them; "massaging" means rubbing. 1.6.1.
Having been permitted, he may lie down. 1.6.2.
Thereafter, having been permitted by the teacher, he himself may enter and lie down. 1.6.2.
And one should not stretch it out toward him. 1.6.3.
One should not stretch out one's feet toward this teacher. 1.6.3.
Some say that there is no stretching out [of the limbs] while one is on a couch. 1.6.4.
Some maintain that when the teacher lies on a bed, it is not a fault for [the student] to stretch out his feet toward him; however, our own position is that there is a fault even in that case. 1.6.4.
And one should not speak while reclining in his presence. || 1.6.5 ||
In the presence of this teacher, one should not speak while sitting or lying down; rather, having stood up, one should speak when it is time to report on one's duties and so forth.
But when addressed while seated, he should reply. || 1.6.6 ||
When addressed by the teacher, he should reply while remaining seated; this applies when the teacher is either seated or lying down. 1.6.6.
Standing up after him as he departs. || 1.6.7 ||
When the teacher speaks while standing, [the pupil] should rise and respond. 1.6.7.
The two subsequent sūtras are clear in meaning:
"One should follow him as he goes. (1.6.8)
One should run after him as he runs. 1.6.9.
One should not walk with one's head covered by shoes, nor with hands occupied. 1.6.10.

Because the wearing of shoes is prohibited later on [ĀpDh 1.7.5] with the statement “not wearing shoes,” the present rule “nor while wearing shoes” is a restatement intended as a counter-exception to the rule “but when on a journey” [ĀpDh 1.6.11]. One should not approach the teacher while wearing shoes, nor with one’s head covered. Nor should one approach him with hands occupied—meaning with hands holding a sickle or similar tools—even if he is in such a state. 1.6.10.
But one who has entered upon a path while still engaged in ritual action may perish. || 1.6.11 ||

"One who has reached the path" means one who has entered upon it. "Engaged in action" means one who has set out toward an action to be accomplished by means of a sacrificial gift and so forth. One who is in such a state may even tread upon [the fire] while wearing sandals. 1.6.11.
If he does not approach [the teacher], [he should perform penance]. 1.6.12.

If he does not sit down—that is, approach and take his seat—in the presence of the teacher, then if he is traveling on a road or engaged in ritual work, he should sit down after removing his sandals and other such items. 1.6.12.
One should attend upon the teacher like a god, without idle talk, with a clear mind, and listening attentively to his words. 1.6.13.

Whichever deity one worships, one should attend upon that deity as one's teacher (*ācārya*). Without idle chatter—idle chatter being useless talk—one should not engage in it; with an undistracted mind, that is, with a mind free from distraction, one should listen to the words of this teacher. 1.6.13.
Not performed by one who has not been formally installed as an assistant. || 1.6.14 ||
The preparation of the ritual seat is well known. Having performed that, one should not sit [in attendance]. 1.6.14.
The wind blows favorably. || 1.6.15 ||

When the wind is blowing from behind, one should sit facing away from it; in the opposite case, one should sit facing toward it. However, sitting with the wind blowing directly against one is prohibited by what will be stated hereafter. Manu also says:
"One should not sit with the teacher when the wind blows against him or when it blows from behind" (MDh 2.203).
Not obstructed by the hand. || 1.6.16 ||
He should not remain propped up; he should not sit with his hands placed on the ground for support. 1.6.16.
Not dependent on anything else. 1.6.17.
He should not lean against anything other than a wall or the like; he should not sit leaning against a wall or similar object. 1.6.17.
He wears the sacrificial thread and has two garments. 1.6.18.

When he has two garments, he should wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with one of them; however, that rule—namely, "Or else, the cord alone may serve the purpose of the sacred thread" (ĀpDh 2.4.22)—does not apply in that case. 1.6.18.
But he who wears his lower garment tucked up is one who is clad in a single cloth. 1.6.19.
But when he has only one garment, then it should be wrapped around his lower body; he must not use even a portion of that long garment as an upper covering. || 1.6.19 ||
The face-to-face [meditation] is directed toward that which is not face-to-face.
Facing the teacher himself, he should attend upon the teacher while not facing himself; seeing only the teacher, he should sit upright in front of the teacher. 1.6.20.
Neither too near nor too far. 1.6.21.
And it would not exist if [the object] were too near or too far. || 1.6.21 ||
As far as he can reach with his two arms while sitting. 1.6.22.
He should sit at such a distance that he can reach the teacher with both arms while remaining seated. 1.6.22.
Not against the wind. 1.6.23.
One should not sit to leeward of the teacher. 1.6.23.
One who studies a single chapter should sit down facing the right arm.
When he studies alone, he should sit down—that is, take his seat—on the right side, facing the teacher’s right arm.
Many [may perform it] according to the available space. 1.6.25.
But many disciples may approach him at their convenience. 1.6.25.
And he remains established in the yoga of neither-sitting-nor-not-sitting.

"Āsanayoga" means the arrangement of a seat; "āsanayogavihita" means one who has been appointed or designated by means of the practice of sitting. While a teacher who has not been so designated by the practice of sitting remains present, one should not sit down oneself. || 1.6.26 ||
And one should not lie down while the other is sitting. 1.6.27.

The phrase "not engaged in lying down" is to be understood according to what precedes it. When the teacher is seated and not engaged in lying down, the student himself should neither sit nor lie down. 1.6.27.
And one exerts effort when desiring to act within the scope of that capacity. (1.6.28)

The middle voice ending (*prasmaipada*) is used here by way of transposition. When the teacher is active, one might desire to perform [the rite] oneself as well. Is this without qualification? It applies within the scope of one's own capacity; that is, if what is being performed by the teacher falls within the range of one's own ability. By the use of the desiderative suffix (*san*) in the word *cikīrṣan*, one should demonstrate merely the desire, and not act independently. Once the desire has been demonstrated, if the teacher grants permission, one may proceed. However, if it falls outside the scope of one's capacity, even the desire should not be expressed. Thus, the reading *cikīrṣet* (one should desire to do) is appropriate. 1.6.28.
And one should not receive a person who stands in the position of a subordinate in his presence. 1.6.29.

The Smṛti tradition designates those other than the Ācārya as *anvaksthānins* (those who stand behind); for it is said, "The Ācārya is the best of gurus" (GDh 2.50), and thus, having considered that their position is subordinate (*anvaksthāna*) in relation to him. One should not perform the ritual salutation (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) to an *anvaksthānin* while in the presence of the Ācārya. 1.6.29.
Or one may recite it by means of the lineage. || 1.6.30 ||
Nor should he mention or praise him according to his station—by his lineage, birth, family, or the like—saying, for example, "This man is a Bhārgava, born of a great family. (1.6.30)
And one should neither rise to meet him nor rise after him. 1.6.31.
He should not even rise up in the presence of his teacher; furthermore, when he has been sitting in the presence of the teacher and rises to depart, he should not even rise up after him. 1.6.31.
Moreover, even if he should be his teacher. 1.6.32.

Even if that person were the maternal uncle or another elder of that teacher, then, since he will state the rule for worship in the passage, "In the case of a meeting between a teacher and a former teacher" (ĀpDh 1.8.19), this [present rule] was stated to prevent the same logic from applying to maternal uncles and others as well. 1.6.32.
But he should move away from his seat and from the place where he was sitting. 1.6.33.
However, he may move from his place and seat for the sake of honoring him. 1.6.33.
Some say that by name he refers to his own teacher, who was a pupil of that [teacher]. 1.6.34.

One should mention that teacher’s pupil by name alone, such as "Yajñaśarman," even if he himself is the pupil's guru; so some maintain. However, our own position is that one must not utter the name of one's own guru. 1.6.34.

But in the case of one who is not related to him as a teacher, even if that person occupies a position subordinate to the teacher, the same respect and conduct toward him is required as toward the teacher himself.

But toward that person in whom there is respect from worldly people due to their knowledge, conduct, and so forth—even in the absence of the relationship of disciple and teacher—one should maintain the same behavior as toward a teacher who occupies the position of a companion; even toward one who occupies the position of a companion, one should behave exactly as toward a companion. 1.6.35.
And having eaten in his presence, one should not rise and offer him the remnants of the meal. 1.6.36.

Having eaten in the presence of the teacher—whether he be eating or not—one should not give him the leavings without rising. The vowel in *utthāna* is long by rule (*chaṇdaso dīrghaḥ*). One should not offer the remains without having performed the act of rising, as it has been prescribed: "Or one should clear the plate for the noble one" (ĀpDh 1.3.40).
Or he may sip water. 1.6.37.
One should not perform even the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) without rising. 1.6.37.
Having addressed him with the words, "What shall I do? [he should wait]. 1.6.38.
Having sipped water and addressed the teacher, "What shall I do? || 1.7.38 ||
Thus ends the sixth section.
He should rise either silently or [with a word]. 1.7.1.

This is an alternative view. Based on the indicative mark of the address "O [Teacher]," one should not perform the sipping of water (ācamana) even after rising; rather, one should sip water only in the presence of the teacher. 1.7.1.
He should not turn his back on the teacher; having circumambulated him from left to right, he may depart. || 1.7.2 ||
Having risen and desiring to go on business, one should not turn away from the teacher with his left side; rather, having circumambulated him clockwise, one should depart. 1.7.2.
One should not look at a naked woman. 1.7.3.
One should not look at a naked woman, upon seeing whom a transformation of the mind occurs. 1.7.3.
One should not smell herbs or trees after having plucked them. 1.7.4.

Annual plants (oṣadhayaḥ) are those that perish at the ripening of their fruit; forest trees (vanaspatayaḥ) are those that bear fruit without flowers—the term also serves as an indication for shrubs and trees. One should not pluck their leaves or flowers and smell them. By the use of the word "plucking," it follows that there is no fault in catching the fragrance incidentally. 1.7.4.
One should also avoid sandals, an umbrella, and a vehicle. || 1.7.5 ||

A vehicle refers to a cart and the like; the word "iti" is intended as an illustration of such types. Regarding this, Gautama states: "One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, idle talk, playing musical instruments, bathing, brushing the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear" (GDh 2.13). 1.7.5.
One should not smile. 1.7.6.
One should not smile. 1.7.6.
"If they smile, let them smile while holding [the vessel]"; for such is the Brāhmaṇa.

If, due to excessive joy, he is unable to restrain himself, then he should cover his mouth with his hand and smile; this is according to the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "he should not smile" (na smayet). 1.7.7.
One should not kiss a woman with the mouth. || 1.7.8 ||

One should not even smell with the mouth a woman, whether she be young or have her limbs anointed after bathing. By the use of the word "mouth," there is no fault in the accidental perception of a fragrance. (1.7.8)
One should not make a request with the heart. || 1.7.9 ||
One should not desire a woman with one's heart or mind, thinking, "May she be mine. || 1.7.9 ||
One should not touch [water] without a specific reason. 1.7.10.
One should not touch a woman without a specific reason. A reason includes occasions such as tying or untying the girdle, supporting her when she has fallen on uneven ground, and so forth. 1.7.10.
"One who is full of passion, whose teeth are red, and who speaks the truth—this is a Brāhmaṇa," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 1.7.11.

"One who has menstrual flow" means one whose body is soiled; "one with red teeth" (*raktadant*) refers to one whose teeth are stained red—the substitution of *dant* for *dat* is Vedic. This means "one with stained teeth. Although both of these conditions are already covered by the rule "one whose fame is lost" (*utsannaślāgha*, ĀpDh 1.2.27), they are stated again because a penance prescribed in the Śruti might apply in the event of their transgression. He will state the penance [for such cases] in the rule "having spoken a falsehood" (ĀpDh 1.26.3). And the Brāhmaṇa text says: "One should be a speaker of truth. 1.7.11.
Whatever knowledge he acquires from his teacher, those who belong to that teacher’s lineage are also his teachers in that [knowledge]. (1.7.12)

Regarding the knowledge that one acquires or studies under one’s own teacher, those who belong to the lineage of that teacher—the *ācāryas*—are also the *ācāryas* of this young student (*māṇavaka*). Even though the knowledge is not received directly from them, nevertheless they are to be treated like an *ācārya*. By the use of the word "in that" (*tasyām*), this rule does not apply to those who belong to the lineage of other branches of knowledge. (1.7.12)
But those others whom he sees [and would otherwise not address], he should then approach and greet. 1.7.13.

While this boy is looking on, or while he is looking at this boy, those others whom the teacher would receive [as students] should also be received by the boy. Is this always so? No, it says: "But then these," meaning in that state. Another says: from that time forward, these are to be received; because of the word "but" (tu), even by one who has returned home [after completing his studies]. 1.7.13.
When there is a gathering of teachers and alms have become available, the alms belong to whichever teacher one follows. 1.7.14.

When a student who is studying the second or third Veda encounters a gathering of teachers—that is, when several teachers have come together—then, when the time for alms has arrived, the alms are dependent upon whichever teacher the student is currently following and from whom he is studying; whatever and however much has been obtained must be reported to him, and its application is to be carried out as directed by him. (1.7.14)
Upon returning from his studies, he should give [the gift] to his mother. || 1.7.15 ||
Having completed his return home from study, he should give to his mother whatever he has acquired prior to his marriage.
The mother shall cause the husband to go [to his own home]. 1.7.16.
The mother shall cause [the daughter] to reach a husband. 1.7.16.
The husband is the guru. || 1.7.17 ||
He too should deliver it to the teacher; it is proper that wealth acquired by the student should go to him. 1.7.17.
Or he should employ it for religious duties. || 1.7.18 ||

He may also employ it for religious duties such as marriage and the like; in the absence of the teacher, the husband [should do so]; in his absence, the mother; and in the absence of all these, the student himself once he has returned home from his studies. || 1.7.18 ||
Having mastered as much of the Veda as he is able, he should, according to his capacity and in accordance with dharma, bring the teacher’s fee.

Having mastered as much of the Veda as he is capable of performing—whether one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas—and having studied it, he should bring a sacrificial fee for his teacher; that is, he should give what has been acquired according to dharma and earned through righteous means, in accordance with his ability. || 1.7.19 ||
This is an exception to the rule of *dharmatā*.
However, if the teacher has fallen into misfortune, he may fetch [the fire] from a fierce man or even from a Śūdra. (1.7.20)

But when the teacher has fallen into misfortune or is in distress, he may bring back the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) by accepting it from an Ugra or from a Śūdra. An Ugra is one born to a Vaiśya woman from a Śūdra father; or it is a twice-born man who performs fierce deeds. 1.7.20.
Some say that at all times, the acquisition of the teacher’s property from a Śūdra or an Ugra is lawful. 1.7.21.

Some maintain that it is lawful—that is, not departing from dharma—for one to procure for the sake of the teacher, whether in times of distress or non-distress, whatever wealth is to be given to the teacher, by means of a Śūdra or even from a Śūdra. In the reading *dhārmyam*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense (to denote the thing itself). 1.7.21.
And having given, one should not speak of it. || 1.7.22 ||
Having thus brought [the gift] and given it to the teacher, one should not proclaim, "This was given by me. || 1.7.22 ||
And having performed it, one should not dwell upon it. || 1.7.23 ||
Even after performing a great service for the teacher during a life-threatening crisis or similar situation, one should not recall or dwell upon it, thinking, "Oh, this was done by me. (1.7.23)
One should avoid praising oneself and censuring others. || 1.7.24 ||
By the use of the particle *iti*, there is also a prohibition of other such things as self-reproach and the like. 1.7.24.
Being sent, he should go to that very place. || 1.7.25 ||

If he is sent by the teacher with the command "Do this," he should undertake and perform that very task, even if it means abandoning a ritual action currently being performed, provided that [abandoning] belongs to the teacher. 1.7.25.
And because there is no coming [of a teacher], the subsistence [of the Veda] is otherwise. 1.7.26.

This is an exception to the rule [ĀpDh 1.1.13]: "And in that very [teacher], the completion of the study and the ritual duties. If the knowledge desired to be acquired does not come forth properly from the teacher—the instructor or preceptor—then, because of its failure to come forth from him, one's livelihood may indeed be found elsewhere with another person from whom it does come forth properly. 1.7.26.
Except for receiving gifts and eating the leftovers, his conduct toward the teacher’s wife is the same as toward the teacher himself. (1.7.27)

The term "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) applies as a supplement to both cases. One should behave toward the teacher’s wives as one does toward the teacher himself. Is this without distinction? No; it is "except for clasping the feet and eating the remnants," meaning that both—clasping the feet and eating the remnants of his food—are to be avoided. On this point, Manu says: "But a young wife of the guru must not be saluted by touching her feet here in this world" (MDh 2.212ab).

Gautama, however, states: “The same applies to his wife’s sons; [but there shall be] no eating of her leftovers, bathing her, adorning her, washing her feet, massaging her, or clasping her feet” (GDh 2.31–32). The use of the singular form *dāra* (“wife”) is a Vedic archaism. 1.7.27.
When thus instructed, he teaches. 1.7.28.

When one who has been instructed and appointed by the teacher teaches, the same conduct as toward the teacher's wife applies toward him. Because the term "teaches" is used in the present tense, this extended application lasts only as long as the teaching continues. (1.7.28)
And toward an elder fellow-student in the holy life. || 1.7.29 ||

The term "teaches" (*adhyāpayati*) does not carry over [from the previous rule]. Because of the specific mention of the word "therein" (*tatra*), one who is aged in both knowledge and years is understood. A *sabrahmacārī* is a fellow student; he is so called because he performs his vow (*vrata*) in the same sacred knowledge (*brahman*). Toward him also, the conduct is as toward the teacher's wife: the teacher takes three-quarters [of the merit] and the pupil takes one-quarter through his own intelligence; one-quarter [of the merit] comes from fellow students, and one-quarter ripens in time.
Thus, because the application [of the rules] is possible in the case of Vedic study. 1.7.29.
Except for eating the remnants of food, his conduct toward the teacher’s son is the same as toward the teacher himself. 1.7.30.

Because of the statement "with the exception of eating leavings," the act of clasping the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) takes place; and this [is done] toward one who is superior in knowledge or age. To that end, the term "one who is more aged" (*vṛddhatara*) is understood to carry over. However, the prohibition of clasping the feet found in the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra* refers to someone other than one who is more aged. (1.7.30)
Even for one who has returned home from his teacher, this same conduct regarding these [occasions] is prescribed by conventional rule.

Even for one who has performed the rite of returning home (*samāvartana*), this very conduct just mentioned—pertaining to the rules of customary practice (*sāmayācārika*) and derived from established custom—is to be observed toward these persons, beginning with the teacher and ending with the son. A specific rule has been stated [in ĀpDh 1.7.28]: "When commanded, he should teach. 1.7.31.
Thus ends the seventh section: [The conduct] of a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) is as follows. 1.8.1.

The term "of one who has returned" (samāvṛttasya) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. We shall now describe the conduct—that is, the mode of life—of a student (brahmacārin) who has returned home but has not yet married. 1.8.1.

Wearing garlands, with his face anointed and his hair and beard smeared, he is sprinkled and rubbed with unguents; he is wrapped and tightly bound, wearing a tunic and sandals, and equipped with wooden shoes. 1.8.2.

*Mālī* means wearing a garland. *Āliptamukhaḥ* means one whose face is smeared with sandalwood paste and the like; the mention of the "face" (*mukha*) is illustrative, based on the statement of Āśvalāyana: "The Brāhmaṇa should first smear his face" (ĀśGṛ 3.8.11). *Upaliptakeśaśmaśruḥ* refers to one whose hair and beard have been treated and refined by being smeared with fragrant substances such as *āmalaka*. *Aktaḥ* means having the eyes anointed with collyrium. *Abhyaktaḥ* means having been rubbed with oil. *Veṣṭitī* means one whose head is wrapped. *Upaveṣṭitī* refers to one whose waist region is wrapped with a second garment. *Kañcukopānaham* is a compound meaning a cloak and sandals; the suffix *ac* is added to form the compound according to Pāṇini 5.4.106. One who possesses these is *kañcukopānahī*; the suffix *in* is applied here according to Pāṇini 5.2.128. In the well-known reading, *kāñcuka* is synonymous with *kañcuka*, and one who possesses it is *kāñcukī*. One who possesses sandals is *upānahī*; the suffix *in* is applied here because the word belongs to the *vrīhyādi* group. *Pāduke* refers to wooden foot-protectors; one who possesses them is *pādukī*. 1.8.2.
And one should not perform or cause these [actions] to be performed by him during his daily observances. 1.8.3.
In the presence of this teacher and others, down to his sons, one should not offer or cause to be offered these garlands and other items in places that come within the range of vision.
And in voluntary actions. 1.8.4.
One should neither perform these nor cause them to be performed. || 1.8.4 ||
An example of this is as follows:
"such as cleansing the teeth, massaging, and scraping. (1.8.5)

"Rinsing the teeth" refers to cleansing the teeth with a twig. "Utsādana" means rubbing the body with unguents. "Avalekhana" is the arranging of the hair into distinct parts using a comb or similar instrument. The word "iti" (and so forth) is used for the purpose of illustration; by it, the prohibition applies to eating, voiding urine, defecating, and other such acts as well. 1.8.5.
And the teacher should not speak of those substances as being in conjunction with himself. 1.8.6.

When that disciple has become a householder, he should not speak in such a way as to show how he has acquired for himself even a single item among those goods provided [to him], nor should he speak in a manner that reveals his desire when the teacher returns to the disciple’s house, thinking, "Oh, what a beautiful eating vessel! and so forth. (1.8.6)
But some say that one who has bathed at the proper time according to the rule, whether invited or arrived on his own, should not turn back from the food brought for him. 1.8.7.

Regarding the rule, “Having studied the Veda, one who is about to bathe,” some maintain that when he has bathed according to that injunction, at that time—whether he has been summoned by the teacher or has approached him on his own—the garland and other items brought and fastened according to the rule should not be removed or taken off. However, our own position is that even then he should remove them, because of the expression “brought according to the rule at the proper time”; thus, starting from the following day, he should indeed remove them. 1.8.7.
One should not sit higher [than his teacher]. 1.8.8.
The suffix *tarap* is used in the sense of the word itself. One should not sit on a seat higher than that of the teacher. 1.8.8.
Likewise, [it applies] to that which has many feet. 1.8.9.
One should not sit on a seat that is lower [than the teacher's] but has many legs. 1.8.9.
Established everywhere. || 1.8.10 ||
He should sit on a seat; having seated the teacher on a stool or similar seat, he himself should sit on a cane chair or the like, for that [chair] stands firmly on the ground on all sides. 1.8.10.
And one should not sit upon a bed or seat that has not been used. 1.8.11.

One should not occupy a bed or seat that has been used by the teacher; one should not lie down on his bed nor sit upon his seat. This same rule applies to other elders, such as one's father. And so Manu has stated without distinction:

"One should not share a bed or seat occupied by a superior" (MDh 2.119). The specific rules for one who has returned home have been concluded. Now follows the remainder of the regulations concerning the student life (*brahmacarya*). 1.8.11.
One should mount a vehicle on the road as has been prescribed. 1.8.12.

A vehicle refers to a cart and the like; when told by his teacher, "Mount," he should mount it afterwards. This is an exception to the previously mentioned prohibition, "He shall avoid the umbrella and the vehicle" [ĀpDh 1.7.5]. Furthermore, the vehicle must be one that the teacher has already mounted, or another [suitable one]. 1.8.12.
And [the use of] the assembly hall, the grinding stone, the bed, and the mat. 1.8.13.

It has been stated that he should mount [the vehicle] when so commanded. The mention of the *sabhā* (assembly hall) is for the purpose of providing an exception to the rule: "He shall attend assemblies and social gatherings" (ĀpDh 1.3.12). A *nikaṣa* is a tool belonging to farmers by which a ploughed field is leveled; when someone has mounted it and another person pulls it, he should mount it even while being pulled by the teacher if so commanded, but he should not fail to mount out of fear of impropriety. A *kaṭa* is a bed made of *vīraṇa* grass; when commanded by the teacher, he should sit upon it together with him. This is the custom during festivals and similar occasions. A *svastara* is a bed of straw, as seen in the injunction: "They lie down on a new *svastara*" (ĀpGṛ 19.9). There too, when commanded by the teacher, he should perform acts such as sitting together. 1.8.13.
Unless addressed by his teacher, he should not speak to him anything other than what is pleasant.
Unless addressed by his teacher, he should not say anything to him other than what is pleasant; however, he may speak pleasant words such as, "A son has been born. (1.8.14)
One should avoid poking at, whispering to, laughing at, addressing by name, calling by name, or sending messages to one's teacher. 1.8.15.

*Vyupatoda* is poking with a finger or the like, which is done for the purpose of confronting [the teacher]. *Vyupajāpa* is whispering repeatedly into the ears. The letter *va* is either a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*) or a scribal error (*apapāṭha*). *Vyabhihāsa* is laughing in his presence. *Udāmantraṇa* is calling out loudly, as one would to a deaf person. *Nāmadeyagrahaṇa* is the utterance of the name assigned by the father on the tenth day; it does not refer to the names of venerable persons such as the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) and so forth. *Preṣaṇa* is giving commands. These should not be performed toward a teacher. By the use of the particle *iti*, there is a prohibition of other similar acts as well, as Manu has said: [Manu 2.197–198]... "One should not utter his name even in his absence alone;
nor should one imitate his gait, speech, or gestures. [MDh 2.199] 1.8.15.
In times of distress, one may make known the purpose [of the act]. 1.8.16.

In times of distress, one should make known one's intended purpose even by means of poking with a pointed object and the like. In the absence of another person, one should inform them through speech rather than sending someone directly; for example: "I have a piercing pain in my side, and it can be relieved by fire, yet no one is present here; what am I to do, unfortunate as I am? (1.8.16)
In the subsequent sūtra, concerning the subject of returning home:
"Living together, he should go to see the teacher in the evening and in the morning, unless summoned. (1.8.17)
Dwelling in the same village, he should go to see his teacher in the evening and in the morning, even if unsummoned, for the purpose of seeing him and not for any other purpose.
And having returned from travel, he should look at her on that very day.
When he has gone to another village and returns, he shall see his teacher on that very day. 1.8.18.
When both the teacher and the sub-teacher are present together, he should clasp the feet of the sub-teacher and desire to clasp the feet of the teacher. 1.8.19.

The teacher of the teacher is the *prācārya*, just as one speaks of a *prapitāmaha* (great-grandfather). When there is a meeting or encounter between the teacher and the *prācārya* due to some business, then [one should act] toward the *prācārya*. The dative case is used here in the sense of the accusative. Having first paid respects to the *prācārya*, one should then desire to pay respects to one's own teacher. This should not be done merely in thought; rather, one should act in such a way that the teacher perceives, "This person wishes to receive me. Otherwise, the instruction would be for a purpose other than what was intended. 1.8.19.
The other should refute [the objection]. 1.8.20.
The other teacher should forbid him, saying, "Child, do not clasp my feet. || 1.8.20 ||
And worship offered in his presence is lost. || 1.8.21 ||
In the presence of this teacher—that is, in his immediate vicinity—the honoring of the teacher must not be omitted; it is not merely the clasping of the feet that is forbidden. 1.8.21.
The subsequent sūtra concerns those who have returned home from their studies:
"And he should go to the teacher's family at intervals for the purpose of seeing him, bringing as much of a gift as he can afford, even if it is only materials for cleaning the teeth. (1.8.22)

The forms *muhūṃś* and *cet* contain the long vowel due to the *anusvāra*, which is a Vedic usage. Here, the elision of repetition (*vīpsā*) should be understood; what is intended is *muhur muhuḥ* (repeatedly). Even while living in another village, he should go repeatedly to the teacher’s family for the purpose of seeing him. "Taking with his own hand" means taking things such as milk products or cakes that are held in the hand, according to his ability. The word *api* indicates that this rule applies even in the absence [of these items]; that is, even in the absence of milk products and the like, one should offer tooth-sticks. The word *iti* serves to indicate the completion of the duties of the pupil. 1.8.22.
In that regard, the conduct toward the teacher [is as follows]. 1.8.23.
In that regard, the conduct—that is, the manner of behavior—of a teacher toward his resident pupil will now be described. || 1.8.23 ||
Desiring him as one would a son, and not concealing anything among all dharmas, he should, being well-disciplined, cause him to grasp the knowledge. 1.8.24.

Desiring that this disciple might attain prosperity just like his own son, he should, without concealing or hiding anything regarding any matters of dharma, cause him to grasp the sciences, being well-prepared, thoroughly attentive, and devoted to the task. 1.8.24.
And he should not obstruct him from his own interests by creating obstacles to his Vedic study, except in times of distress. 1.8.25.

And one should not obstruct this student in his own affairs by causing an interruption to his studies. "Obstruction" means making him dependent (depriving him of independence). Because of the statement "except in times of distress," obstruction—even by means of an injunction to study—is not a fault when there is an emergency. 1.8.25.
A pupil who has surrendered himself to his teacher becomes as if no longer a pupil when he displays incompetence toward his guru. 1.8.26.

The term "āpadyamānaḥ" (falling into) implies the sense of the causative verb (*ṇyartha*). A pupil who, having properly surrendered himself to two teachers, displays incompetence toward his primary guru by saying, "This point was not correctly stated by him," is no longer a pupil; the meaning is that he should be abandoned. On this point, Manu says:
"Where neither dharma nor artha exist, nor even service of the appropriate kind, there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil. (MDh 2.112)

Another says: A pupil who, through the actions of speech, mind, and body, falls into incompetence and remains ill-disposed toward his teacher, not serving him in a fitting manner—he is no longer a pupil. 1.8.26.
Even a teacher becomes one who is not a teacher if he neglects sacred learning. 1.8.27.

"Even a teacher becomes a non-teacher"—the meaning is that he is to be abandoned. What is he doing? Avoiding what has been heard [from the scriptures], while imparting knowledge through various such pretexts. 1.8.27.
And one should constantly find fault with him regarding his transgressions. || 1.8.28 ||
When offenses have been committed, he should constantly reprove this disciple, saying, "This which you have done is improper. || 1.8.28 ||
Intimidation, fasting, touching water, and avoidance [of the offender] are the punishments, according to the gravity of the offense, until [the transgression] has ceased. 1.8.29.

*Abhitrāsa* is the production of fear by means of ropes, bamboo whips, and the like. *Upavāsa* is the omission of food. *Udakopasparśana* is bathing with cold water. *Adarśana* is acting so that the person does not see himself, such as forbidding him entry into the house; in all these cases, the suffix is applied to the causative form (*ṇyanta*). These are the punishments for a student, to be applied individually or collectively according to the measure of the offense—that is, in proportion to the degree of the transgression—and they continue until his desistance, meaning they persist as long as he does not turn away from those offenses. (1.8.29)
He should dismiss him with the words: "Having completed the practice of celibacy, may you be one who is not separated from other dharmas. (1.8.30)

"Having thus lived the life of celibacy and returned from the teacher's house"—the meaning is that he has performed the rite of returning home (*samāvartana*). To him who is in such a state, [the father] should say: "Become one who is not separated from those duties (dharmas) for whichever stage of life (*āśrama*) he is about to enter; be such that you do not become separated from those duties. Having said this, he should dismiss him, releasing him to enter that stage of life. 1.8.30.
Thus ends the eighth section;
thus ends the second chapter in the *Ujjvalā*, the commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Having commenced the term on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one shall not study during the first watch of the night for one month. 1.9.1.
Thus have been stated the duties pertaining to the student and the teacher. Now, the duties regarding study as determined by place and time are being declared:
"Whichever new moon (*darśa*) occurs while the sun is situated in Aries and the subsequent signs, those twelve months ending with that [new moon] are traditionally known as Caitra and the others."
Among those, whichever is the full moon day (paurṇamāsī) is traditionally designated as Caitrī and so forth;
the determination [of its name] is based on the conjunction of the moon with a particular lunar mansion (nakṣatra), such as Citrā.

Thus, when the sun is situated in Leo, on the full moon day that falls in the middle of the lunar month ending with the new moon, that is the Śrāvaṇī. Whether there is a conjunction with the Śravaṇā asterism or not, having commenced the term (*adhyāya*) on that Śrāvaṇī full moon and performed the *upākarma* ceremony according to the rules prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, one should study the Veda. While studying, during the first part of the night—the period of *pradoṣa*—for one month, one should not study; that is, one should not perform the study for memorization (*grahaṇādhyayana*) nor the study for retention (*dhāraṇādhyayana*). Because of the mention of *pradoṣa*, there is no fault in studying after that time, even during the night. (1.9.1)
One should cease [the study] on the full moon day of the month of Taiṣya, or under the asterism Rohiṇī.

*Taiṣī* is the full moon day conjoined with the asterisms Tiṣya (Puṣya); it is like *Śrāvaṇī*. On that day one should cease [studying] and perform the *utsarjana* ceremony. Its procedure is also exactly as stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Or, on *Rohiṇī*: in the month of Taiṣa, on the *Rohiṇī* that precedes Tiṣya, one may likewise cease. During these two options, one should study for five months. 1.9.2.
Some say four months and a half-fifth [of a month]. 1.9.3.

Those for whom there are four and a half months are called *ardhapañcamāḥ*. Some maintain that one should study for four months plus an additional half-month. According to this view, the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) takes place on the full moon of *proṣṭhapada*; or, based on the observation of other scriptures, the conclusion (*utsarjana*) is brought forward. Once the conclusion has been performed, until the full moon of *śrāvaṇa*, during the bright fortnights one should engage in the memorization (*dhāraṇa*) of the Veda, and during the dark fortnights, the study of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) such as grammar. Then, having performed the commencement again on the full moon of *śrāvaṇa*, one engages in the study of grasping (*grahaṇa*) those portions not yet mastered. This has been explained in detail in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* (1.9.3).
One should avoid reciting the Nigamas. 1.9.4.
*Nigamas* are crossroads or the roads leading out of a village, so called because they are traversed by people according to fixed rules; in such places, he should avoid study of every kind. (1.9.4)
Or he may study on ground smeared with a ball of cow-dung from a bull. || 1.9.5 ||
Having smeared himself with a lump of dung from an ox, he should study in inhabited areas. 1.9.5.
In a cremation ground, [the boundary extends] everywhere for the distance of a throw of a yoke-pin. 1.9.6.

One should avoid studying in a cremation ground. "In all directions" means in every direction for the distance of a *śamyā*-throw. Because of the use of the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*), it is understood that this refers to the area within that distance. A *śamyā* is a wooden pin; the area within which it falls when thrown is the limit from which one must stay away. (19.6)
When a village or a field has been settled upon, there is no suspension of study. 1.9.7.
When a cemetery has been settled upon as a village or as a field and has been taken possession of, then it is not a time for suspension of study; one must indeed study. 1.9.7.
But while that very place is being known [as such], one should not study there. 1.9.8.
But when that cemetery is recognized as "this is that place," then one should not study in that very area, nor even within the distance of a *śamyā*-throw. 1.9.8.
A Śūdra and an outcaste are like a cremation ground. 1.9.9.
One should not study even within the range of a *śamyā*-throw from a *śūdra* or an outcast (*patita*). 1.9.9.
"Some say [it means] 'in the same house'. 1.9.10.
Some maintain that within the same house, a Śūdra and an outcast (patita) are to be avoided, but not beyond the range of a wooden pin's throw. 1.9.10.
But in the case of a Śūdra woman, there is no suspension of study only when looking at her or being looked at by her. || 1.9.11 ||

But when there is mutual looking between [a Śūdra man and] a Śūdra woman, at that very moment there is a suspension of study; it is not so when they are in the same house, nor even within the range of a throw of a wooden pin (śamyā). || 1.9.11 ||
Likewise, [the same applies] when one has sexual intercourse with another woman who has transgressed her caste. || 1.9.12 ||

Even in the case of a woman who, though not a Śūdra, has transgressed the bounds of her caste during sexual intercourse by approaching a man of a lower caste, there is likewise a suspension of study upon seeing her or being seen by her. 1.9.12.
When about to study the Veda, if he desires to speak with a woman in her courses, he should first speak with a Brāhmaṇa;
having spoken with that Brāhmaṇa, he may then speak with her, and only after speaking with the Brāhmaṇa should he study the Veda; in this way, there is the highest welfare for her offspring.

If one who intends to study this Veda desires to converse with a woman of impure garments (*malavadvāsas*), that is, a menstruating woman, he should first converse with a Brāhmaṇa and only afterwards with her. Having conversed with her, he must again converse with a Brāhmaṇa before he may study. What happens when this is done? In this way, for the offspring she will bear, there shall be spiritual welfare (*niḥśreyasa*) or worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Or rather, the "spiritual welfare" consists in the excellence of the offspring itself. Because of the expression "welfare of the offspring," this [procedure] need not be performed when conversing with widows and the like. (1.9.13)
A corpse within. 1.9.14.
And one who is a Cāṇḍāla within. 1.9.15.

One should not study in a village where a corpse is present. By this, the case of "where a *caṇḍāla* is within" is explained. *Caṇḍāla* is the same as *cāṇḍāla*. In both instances, the nominative case is to be understood in the sense of the locative, or it should be seen as an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of a case ending.
But for those [texts] that have been brought forth, there is no suspension of study within their boundaries. || 1.9.16 ||
But when corpses have been carried out beyond the boundary of the village, then there is no suspension of study there. 1.9.16.
And in the forest, at the time of the [first] appearance. 1.9.17.
And in a forest, as far as a corpse or a Caṇḍāla is visible, there is no study. 1.9.17.
And on that day, when those from outside the village have arrived. 1.9.18.
The outsiders, such as the fierce Niṣādas and others, are adversaries. When they have arrived in the village, there is a suspension of study on that day; one must not study on that day. 1.9.18.
Even when [the causes] exist. 1.9.19.
When virtuous persons who are great by virtue of their learning, conduct, and other qualities have arrived in the village, that day is one on which study is suspended. 1.9.19.
If there is thunder during the twilight or at night, [one should remain standing]. || 1.9.20 ||

*Saṃdhi* means twilight. When there is thunder during that *saṃdhi*, that is, when there is the rumbling of clouds, one should not study at all throughout the night. This rule applies during the rainy season; for other seasons, more will be stated later. (1.9.20)
Up to the end of dreams, as in lightning. 1.9.21.

"Up to the time of sleep": the last [syllable] is long and the penultimate is short; this reversal is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*) or a scribal error. When lightning occurs during the twilight, there is no study for the night until the time of sleep, but not for the entire night. The night "until the time of sleep" means it remains for one watch (*prahara*). 1.9.21.
Thus it has been stated regarding the evening twilight. Regarding the morning twilight, he says:
"Until near dawn, or as long as one can discern the dark or the ruddy [cow] from the distance of a *śamyā*-throw; at that time, if it is lightening, the day is accompanied by the onset of night."
A time unfit for study. || 1.9.22 ||

*Upavyuṣam* means near dawn. Even there, when lightning flashes—that is, while lightning is present—the day until the following evening is a period of non-study. After the evening (pradoṣa), study may take place at night. Or, for as long a time as it takes to recognize a black or a red cow standing within the range of a *śamyā*-throw; the construction is: "when lightning flashes near dawn during that amount of time. A red cow (*rohiṇī*) is a cow of reddish color. When the word *iti* is employed, the accusative case is used. The specific manner of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) in that instance is to be considered. 1.9.22.
In the small hours of the night, by the sound of thunder. || 1.9.23 ||

The entire third part of the night is the *apararātra* (the latter part of the night). When this is divided into three parts, the first portion is the *mahārātra* (great night), and the last is the *dahra* (small [portion]). During that *dahra* of the *apararātra*, on account of the thundering of clouds, there is no study for the day including the preceding evening. 1.9.23.
"Some say [it may be performed] after midnight. 1.9.24.
Some maintain that after midnight, if there is thunder, the entire day including the evening is unfit for study; however, our own view is that it is only for a short duration. 1.9.24.
And likewise when cows are confined. 1.9.25.
When cows are seized by bandits and the like, there is a suspension of study for that duration of time; "seizure" (avarodha) means the obstruction of their exit from the village. 1.9.25.
And [the same applies] to those who are to be executed, up to the point at which they are actually slain. || 1.9.26 ||
When there is an execution of those deserving of death, such as thieves and others, there is no study for as long as the time it takes for them to be executed. (1.9.26)
One who is mounted on the back of domestic animals should not recite [the Veda]. 1.9.27.
One who is mounted on the back of animals such as elephants or horses, or while sitting upon them, shall not study. 1.9.27.
On the new moon days, [one should fast] for a day and night. || 1.9.28 ||
One should not study for two days and nights on the new moon days (*amāvāsyā*); that is, on those days and on the preceding fourteenth days (*caturdaśī*). And so says Manu:
"On the new moon and the fourteenth days, on the full moon and the *aṣṭakā* days... [MDh 4.113cd].
Thus ends the ninth section, concerning the Cāturmāsya festivals. 1.10.1.

The term *cāturmāsya* refers to that which occurs in four months (*caturṣu māseṣu*). This is a designation for the three full-moon days (*paurṇamāsī*) on which the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices are performed. Which are those? They are the full moons of Phālguna, Āṣāḍha, and Kārttika. Regarding the sacrifice called *Cāturmāsya*, since the rule "that which occurs therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*) is already in effect, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām aṇ*). On those *Cāturmāsī* days, as previously stated, there is a suspension of study for two days and nights. Gautama, however, states this explicitly with his own words: "The full moon of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha" (GDh 16.32). On other full-moon days and on the first days of the lunar fortnights (*pratipat*), there is a suspension of study according to the statements of other scriptures. As Uśanas says: "There is a suspension of study for branches of knowledge excluding the Epics and Purāṇas," and "One should not reflect [on sacred matters] on the *pratipats*. Thus, the authority for the exclusion of the fourteenth day alone is another scripture. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:

On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, the eighth day, during the eclipse of Rāhu, at the transitions of the seasons, after eating, and after accepting an offering from a funeral ceremony (śrāddha). [YDh 1.146] || 1.10.1 ||
The Vairamaṇa, the Aṣṭākya, and the Aupākaraṇa [are] three-day rites performed for the teachers. 1.10.2.

*Viramaṇa* means cessation; that itself is *vairamaṇa*, and [the word refers to] in that *vairamaṇa*. In the reading where the nominative case is used, the nominative has the sense of the locative. "Toward elders" (*guruṣu*) refers to fathers-in-law and others. "When they have passed away" (*saṃsthiteṣu*) is understood from the context. *Aṣṭakya* is simply *aṣṭakā*; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of the base itself. The augment *vṛddhi* was applied at the beginning, though it occurs in the middle [of the compound]. *Aupākaraṇa* is simply *upākaraṇa*. On these occasions, there are three-day periods free from study. Among those, in the case of elders, the three days begin from the day of death; in the other cases, however, one should not study on the previous day, the following day, and that very day. Regarding this, Gautama says: "The three *aṣṭakās* [require] three nights... [and] on both sides of the annual [term]" (GDh 16.38, 40). The study that takes place after the *upākaraṇa* and before the *utsarjana* is the "annual" (*vārṣika*); the meaning is that there are three nights also for the rites performed on both sides of that—both at its beginning and at its end. And Uśanas has stated clearly: "At the *upākarma* and the *utsarga*, a three-night suspension [of study] is prescribed. (1.10.2)
Likewise, regarding relations and kinsmen (1.10.3):

even when those kinsmen who are closely related—such as brothers, their sons, paternal uncles, and so forth—have died, there is likewise a three-day suspension of study. This rule applies to the religious student (*brahmacārin*). However, for those under ritual impurity (*āśauca*), the suspension of study lasts as long as the impurity itself, as established in other scriptures. Regarding this, Manu says:
"In both cases, for ten days the food of the family must not be eaten."
Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic recitation are suspended in both cases: at birth and at death. 1.10.3.
Upon the death of a mother, a father, or a teacher, the period of impurity lasts twelve days.

When one's mother or other [relatives] have died, there is a suspension of study for twelve days. This rule applies even to householders. Some maintain that the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) also lasts for that same duration; we say "no," because this occurs in the section concerning the suspension of study. 1.10.4.
And among those, there is contact with water for that same duration of time.
Regarding [the death of] one's mother and others, it is even more so—one must perform the ritual bath every single day for that duration, not merely abstain from Vedic study.
And the shaving of those who have experienced [the death]. || 1.10.6 ||

"Anubhāvinaḥ" refers to those who have followed after, having been born later—that is, those younger than the deceased; for them, there is also the shaving of the hair. Regarding the suffix *ṇa*, although it would be required by the rule "kṛty-a-caḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.29), there is an optionality provided by the rule "ṇer vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 8.4.30). Others, however, maintain that the shaving applies to all those experiencing the sorrow (*śāva*) of the deceased. Another says: "anubhāvinaḥ" means those entitled to the water-offering (*udakārhāḥ*); for them, there is the shaving upon death. 1.10.6.
Some say that those who have returned from their studies should not sow [seeds] except in a monastery. 1.10.7.

The monastery is the initiation for sacrifice; therefore, some think that one should not shave elsewhere until the initiation has been completed. But our own view is that one should indeed shave. 1.10.7.

In this regard, he cites a Brāhmaṇa passage to state that shaving is inauspicious and to provide a resolution for it by means of a secondary injunction: "Moreover, there is this Brāhmaṇa: 'This [head] is indeed empty and uncovered when it is shaven; that which is the tuft of hair (śikhā) is its covering. 1.10.8.

An empty vessel, such as a jar, is hollow within. This [vessel] is "uncovered," meaning it is devoid of a lid, just as this one called *muṇḍa* (the shaven-headed) is. The "covering" (*apidhāna*) of that empty [vessel] is what is called the *śikhā* (the topknot). By this, it is shown that the prohibitive scripture, together with the *śikhā*, has the purpose of prohibiting the shaving [of the head]. 1.10.8.
How then is the statement in the *sattras*, "They shave following the crest for the sake of prosperity" (*TS* 7.4.9), to be understood? He says: because of its superior force;
however, in the *sattras*, there is shaving of the crest due to that specific scriptural injunction. (1.10.9)
This is clear. 1.10.9
Some say that [the impurity lasts] for three days and nights in the case of a teacher (ācārya). 1.10.10.
Some maintain that when an Ācārya has passed away, one should avoid Vedic study for three days and nights; however, our own position is as previously stated: twelve days. 1.10.10.
In the case of a gathering of Vedic scholars who have not been together for a full year, [he should give] one [cow]. 1.10.11.

The author will speak of the *śrotriya*. Upon the completion of such a person's [study], provided that less than a full year has elapsed since it was heard, there is a suspension of study for one night or one day and night. Here, because of the mention of "completion" (*saṃsthā*), this same cause applies to the suspension of study even in the case of the death of a teacher and others.
"Co-religious student," say some. 1.10.12.

Some, however, desire that the suspension of study mentioned immediately above applies only upon the death of a fellow religious student (sabrahmacārin), and not upon the death of an ordinary Vedic scholar (śrotriya).
When a Vedic scholar arrives, one who desires to study, or one who is already studying, should study only after having obtained permission. 1.10.13.
When a learned scholar (śrotriya) has arrived, one who desires to study or is already studying should do so only after having obtained his permission. 1.10.13.
Or he may teach [the Veda]. 1.10.14.
"Desiring to teach, or while teaching"—this is understood from the context. He too, having obtained permission, should teach a learned *śrotriya* who has arrived. (1.10.14)
And in the presence of the teacher, having said "Recite, sir," he should study. 1.10.15.
While performing the memorization or the recitation of the Veda, if the teacher is present, he should say, "Recite, sir," and then proceed to study. 1.10.15.
Or he may teach [the Veda]. || 1.10.16 ||
Even when teaching while the teacher is present, he should teach only after speaking in this very manner. 1.10.16.
One should show hospitality toward both types of persons: one who desires to study and one who has already studied. 1.10.17.

In both cases, at the beginning and at the end of the study, a formal salutation must be performed: at the beginning for one desiring to study, and at the end for that which has been studied. 1.10.17.
Or, while others are reciting, if someone else should intervene, one should continue reciting after emitting that very same sound. 1.10.18.

The plural number is not restrictive. Furthermore, when those who are studying are interrupted by another person entering between them, they should likewise continue their study after uttering this very expression, "Recite, sir! Because the instruction is given to each individual, the singular number is used; [thus it is said] "they should study.
The barking of dogs and donkeys, the howling of jackals, the cries of hyenas and owls, all sounds of musical instruments, and the sounds of weeping, singing, and Sāman chants. 1.10.19.

The sounds of many dogs and donkeys—due to the use of the plural number; the female jackal (*salāvṛkī*) is a sub-species of the wolf, though others call her the female hyena (*kroṣṭrī*); since gender is not intended to be significant, the male is also included, as seen in such passages as "Indra [gave] the *yatīs* to the *sālāvṛkas*" (TS 6.2.7); in all these cases, the first vowel is long, and this very sound is employed here in its modified form; the *ekasṛka* is a solitary wandering jackal; the *ulūka* is the owl, the "fearful by day"; and the sounds of these, as well as the sounds of musical instruments (*vāditrāṇi*) such as the lute, flute, drum, and so forth, and all their sounds—including the sounds of weeping, singing, and the chanting of *sāmans*—when heard, are causes for the suspension of study (1.10.19).
And in another Vedic school, there is no study of the Sāmans.

The Sāman should not be studied in the vicinity of another Veda, because "the designation Sāman applies to the melodies" (PMS 2.1.36). Others hold that the word Sāman refers to the Veda itself by virtue of its connection with those melodies. 1.10.20.
And in all vocal actions, wherever they may be combined. || 1.10.21 ||

In all cases involving verbal actions such as abuse, ridicule, and the like, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*), provided that those sounds would otherwise mingle with the sound of Vedic recitation. (1.10.21)
Having caused [the disciple] to vomit, [he should perform the rite] until the end of the dream. || 1.10.22 ||
Chardana means vomiting; having performed that, one should not study until the end of the dream. || 1.10.22 ||
Or, having consumed clarified butter. 1.10.23.
Or alternatively, having consumed clarified butter, he may study.
A foul odor. 1.10.24.
An offensive odor; and its perception is a cause for the suspension of study. 1.10.24.
And that which is sour when combined with oneself [is also to be eaten]. 1.10.25.

That which was cooked by the process of time and has become sour is called *śūkta*. As long as it remains undigested within one's own stomach while in contact with oneself, or as long as there is eructation corresponding to that state, for that long it is a cause for the suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*). (1.10.25)
And having eaten at the wrong time of day. 1.10.26.
The word "should not study" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Therefore, one should eat only after having studied. 1.10.26.
And [the same applies] when the two hands are wet with water. || 1.10.27 ||
"Having eaten" (bhuktvā) is the very [term used]. Having eaten, one should not study as long as both hands are wet with water. Some do not carry forward the word "having eaten" (bhuktvā). 1.10.27.
Having eaten food prepared for the deceased (pretas), there is a suspension of Vedic study for one day and night. || 1.10.28 ||

One who has died but for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has not been performed is a *preta*. Having eaten food offered for his sake, one should not recite the Veda during that day until the onset of night (*pradoṣa*). After *pradoṣa*, there is no fault. Regarding this, Manu says:
"As long as the odor and the smear of food offered at a single-ancestor rite remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long he should not proclaim the Veda" (MDh 4.111).
And until its maturation. 1.10.29.
If, however, within that time that food has not been digested—that is, has not reached its transformation—then he should not study because of that lack of digestion.
But one who lacks faith should cover [the fire] with it. 1.10.30.

Whether that [food] has been digested or not, one should finish it with food that is not part of a *śrāddha* offering; the meaning is that one should eat non-*śrāddha* food on top of it. Some, however, because of the expression "with food that is not a *śrāddha*," believe that even in the preceding case, the term *śrāddha* is intended to refer specifically to food for the deceased (*pretānna*). 1.10.30.
Thus ends the tenth section;
and this [rule] regarding the commencement of the book applies also to one who has no mother. 1.11.1.

The commencement of a *kāṇḍa* and the instruction for the *kāṇḍavrata*: on that day, having eaten the food of one who has no mother, there is a suspension of study for the day including the evening (*sapradoṣam*). Another says: the word "having eaten" does not carry over [from the previous rule]. And thus, later on, the mention of "having eaten" occurs again. When the commencement of a *kāṇḍa* is the occasion, there is a suspension of study for the day including the evening for a student (*māṇavaka*) who has no mother. By this, the subsequent case is explained. 1.11.1.
And [the same applies] for one who has no father at the conclusion of a section (kāṇḍa). || 1.11.2 ||
The completion of a section [of study] is the release from the vow. 1.1.2.
And some say that one should eat at the sacrifice of those gods who have human natures. 1.11.3.

Those who, having been human beings, have become gods through eminent asceticism (*tapas*)—such as Nandīśvara, Kumāra, and others—are "gods of human nature. Regarding their sacrifice, some hold that on the day one eats at a meal for Brahmins intended to please them, the entire day including the evening is a time when study is forbidden (*anadhyāya*). Others hold that it is so when gods in human form are being worshipped. (1.11.3)
There is no suspension of study on account of stale rice or raw meat. 1.11.4.

This is an exception to the rule [ĀpDh 1.10.28] stating "prepared by a *preta*. "Stale" means those kept overnight. When rice grains received yesterday are cooked and eaten today, there is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*). Likewise, there is no suspension of study even if raw meat is eaten on that same day. Others maintain that "stale" refers to food kept overnight; according to the expression "by stale [food]," there is a suspension of study for the entire evening (*sapradoṣam*) after eating such food on that day. 1.11.4.
Likewise with the roots and fruits of medicinal herbs and forest trees. || 1.11.5 ||

By the mention of "herbs" (*oṣadhi*), climbing plants (*vīrudh*) are also included; by the mention of "forest trees" (*vanaspati*), even mere trees are included. There is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) even if one eats their roots—such as the *sūraṇa* tuber—and their fruits—such as mangoes—whether ripe or unripe, on that very day. Others, however, maintain that this applies only if they have become stale (*paryuṣita*). (1.11.5)
On the day on which one begins a section (kāṇḍa) or on which one performs the introductory recitation (anuvākya), one should not study that [section] on that day. 1.11.6.

On whichever day a particular section (*kāṇḍa*) has been formally commenced, one should not study that section on that very day. Likewise, having performed the commencement ceremony (*upākaraṇa*) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should begin the recitation of the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for whichever section is to be studied on another auspicious day; one should not study that section on that very day. The word "day" (*ahar*) is an elliptical expression for a full day and night (*ahorātra*). (1.11.6)
And at the commencement and completion of the recitation of the Pārāyaṇa, [he should offer oblations] for that Veda. || 1.11.7 ||

When one who studies many Vedas performs the complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of a single Veda, on that day he shall not study that specific knowledge once the preparatory rite (*upākaraṇa*) and the concluding rite (*utsarjana*) of that recitation have been performed. This very rule indicates that the preparatory and concluding rites apply to the *pārāyaṇa* as well. Because of the expression "that knowledge," there is no fault in studying other branches of knowledge [on that day]. (1.11.7)
Wherever there is a roaring wind on the ground, or a rustling of grass, or where it rains and streams flow down; || 1.11.8 ||

"Ghoṣavān" means audible to the ear. "Tṛṇasaṃvāha" refers to that which carries away—meaning it lifts up and moves along—the grasses standing upon the ground; or, when the clouds rain, it causes the streams of water to flow forth or scatter them. In whatever region such a wind blows, one should not study for as long as that time lasts. Regarding this, Manu says: "When the wind is audible to the ear at night, or during the day when it raises a cloud of dust... (MDh 4.102). || 1.11.8 ||
The subsequent sūtras are established by their literal meaning: "And at the junction of a village and a forest. (1.11.9)
And on the high road. 1.11.10.
And having returned from a journey abroad, one should study on that day until the time for the next meal. || 1.11.11 ||

When some among those studying together depart due to certain causes while others remain with the teacher, one should not study that day the portion being studied together. Others maintain that one should not study on the day when those who have been away meet again. 1.11.11.
And in voluntary acts. 1.11.12.
"One should not study at all. (1.11.12)
An example of this is as follows:
"such as washing the feet, massaging, and anointing with ointments. (1.11.13)
The substitution of *ṇ* is either accidental or a corruption of the text. 1.11.13.
For that long, one should neither study nor teach. || 1.11.14 ||
During those times of his own leisure, he should avoid both studying and teaching for that duration. 1.11.14.
At the two twilights. || 1.11.15 ||

“While the light still remains, until the light is seen again” (GDh 2.11). This refers to both twilights; during that time, one should neither study nor teach. This same rule applies subsequently as well. 1.11.15.
The subsequent sūtra is established by the mere recitation [of the rule]. Likewise: "one who has climbed a tree" (vṛkṣam ārūḍhaḥ). 1.1.16.
And he has plunged into the waters. || 1.11.17 ||
And at night, when it is uncovered. || 1.11.18 ||
"Open door" means one that is unbarred. One should not study there at night. 1.1.18.
And also during the day when [the sun] is obscured. || 1.11.19 ||
It should have its doors closed and be shut up; there, one should not study during the day. 1.11.19.
The recitation of the Anuvākas is not prescribed during the months of Āṣāḍha and Vāsantika.

The *vāsantika* is the spring festival (*vasantotsava*), which occurs on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra. By the word *āṣāḍha*, some such festival as the Indra-festival (*indrotsava*) and others, which are held in that month, are intended. On those two days, the study of the *anuvākas* is not prescribed. Because of the mention of the term *anuvāka*, there is no fault in studying less than that. Another says: because of the mention of the term *anuvāka*, the prohibition applies only to the *mantras* and the *brāhmaṇas*, and not to the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*). 1.11.20.
And [the same applies] to a constant question asked in an improper manner. 1.1.21.

The *nityapraśna* is that Vedic study which consists of the constant recitation of questions; it is the *brahmayajña*. Its study of an *anuvāka* without the prescribed method—which will be described below—is not ordained. Although the study of the *brahmayajña* is obligatory (*nitya*), it must nevertheless not be performed lacking even a single ancillary part. Therefore, if one forgets to perform it after having eaten the morning meal, there is only an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and no performance of the *brahmayajña*. As Manu says: "In the case of the transgression of obligatory rites enjoined by the Veda, and upon the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the expiation is fasting" (MDh 11.204).
The procedure for that [is as follows]. 1.11.22.
The procedure for that constant questioning will now be explained. || 1.11.22 ||

Having refrained from his morning meal, having gone to the edge of water, being self-restrained and pure, he should recite the Veda in a clean place according to the lesson, or recite it aloud while letting it go.

Having not yet eaten his morning meal and having not yet eaten during the day, he should go to the edge of water—that is, near water—and being restrained (prayata), purified by bathing, wiping, and so forth, he should study in a clean place in either the eastern or northern direction, where no roof is visible, according to the lesson and according to the recitation, without omitting any supplementary passages (anuṣaṅga). "Omitting" means that he should study from the beginning on the first day and subsequent days, but on the second day and following, he should omit what was studied on the first day and so forth, and then study beyond that. "With the voice" means aloud. 1.11.23.
And one should not recite [the Veda] mentally during the forbidden times for study.
And during a period when study is prohibited, one should mentally recite the daily lesson.
They declare that the mind is unfit for study when lightning is imminent, during thunder, when there is a lack of ritual purity, when eating the food of the deceased, and during mist. 1.11.25.

When lightning is imminent and unceasing, when thunder is near, when there is a lack of self-purification due to impurity, and when one has eaten the food of a *preta*, and while the mist—that is, the heavy snow—is present—they prescribe the avoidance, meaning they forbid, the mental study of the Vedas just mentioned. 1.11.25.
Some [maintain that this applies] specifically at the Śrāddha meal. 1.11.26.
However, some teachers maintain that mental [repetition] is prescribed only during the Śrāddha meal, and not during lightning and other such occasions. 1.11.26.
Where lightning, thunder, and rain should occur together outside of the rainy season, there shall be a suspension of study for three days. || 1.11.27 ||

Regarding the non-season (*apartu*): in whatever region a particular rainy season occurs, the time other than that is the non-season; if lightning and so forth should occur together there, then there is a suspension of study for three days. || 1.11.27 ||
According to some, [the ground is purified] as far as the earth remains dry. 1.11.28.
Some maintain that the suspension of study lasts for as long as time as it takes for the ground to become free of water.
One may eat of these [roots, fruits, and grains] either singly or in pairs until the time [of the next meal]. 1.11.29.

Among these, such as lightning and the rest, when there is a conjunction with one or two of them, there is a suspension of study for as long as the time [of the phenomenon] lasts; the meaning is that on the following day, it continues until that same time has arrived. || 1.11.29 ||
During an eclipse of the sun or moon, an earthquake, thunder, a meteor, or a fire-omen, there is a time for all branches of knowledge at any hour, regardless of the specific time of day. 1.11.30.

The mention of the sun and the moon is for the purpose of excluding Jupiter (*bṛhaspati*) and the other planets. "In an earthquake" means during a tremor of the earth; "in a subterranean roar" means during a thunderclap; "in a meteor" means during the fall of a shooting star; "in a fire-omen" means during the burning of a village or similar conflagration. On these occasions, regarding all branches of knowledge—namely:
the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive system of Nyāya, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras; for these indeed are the fourteen branches of learning.

For those [periods] thus mentioned, there is a suspension of study at all times, both during the [proper] season and outside the season, and at improper times. Because of the statement "of all," some hold that the prohibition applies only to the Vedas; others hold that it applies to the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) as well. 1.11.30.
In the case of clouds out of season, a halo around the sun or moon, a rainbow, a mock sun, a fish-shaped apparition in the sky, a foul odor in the wind, and mist— in all these instances,
the impurity lasts for as long as they persist. (1.11.31)

When a cloud is visible while separated from the sky, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for as long as it remains visible.
