This same rule should be applied to halos around the sun and other such phenomena. Even here, there is no fault if the halo belongs to Jupiter or other auspicious planets. A rainbow is well known. A *pratisūrya* (counter-sun) is a form resembling the sun appearing near the actual sun. A *matsya* (fish) is a star with a tail-like shape. [The compound] *matsyābhram* is a collective dvandva in which the gender has been changed according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). For all these, as well as for the three beginning with wind—namely, when there is a noisy wind, a foul odor, or mist (*nīhāra*, i.e., frost)—there is a suspension of study for that duration. The mention of "wind" and the others is intended to include by implication (*upalakṣaṇa*) the previously mentioned dogs, donkeys, and so forth. The repetition here is for the purpose of prescribing the duration "for that time. Since the inclusion of dogs, donkeys, etc., could have been made right here, the purpose of their placement in the previous section is to be considered. (1.11.31)
When the wind had ceased for a moment.
When there is a sound of wind, even when it has ceased, there is a suspension of study for a mere moment; two *nāḍikās* constitute a *muhūrta*. 1.11.32.
"Born from a female jackal, one-legged"—this concludes the section on dreams. 1.11.33.
This is an exception to the rule "for that length of time"; the words *salāvṛkī* and *ekasṛka* have been explained. 1.11.33.
And at night, he should not go out into the forest unless he is naked or without gold. || 1.11.34 ||
At night, one should not study in a place devoid of fire or devoid of gold, nor in the forest. 1.11.34.
And one should not study the Veda if it has not been previously taught, nor during the intercalary months.

The period from after the *utsarjana* until before the *upākaraṇa* is the non-season (*apartu*). During that time, one should not study any portion of the Veda (*chandas*) that has not been previously studied, nor any new material; that is, the study for the purpose of memorization (*grahaṇādhyayana*) must not be performed during the non-season. Even though it is said, "One should cease [study] on the full moon of the month of Taiṣya or under the asterism Rohiṇī" [ĀpDh 1.9.2], nevertheless, in response to the inquiry as to for how long that cessation lasts and from what kind of study, it is stated: for this duration, the study for the purpose of memorization must not be performed. However, there is no fault regarding the study for the purpose of retention (*dhāraṇādhyayana*). Likewise, because of the expression "of the Veda" (*chandasaḥ*), there is no fault even in the study for memorization of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). 1.11.35.
And at the time of dusk. 1.11.36.

One should not study what has not been previously learned during the evening twilight, even during the ritual season (*ṛtu*). As for the rule, "One should not study during the evening twilight for a month" (ĀpDh 1.9.1), that is intended as a prohibition against even the memorization (*dhāraṇā*) of the texts. Another says: on that night when the twelfth and thirteenth lunar days overlap, one should not study during the evening twilight—neither what has not been previously learned nor what has been previously learned. This is the practice both during the ritual season and outside of it. 1.11.36.
It is traditionally taught as being for all times. 1.11.37.
That which has been handed down is "studied"; that should be studied at all times, both during the intervals [between the seasonal sacrifices] and at evening, at every moment. || 1.11.37 ||
As it has been stated: "Other than this, [the rules apply] in assemblies. (1.11.38)

Therefore, for reasons other than those mentioned in this section on the suspension of Vedic study (*anadhyāya*), one should observe the causes for the suspension of study as they are stated in the *Mānava* and other *Dharmaśāstras* concerning assemblies. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: "In the event of a forest fire, a mountain collapse, or during rains of stones, blood, or dust, the suspension lasts until the same time the next day" (VaDh 13.35). Yama says:
"One should never study beneath a *śleṣmātaka*, a *śalmali*, or a *madhūka* tree, nor under a *kovidāra* or a *kapittha*."
“One should not study in the vicinity of battlefields, pleasure gardens, or deities. (1.11.38)
Thus ends the eleventh section;
thus ends the third chapter in the commentary on the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
"Austerity and Vedic study," so says the Brāhmaṇa. 1.12.1.

That which is this constant private recitation (*svādhyāya*) is austerity (*tapas*); the meaning is that it accomplishes as much as the austerity characterized by the *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth, would accomplish over the same period of time. || 1.12.1 ||
Regarding this, it is heard: "Whether he recites his private Vedic study while standing, sitting, or lying down, he performs austerity; for private Vedic study is indeed austerity. 1.12.2.

In that very *Brāhmaṇa*, the rule for times of distress (*āpatkalpa*) is heard: "If he is standing or sitting... In that context, the primary rule (*mukhya kalpa*) is stated in the *Brāhmaṇa* itself: "Having spread out a great quantity of *darbha* grass and made a lap, one should study the sacred texts while sitting facing the east," and so forth. Here, however, the mention of "sitting" is intended merely to indicate some form of seated posture. In every case, the meaning of the *Brāhmaṇa* is: "For one who is studying, that indeed constitutes the performance of austerity. Manu also says: "He truly performs the highest austerity even unto his fingertips."
"He who, even while wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily according to his ability" (MDh 2.167).
By the word "sragvī" (wearing a garland), he indicates that it may be done at will. 1.12.2.

Having thus stated that the restriction for the performer is not to be excessively observed even in times of distress, he speaks also regarding the proper time, citing the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa: "This private recitation (svādhyāya) is indeed the sacrifice to Brahman;
its *vaṣaṭ*-calls are when it thunders, when it lightens, and when..."
When the wind thunders, when it blows, when it thunders while lightning flashes,
or when the wind is blowing while thundering— he should indeed continue to recite for the sake of ensuring that the *vaṣaṭ* calls are not rendered futile. 1.12.3.

Moreover, "private recitation" (*svādhyāya*) is what is called the "sacrifice to Brahman" (*brahmayajña*). "Brahman" is the Veda; the sacrifice is that which has this as its means, just as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices have sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and the like as their means. The two particles *ha vai* indicate well-known tradition. For that sacrifice, these things about to be mentioned—the thundering and so forth—are the *vaṣaṭkāra*s. Because of the use of the plural number, all those intended for the purpose of offering—such as the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* and the *svāhākāra*—are included. Thundering is the sound of the clouds. Flashing is the activity of lightning. Crashing is the falling of thunderbolts, for there is the scriptural observation: "The crashing is the sign. "Vāyati" is a form of the root *vai*, meaning "to dry up. The sense is that it blows in such a way that a moist place becomes dry. Since these are the *vaṣaṭkāra*s of the sacrifice to Brahman, therefore one should indeed study even when conditions such as thundering exist that would otherwise cause a suspension of study; one should not refrain from studying on the grounds that it is a time for non-study (*anadhyāya*). The meaning is that one should perform the sacrifice to Brahman. For what purpose? To ensure that these *vaṣaṭkāra*s are not in vain—that is, to prevent them from being useless. Otherwise, these *vaṣaṭkāra*s would be futile. And in that case, it would be as if the Adhvaryu priest did not offer the oblation when the Hotṛ priest has uttered the *vaṣaṭ*. 1.12.3.
In another recensional branch (śākhā), the completion of the sentence occurs [at that point]. 1.12.4.
In another recension of that Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa, the sentence reaches its conclusion; yet, it does not terminate there. 1.12.4.
He recites that very same passage from another branch:
"Now, if the wind should blow, or it should thunder, or lightning should flash, or a thunderclap should strike, one should utter a single Ṛc, or a single Yajus, or a single Sāman: 'Bhūḥ!'"
"Bhuvaḥ suvaḥ! I offer truth in austerity through faith"—this is what he means. By this, indeed, his private Vedic study for that day becomes properly undertaken. 1.12.5.

The word "ante" (at the end) is to be supplied [from the previous rule]. When wind and other such obstacles are present, one should recite a single *ṛc* at the appointed place; during the study of the Yajurveda, a single *yajus*; during the study of the Sāmaveda, a single *sāman*; or, in the case of all the Vedas, one should utter the *yajus* beginning with "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar," and not merely the introductory question as before. By this much alone, on that day, his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) becomes undertaken, accepted, and mastered—that is, the meaning is that it has been studied. However, some consider the passage beginning with "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar" to refer to the study of the Brāhmaṇa portion, and not to the *Sāvitrī*. 1.12.5.

But why is the completion of the sentence accepted from the other recension cited in the *Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇa*, rather than merely following what is heard [in that specific text]? To this he says: "This being so, it is not contradicted by the established tradition of the Āryas. (1.1.6)

This being so, when this conclusion of the sentence is thus accepted according to the *āryasamaya*—the *āryas* being the cultured ones such as Manu and others, and their *samaya* being their established rule—it remains uncontradicted. Otherwise, it would be contradicted. 1.1.6.
How so?
For they teach [rules regarding] study and non-study; that would be purposeless if one were to disregard the Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa. 1.12.7.

For the noble ones indeed teach both the permitted time for study (*adhyāya*) and the forbidden time for study (*anadhyāya*). That teaching would be purposeless if the student were to regard the *Vājasaneyi-Brāhmaṇa* exactly as it is heard [in the text]. (1.12.7)
He says: "Let this be purposeless, because it contradicts the Veda. To that he replies: "For the tradition of the Noble Ones has no perceivable cause. (1.12.8)

Regarding this traditional doctrine (*āryasamaya*) concerning the days suitable and unsuitable for Vedic study, no specific reason is apprehended therein—just as in the case [of the rule]: "One gives the cloth used for the *vaisarjana* oblation to the *adhvaryu* priest. Since this traditional doctrine is a means of valid knowledge by way of inferring a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) even when no reason is apprehended, it is therefore proper that the sentence be concluded right there. For in this way, there is no absolute contradiction even with the *Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa*. Furthermore, the instruction regarding non-study days is purposeful insofar as it pertains to extensive Vedic study. In the Sūtra, the absence of the *ṇatva* substitution (the nasalization in *agṛhyamāṇakāraṇaḥ*) is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). 1.1.2.8.

What, then, is this *smṛti* that prescribes non-study even during the *brahmayajña*? In the *Mānava-dharmaśāstra*, on the contrary, it is heard: "In the case of the daily (*naiṣṭhika*) recitation, there is no non-study, for that is remembered as a *brahmasattra*" (MDh 2.106). The general instruction regarding non-study, however, finds its application elsewhere than in the *brahmayajña*. Therefore, such a *smṛti* must be sought. If that were so, would it not follow that there is non-study of the mantras even in the *agnihotra* and other rites? He says: No.
It is heard that there is a suspension of study regarding sacred knowledge (*vidyā*), but not regarding the application of mantras in ritual action (*karmayoga*). 1.12.9.

*Vidyā* means knowledge or study; regarding that, a prohibition of study (*anadhyāya*) is heard, but not for the employment of mantras in ritual action. The reason has been stated in the *Paribhāṣā*: "Because it is a different matter" (ĀpPar 1.40). For the employment of mantras in ritual action is indeed for a different purpose, whereas study is for the sake of grasping [the text], since its purpose is to illuminate the meaning of what is to be performed. And thus, it must be considered whether or not study continues during the course of a complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) when a period of non-study (*anadhyāya*) occurs. The same applies to the muttering (*japa*) of the Rudra-hymns and others. 1.12.9.

But how can the tradition of the noble ones (*āryasamaya*) be an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), given that it is impossible for them to possess knowledge of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*)? To this he replies:
"The injunctions spoken by the Brahmins have perished; their recensions (*pāṭha*) are inferred from their application (*prayoga*). (1.1.10)

"Prescriptions" (*vidhayaḥ*) are those actions that are enjoined; all of them, even those belonging to the *Smṛtis*, are stated in the *Brāhmaṇas* alone. [Objection: But surely the *Brāhmaṇas* are not found at present. [Reply: True; their recensions have been lost due to the weakness of the students. [Question: How then does their existence [at present] come about? [Answer: They are inferred from practice. Practice consists of both the codification of the *Smṛtis* and actual performance; therefore, it is inferred that the *Brāhmaṇas* were obtained by Manu and others. Otherwise, how could they remember or perform [the rites]? And their connection with the Veda is indeed possible. (1.1.10)
Now, as an incidental digression, forgetfulness is discussed:
"But where there is activity resulting from the perception of pleasure, there no scripture exists. (1.12.11)

But where there is engagement in such matters as the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter due to the perception of pleasure, a scripture with a lost textual tradition is not inferred in those cases, because pleasure itself serves as the cause for engagement. (1.1.11)
And therefore:
following after that, one prepares for hell. 1.12.12
One who performs such an injunction leads only to hell. || 1.12.12 ||
Now follow the rules declared by the Brahmins. 1.12.13.

Thus, it has been stated that those practices established by tradition (smṛti) and custom have their root in the Śruti. Now, however, certain injunctions that are explicitly stated in the Brāhmaṇas themselves are being explained for the purpose of including them within the category of Smārta rules. Consequently, if one violates them, the expiation required is precisely that which is occasioned by the violation of a Smārta rule. || 1.12.13 ||
For them, there is the praise: "great sacrifices" and "great sessions. || 1.12.14 ||

Regarding those [five sacrifices] about to be described, there is a praise of them as "great sacrifices" (*mahāyajña*) in the *Svādhyāyabrāhmaṇa*, and there is also a praise of them as "great sacrificial sessions" (*mahāsattra*) in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* and other texts. By using the term "praise," [the author] indicates that this is merely a figurative description and not a formal name intended for the extension of ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*). Consequently, neither the properties stated for the great sacrifices—that is, the Soma sacrifices—such as "one should not perform the Soma sacrifice by bypassing one's elder brother," nor the properties of the great sacrificial session, the *Gavāmayana*, such as "those who have already performed their first sacrifice should sacrifice," apply to the five great sacrifices that are about to be described. (1.12.14)
Who, then, are they? He says: "The daily offering to beings (bhūtabali) and giving to humans according to one's ability. (1.12.15)

Thus ends the twelfth section: the offering of *svāhā* to the gods with fuel as the limit; the offering of *svadhā* to the ancestors with a vessel of water as the limit; and the private recitation of the Veda. 1.13.1.

In the *vaiśvadeva* rite, the *bhūtabali* (offering to beings) must be given day after day to the beings according to the method of offering oblations (*baliharaṇa*) that will be described. This is the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*). And one should give gifts to humans according to one’s ability; this is the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*). To the gods, an offering is to be made with the utterance of *svāhā*, even down to a piece of wood if there is no food available; even a piece of wood should be given according to the procedure stated for the *vaiśvadeva*. This is the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*). Some consider this oblation to be distinct from the *vaiśvadeva* oblations; they desire the mantra “*devebhyaḥ svāhā*” and they desire the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) “I shall sacrifice with the sacrifice to the gods. We, however, do not agree with that, as we have already stated in the *Gṛhyasūtra* itself [on ĀpGṛ 7.16]. Some say that because of the statement “even down to a piece of wood,” the *vaiśvadeva* must be performed somehow or other even when eating is omitted due to a lack of food, since it is a refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*). Others, however, maintain that since it is a refinement of the food (*aśanīyasaṃskāra*), the *vaiśvadeva* need not be performed when eating is omitted. To the ancestors, an offering is to be given with the utterance of *svadhā*; because of the mention of a vessel, it should be given along with the vessel. This is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). As for the study of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), it is the obligatory daily recitation (*nityasvādhyāya*) beginning with the rule “the rule for that” [ĀpDh 1.11.22]. This is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). The word “iti” marks the conclusion, meaning “these are the great sacrifices. Furthermore, this order of instruction is not applicable to the performance; rather, the performance follows the order: sacrifice to Brahman, sacrifice to the gods, sacrifice to beings, sacrifice to the ancestors, and sacrifice to humans. (1.13.1)
In this context, he speaks of worship:
"Worship should be performed for those who are superior by virtue of their caste. (1.13.2)

Those who are superior by caste and more highly esteemed must be honored by those of lower caste through following them on the road and similar acts, as well as with perfumes, garlands, and so forth during festivals. || 1.13.2 ||
And [he should show respect] toward those who are older. 1.13.3.

One should also perform worship for those of the same caste (*sajātīya*). Because of the mention of the suffix *-tarap* (indicating comparison), this includes those who are superior by virtue of knowledge, age, or occupation. Some say it includes even those who are inferior; thus Manu says: "Even a Śūdra who has reached the tenth decade [of life]" (MDh 2.137). 1.13.3.

It has been stated that worship should be performed; he now says that joy, which is contrary to that, must be avoided: "The joyful man becomes arrogant; the arrogant man transgresses the Dharma; and indeed, upon the transgression of Dharma, there is hell. (1.13.4)

*Harṣa* (joy) is a modification of the mind caused by the attainment of what is desired and so forth; one who is possessed of that is *hṛṣṭa* (joyful). One *darpati* or *dṛpyati* (is arrogant). *Darpa*, *garva*, and *abhimāna* are synonyms for pride. An arrogant person transgresses the Dharma because of his stubbornness regarding the honoring of those worthy of honor and other such duties. The words *khalu* and *punar* are used as sentence ornaments. Indeed (*khalu*), when there is a transgression of the Dharma, hell (*naraka*) follows; he falls into the abyss. Therefore, joy, which is the root of the transgression of the Dharma, must not be indulged in. Although joy is also mentioned among the faults to be avoided in the section on natural defects [ĀpDh 1.23.6], this present undertaking is for the purpose of avoiding joy here, because it is a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*) as will be explained. 1.13.4.
No instruction exists for one who has returned home. || 1.13.5 ||

A teacher should not issue a formal injunction to a student who has completed his studies, such as "this must be done by you. Just as commands were given during the period before graduation—such as "fetch a water-jar" and so forth—it is not so now. However, if he acts according to his own inclination, he is not to be forbidden. 1.13.5
The syllable *oṃ* is the gateway to heaven; therefore, one who is about to study the Veda should commence with this. 1.13.6.

The syllable *oṃ* is the *praṇava*. It is like a door to heaven; just as the interior of a house is reached through a door, so too is heaven reached by means of this. Therefore, one who is about to study the *brahma-veda*—the means for attaining heaven—should begin the study by first uttering this *oṃ*, even if it has not been explicitly prescribed, and thus commence. 1.13.6.
And by engaging in other such idle talk with worldly speech, one turns away from the Brahman.

Idle talk (*vikathā*) is discourse not conducive to study; having engaged in that or something else, one should undertake this [study] and so forth. This being the case, the *brahman*—the Veda—is distinguished from worldly speech; it does not become mixed with it. (1.13.7)
Furthermore, he praises the syllable *oṃ* itself: "And in sacrifices, these and others are the invocations. (1.13.8)

In sacrifices such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and others, these and similar utterances beginning with *oṃ* constitute the *prasava*s, which are formulas of authorization; for instance, in the Soma sacrifice, there are [the commands] to Brahmā and others: “*oṃ praṇaya*,” “*oṃ nirvapa*,” and “*oṃ studhvam*. (1.13.8)
And in the world, for rites intended for prosperity, there would be only such sentences as these:
"An auspicious day! Welfare! Prosperity! (puṇyāhaṃ svasty ṛddham). 1.13.9.

Just as in sacrifices there are invocations such as *oṃ*, so too in the world, in rites for prosperity such as marriage and the like, there should be sentences beginning with these very [words]. He illustrates them with the word "as follows" (*yathā*). In the recitation for a "holy day" (*puṇyāhavācana*), having caused [the officiants] to say, "Oṃ! May you, sirs, declare the holy day for the rite," he speaks. The respondents reply, "Oṃ! Let there be a holy day for the rite. Likewise, having caused them to say, "Oṃ! May you, sirs, declare well-being for the rite," the others say, "Oṃ! Well-being for the rite. Having caused them to say, "Oṃ! May you, sirs, declare success for the rite," the others say, "Oṃ! Let the rite succeed. Therefore, the syllable *oṃ* is thus praised. (1.13.9)
One should not perform the recitation at an improper time or with difficulty, except by omitting the three-fold proclamation and the three-fold simultaneous utterance. 1.13.10.

*Samaya* means service; without that, one should not compose a new work—a difficult, painful, and hard-to-comprehend text. The verb *karoti*, which expresses action in general, is used here in the sense of both studying and teaching. Without such service, even a student should not study a difficult text, nor should a teacher teach it. And so Manu says:
"Where neither virtue (*dharma*) nor wealth (*artha*) are found, nor likewise the corresponding service, there knowledge should not be sown, just as good seed is not sown in barren soil. (MDh 2.112)

Is this [requirement] without distinction? No, he says: "excepting the threefold proclamation and the threefold simultaneous speech. When only the threefold proclamation or only the threefold simultaneous speech is performed with reference to either one, service need not be expected. Beyond that, however, it must be expected everywhere.
"O Brahmin, one must speak without hesitation," so says Hārīta. 1.13.11.

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is uncertainty; its absence is non-doubt (*avicikitsā*). Hārīta, the teacher, maintains that as long as [doubt] has not arisen, one must go toward the *brahman*—that is, one must proceed according to the prescribed rules. According to this view, one must likewise attend with a desire to hear even during the threefold recitation and the threefold simultaneous utterance. Because of the mention of *brahman*, this rule does not apply to the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). 1.13.11.
There is no access outside the Veda. || 1.13.12 ||

Regarding the hearing of poetry, drama, and the like, which fall outside the Veda, there is no inclination or desire to listen, even though such things may be useful for the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda. (1.1.12)
One should attend upon the teacher who has been instructed and is teaching, until the study is completed. 1.13.13.

He who, being commanded by the teacher, teaches him, should attend upon him from the beginning of the study until he has taught him. Regarding the sūtra, “When he teaches him as thus commanded,” [ĀpDh 1.7.28], conduct toward him is said to be like that toward the teacher’s wife; and in that context, the phrase “except for attending upon [the teacher]” [ĀpDh 1.7.27] applies. Therefore, this present section is commenced for the purpose of prescribing such attendance. 1.13.13.
Some say that an Arhat is eternal. 1.13.14

If he has been instructed and becomes an Arhat through knowledge, virtuous conduct, and so forth, then some maintain that one should attend upon him constantly; however, his own view is that this should continue only as long as the study lasts. 1.13.14
No going exists. || 1.13.15 ||
Even if he is an Arhat, nevertheless, that service and obedience which is due toward a teacher should not be performed toward him. 1.13.15.
But for the elders: || 1.13.16 ||

The word *tu* has the sense of *ca* (and). For elders and for pupils, there is no obligation to rise; a pupil who is younger than an elder pupil need not show service to a teacher who is older [in age]. Some say this applies after the period of study; others say it applies even during the time of study. Some say that even a younger pupil must not perform the act of rising (*gati*) toward an elderly person. 1.13.16.
When there is mutual application within the Veda, no other course is found. || 1.13.17 ||

Even when there is a mutual exchange of instruction regarding the Brahman—that is, concerning the Veda—such as when a follower of the Rigveda studies the Yajurveda from a follower of the Yajurveda, and he likewise [studies] the Rigveda from him, even then no service should be rendered to one another. (1.13.17)
Regarding this, he states the reason himself: "They teach that Brahman increases. 1.13.18.
The Brahman prospers for both; the teachers teach that this very increase of the Brahman is what constitutes service. 1.13.18.

"When the settling [of the marriage] has taken place, he should dwell for two months every year in the teacher's household with a concentrated mind, desiring further learning"— so said Śvetaketu. 1.13.19.

"Desiring further instruction, a man—even when his household duties have been settled and his marriage performed—should live for two months each year at the teacher's house with a concentrated mind; this is what the teacher Śvetaketu believes. 1.13.19.
In this context, it is Śvetaketu himself who speaks to his disciples as the reason for [his knowledge]:
"For by means of this yoga, I have heard more than before. (1.13.20)
By this aforementioned method or means, I have acquired more learning—indeed, a greater amount—than during my previous period of studentship; therefore, you too should do likewise. 1.13.20.
That is contradicted by the scriptures. 1.1.21.
This statement of Śvetaketu is contradicted by the scriptures, such as the Śrutis and others. 1.13.21.
To the question "How so?", he says: "For when the settling [of the bride] has taken place, the regular [sacrificial] rites are prescribed. (1.13.22)

The word *hi* indicates the reason: because, once one has entered [the householder stage], the regular (*naiyamikāni*), obligatory (*nitya*) rites are prescribed as things that must necessarily be performed. 1.13.22.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.
What, then, are those? The Agnihotra sacrifice and guests. 1.14.1.
The fire-sacrifice, guests, and the honoring of guests.
As all living beings live by depending upon their mother, so do all mendicants live by depending upon the householder. (VaDh 8.16)
And whatever else is likewise connected [to this]. 1.14.2.

Such are the duties, including the ancestral offerings and the twilight devotions. For one who is thus occupied day after day with these rituals, there is not even an opportunity to scratch his head; how then could he dwell in the teacher’s household for two months at a time? || 1.14.2 ||
If someone should urge him for the sake of Vedic study, he should not refuse that person. 1.14.3.

If a young student should urge an Ācārya with the purpose of study, saying, "I am your disciple; teach me, who have come to you for refuge," he must not refuse that young student. The word *ca* (and) is used here for emphasis. 1.1.4.3.
Is this without distinction? No, he says:
"And one should not see any fault in this. (1.14.4)

The particle *caṇ* exists, according to [Pāṇini 8.1.30]: "In the presence of particles such as *yad*, *yadi*, *iha*, *anta*, *ku*, *vit*, *na*, *cet*, *caṇ*, *kaccit*, *yat*, and *trā* [the augment *ṭi* is applied]. Since it occurs in the sense of *ced* ("if"), as seen in examples such as *indraś ca mṛḍayāti naḥ* (RV 2.41.11), this is its usage here: "If he should not perceive a fault in this young boy—a reason for not teaching him. (1.14.4)
If there were no such thing as chance, then movement would be impossible in that case.

When students are studying together, if for some reason—without any visible cause, but due to dullness of intellect or the like—there should be a failure in study such that the portion learned does not come forth as it does for other students, then in the face of that failure caused by chance, the student’s only recourse is service toward that teacher. And so Manu says:
"Just as a man digging with a spade obtains water, so the one who desires to hear obtains the knowledge residing in the teacher" (MDh 2.218).
"The teacher should instruct him who has served him excessively with his whole being. || 1.14.5 ||
Service toward one's mother and father is to be performed as toward a teacher. 1.14.6.

By the mention of "mother," the grandmother and great-grandmother are also included; by the mention of "father," the grandfather and great-grandfather are included. All these must be served just as one's teacher. 1.14.6.
One who has returned home from his studies must pay homage to all his teachers. || 1.14.7 ||
Those already mentioned and those not yet mentioned—the elder brother, the maternal uncle, and so forth—all elders must be saluted daily by one who has returned from his teacher's house.
And upon reunion after having been away.
If one has returned from traveling abroad oneself, or if the teachers have returned from traveling abroad, then they too should be welcomed with respect. || 1.14.8 ||
One should show respectful salutation to brothers and sisters according to their seniority, as previously described. || 1.14.9 ||
Although this was already established by the preceding rule, this statement is for the sake of specifying the order: "according to seniority, as before. (1.14.9)
And the daily worship is performed according to the instruction.

"In accordance with the instruction, ‘Worship should be performed for those superior by caste, and for those who are more elderly’ (ĀpDh 1.13.2–3), that worship which is obligatory must also be conducted according to the aforementioned order of seniority. 1.14.10.
One should rise to greet and salute officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger than oneself. 1.14.11.

"He who has been a master of the Veda for three years deserves a salutation" (ĀpDh 1.14.13)—so he will state later. By this, even officiating priests and others who are younger in age are to be saluted; when they salute him, he should rise and greet them in return, not remaining seated at ease as one would with others. Therefore, this alone is the honor due to those who are superior. 1.14.11.
Or he may accept [the gift] in silence. 1.14.12.
Alternatively, having risen, he himself should also silently attend to them; the choice depends on their learning, conduct, and other qualities.
Now those who are to be saluted are described: A ten-year-old fellow citizen, a five-year-old fellow student, and a Vedic scholar three years senior deserve a formal salutation. (1.14.13)

The term *paura-pauram* refers to fellow citizens, and *paura-sakhyam* refers to friendship with them, which is based on service and so forth; this constitutes the ground for salutation. Of what nature is it? It is characterized by an interval of ten years. The intended meaning is that a fellow citizen who is more than ten years older is to be saluted even if he is not a *śrotriya*. However, the phrase "friendship of five years" (*pañcavarṣaṃ tu cāraṇaṃ sakhyam*) is to be understood as a connected whole. The word *cāraṇa* is conventionally used for those who study the Vedic branches (*śākhā*). Their friendship lasting five years is the ground for salutation. Regarding the *śrotriya*, the author will state later [ĀpDh 2.6.4]: such a person deserves salutation merely by being three years senior; he does not depend upon prior acquaintance. (1.14.13)
When a difference in age is known, one who is older is to be saluted with the *abhivādana* greeting.

This statement is for the purpose of establishing the sequence: when a difference in age is known, first the salutation must be performed toward the older person—that is, the greeting should be offered—and afterwards toward the younger person. || 1.14.14 ||
One who has fallen into a precarious situation need not pay homage to a teacher. || 1.14.15 ||

Whether standing in a high place or a low place, or situated on uneven ground, one should not perform the salutation (*abhivādana*) to anyone other than the teacher (*guru*). However, one must certainly salute the teacher, because it is improper to remain silent when seeing him. (1.14.15)
Or, having climbed up after him, he should offer his salutation.

This refers to the case of those who are not gurus. Wherever that person who is to be saluted is standing, one should salute him either by climbing up after him or by descending down after him; for the latter rule is also to be understood here, as the underlying principle is the same. However, it has been stated that in the case of a guru, the salutation must be performed the very moment he is seen.
But in all cases, one should rise and offer a respectful greeting.
In all cases, whether toward a superior or one who is not a superior, one must rise up before offering salutation. || 1.14.17 ||
The two subsequent sūtras are established by their literal meaning: "One should not salute [a person] with indifference. (1.14.18)
To one who is thus striving. || 1.14.19 ||
And one who is not purified shall not return a greeting. M 1.14.20
If someone should greet one who is impure out of ignorance, even so, that impure person must not return the greeting.
Women who are of equal age [to their husbands]. || 1.14.21 ||
Whatever is the age of the husband is indeed the age of the wives; therefore, salutation toward the senior wife and others is performed in accordance with that [age]. (1.14.21)
One should not offer salutation while wearing shoes, with one's head wrapped, or with hands occupied. 1.14.22.
"With hands steady" means having sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, and so forth in his hands, or else having a sickle and such in his hands; the rest is well known. || 1.14.22 ||
Women, as well as Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, are not addressed by their personal names, but by pronouns.

One should greet women using only their generic name, saying, "I, [name], greet you," and not by their specific personal name, such as, "I, Devadatta, greet you. The same applies to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. 1.14.23.
Some say [he should not eat] his mother or the wife of his teacher. 1.14.24.

One should also salute one's mother and the wife of a teacher using their general titles (*sarvanāman*) alone, and not by name; so some maintain. However, his own view is that they should be saluted by name alone. (1.14.24) He states that there is no salutation based on age for one of a lower caste:
"A ten-year-old Brāhmaṇa and a hundred-year-old Kṣatriya..."
Know that those two were father and son; of them, the Brāhmaṇa was the father.

This is the instruction of the teacher to the disciple. The particle *sma* is used for the purpose of completing the verse. "Brāhmaṇa" and "Kṣatriya" are indicative terms for the highest and lowest castes. "Know" means understand. The rest is clear. (1.14.25)
One should ask a virtuous person who is younger in age or a companion. || 1.14.26 ||

This refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa, since specific rules for Kṣatriyas and others will be stated later. A *vayasya* is one who is equal in age. One should ask a Brāhmaṇa who is younger than oneself or of equal age, when met on a road or elsewhere, about his welfare, saying: "Is all well?
The Kṣatriya is free from disease. || 1.14.27 ||
One who is free from illness is healthy; one should ask him: "Are you free from illness? || 1.14.27 ||
The Vaiśya is indeed not lost. 1.14.28.
"Are your cattle and wealth not lost? || 1.14.28 ||
"Health," [he says] to a Śūdra. || 1.14.29 ||
To a Śūdra [he asks]: "Are you healthy? Are you free from illness? (1.14.29)
One should not pass by a Vedic scholar (śrotriya) without having spoken to him. || 1.14.30 ||
One should not pass by a learned Vedic scholar encountered on the road without speaking to him. 1.14.30.
And [he should not look at] a woman in the forest. || 1.14.31 ||

The mention of the "forest" is an illustration for any region that is dangerous. Having seen a woman there alone, one should not pass by her without speaking. And the conversation should be like that with a mother or a sister: "Sister, what may I do for you? You must not be afraid. (1.14.31)
Thus ends the fourteenth section;
thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Ujjvalā*, the commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Intending to prescribe sipping water (ācamana) as a subsidiary element for all ritual acts, he states the rules pertaining to its application:

"In the service of gurus, elders, and guests; during the fire-oblation (homa), the rite of recitation (japa), eating, sipping water, and Vedic study, one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī). (1.15.1)

When attending upon gurus—such as teachers and others—as well as other elders, venerable persons, and guests; when performing a *homa* (other than that for the ancestors) along with its constituent parts; during the act of recitation (*japa*); during eating and sipping water (*ācamana*); and during the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), one should wear the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). The *yajñopavīta* is a specific manner of arranging the garment: "He raises the right arm and wears the left [under the right arm]"—so says the Brāhmaṇa [Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.1]. In the absence of a cloth, he will state an alternative rule: "Or else, even a cord may serve the purpose of the sacred thread" [Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.4.22]. Manu has also said this.
"The sacrificial thread (*upavīta*) of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward, and triple-stranded" (MDh 2.44);
and "When the right hand is raised, a twice-born man is said to be wearing the sacrificial thread" (MDh 2.63).
Since these rules prescribe the sacrificial thread for these specific rites, it is not mandatory during other times. 1.15.1.
Having sipped water from water situated on the ground, one becomes pure. || 1.15.2 ||

Waters on the ground are pure when they can satisfy the thirst of a cow, provided they are not contaminated by impurities and possess their natural odor, color, and taste. Water that satisfies a cow's thirst, remaining in its natural state upon the earth, is pure. (MDh 5.128; YDh 1.192)
Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Goats, cows, buffaloes, and a Brāhmaṇa woman who has recently given birth become pure after ten nights, as do rainwater that has reached the ground."

Thus says Manu. "When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, all rivers are in their menses," so it is stated in another Smṛti. Having sipped water (ācamana) from waters free from such defects, one becomes pure (prayata). For the sake of purification, the sipping of water must be performed using water that has reached the ground. 1.15.2.
Or he may cause one who is purified to sip water.

Or, if another person who is pure should cause him to sip water, he also becomes pure. In no case does sipping water with water poured from the left hand constitute the rite. By this it is indicated that the teacher does not approve of the carrying of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) mentioned in other treatises; for the learned practice sipping water themselves using either a gourd vessel or a coconut shell.
One should not sip water while raindrops are falling. 1.15.4.

Some maintain that since there is no possibility of the aforementioned *ācamana* for the purpose of purification occurring in the streams of rain, this [verse] is a prohibition against drinking for one who is thirsty. Others say: precisely because of this prohibition, there is certainly no *ācamana* for the purpose of purification in the case of streams from water-jars and the like situated on a carrying-net (*śikya*) or similar supports. (1.15.4)
Likewise, in the water of a fissure. 1.15.5.
A *pradara* is a section of ground that has split open of its own accord; one should not sip water (*ācamana*) from water located therein, even though it is situated on the earth.
And [the same applies] to those who have been punished with hot [liquids], even though they were innocent. 1.15.6.

One should not rinse with water that has been heated without a specific reason. There is no fault when there is a reason such as fever and the like. Because of the mention of "heated" water, there is no fault in using water that has been boiled and then cooled. Thus, in the Smṛtis, the prohibition generally applies only to water that is hot. 1.15.6.
With empty hands, having raised his arms, he should touch water. || 1.15.7 ||

*Vaya* is a name for a bird. He who, having his hands empty, raises his hand to strike a *vayas*—that is, a bird—in order to drive it away, should, after doing so, touch water with that very same hand. Because of the expression "empty-handed," there is no fault in raising a hand that holds a piece of wood or a clod of earth. Some say that "touching" (*upasparśana*) refers to sipping water (*ācamana*). (1.15.7)
One should not remain even for a moment lacking in self-restraint regarding the domain of one's power. || 1.15.8 ||

If one is capable, one should not remain even for a moment without being purified. Upon seeing water suitable for sipping (ācamana), one may perform the voiding of urine, feces, and so forth, provided that one is able to restrain the urge for that duration of time. 1.15.8.
Or naked. 1.15.9.

The phrase "there should not be [lack of clothing] even for a moment" is connected [to the previous rule], as is the qualification "within one's capacity. There is no fault if, due to a wound or similar reason, one is unable to cover the private parts. 1.15.9.
For one who is in water, no support is found. || 1.15.10 ||

That by which one becomes purified is "purification," namely, sipping water (*ācamana*). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of an instrument. That [purification] does not occur for one who is in water; even while sitting in the midst of water, one should not sip water. (1.15.10)
But having crossed over, one should sip water for purification. || 1.15.11 ||

The meaning that "one should sip water after having crossed onto the bank, but not while in the water" need not be enjoined, as this has already been established by the preceding rule. Therefore, this is the meaning: when one crosses a river by boat or by some other means, then, having crossed it and reached the opposite bank—even if he is already pure—he should sip water; for even the act of crossing a river or similar body of water is a cause for sipping water. The particle *tu* (but) is used in the sense of *api* (also). (1.15.11)
One should not place fuel that has not been sprinkled with water into the fire. 1.15.12.

One should not place, nor throw, fuel that has not been sprinkled with water into a fire—whether it be a Vedic (śrauta), traditional (smārta), or worldly (laukika) fire. Some, however, do not accept this rule regarding the worldly fire. 1.15.12.
On a defiled mat, one who is pure should consider himself pure provided he does not touch others who are impure. 1.15.13.

Gautama says: “Upon touching one who has fallen from his caste, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, a corpse, or one who has touched any of these, one becomes pure by bathing with one’s clothes on. Regarding that subject, this is stated: a heap of straw and the like that has been well-spread out for the purpose of lying down or sitting upon is called a *svastara*. The formation of the word is established because it is seen among the *pṛṣodarādi* group. When the distinction between the roots and tips of the straw and so forth is not perceived due to extreme smoothness, it is called *mūḍha*. A *svastara* that is *mūḍha* is a *mūḍhasvastara*. If someone who is pure (*prayata*) should sit upon such a *mūḍhasvastara* where impure persons such as those who have fallen from their caste are already seated, provided he does not touch them, then he may consider himself pure; just as one who is pure considers himself pure, thinking “I am pure,” so indeed should he consider himself. In such a case, the rule regarding contact with those who have touched the impure (*tatspṛṣṭinyāya*) does not apply. 1.15.13.
Likewise, when grass and wood have been buried [in the ground]. || 1.15.14 ||
The principle of contact does not apply to grass and wood that have been buried in the ground. 1.15.14.
Having sprinkled it with water, he should put on the garment. || 1.15.15 ||
One should use or wear even a clean garment only after sprinkling it with water. Another teacher says: "Even for an impure garment, sprinkling alone is the cause of purification. 1.15.15
One who has been bitten by a dog should immerse himself in water along with his clothes.

"Struck by a dog" means touched by one. Even if the garment has not been touched by the dog, nevertheless, he who is wearing clothes must plunge into water found on the ground—that is, he should bathe in water that is not drawn out [from a well or tank]. However, for one who has been bitten, there is an expiation prescribed in another Smṛti. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says:

"A Brāhmaṇa who has been bitten by a dog, having gone to a river that flows to the ocean and having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), becomes pure after consuming clarified butter. [VaDh 23.31]
Aṅgiras says: A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) bitten by a dog is purified in three nights;
a householder (*gṛhastha*) in two nights; and one who maintains the *agnihotra* fire in one day.
For one bitten above the navel, that same [penance] shall be doubled;
it shall be tripled for a bite on the face, and quadrupled if it occurs on the head.
One born from the womb of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra becomes pure by bathing alone;
however, for one who dwells in the forest and likewise for one who has renounced the world, it is double that amount.
If a Brahmin woman is bitten by a dog, she should fix her gaze upon the moon;
but when the moon is not visible, what then is the expiation?
One should look toward whichever direction Soma has gone;
that [direction] becomes purified by the path of Soma and is cleansed by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Or, having washed that spot, touched it with fire, washed it again, and sipped water, he becomes pure. || 1.15.17 ||

Having washed a place touched by a dog, and having touched it with fire, and having washed it again, and having washed his feet, he becomes pure after sipping water (ācamana). This is an optional rule based on circumstances: "Whatever limb, excluding the hands and the area above the navel, is defiled, the procedure for bathing is prescribed there; however, for areas below that, washing is ordained."
Thus, because it is seen in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]. 1.15.17.
One who has not yet offered the oblation should not sit near the fire. 1.15.18.

Being unpurified, one should not sit near the fire; that is, one should not remain in proximity to the fire at a distance from which heat is perceived. In this case as well, there is no fault if one is unable [to avoid it]. 1.15.18
"Only the distance of an arrow's flight," say some. 1.15.19.
Some maintain that one should not sit closer than the distance of an arrow’s length from the fire; one should not sit so near that the heat is perceived, or perhaps not at all. 1.15.19.
And one should not blow upon it. 1.15.20.
"Unrestrained"—this is the rule. One who is unrestrained should not blow upon this fire; there is no fault for one who is restrained.
One should blow upon the fire with the mouth, for from the mouth fire was born.

Because this is seen in another Smṛti; and because it is seen in the Mānava [Dharmaśāstra] that "one should not blow upon the fire with the mouth" (MDh 4.53ab), there is an option between the two. Another says: since it is seen in the Śrauta section of the Vājasaneyaka that "Fire was born from the mouth; therefore, one should kindle it with the mouth," blowing with the mouth applies only to the Śrauta rites, while the prohibition applies elsewhere in the Smārta context. Others, however, desire kindling by means of a hollow reed or an iron tube; for in this way, by the continued application of the mouth's function, the Śruti is honored, and since there is no fear of saliva-drops falling, the Smṛti prohibition is also maintained. 1.15.20.
One should not place [the fire] upon a couch. 1.15.21.
One should not place the fire beneath a bed; however, there is no fault in this even if one is unable to do so. 1.15.21.
In a village with abundant fuel and water, where the means of purification are under one's own control, it is lawful for a Brāhmaṇa to dwell. 1.15.22.

In a village where fuel and water are abundant, the residence of a Brāhmaṇa is lawful (*dhārmya*). Even there, however, it is not everywhere. What then? Only in a place where purification (*prāyatyam*), such as the washing of urine, feces, and so forth, is under one's own control. But where water is available only from wells, one should not dwell there even if there are many wells. By the mention of "Brāhmaṇa," there is no such restriction for other castes. And by the mention of "village," one should likewise not dwell in such places as cowherd settlements (*ghoṣa*) and the like. (1.15.22)

Having voided urine or feces, having washed away the smears of urine and feces, the smears of food, the smears of leavings, and those smears of semen, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure. 1.15.23.

Having voided urine or feces and having discarded them, one should wash away with water and earth all those smears of that urine or feces—whether they remain in that spot or have fallen in another place—including all such smears of food, whether they are from what was left over or from what was not left over; likewise, one should wash away all smears of semen occurring during sleep or sexual intercourse. After washing the feet even if they are free of smears, and then sipping water (ācamana), one becomes pure. Since neither the quantity nor the number of applications of earth has been specified here, it is intended that one should use as much as is necessary for the removal of odor and smears. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"One should perform purification diligently until the odor and the stain have been removed.
Thus [it is said]. Devala, however, has stated it quite explicitly:
"One should perform purification for as long as one considers oneself to be pure."
"The number of purificatory acts for cleansing is not prescribed by the learned.
Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"When urination or defecation has been performed, there shall be no cleansing while remaining within a body of water."
"But having extracted [the mantra] from elsewhere, one should always perform it with a concentrated mind. (1.15.23)
Thus ends the fifteenth section:
One should not sip water while standing or while stooping. 1.16.1.

"One should not sip water while standing or while stooping. This prohibition cannot be maintained. Why? Because he will state later: "Sitting, one should sip water three times" [ĀpDh 1.16.2]. Therefore, just as sipping water does not occur for one who is lying down, it likewise does not occur for one who is standing or stooping. If that is so, then this is not a prohibition of the sipping of water for the purpose of purification. What then? It is a prohibition of drinking water. And thus says Gautama: "One should not drink with cupped hands; nor while standing" [GDh 9.9–10].

Another says: from this very prohibition, it follows that rinsing the mouth (ācamana) is permitted for one who is standing or bowing down in certain circumstances; when water on the ground is unfit for the purpose of a bathing place (tīra), rinsing the mouth may be performed by one standing in water reaching up to the thighs or the navel. In the *Gautama-dharma-sūtra* as well, because of the division of the sūtra as "one should not rinse the mouth while standing with drawn-up water" (GDh 9.11), the prohibition applies specifically to one standing with drawn-up water. 1.16.1.
Now follows the rule for sipping water (ācamana): Seated, one should sip water three times with water that reaches the heart. (1.16.2)

"With water"—the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative. Here, what is not explicitly stated is supplemented by the statements of other Smṛtis: "Seated in a clean place, but not on a seat; at the end of a meal, however, on a seat; having placed the right arm between the thighs; seated facing east or north; a Brāhmaṇa should sip and drink water that reaches the heart—water which, when held in the palm, is such that a bean sinks in it—and which is free from foam and bubbles, after having looked at it three times. A Kṣatriya [should drink] until it reaches the throat; a Vaiśya, until it reaches the palate; a Śūdra, once, merely touching the tongue. (1.16.2)
He should wipe his lips three times.
One should wipe it clean. 1.16.3.
Some say [the word] "twice. 1.16.4.
The conceptualization is equal. 1.16.4.
One should touch [the water] once. || 1.16.5 ||
One should touch the two lips with the three middle fingers alone. || 1.16.5 ||
Some say twice. 1.16.6.
The conceptualization is equal. 1.16.6.
Having sprinkled his left hand with water from his right hand, he should touch his feet, his head, and his sense organs—the eyes, the nostrils, and the ears. (1.16.7)

Having sprinkled his left hand with his right hand, as well as his feet and head, he should touch the sense organs with his fingers. Regarding the engagement of all the sense organs, [the text] specifies them as: "the eyes, the nostrils, and the ears. The mention of "sense organs" (*indriyāṇi*) is merely for the purpose of stating their nature. Among these, one should touch the two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger—some say simultaneously, others say separately. One should touch the two nostrils with the thumb and the index finger, and the two ears with the thumb and the little finger. Since simultaneous action is impossible here and separate action is certain, it is logical that in the preceding cases as well, the action is performed separately. (1.16.7)
Then he should touch water. 1.16.8.
Immediately after touching the sense organs, one should wash both hands. || 1.16.8 ||
But when about to eat, even if he is already pure, he should sip water twice, wipe his mouth twice, and touch [the lips] once. (1.16.9)

Even when already pure (*prayata*), one who is about to eat should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice. Herein is the distinction: one should wipe [the mouth] twice, not optionally three times; one should touch [the lips] once, not optionally twice. Because of the statement "even when already pure," the Teacher’s intention is that the sipping of water twice applies in all cases where one is not already pure. Regarding this, there is another Smṛti:

"Having sneezed, having slept, having eaten, having spat, and having spoken untruthful words, as well as after putting on a garment, one who has already sipped water should sip water again. (MDh 5.145ab; YDh 1.196) || 1.16.9 ||
Having touched the lips at their dark edges, one should sip water for purification. 1.16.10.

The two lips begin from the roots of the teeth. Therein, the hairless portion is dark; the area inside it is hairy. Having touched the edges of the lips [at that point], one should sip water for purification (*ācamana*). One should touch the hairless portion of the lips with a finger or a piece of wood and then sip water for purification.
One does not become impure by having food in the mouth due to the presence of facial hair, as long as one does not touch it with the hand. 1.16.11.

When there are hairs of the beard inside his mouth, he does not become impure by their being within the mouth as long as he does not touch them with his hand. However, upon touching them, he becomes impure and must therefore sip water (*ācamana*). From this very prohibition it is known that even the presence of any substance whatsoever within the mouth is a cause for impurity. 1.16.11.
Regarding those drops that are perceived falling from his mouth, sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed for them. 1.16.12.

Regarding the drops of saliva falling from one who is speaking, *ācamana* (sipping water) is prescribed for those that are perceived by the eye or by touch—that is, for those that are capable of being perceived. However, concerning the recitation of the Veda, Gautama states: "When one recites the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, those drops which are perceived on the body do not require *ācamana*" [GDh 1.16.12].
Some say that one should not sip water (ācamana) from those [vessels] that rest upon the ground. 1.16.13.

Some maintain that one need not sip water (ācamana) for those drops which fall on the ground and not on the body [cf. MDh 5.142; YDh 1.195; ViDh 23.54; BDh 1.10.34]; however, his own opinion is that one should sip water even for those. 1.16.13.

Upon dreaming, sneezing, touching phlegm or tears, touching blood, hair, fire, cows, a Brahmin, or a woman; upon walking along a high road; upon touching something impure; upon touching a person who is not ritually pure; and upon putting on the waist-knot (nīvī)—one should touch water. 1.16.14.

Upon dreaming (svapnaḥ) or sleeping (svāpaḥ), upon sneezing (kṣavathuḥ) or coughing (kṣutam), upon touching nasal mucus (śiṅghāṇikā) or tears (aśru), upon touching blood (lohita), hair on the head or fallen on the ground, or the four [substances] beginning with fire; having walked along a high road (mahāpatha); having touched impurity (amedhya)—such as the urine or feces of animals other than cows, or the spittle used for betel—and having touched a person who is not pure (aprayata); and having put on the *nīvī* (which refers to the lower garment by association with that term)—one should touch water. In some cases there is bathing (*snānam*), in others sipping water (*ācamanam*), and in others merely touching; [the rule applies] according to what degree one considers oneself purified. 1.16.14.
Or moist cow dung, or herbs, or the earth. || 1.16.15 ||

"He should touch [water]"—this much is the rule. The word "moist" (*ārda*) is connected with all three [options] by modifying its gender and number accordingly: either moist dung, or moist plants, or moist earth. This is an optional alternative to all that was previously mentioned. 1.16.15.
Thus, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) has been explained along with its specific characteristics.
Now follows the section on forbidden foods:
meat cut with a knife intended for killing is unfit for consumption. 1.16.16.

The mention of "taking up a sword" is an illustration that includes other weapons such as razors and the like; for meat that has been cut with a sword intended for the purpose of killing at the time of cooking is unfit to be eaten. (1.16.16)
One should not cut off a piece of the cake with the teeth. 1.16.17.

The mention of "cake" (*apūpa*) is an elliptical expression that includes roots, fruits, and so forth. The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative. One should not bite a cake with one's teeth; rather, having cut it off with the hands or other means, one should eat it. (1.16.17)
In whose family one may die, food must not be eaten there during the ten-day period of impurity. || 1.16.18 ||

If someone in a family dies while the period of *asapiṇḍatā* (non-participation in funeral rites) remains, one must not eat there as long as the ten-day period has not elapsed. The term "anirdaśa" (not ten days) is an indicative mark for the duration of impurity (*āśauca*). Therefore, for Kṣatriyas and others, the period is longer, and for those with a *pakṣiṇī* (two nights and the intervening day) period of impurity, it is shorter. 1.16.18.
Likewise, when the woman who has given birth has not yet arisen [from her confinement]. || 1.16.19 ||

*Sūtakā* means *sūtikā* (the woman who has recently given birth); [the meal is forbidden] while she has not yet risen. "Rising" (*utthāna*) refers to the removal of the water-jars and other items placed in the lying-in chamber; and this occurs on the tenth day, because it is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "when she has risen on the tenth day" (*ĀpGṛ* 15.8). Since this [period] also serves as an indicator for the duration of ritual impurity (*āśauca*), one must abstain from eating for as long as that impurity lasts. Regarding this, Aṅgiras says: "For those who maintain the *agnihotra*, there is no fault in eating [during the impurity] of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas; however, during impurity caused by childbirth (*sūtaka*) or death (*śāva*), [they may eat] after the collection of the bones. (1.16.19)
And [the same applies] when there is a corpse inside. 1.16.20.

As long as a corpse has not been carried out from the village, one must not eat there; however, within a distance of a hundred bows (dhanuḥśata) is the customary practice. Even there, they eat after having raised a lamp and placed a water-pot nearby, provided that the house does not belong to a family of the same lineage.
Food defiled by one who is impure is "impure," but it is not, however, unfit to be eaten. (1.16.21)

That which is touched by one who is unpurified (*aprayata*) or impure (*aśuci*) becomes unpurified. However, even that which is impure does not necessarily become unfit for consumption. What, then, is the distinction between the unpurified and the unfit for consumption? It is said: food that is unpurified becomes purified and fit for consumption if it is placed on fire, sprinkled with water, touched by ashes or clay, or consecrated by speech. But garlic and the like are unfit for consumption under no circumstances whatsoever. (1.16.21)
But food offered by a Śūdra who is not self-restrained is unfit to be eaten. 1.16.22.

However, food brought by a Śūdra who is not restrained is unfit to be eaten, whether it has been touched or untouched [by him]. Others say that it is only when it has been touched that it is unfit. 1.16.22.
And in whatever food there may be hair. 1.16.23.

That too is unfit for consumption. And this refers specifically to food that has been cooked while already containing a hair from one who has fallen (from his caste). However, regarding food that comes into contact with a hair only after it has been cooked, other Smṛtis state that it becomes fit for consumption after being purified by the addition of ghee and so forth. 1.16.23.
Or any other impure substance. || 1.16.24 ||

Furthermore, any other impure substance such as fingernails and so forth that might be in the food is also unfit for consumption; this is to be understood as before. On this point, Bodhāyana states: “Having seen hair, insects, nails, body hair, or mouse-dung, one should remove only that much of the food and eat the remainder” [BDh 2.12.6]. Vasiṣṭha, however, says: “One may at will discard hair, insects, and the like, sprinkle the rest with water, scatter ashes over it, and consume it after pronouncing a word of purification” [VaDh 14.23]. 1.16.24.
Touched by impurities. || 1.16.25 ||
That which has been touched by impure things such as *kalañja*, onions, and the like, is unfit for consumption. 1.16.25.
Or like a worm that dwells in impurity. 1.16.26.
"In which food there might be hair" (ĀpDh 1.16.23)—this phrase is connected even though it is separated by intervening words. An impure-insect is one called the "putrid-egg insect. 1.16.26.
Or the tail of a rat. 1.16.27.

The connection is as before. "Mūṣikalā" means mouse-dung or a limb of a mouse. The term "mouse" applies to both cases collectively; that food in which there is a limb of a mouse, such as a tail or a foot, is also unfit for consumption. (1.16.27)
Or [a place] trodden upon by feet. 1.16.28.
Even that which is touched by the foot of one who is self-restrained is unfit for consumption.
Or likewise with the *sic* [suffix]. 1.1.6.29.
The fringe of a garment (*sic*): whatever has been touched by the fringe of a cloth that is being worn is also unfit for consumption. (1.16.29)
Or it is seen by a dog or by a vessel used for husking grain. 1.16.30.

The word "seen" (*dṛṣṭam*) is to be connected with each [term]. That which has been seen by a dog, or that which has been seen by one who is an *apapātra*—that too is unfit for consumption. Fallen persons (*patita*), *caṇḍālas*, women who have recently given birth (*sūtikā*), menstruating women (*udakyā*), and so forth, are *apapātras*; they are "removed from the vessel" (*apagataḥ pātrebhyaḥ*). For they do not obtain the right to eat from a vessel. (1.16.30)
Or likewise, that which has been offered with a sword. || 1.16.31 ||
Even that which is offered by the hem of a garment, though it be pure and unwashed, is unfit for consumption. (1.16.31)
Or it was brought at night by a female slave. || 1.16.32 ||

Food brought by a female slave at night is unfit for consumption. Because of the specification of the feminine gender, there is no fault if it is brought by a male slave. Others consider the gender to be irrelevant. Because of the mention of "at night," there is no fault if it is brought during the day. (1.16.32)
Thus ends the sixteenth section:
where a Śūdra might touch [the water]. 1.17.1.

If a Śūdra should touch [the food] while one is in the state of eating, then one should not eat even then. Some hold that because of the mention of "one who is eating," there is no impurity (aprāyatya) when a Śūdra touches [the food] at other times. Others, however, maintain that impurity always exists; the prohibition regarding the state of eating is intended to indicate that it is particularly excessive at that time. 1.17.1.
Or [one should not eat] in the same row as those unworthy [to sit]. 1.17.2.

The word "or" (*vā*) occurs everywhere in the sense of conjunction. Those who are devoid of noble birth, learning, and virtuous conduct are unworthy; one should not eat in the same row as them. (1.17.2)
Or while [others] are eating, he should not rise up from his seat to offer them the leftovers or to rinse his mouth. 1.17.3.

The phrase "in the same row" (*samānapaṅktau*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. When many are eating in the same row, if one person, without rising, should stop eating and give his leavings to disciples and others, or should rinse his mouth (*ācāmet*), then the others in that row must not eat. Therefore, when many are eating, one should not stop in the midst of the meal; they call such a person a "thorn in the meal" (*bhojanakaṇṭaka*).
Or where they might give food after having reviled [the recipient]. 1.17.4.
Having reviled them thus, saying, "O fool, O son of a widow, eat poison!", even if they should give food there, that too is unfit to be eaten.
If it has been smelled by humans or by other impure things. 1.17.5.

Food smelled by humans or others, such as cats and the like, that are impure, is unfit for consumption. Because of the use of the prefix *ava-* in the word *avaghrātam*, there is no fault if the odor is smelled from a distance. (1.17.5)
One should not eat on a boat. 1.17.6.
One should not eat while seated on a boat, nor even from a clean vessel.
Likewise, in the case of a palace. 1.17.7.
A palace made of wood is a wooden bed; one should not eat even there. 1.17.7.
But one should eat on ground that has been prepared. || 1.17.8 ||

Even when eating on the ground, one should eat on ground that has been prepared with cow dung and other such materials. Another says: even in a palace, when it has a prepared floor—not merely one made of wood—one may certainly eat there. 1.17.8
One should eat from an unbaked earthen vessel. 1.17.9.

If one should eat from an earthen vessel, then it must be eaten before it has been consecrated (*anāprīta*). *Āprīta* refers to that which has been employed for some purpose, such as cooking or the like.
If it is not pleased, [it is] burnt up. 1.17.10.
If it is obtained while still raw, then one should eat it there after having had it roasted on all sides by fire. || 1.17.10 ||
The iron [vessel] was polished and purified. || 1.17.11 ||

Iron—that is, a vessel made of iron such as bell-metal (kāṃsya) and the like—becomes pure when scrubbed with ashes and other substances. In this regard, it should be understood according to other Smṛti texts that bell-metal is purified by ashes, copper by acid, silver by cow dung, and gold by water alone, and so forth. 1.17.11.
It is carved out of wood. || 1.17.12 ||
A wooden vessel, when scraped and planed, becomes pure when it is thoroughly cleansed. || 1.17.12 ||
According to the traditional scripture, in the sacrifice.

The sacrificial vessels, however, become purified and ready for use according to the traditional injunctions. For example: the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle is washed with water using *darbha* grass; the *soma* vessels are washed at the *mārjālīya* shed; and the *ājya* vessels are washed with warm water. 1.17.13.
One should not eat food that has not been offered. 1.17.14.

A *āpaṇa* is a marketplace or bazaar. What is purchased or obtained there is called *āpaṇīya*; one should not eat that, even if it is cooked food. There is no fault, however, in the case of rice and similar grains. 1.17.14
Likewise, among the flavors, having excluded raw meat, honey, and salt. 1.17.15.
Regarding flavors, one should not consume the substances that constitute those flavors, even if they are available for purchase, with the exception of raw meat and similar items. 1.17.15.
But one should employ oil and ghee after having placed them in water.

However, one may also use oil and ghee that are for sale in the market, provided they have been purified by placing them in water and pouring [the water] out after boiling; others explain that one should mix them with water in such a way that no conflict with the purpose arises. 1.17.16.
Cooked food that has stood overnight is unfit to be eaten, drunk, or consumed.

Prepared food (kṛtānna) is cooked food; that which has become stale, having been cooked on the previous day, is unfit for eating, drinking, or consuming. It is, as appropriate, hard and coarse, liquid, soft and coarse, prepared, or oily. 1.17.17.
And fermented sour gruel. 1.17.18.
Śukta is that which has become sour through the process of time; even if it is not stale, it is unfit to be eaten, drunk, or consumed. 1.17.18.

Except for molasses, flattened rice, rice grains, milk-rice, *bharuja* beans, parched grain flour, vegetables, meat, flour preparations, dairy products, medicinal herbs, forest plants, roots, and fruits. 1.17.19.

The two methods just mentioned should be understood as excluding molasses (*phāṇita*) and the like. *Phāṇita* is a specific kind of syrup; some say it is sugarcane juice. *Pṛthuka* refers to flattened grains of parched (*bharjita* or *mṛṣṭa*) rice. *Karamba* is a mixture of curd and barley meal, which is well known as *karambha*. In the Veda, both forms occur: “He offers with *karambas*” (*karambair juhoti*, TaitBr 3.8.14) and “Parched grains, *karambha*, and parched grain flour” (*dhānāḥ karambhaḥ parivāpaḥ*, TS 6.5.11). *Bharuja* refers to parched barley. *Kṣīravikāra* refers to products derived from milk, such as curd and so forth. The rest is well known. (1.17.19)
Now, this is a supplement to the rule "and sour food" (ĀpDh 1.17.18):
"And sour food that has not been mixed with anything else. (1.17.20)

That which is conjoined with another substance is *parayoga*; that which is other than this is *aparayoga*. Only that [sour gruel] which is *aparayoga* is to be avoided. However, sour gruel that has merely been touched by another substance such as curd is indeed fit for consumption. Thus, the qualification "not conjoined with another" (*aparayogam*) should have been stated in the preceding rule itself; or rather, let this very [present] sūtra stand [as the definition]. The composition of two separate sūtras, however, was done at the discretion of the Teacher, just as he first stated generally, "The sounds of the *salāvṛkī*, the *ekasṛkā*, and the owl," and subsequently specified, "In the case of the *salāvṛkī* or the *ekasṛkā*, [the food is forbidden] until one falls asleep. (1.17.20)
All intoxicants are not to be drunk. 1.17.21.
All intoxicants that cause exhilaration are unfit to be drunk; however, in this matter, the determination is made according to other Smṛtis. On this point, Manu says:
"Gauḍī, Mādhvī, and Paiṣṭī are to be known as the three kinds of *surā*.
Just as one [kind] is not to be drunk, so all [three] are forbidden for the best of the twice-born" (MDh 11.95).

However, liquor other than *surā* must never be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa. Thus says Gautama: "Liquor is always forbidden for a Brāhmaṇa; but for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, it is forbidden only while they are students (*brahmacārin*)" (GDh 2.20). 1.17.21.
Likewise, milk from an elk. 1.17.22.
The ewe is a sheep; her milk is not to be drunk. 1.17.22.
The milk of a camel, the milk of a doe, the milk of a cow that has recently calved, and the milk of a woman who has recently given birth [are forbidden]. || 1.17.23 ||

The female camel (*uṣṭrī*) and the female deer (*mṛgī*) are well known. That which, being pregnant, gives milk is known in another treatise as *saṃdhinī*. Others say it refers to one who performs the oblation at the same time [as the cow]. That which brings forth more than one fetus in a single birth is a *yamasū* (twin-bearer). The milk of camels and the like is unfit for drinking. By the use of the word "and so forth" (*iti*), the milk of one-hoofed animals of this kind is also unfit for drinking. And so says Manu: "The milk of all wild animals except the buffalo, the milk of females, and all fermented acids (*śukta*) must indeed be avoided."
"The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, camel's milk, the milk of one-hoofed animals,
sheep's milk, the milk of a *saṃdhinī* cow, and the milk of a cow whose calf has died. [MDh 5.8–9] || 1.17.23 ||
And [the milk] of a cow within ten days of calving. 1.17.24.
A "dhenū" is a cow that has recently calved; the word "ca" (and) includes goats and buffaloes as well, according to the observation in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "Goats, cows, and buffaloes...
Likewise, [the same applies] to sweet water and medicinal herbs. 1.17.25.
The medicinal herbs intended for liquor are the *oṣadhayaḥ*; food, which is a modification of them, is what is to be eaten. 1.17.25.
Karañja, palāṇḍu, and parārikā. || 1.17.26 ||
*Karañja* is red garlic; *palaṇḍu* is white [onion]; *parārikā* is black [onion], well known among the Mlecchas by the name *ḍuṇḍubha*. These are also unfit for consumption. 1.17.26.
He says in brief that it is not possible to recite [the text] word for word:
"And whatever else they proclaim" (1.17.27).
Furthermore, whatever else is described as such by the learned and avoided by them, that too is unfit to be eaten. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Garlic, leeks, onions, mushrooms, and things produced from impure matter are unfit to be eaten by the twice-born. (MDh 5.5)
"For what is unfit to be eaten?"—thus says the Brāhmaṇa. 1.17.28.
The *kyāku* mushroom—this too is unfit for consumption, it is not to be eaten. The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose already explained. 1.17.28.
The single-hoofed animals, camels, gayals, village pigs, śarabhas, and boars. || 1.17.29 ||

"Meat" is understood by implication. "Single-hoofed animals" refers to horses and the like. The *gavaya* is a beast resembling a cow. The *śarabha* is an eight-legged wild deer. Others are well known. The meat of these [latter] is not to be eaten. (1.17.29)
The milk of a cow and the urine of a bull may be consumed. 1.17.30.
The meat of a cow and a bull is to be eaten; this is a counter-exception to the prohibition of beef. 1.17.30.
"The dung of a bull" is the Vājasaneyaka text. 1.17.31.
The Vājasaneyins record in their tradition that the flesh of the ox is not only edible, but even sacrificially pure. 1.17.31.
The cock is the chief among birds that scatter grain. 1.17.32.

The phrase "even if it is distant" is connected with "unfit to be eaten. Those birds such as peacocks that scatter and eat insects, grain, and so forth with their feet are called *vikira* (scatterers). Among them, the domestic cock (*kukkuṭa*) is not to be eaten; according to another *smṛti*, this refers to the domestic one and not the wild one.
The water-fowl is the foremost among those that strike with their beaks.

Those that peck with their beaks and then devour their prey are the "peckers" (pratuda), such as woodpeckers and the like. Among them, only the *plava* is not to be eaten. The *plava* is a specific type of crane known as the *śakaṭabila*. || 1.17.33 ||
The flesh-eater. 1.17.34.
*Kravya* means flesh; those who eat that alone are *kravyādas*, such as vultures and other scavengers. They too are not to be eaten. || 1.17.34 ||
And swans, cranes, ruddy geese, and garuḍas. || 1.17.35 ||
The *haṃsa* is well known. The *bhāsa* is shaped like a hawk with a thick beak. The *cakravāka* moves about in pairs. The *suparṇa* is a hawk. These are also not to be eaten. (1.17.35)
With the exception of the *kruñca*, *krauñca*, *vārdhrīṇasa*, and *lakṣmaṇa*.

The *kruñca* birds move in flocks; the *krauñca* birds move in pairs. These are not to be eaten. In the Sūtra, the case-ending in the word *krauñca* is elided by Vedic license (*chāndasa*). Are the *kruñca* and *krauñca* birds not to be eaten without distinction? No, he says: "except for those characterized as *vārdhrāṇasa*. Those whose heads are white or red are called *lakṣmaṇas*.
