They are further specified as *vārdhrāṇasas*. *Vārdhra* means hide; those whose noses have that shape are thus called *vārdhrāṇasas*. Excluding such *lakṣmaṇas*, the *kruñca* and *krauñca* birds are not to be eaten. Others, however, say that this is a prohibition regarding the four species beginning with *kruñca*, which would otherwise be subject to the general prohibition of eating "meat-eaters" (*kravyāda*). In that context, *lakṣmaṇā* refers to the female crane (*sārasī*). The short vowel in *lakṣmaṇa-varjam* is according to Pāṇini 6.3.63: "In names and in Vedic usage, the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are frequently elided. The same applies to the word *kruñca* and others when they end in the feminine suffix *ṭāp* (forming *kruñcā*). 1.17.36.
Among five-toed animals, all are permitted except for the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the rhinoceros, the hare, and the pūtikhaga (stinking bird). 1.17.37.

The five-clawed animals include humans, monkeys, cats, and others. Among them, with the exception of seven—beginning with the *godhā*—the rest are not to be eaten. The *godhā* is large-bodied and resembles a lizard (*kṛkalāsa*). The *kacchapa* is the tortoise. The *śvāvit* is a species of boar whose hair is shaped like iron arrows (*nārāca*). The *śaryaka* is the porcupine, whose skin is used to make armor; "śvāvit-śalyaka" is the correct reading. Some, however, read "chakāra," deriving it from the letter *cha*. The *khaḍga* is a specific kind of deer whose horn is used as an oil-container. The *śaśa* (hare) is well known. The *pūtikhaṣa* has the form of a hare and is well known in the Himalayas. (1.17.37)
And fish are not to be eaten by a servant. 1.17.38.
Among fish, the one called *ceṭa* is not to be eaten; others may be eaten. 1.17.38.
Those with serpent-heads, those with soft chests, the flesh-eaters, and others who are deformed, such as those with human heads. || 1.17.39 ||

Even that fish whose head is like a serpent’s is not to be eaten. The *makara* is soft-bodied. And those such as the *śiṃśumāra* (porpoise) and others that eat raw flesh are also inedible. Furthermore, those fish other than those mentioned which have deformed shapes are likewise forbidden; for example, those with human heads, those called *jalamanuṣya* (water-men), and *jalahasti* (water- elephants) and the like—all these are not to be eaten. Regarding this, Manu says: “The one who consents, the one who dissects, the slayer, the buyer and seller, the one who prepares it, the one who serves it, and the eater—all these are killers.”
"He shall devour me in the next world, whose flesh I eat here"—
the wise declare this to be the true nature of "flesh" (māṃsa).
“There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse; this is the natural inclination of living beings, but abstention bears great fruit. (MDh 5.51, 55, 56).
The meaning is that even regarding those things not expressly forbidden, abstaining from consumption is indeed superior. 1.17.39.
Thus ends the seventeenth section;
thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Ujjvalā*, the commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.

Thus, food that is defiled by its cause (*nimitta*), defiled by time (*kāla*), and defiled by its kind (*jāti*) has been declared unfit for consumption. Among these, that which is defiled by its cause is exemplified by such rules as, "if a member of his family dies" (ĀpDh 1.16.18) and so forth; that which is defiled by time is food that has become stale and the like; and that which is defiled by its kind is the *kalañja* bird and the like. Now, having permitted certain things that are impure by way of acceptance (*pratigraha*), he prohibits others.
Honey, raw grain, a path, meat, land, roots and fruits, protection, pasture-land, a dwelling, and fodder for draft animals—these may be accepted even from one who is fierce. (1.18.1)

Honey, whether ripe or unripe; raw grain such as rice and the like; *mārga*, which is the product of a deer, namely its meat; land, meaning a field for growing rice and so forth—others say it means any place; roots and fruits, such as radishes, mangoes, and the like; protection, meaning the granting of safety; a *gavyūti*, meaning a cow-path; a *niveśana*, meaning a house; and fodder, such as straw and the like, for a *yugya*—that is, a draft ox that pulls a yoke—these may be accepted even from an *ugra*, even when there is no famine. An *ugra* is a twice-born man of sinful conduct, or one born of a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother. The mention of the term *ugra* is intended to include others of similar character. (1.18.1)
Hārīta says that these [foods] also are not [permissible] if they have not been brought by a pupil. 1.18.2.
Master Hārīta maintains that even these items, such as honey and the like, are to be accepted only when brought by a pupil, and not when taken directly from a hunter. 1.18.2.
Or they may take raw [grain]. 1.18.3.
"The twice-born may take raw grain from the aforementioned [sources] themselves," such is the view of the teacher Hārīta. 1.18.3.
Or of prepared food that has lost its flavor.

In the absence of raw grain, they may take a small amount of prepared food that is tasteless and unmixed with salt or other flavors; this is understood from the use of the genitive case, meaning they should take it either by themselves or as brought by a pupil. (1.18.4)
There would not be abundance of food. || 1.18.5 ||

By that which has been prescribed in the two rules just mentioned, they would not be well-supplied or fully satiated; rather, they should take only as much as is necessary for the maintenance of life, and not as much as would result in complete satiety. 1.18.5.
If he himself does not perform the rite, he may consume [the food] after giving gold or an animal. || 1.18.6 ||

But when, due to famine, one cannot obtain a livelihood for oneself, let alone for those one is obligated to support, then even if one lacks a means of subsistence oneself, one may eat prepared food wherever it is obtained. Regarding this, there is a rule concerning the quality of the gift: having given gold, one should eat only that which has been prepared, after touching it with gold from above. By this, the rule "or having given an animal" is explained. The animal is fire, because of the indicative mark of the mantra, "Fire was the animal" (TS 5.7.26), and because of the observation of the worship of fire with the *gosūkta*. 1.18.6.
One should not settle into them excessively. || 1.18.7 ||
But he should not sink down utterly. 1.18.7.
Having obtained a livelihood, he should desist [from further worldly activity]. || 1.18.8 ||

When a prescribed means of livelihood (*vṛtti*) is obtained, one should desist from that which is forbidden; however, one should not remain in that very [forbidden state] according to the maxim: "Why cover up [the wound] once it has already been inflicted? Regarding this, the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* states: "When the Kurus were devastated by hailstorms, Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa lived as a wanderer with his wife in the village of a wealthy man (*ibhya*), subsisting on gleaned grain. He begged from the wealthy man who was eating some boiled beans... and so forth (*ChU* 1.10.1–2). There is also a Vedic mantra: "Out of necessity (*avartyā*), I cooked the entrails of a dog" (*RV* 4.18.13). "Out of necessity" means due to the absence of a livelihood. Another says: in a famine, or when one lacks a livelihood oneself, one may live anywhere with a lowly giver until that [famine] ceases, eating whatever is available; having given him any amount of gold or any kind of animal, one should not settle there permanently, but should desist once a livelihood is found. (1.18.8)
Having thus described the mode of conduct in times of distress, he now states the mode of conduct in times of plenty when there is no distress:
"A student who has completed his vows must not eat the food of the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya. (1.18.9)
A twice-born man who has completed his studies shall not eat in the house of the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya.
By nature, the food of a Brāhmaṇa is fit to be eaten; it becomes unfit to be eaten only for a specific cause.
The food of a Brāhmaṇa, however, may be eaten by its very nature and inherent quality; it is only for a specific reason that it becomes unfit to be eaten. 1.18.10.
He states the reason:
"In that case where one performs an act requiring expiation when [the rule] prescribes expiation. (1.18.11)

When one devotedly performs obligatory rites such as the Agnihotra and Vaiśvadeva, or rites for prosperity, without performing the required expiation—even when he is subject to an expiation prescribed for himself, such as breath-control (prāṇāyāma), fasting, or the Pathikṛt sacrifice—then for this reason, the food of such a person is unfit to be eaten by a Brāhmaṇa. 1.18.11.
One may eat [the food] of one who has completed his penance. || 1.18.12 ||

The food of one by whom the *nirveṣa*—the expiation—has been performed should be eaten; there is no fault in eating it. Because the suffix *-ta* denotes the past tense, [the food] must not be eaten even while the *nirveṣa* is being performed. What then? Only when it has been performed (*carite*). 1.18.12.
Some maintain that food may be eaten from all social classes provided they abide by their own respective duties, with the exception of Śūdras. 1.18.13.
Some maintain that food may be accepted from the three castes—excluding the Śūdra—who abide in their own respective duties, but not from a Brāhmaṇa alone. 1.18.13.
And for him as well, who has been brought [to this state] by the Dharma.

The food of that Śūdra also may be eaten if he has approached for the sake of dharma and has become a dependent. Because of the mention of "dharma," the food of one who has approached for the sake of wealth is not to be eaten; and this is a rule for times of distress. 1.18.14.
In this case, it is an injunction regarding a secondary quality (guṇavidhi):
having given gold or a sacrificial animal, one may eat; one should not settle down permanently, but upon obtaining a livelihood, one should desist. 1.18.15.
The [section] is concluded. || 1.18.15 ||
Food from the Saṃgha is not to be eaten. 1.18.16.
The *saṃgha* is a group; whatever food belongs to it is not the property of a single individual, and therefore it is not to be eaten, even if they should all give it [to one].
And that which is proclaimed. 1.18.17.
That which is given after one has cried out "Come, you who desire to eat! and summoned [the guests] from all sides is called *parikruṣṭa*; that is unfit to be eaten. 1.18.17.
And [he should not eat] the food of all those who live by their craft. || 1.18.18 ||
The food of all those Brāhmaṇas who subsist by the arts of painting, the creation of variegated images, and so forth, is also unfit to be eaten. 1.18.18.
And those who live by the sword. 1.18.19.
The food of those who live by the sword is also unfit to be eaten, with the exception of a Kṣatriya, because for him it is prescribed. 1.18.19.
And those who have resolute faith. 1.18.20.
The phrase "those who live by" requires an object. A *ādhi* is the taking of wages after having provided lodging for others in one's own house; it is what is commonly known as *stoma*. As it is said:
"But he who, having built a hut on another's land, should dwell there after giving a *stoma* [as rent].

Those who live by such a *ādhi* are also those whose food is not to be eaten. However, as for those who live by the *ādhi* that is commonly known [as interest], their food is established as unfit to be eaten precisely because they are usurers (*vārdhuṣika*). (1.18.20)
The physician. || 1.18.21 ||

"His food is not to be eaten"—this is understood from the context. A "physician" (bhiṣaj) is one whose livelihood is medicine. However, those who treat snakebites and other ailments for the sake of dharma alone are indeed those whose food may be eaten. (1.18.21)
One who lives by usury is also one whose food must not be eaten. || 1.18.22 ||
One who has been initiated but has not yet purchased the King [Soma] is called *dīkṣita-akrītarājaka*.

One who has been initiated—that is, one consecrated by the Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi sacrifice—is likewise forbidden from eating the food of others until he has purchased the King [Soma], that is, until he performs the purchase of the Soma. 1.18.23.
Only at the conclusion of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice. || 1.18.24 ||

The phrase "it is to be eaten" (*bhoktavyam*) requires reference to what is about to be stated. There is another view: that it is only when the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice has been concluded—that is, completed—that it may be eaten, and not before. (1.18.24)
Or, once the omentum has been offered, the consecrated person may eat. 1.18.25.

The food of one who has been initiated (dīkṣita) may be eaten either when the omentum (vapā) of the animal sacrificed to Agni and Soma has been offered, or [at other times]. Thus says the Bahvṛca Brāhmaṇa: "One should eat when the omentum has been offered. (1.18.25)
He states another alternative: "Or, when it has been designated for the sake of a sacrifice, they may eat from the remainder; for so says the Brāhmaṇa. (1.18.26)

"When the declaration has been made, 'This is for the sake of the sacrifice,' the Brahmana states that they should eat from the remainder. The mention of "Brahmana" is so that there may be no forgetfulness regarding the engagement [with the rule] based on the perception of satisfaction; thus, the Brahmana is indeed directly authoritative in this matter. (1.18.26)
Eunuch. 1.18.27.
A eunuch; he too is one whose food should not be eaten. 1.18.27.
He is the one who carries out the commands of kings. || 1.18.28 ||
Because of the plural number in the word "rājñām" (of kings), there is also a prohibition against one who carries out the commands of a village headman or similar authority. || 1.18.28 ||
One who performs sacrifices with clarified butter. 1.18.29.

And he who sacrifices with non-offerings such as human blood and the like—for instance, in malevolent rites [ābhicāra] where it is said, "having made the blood of the one whom he intends to harm the sacrificial portion (avadāna)"—his food also must not be eaten. 1.18.29.
And the practitioner. || 1.18.30 ||
A spy, a secret agent, or an informer—his food also must not be eaten. 1.18.30.
And one who has gone forth by an improper method. || 1.18.31 ||
Those such as the Śākyas who have gone forth without following the prescribed rule are also persons whose food should not be eaten. || 1.18.31 ||
And he who abandons the sacred fires. || 1.18.32 ||
"By not following the rule" means precisely this: he who abandons the sacred fires without performing the *utsargeṣṭi* sacrifice is also one whose food must not be eaten. (1.18.32)

And he who avoids all [food], yet eats everything, who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) but has been expelled from his community (nirākṛti), and who is the husband of a Śūdra woman (vṛṣalīpati). || 1.18.33 ||

He who excludes everyone from food and does not eat anywhere himself, nor feeds anyone else; and he who eats the food of all, that is, the food of everyone—even these two are persons whose food must not be eaten. The word "learned in the Vedas" (*śrotriya*) applies as a supplement to both cases, meaning that even if one is learned in the Vedas, his food is still not to be eaten. "One who has been expelled" (*nirākṛti*) means one who has ceased Vedic study; others say it refers to one who has abandoned his religious vows (*nirvrata*). He too is one whose food must not be eaten. "The husband of a *vṛṣalī*": in the case of a marriage in the prescribed order, he whose *vṛṣalī* wife lives while the other wives have died is the "husband of a *vṛṣalī*. Even if such a person is learned in the Vedas, his food is not to be eaten. (1.18.33)
Thus ends the eighteenth section:
one who is intoxicated, insane, bound, blind, or sitting in protest, as well as one who causes another to sit in protest, [is exempt] for that duration of time. 1.19.1.

*Matto* means one who has reached a state of transformation through the consumption of intoxicants; *unmattaḥ* means one who is deluded; *baddhaḥ* means one who is shackled; *aṇikaḥ* refers to one who learns from his son, which is censured in the scriptures as being a "son-teacher" (*putrācārya*). *Pratyupaviṣṭaḥ* is one who, for reasons such as a debt, sits down beside a debtor after having obstructed him; whereas the *pratyupaveśayitā* is one who, not providing relief to that person, sits with him at will for a very long time. These individuals, beginning with the intoxicated, are those whose food is not to be eaten for as long as the state of intoxication and so forth persists. Another says: *aṇikaḥ* means a debtor, the giver of a debt; this is an epithet of the one who sits in opposition (*pratyupaveṣṭṛ*).
Who is the one who has eaten? 1.19.2.

"If these are persons whose food is not to be eaten, who then is one whose food may be eaten, and whose food is fit to be consumed? Although it is understood that if these are said to be those whose food is not to be eaten, the remainder are those whose food is to be eaten, nevertheless, this introduction by way of a question is for the purpose of presenting various opinions. 1.19.2.
"One who should desire [this]," so says Kaṇva. 1.19.3.
The sage Kaṇva maintains that whoever makes a request may eat from that [vessel], with the exception of what is forbidden. 1.19.3.
"It is merit," says Kautsa. 1.19.4.

Since it has been stated, "Of all castes abiding in their own duty" (ĀpDh 1.18.13), all those who are meritorious have food that may be eaten. However, the mention of "meritorious" here is for the sake of emphasizing excellence. Kautsa maintains that one who is endowed with austerity, burnt offerings, recitations, and his own duty is "meritorious"; according to Kautsa's view, such a person has food that may be eaten even if he does not himself solicit it. 1.19.4.
"Whoever may give [it]," says Vārṣyāyaṇi. 1.19.5.
"Whoever is constantly disposed toward giving, whether he be meritorious or demeritorious, his food may be eaten," said Vārṣyāyaṇi. And so too Manu says:
"The food of a liberal man is purified by faith; that of another is destroyed by a lack of faith.

The justification for this is as follows: if the dust [of sin] residing in a person is stationary, it must be experienced; however, if it is mobile, one becomes free from fault through giving. 1.19.6.

*rajas* is evil. If that [evil] residing in the person who committed the act remains stationary—that is, stable—and does not perish without [the recipient] experiencing its fruit, then even when it is transferred through acceptance, it must be experienced by the recipient because there is no transition [of the karma itself]. However, if it is mobile and perishes even without being experienced, then, since evil does not remain for even a moment in one whose nature is constant giving, how could there be any fault in the recipient?
Pure alms should be eaten; likewise, Ekakuṇika, Kāṇva, Kutsa, and Puṣkarasādi [did so]. || 1.19.7 ||

"Alms obtained by one who is righteous and diligent are pure; they may be eaten"—this is the position of the group beginning with Ekata. Puṣkarasādi’s son is Pauṣkarasādi. The absence of *vṛddhi* in the first syllable is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). 1.19.7.
The Vārṣyāyaṇīya [recension] contains everything. 1.19.8.

"Sarvatopeta" means endowed with everything. This is a grammatical quality derived from the Vedic *chandasa*. "Upeta" means obtained without being asked for. According to the opinion of Vārṣyāyaṇi, that food which is obtained in this way may be eaten even if it comes from everyone. 1.19.8.
Now he states his own view:
"One who desires merit must enjoy [the fruit]. (1.19.9)
The combined positions of Kaṇva and Kautsa constitute the position of the Teacher. 1.19.9.
Even merit should not be enjoyed if it is not desired. 1.19.10.

He who, even when requested, repeatedly says "no," and only with great difficulty has his desire fulfilled, is said to be one who does not desire [the gift]. The food of such a person is also unfit to be eaten. Another explains: "anīpsataḥ" is a genitive in the sense of the agent; thus, the food of such a person is not to be eaten, provided that while begging, he himself does not desire it due to prior enmity or similar reasons. (1.19.10)
One should eat whatever is obtained from wherever it may come. 1.19.11.
That which was stated as "endowed with everything" (sarvatopeta) is repeated here for the purpose of specifying particular details. 1.19.11.
Hārīta says that this [permission] must be preceded by a formal injunction from another. 1.19.12.

"Today I shall bring this for you; therefore, it should be accepted by your honor"—this is *niyoga* (a formal request). The absence of that is *aniyoga*. There is again a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). Two negatives convey the original meaning: *ananiyoga* is *niyoga*. If that [food] was previously offered, it is not to be eaten. 1.19.12.

Now they cite two verses from the Purāṇa: "Prajāpati considered alms that are being offered, brought forth, and not previously announced as fit to be eaten even from one who has committed evil deeds."
Neither do his ancestors eat for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, he who harbors malice toward her.
Thus [ends the section]. 1.19.13.
Moreover, in the Purāṇa it is said: "Cosmic creation, secondary creation, genealogies,
the periods of the Manus, and the accounts of dynasties— this is the Purāṇa characterized by five features."

In such circumstances, regarding food that is about to be given and so forth—food that is held up and supported by both hands, brought [to the door] by the giver himself, or previously announced—even from one who has committed a transgression, Manu Prajāpati considered it fit to be eaten. This is because, as seen in the case of Dakṣa, "Manu is Prajāpati in whom [the law resides]. But for him who treats such food with contempt and rejects it, his ancestors do not eat the *kavya* (offerings to the manes) for ten and five years; and Agni likewise does not carry the *havya* (offerings to the gods) for that same duration. This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to censure the rejecter. (1.19.13)
The food of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a snarer, an unchaste woman, and a eunuch—these are not to be eaten. 1.19.14.

A *cikitsaka* is one who makes his living as a physician. A *mṛgayu* is a hunter, a killer of wild animals. A *śalyakṛnta* is an *ambaṣṭha*, a cutter of tumors and the like with a surgical instrument. A *pāśī* is one who possesses snares; he is a catcher of deer and other animals by means of a net. A *kulaṭā* is a woman who wanders among families, that is, an unchaste woman. A *ṣaṇḍaka* is a third gender (a eunuch). The food of these—beginning with the physician—is not to be eaten (*anādyam*). The repetition of the physician and the eunuch is for the purpose of prohibiting them even when they are [otherwise] prepared to eat. If that were so, then their inclusion in the previous [list] would have been impossible. In that case, this prohibition belongs to the author of the Sūtra, while this [present verse] is an ancient śloka; thus there is no redundancy. (1.19.14)
Moreover, they cite this:

"The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the eater of food; the innocent man is defamed by one who falsely accuses him; a thief is released by the king, and he who utters falsehood brings about a mixture of sin. (1.19.15)

One who has studied the Veda together with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is a *bhrūṇa*; he who has killed such a person is a *bhrūṇahan*. He "smears" or defiles the eater of food. What [does he smear]? From the context, it is understood that it is "sin" (*enas*). The sin of the killer of a *bhrūṇa* transfers to him who eats his food. Therefore, even if it is offered, his food is not to be eaten. This completes the section consistent with the context. The other [verse] was recited while an ancient verse (*purāṇaśloka*) was being read: "He who falsely accuses one who is sinless, saying 'This was done by you,' smears that sin upon the one he accuses. But Manu says:

By saying "he has fallen" regarding one who has not fallen, or again, by calling a thief a "thief," one incurs an equal fault through such speech; if it is false, one becomes a partaker of double the fault.

Thus he states the doubling [of the penance]. That is to be understood as applying to repeated practice; for he will say later, "The thief with disheveled hair" (ĀpDh 1.25.4). This very point constitutes the meaning of the third quarter [of the verse]. There is no tautology because the agents differ. *Saṅgara* means a promise or a vow, as in the expression *satyasaṅgara* ("one whose promise is true"). He who, having promised, does not give, is one whose promise is false (*anṛtasaṅgara*). The letter *k* is a Vedic archaism. By begging from such a person, one transfers the sin to oneself. Therefore, what has been promised must be given. 1.19.15.
Thus ends the nineteenth section;
thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Ujjvalā*, the commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
One should not practice the teachings by placing worldly interests ahead of them. 1.20.1
One should not practice the teachings by placing before oneself, or having in mind, this worldly aim or purpose known in the world, which consists of fame, gain, and honor. 1.21.1
What is the reason?
For they become fruitless in the case of prosperity. || 1.20.2 ||

For indeed, when dharmas are performed in this manner, they become fruitless at the time of the result, which is worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). For he practices dharma for the sake of the world, not out of faith that "it must be done"; and without faith, dharma does not accomplish its fruit, according to such scriptural passages as, "He who indeed lacks the undertaking of faith" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.6.8). || 1.20.2 ||
Should that which has visible fruit now be abandoned? No, he says.

Just as when a mango tree is planted for the sake of its fruit, shade and fragrance arise as secondary benefits; so too, while practicing the Dharma, worldly advantages arise as secondary benefits. 1.20.3

The word *tad* (that) is used here to introduce the statement. For an *āmra* tree is planted—that is, established—for the sake of its fruit. When that tree has been planted for the sake of the fruit, shade and fragrance arise as secondary consequences (*anūtpadyete*). In the same way, when one practices righteousness (*dharma*), benefits such as fame and the like arise and are produced as secondary results; they are to be accepted in that very manner, and not as the primary objective. Thus it is said: "Just as water sprinkled for the sake of sugarcane also waters the grasses and creepers, so too a man conducting himself according to the path of righteousness attains fame, desires, and wealth."
Thus [ends the section]. 1.20.3.
If they do not arise, there is no loss of the Dharma. || 1.20.4 ||
Even if wealth does not arise by chance, dharma nevertheless exists; and since that is an independent human goal, what is the use of other things? 1.20.4
Free from envy, he should be difficult to deceive regarding the talk of deceivers, rogues, nihilists, and fools. || 1.20.5 ||

A *kuhakā* is one who is pure in public but acts according to his own whims in private; a *śaṭha* is one who is deceitful and crooked-minded; a *nāstika* is one who denies the existence of life after death; a *bāla* is one devoid of learning. One should not be envious (*asūyu*) regarding their doctrines. Through envy, hatred is indicated; thus, one should not be a hater. Taking them as objects, one should not even harbor hatred toward them. Likewise, one should be difficult to deceive (*duṣpralambha*). "Deception" (*pralambhana*) means misleading or proclaiming false results, as seen in the rule: "The roots *gṛdh* and *vañc* are used in the sense of deceiving" (Pāṇini 1.3.69). To be "difficult to deceive" means to be impossible to mislead or to incite by proclaiming false results. The meaning is that even if one is deceived by the doctrines of the *kuhakā*s and others, one should not fall under their influence. (1.20.5)
He speaks of the possibility of deception:
"We two do not practice dharma and adharma," nor do the gods, gandharvas, or ancestors declare, "This is dharma; this is adharma. (1.20.6)

The form *āvām* is a Vedic (chāndasa) form; in the common language (*bhāṣā*), however, by the rule "and in the dual of the first person in the common language" (Pāṇini 7.2.86), the substitution of *ā* would apply. For if dharma and adharma were embodied beings moving about like cows or tigers, saying "We two are ourselves," or if gods and others possessing superior knowledge were to say "These two are dharma and adharma," then there would be no deception in debates concerning tricksters and the like; but since that is not the case, deception is possible. Furthermore, this should be observed here: dharma and adharma are not within the scope of perception and the other means of knowledge, but are rather to be understood from the eternal and faultless Veda, or in its absence, from the Dharmaśāstras which have that as their source. 1.2.6.6.
But where it is difficult to determine the application of the subject matter, such as in the case of penances and the like, he states the decision:
"That which the noble ones praise when it is being performed is dharma; that which they condemn is adharma. (1.20.7)

The noble ones (*āryāḥ*) are the cultured members of the three *varṇas*. Because of the plural number, there are either four or three; as Manu says: "A council (*parṣad*) consists of four who know the Veda and the Dharma, or even those learned in the three Vedas; whatever it declares shall be the Dharma, or [it may be declared by] a single person who is most excellent in the knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātma*). (YDh 1.9)
Thus [ends the section]. 1.20.7.
Now, he states that even when the Vedas and the Smṛtis are not directly perceived, Dharma is to be practiced by understanding it from the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*):
"The conduct of the Āryas— who are perfectly disciplined, aged, self-possessed, and free from greed— is consistently observed in all regions."
One should cultivate a resemblance in conduct with those who are free from hypocrisy. 1.20.8.

"Properly trained" means endowed with discipline (*vinaya*) according to such rules as "he should be dependent upon his teacher" (ĀpDh 1.2.19). "Elderly" means those whose age is mature; this was stated because even in youth one might fall under the sway of sensual objects. "Self-possessed" means those who have conquered their senses. "Free from greed" means not being miserly. "Not hypocritical" means not bearing the banner of unrighteousness (*adharmadhvaja*), and being consistent in conduct whether in solitude or in public. One should adopt the conduct—that is, the practice and observance—which is unanimously and invariably agreed upon by such noble persons (*ārya*) throughout all regions; it is not restricted to a limited area like the marriage of a maternal uncle's daughter and so forth. One should act in conformity with that. Their practice is not without foundation, for there exists the experience of Vedic Brāhmaṇas whose recensions (*pāṭha*) have been lost. (1.20.8)
In this way, one conquers both worlds. 1.20.9.
Thus, performing the practice rooted in the Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous, one conquers both worlds—this one and the next. 1.20.9.
Trade is not prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa. 1.20.10.

Trade, consisting of the business of buying and selling, is not prescribed as a livelihood for a Brāhmaṇa when performed by himself; this is a restatement of what is already established, intended to introduce an exception. (1.20.10)
In times of distress, he may engage in trade, avoiding those goods that are forbidden for sale.

The non-availability of the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa constitutes an emergency; when that exists, there is [permission for] trade goods. The genitive case is used in the sense of the object according to Pāṇini 2.3.57, *vyavahṛ-paṇoḥ samarthayoḥ*. He should engage in trade; "trade" (*vyavahāra*) consists of both buying and selling, meaning he may purchase and sell trade goods. He does so while excluding—that is, avoiding—those items which are not to be traded, as will be mentioned later. This is an illustration of the entire livelihood of a Vaiśya. And by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*), the livelihood of a Kṣatriya is thereby established. Thus says Gautama: "In the absence of that, the livelihood of a Kṣatriya; in the absence of that, the livelihood of a Vaiśya" (GDh 7.6–7). 1.20.11.
He states the items that are not for sale:
human beings, liquids, dyes, perfumes, food, hides, a cow that has recently calved, phlegm, water, young sprouts, fermenting agent, ants, black pepper, and grain.
Flesh, weapons, and hope for good deeds. || 1.20.12 ||

"Human beings" refers to slaves and the like. "Flavors" (*rasa*) refers to molasses, salt, and so forth, or milk and the like. "Dyes" (*rāga*)—so called because one is colored by them (*rajate ’nena*)—or things that are themselves colored (*rajyante*), such as cloth and the like; these include safflower and other such substances. "Fragrances" (*gandha*) refer to sandalwood and the like. A "barren cow" (*vaśā*) is a cow among cattle that does not bear calves. "Glue" (*śleṣman*) refers to lac and similar substances, by which separated items such as leather are joined together. As it is seen in the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*: "One should join together with glue a piece of leather, or something else that is separated. "Sprouts" (*tokmāni*) are rice and other grains that have slightly germinated. "Ferment" (*kiṇva*) is the substance that serves as the base for liquor. "Good deed" (*sukṛta*) is merit; its fruit is the "hope for a good deed" (*sukṛtāśā*). The remaining terms are well known. Having excluded these non-saleable items, one may trade in other commodities. Although the phrase "having excluded human beings and the like" would have sufficed, the explicit mention of "non-saleable items" is intended to exclude other things designated as non-saleable in other Smṛtis. Regarding this, Manu says: [text follows].
One should exclude all liquids, prepared food along with sesame seeds,
stones, salt, domestic animals, and human beings.
And all woven cloth, whether dyed or even if undyed— including hemp, linen, and wool—
as well as fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs.
Water, weapons, poison, meat, soma, and all types of perfumes;
milk, alkaline substances, curd, clarified butter, oil, honey, molasses, and kusha grass.
"All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and all one-hoofed animals" (MDh 10.86–89). || 1.20.12 ||
But one should especially not sell sesame seeds or rice among the various grains. 1.20.13.

Among grains, one should especially and emphatically not sell sesame seeds and rice; one must not sell them. There is an option regarding other grains. This prohibition does not apply to those produced by oneself. For it is heard in the *Mānava* (Manusmṛti):
"A farmer, having himself cultivated them through agriculture, may at his pleasure sell pure sesame seeds for the sake of dharma, provided they have not been kept for long" (MDh 10.90).
Thus [ends the section]. 1.20.13.
And their mutual exchange is not prescribed. || 1.20.14 ||
Exchange is barter; for those items whose sale is prohibited, even their mutual exchange with one another is not permitted—that is, it is prohibited—and should not be performed. || 1.20.14 ||
Among those very [beings], a restriction is also permitted for some:
food with food, humans with humans, juices with juices, fragrances with fragrances, and knowledge with knowledge. (1.20.15)

The meaning is that there is indeed an exchange between items beginning with food and ending with knowledge. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Liquids may be exchanged for liquids, whether they are equal or inferior... sesame, rice, cooked food, knowledge, and human beings are prescribed for barter" (VaDh 2.32, 39). However, there is a specific rule in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]:
"Liquids may be bartered for liquids, but salt must never be bartered for liquids;
prepared food for unprepared food; and sesame for grain in equal amounts" (MDh 10.94).

In the Gautama-smṛti, however, it says: "But there is a restriction: [the exchange] of liquids for liquids, and of animals for animals; but not of salt for cooked food. However, in the case of cooked food, [exchange may occur] with something of equal or unequal value" (GDh 7.16–21). Therefore, one should not suspect that the prohibition [of bartering knowledge] continues to apply here. Furthermore, it was stated previously: "When Brahmins employ their [knowledge] among themselves, no [other] means of livelihood exists" (ĀpDh 1.16.17). It should be understood that the sale of sciences is prohibited precisely because of this permission regarding restricted exchange. 1.20.15
He shall engage in trade with goods that have not been purchased for resale.
He should trade in those commodities which are not purchased, but are either produced by himself or brought from the forest. || 1.20.16 ||
Thus ends the twentieth section: [one may subsist] on muñja grass, balvaja grass, roots, and fruits. 1.21.1.
Muñja and balvaja are specific types of grass. 1.21.1.
With grass and wood that have not been altered. || 1.21.2 ||

The modification of grasses is their state as ropes and the like; the modification of wood is their state as pillars and the like. Although [the state of being a modification] is already established by the fact of being grass, the mention of *muñja* and *balvaja* grasses is for the sake of illustrating the specific types of modifications. 1.21.2.
One should not settle into extreme attachment. || 1.21.3 ||

Even if forbidden items are involved, he may subsist by selling or bartering them, but he must not settle into such a practice excessively, lest he perish. Thus says Gautama: "In every way, however, if one is unable to subsist otherwise, one may do so provided it is not through the work of a Śūdra; even that, some say, is permissible when there is danger to life" (GDh 7.22–23). Manu also says:
"He who, having fallen into a situation where his life is at stake, eats food from whatever source it may come, is not tainted by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud" (MDh 10.104).
Thus [ends the section]. 1.21.3.
Having obtained a livelihood, he should desist [from further worldly activity]. 1.21.4.
The [section] is concluded. 1.21.4.
No social interaction exists with those who have fallen [from their status]. || 1.21.5 ||
"Outcasts" refers to thieves and others who will be mentioned hereafter; one must not engage in any transaction with them. Regarding this, Manu says:
"One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or marriage, but not through traveling, sitting, or eating together. (MDh 11.181)
Through [the use of] vehicles and the like, one falls after a year; however, through officiating at sacrifices and the like, one falls immediately. || 1.21.5 ||
Likewise, [one should not eat] from improper vessels. 1.21.6.
Those who are "excluded from the company" (apapātra) include Caṇḍālas and others; one must not engage in social or commercial dealings with them. 1.21.6.
Now, the transgressions leading to loss of caste. 1.21.7.
Falling away from the duties of the twice-born is degradation; the actions that cause this shall now be described. 1.21.6.

Theft, false accusation, murder of a man, abandoning a Veda-student, causing an abortion, sexual intercourse with the mother, the father, or other relatives by birth—including their offspring—and sexual intercourse with a woman, drinking liquor, and forbidden sexual union. 1.21.8.

Theft (*steya*) is the stealing of gold. Calumny (*ābhiśastya*) is the killing of a Brāhmaṇa; for it will be stated later that one who kills even a mere Brāhmaṇa is "accused" (*abhiśasta*). Killing a person (*puruṣavadha*) is the killing of one belonging to the human species; by this, the killing of a woman is also included. Abandoning the Veda (*brahmojjha*): *ujjha* means abandonment (*utsarga*), with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*); the change of gender is Vedic. "Veda" (*brahman*) refers to the sacred knowledge; the destruction of that which has been studied is "abandoning the Veda. Causing an abortion (*garbhaśātanam*) is the destruction of the fetus through the administration of medicines and the like. Sexual intercourse with female relatives of the mother—such as a maternal aunt (*mātṛṣvasṛ*) and others—or with female relatives of the father—such as a paternal aunt (*pitṛṣvasṛ*) and others—together with their offspring: this means sexual intercourse with a maternal aunt, a paternal aunt, their daughters, and the daughter of a maternal uncle (*mātulasutā*).
"Surā is to be known as threefold: that distilled from molasses (gauḍī), that from honey (mādhvī), and that from flour (paiṣṭī).

Just as one [type] is not to be drunk, so all are [forbidden] by the best of the twice-born. Thus, according to the *Mānava*, "drinking surā" (surāpāna) is the drinking of that surā which is prohibited. "Those unfit for association" (asaṃyogāḥ) refers to those such as those born of inverse unions (pratiloma) who are unworthy of association; association with them, such as living in the same house, is "association with the unfit" (asaṃyogasamyoga). These are the causes of falling (patanīyāni). 1.21.8.
Having approached the wife of a teacher, the friend of a teacher, and others who are the wives of others; || 1.21.9 ||

The short vowel in the word *sakhī* is a Vedic (chāndasa) anomaly. A "guru-sakhī" is a friend of one's mother and others; a "guru-sakhī" is a friend of one's father and others. Having gone to her—what follows?—"he falls," as is heard later in the text. And having gone to other [women], namely the wives of others (*paratalpa*), he falls. By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is indicated. 1.21.9.
Some say that one does not fall [into hell] for violating the bed of a Guru. 1.21.10.

Some maintain that there is no loss of caste (*pātitya*) in approaching another man’s wife, provided it is not the wife of one's teacher; for although they are generally declared to be causes of falling, the relative gravity or lightness of the offense must be considered when determining the expiation. (1.21.10)
But the practice of unrighteousness is constant. || 1.21.11 ||
The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "and. The constant practice of unrighteous acts other than those already mentioned is also a cause for falling [from one's status]. 1.21.11.
Now, the things that cause impurity. 1.21.12.
They are called "impurity-producing" because they make a person impure; those actions will now be described. 1.21.12
Sexual intercourse with Śūdra women by noble (Ārya) women. 1.21.13.
Sexual intercourse with a Śūdra woman causes impurity for women of the three higher castes.
The eating of forbidden meat. 1.21.14.
The consumption of the flesh of those animals whose meat is forbidden causes impurity. 1.21.14.
An example of this is as follows: [the meat] of a dog, of a human, and of domestic fowl and pigs, and of carnivorous beasts. (1.21.15)

Because of the mention of "village-dwellers" (*grāmyāṇām*), there is no prohibition regarding those that dwell in the forest (*āraṇyānām*). *Adaḥ* means "eating" (*adanam*); the suffix *asun* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Those whose eating has raw flesh (*kravya*) as its object are *kravyādasaḥ*—vultures and the like, whose livelihood consists solely of meat. (1.21.15)
The consumption of the urine and excrement of human beings. 1.21.16.
The mention of urine and feces is also an elliptical indication for semen. 1.21.16
The eating of the leavings of a Śūdra and the acceptance of food from unworthy persons by Āryas [are forbidden]. 1.21.17.

Eating the remnants of a Śūdra causes impurity for the noble ones of the three higher castes; likewise, those who are excluded from the vessels [of the twice-born]—namely, those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) and women—and sexual intercourse with them. 1.21.17.
Some say that these also are causes for expulsion. 1.21.18.
Some maintain that those acts which have been enumerated as causing impurity are also causes for loss of caste (*patanīya*). 1.21.18.
Therefore, other [types of food] are defective and cause impurity. || 1.21.19 ||
Actions other than those mentioned, such as improper acceptance of gifts, violence, and so forth, which are defective, become causes of impurity. 1.21.19.
Having recognized a fault, one who was previously [pure] should not proclaim it to others regarding one who has fallen;
rather, he should avoid him in matters of dharma. 1.21.20.

Having learned of a transgressor’s fault that is unknown to others, one should not be the first to report it to them. Even if one knows it oneself while it remains unknown to others, one should not announce it to others beforehand; rather, one should personally exclude him from religious duties so that others do not find out. Otherwise, one becomes a transgressor. (1.21.20)
Thus ends the twenty-first section;
thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Ujjvalā*, the commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
One should practice internal yogas that are consistent with reason and free from worldly attachment. || 1.22.1 ||

The acts that cause one to fall from caste and those that cause impurity have been described. Now, intending to state the expiations for them, [the author] first introduces self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) and the yogas conducive to it, because that knowledge itself is the primary expiation due to its power to remove all sins. For it is heard in scripture:
"The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed, and his karmas are exhausted when He, who is both the higher and the lower, is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
“And just as a tuft of *iṣīkā* grass thrown into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed” (ChU 5.24.3). Yājñavalkya also said:
“Of the acts of sacrifice, ritual conduct, self-control, non-violence, charity, and Vedic study, this indeed is the supreme dharma: that one perceives the Self through yoga” (YDh 1.8).

"Internal states" (*adhyātmabhāvān*) means internal (*adhyātmikān*). The absence of *vṛddhi* (the lengthening of the vowel) is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). One should practice—that is, cultivate—the methods (*upāyān*) such as non-anger and so forth, which will be described below, which cause one to attain the self, which are the causes for the concentration of the mind, which are consistent with reason (*nyāyasaṃhitān*), and endowed with logical justification (*upapattisamanvitān*). For these are logically established for the purpose of destroying defects such as anger. "Distracted" (*naiścārikān*) means that "distraction" (*niścāraḥ*) is the outward scattering of the mind; those factors such as anger to be described below which lead to that are "distracting," and [these methods] are their opposites. When non-anger and the others are present, the mind, by nature not wandering outward, remains steady, focused on an internal object. Therefore, one should practice them; that is, in order to attain the self, one should effect the concentration of the mind characterized by non-anger and the rest. 1.22.1.
But is the Self to be attained through effort? "Yes," he said. "There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self. 1.22.2

There is no other gain superior to the attainment of the Self; therefore, one should apply effort for its realization. But what is this Self? It is the inner self (*pratyagātman*). Now, is it not already eternally attained? For surely it cannot be unattained by itself. True; however, due to contact with *prakṛti*, it has assumed the qualities of that [nature] and thus becomes, as it were, one whose true nature is lost. For the *puruṣa* is eternally connected with *prakṛti*. And that connection is such that their mutual distinction is not known. The attributes of one are superimposed upon the other, just as when milk and water are mixed, one does not know "this much is milk" and "this much is water," nor "in this space is the milk" and "in this space is the water. Or, as when fire and an iron ball are joined, those attributes of fire such as heat and luminosity are superimposed on the iron ball, and those attributes of the iron ball such as hardness and length are superimposed on the fire. Thus, the perception there is: "one single object is hot, luminous, long, and hard. Similarly here too, the attributes of the *puruṣa* such as consciousness are superimposed on *prakṛti*, and the attributes of *prakṛti* such as the transformations of pleasure, pain, and delusion are superimposed on the *puruṣa*. Consequently, the worldly usage arises: "one single entity is conscious, a mass of pleasure and so forth, and subject to transformation. In reality, however, within that aggregate, the unconscious part is what transforms, while the conscious part merely follows along with it. In whatever form it transforms, it undergoes an identification with that form. Just as ghee existing in the state of milk enters even that state when the milk transforms into the form of curds, so it is here as well. This is expressed in the text: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6). Even in the act of creation, the agency of the Self is precisely this: being the instrumental cause by way of being the enjoyer. Thus, although the Self is by nature pure, having attained non-difference from *prakṛti*, it comes to possess its attributes. In this same manner, through its modifications—beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), then the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and so on down to the body—it should be understood that [the Self identifies]: "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am a god," "I am a human," "I am an animal. For one who has come to such a state, the recovery of his true nature is required, like that of a prince raised among low-born people. For example: one who has been brought up since childhood by hunters and others among their own children, perceiving himself as belonging to that species, becomes as if he has recovered his true nature when his mother tells him who he really is. Likewise, the Self, led to a different state of being by the inevitable *prakṛti*, is led back to its true nature by the Śruti—"That thou art"—which stands in the place of a mother: "That which is such a pure reality, that indeed you are; it is not as you think, namely 'I am a human,' 'I am suffering,' and so forth. It is just as when a prince is told, "You are that king. Now, one might object: "In 'That thou art,' identity with Brahman is being stated. Who says "no"? Brahman is not other than the Self. Furthermore, is this Self one, or is it manifold? What is the use of knowing this? You yourself are of such a nature—a single essence of consciousness, eternally pure, which has become as if sullied through contact with impurity; liberation is your separation from that. If, once you are liberated, others still exist, they will continue to transmigrate; what loss is that to you? Or if they do not exist, even then what gain is that to you? Enough of this; this is a great discourse. On this point, there are these verses: [The verses follow.]
Having grown up for a long time in the dwelling of the low-born together with their sons,
the prince comes to regard even himself as belonging to that same class;
likewise, the Puruṣa, dwelling in the aggregate together with Mahat and the other principles, [regards itself as one with them].
Fie upon him who falsely considers his own self to be defiled by pleasure, pain, and delusion!
Having heard from the mouth of his mother exactly as it was— that "You are that very king who was a donor devoted to enjoyment, possessed of complete wealth, and the punisher of evildoers"—
the man, having become a king, strives for that which is indeed according to reality; so too is the person awakened.
Having heard "That thou art," and having cast off all evil, one becomes Brahman itself.
Thus, even though many princes have reached such a state,
they do not suddenly abandon their mutual distinctions and all attain oneness;
rather, they remain separate and distinct in their own supreme abodes.
If they are called "knowers of the field" (kṣetrajña) based on the primordial statement regarding reality, what harm is there to the doctrine of difference?
If even one among them should ever attain his own sovereignty through his mother’s word, what harm is there to him, since others remain in a different state?
Or, if the others were not to exist at all, what would be the loss to him? His course of action remains the same.
We do not insistently determine the identity or the difference of men as such.

Therefore, the knowledge of the Self required here is being taught. And that is threefold: hearing (*śruta*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*dhyāna*), according to the scriptural injunction: "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5). Among these, *śruta* is the knowledge produced by words such as those of the Upaniṣads. *Manana* is the investigation through logical reasoning. When the Self has thus been heard and reflected upon, *dhyāna* is the uninterrupted contemplation with an undistracted mind, which is the cause of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). || 1.22.2 ||
To establish that [goal], he first states the knowledge derived from the Vedas.
In this regard, we shall cite the verses concerning the attainment of the Self. 1.22.3.

The word *tatra* is used here as an introductory phrase. *Ātmalābhīyān* means those whose purpose is the attainment of the Self; the suffix *śa* is applied according to its appearance in rules such as *anupravacana*. We shall cite—that is, having extracted—we shall set down in this work the verses (*ślokas*), which are composed in metrical feet, that belong to the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣad-mantras*). || 1.22.3 ||
All living beings are indeed cities of the one who dwells in the cave, who is never slain and is free from blemish.
Those who attend upon Him, whose abode is the moving [world] yet who is immovable, they become immortal. (1.22.4)
It conceals that which is known as primordial nature (*prakṛti*);
that which is remembered as the cause, the immeasurable Brahman, the primary matter (*pradhāna*), nature (*prakṛti*), the source of birth (*prasūti*).
It is the self (*ātman*), the cave, the womb, the beginningless and endless field (*kṣetra*), and likewise the immortal and the imperishable (*akṣara*).

This is because it is seen thus in the Purāṇa: "The Self is said to 'lie in the cave' (guhāśaya) because He lies within it, remaining in a state of non-separation from it. "The one unborn [Self] lies down by the side of the one unborn [Prakṛti]—who is red, white, and black, who gives birth to many offspring of similar form; while another unborn [Self] abandons her after she has been enjoyed. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5)

And there is another mantra: "Of the one who is not slain," for he is not slain even when the body is slain; thus it has been said by the Blessed One: "It is not slain when the body is slain" (BhG 2.20). "Of the stainless one," that is, the one free from taint; for all qualities such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) belong to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), while they are merely superimposed upon the Self (*ātman*). For such a Self, all living beings—from Brahmā down to the animals—possessing vital breaths and the like, are "cities" (*pūḥ*), meaning bodies that are places of experience. Just as a king, dwelling in a city, enjoys pleasures brought to him by his ministers, so too this [Self], dwelling in the bodies of gods and others, enjoys the pleasures presented by the instruments of perception. Those who attend to—that is, worship—Him who is thus described, who is immovable because He is omnipresent, yet whose abode is moving; "abode" (*niketa*) means place, namely the body, and He whose abode is moving—those who realize, "I am of such a nature," they become immortal, that is, liberated. (1.22.4)

Therefore, he says that this [Self] is to be worshipped by means of abandoning attachment to sense objects: "Whatever is called 'this' or 'that' in the world—that object—having shaken off this, the wise man should practice [meditation upon] that which dwells in the cave. (1.22.5)

In the phrase "yad idam viṣayam etat," the change of gender everywhere is Vedic; likewise, the letter *da* replaces the *ta* of the word *iti*. The word *iti* denotes well-known fact (*prasiddhi*), while the word *ha* denotes wonder (*āścarya*). By the repetition of the word *iti*, the internal distinctions among the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, are set forth. For those whose minds are carried away by sense-objects say: "Such indeed was her song," "Such indeed was her pleasant touch," "Such indeed was her form, like refined gold," "Such indeed was her most delicious lip-jewel," and "Such indeed was her fragrance, satisfying to the nose. In this way, the distinction between divine and human [objects] is also to be understood. Here, another word *iti* is to be supplied immediately after: "iti ha iti ha"—that which is called an object in the world. The singular number is used with reference to the generality. Having shaken off this [object], the wise and intelligent man should abide in that which dwells in the cave (the heart). 1.22.5.
He states the reason for abandoning sense objects:
"Having not found this welfare even within myself, practice what is beneficial and not what is harmful;
then I shall seek among others the station of the virtuous with total detachment."
The great body of splendor, the Lord established everywhere.

This is the teacher’s address to the disciple. There are two reasons for abandoning sense-objects here: their dependence on others and their harmful nature. [The disciple says: "I did not perceive that Great One—who is great by virtue of his qualities, whose body is of splendor, a mass of radiance, self-luminous—as described in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: 'The Self, O King, is the light of the sun' (6.3.2); who is established everywhere, all-pervading, the Lord, independent; who dwells in the cave [of the heart] in such a manner. For so long, O Self (*ātman*)—here the singular ending of the locative case is elided—I, having failed to obtain Him within this my own aggregate (*saṃghāta*) without depending on anything else, sought Him among other things, such as the senses, toward each respective object (*viṣaya*). [The present tense is used in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*): I was seeking Him. But now, having obtained Him, I am no longer such [as I was before]. You too should resort to this very beneficial, virtuous station, the path of the good, and not to what is harmful—the pursuit of sense-objects. (1.22.6)
Furthermore, he describes what that [Self] is like:
"He who is eternal among all beings, wise, immortal, and firm;
bodiless, soundless, formless, and intangible; great and pure."
He is the all, the ultimate limit; he is indeed the equinox, and he is the city of Vaibhājana.

Among all beings—the multitudes beginning with humans—that which is eternal and does not perish even when they perish; which is wise (*vipaścit*), intelligent (*medhāvī*), and of the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*); which is immortal (*amṛta*) because, being eternal, its very nature is deathlessness; which is fixed (*dhruva*), uniform, and free from modification—meaning that its eternity is not merely as a substrate of change like the *pradhāna*, but as its own essential nature; which is bodiless (*anaṅga*), devoid of limbs such as hands and feet; which is without sound and without touch (this being an illustration for the qualities of the elements), meaning it is devoid of qualities such as sound; which is without a body, being even free from the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*); which is great (*mahān*) and pure (*śuci*)—where "greatness" qualifies purity, meaning it is absolutely pure in the ultimate sense; it is "all" by way of non-difference from primordial nature (*prakṛti*). And it alone is the supreme goal (*paramā kāṣṭhā*), because there is nothing further to be reached beyond it. It is the "equinoctial" (*vaiṣuvatam*): the day called the *viṣuvān* occurs in the middle of the *gavāmayana* sacrifice, as seen in the text: "They approach this twenty-first day... the *viṣuvān* in the middle of the year. The *viṣuvān* itself is the *vaiṣuvatam*. Just as that occurs in the middle of the year, so does this [Self] occur in the middle of the limbs. For the *Bahvṛca-brāhmaṇa* says: "For he is the middle, the Self of the limbs. It is the city of Vaibhājana: *vibhājana* means that which is to be enjoyed through various paths; that itself is *vaibhājanam*. [The suffix -aṇ is applied according to the rules for] *prajādi* and *anuśatikādi*. Just as a prosperous city is to be reached by all seekers, so too is this [Self]. 1.22.7.
Whoever should practice that in every respect and always act in accordance with it—being disciplined, he who perceives that which is subtle and difficult to see shall rejoice in the world. (1.22.7)

Whoever would thus practice—that is, worship—such a Self; whoever would always act with complete conformity toward Him in all places and in all conditions, conformity consisting of the avoidance of what is prohibited and the performance of obligatory and occasional duties; and whoever, becoming disciplined and concentrated, should behold this one who is difficult to see, subtle, and profound, and realize Him directly—he rejoices in the world free from suffering, established in his own glory, devoid of all misery; or, even while in the state of transmigratory existence, he experiences his own unsurpassed bliss which was previously concealed. || 1.22.7 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second section:
Seeing all beings within the Self, the wise sage who reflects shall not be deluded;
he who sees the Self everywhere is indeed Brahman.
He shines resplendently upon the vault of heaven.

Seeing all beings as subservient to the Self within the Self—knowing this through the Upaniṣads and other scriptures, and subsequently reflecting upon it and determining it through reasoning—he who does not become deluded, who does not fall into confusion in the interim, being wise and intelligent, and who thereafter perceives the Self as subsisting everywhere as the presiding Lord and realizes It directly, he indeed is a Brāhmaṇa, a knower of Brahman; established in his own glory, which is like the vault of heaven, he shines forth and is self-luminous. 1.23.1.
Subtler than a lotus fiber, he who stands pervading all;
greater than the earth, he is the eternal one, encompassing all.
Having begun, he remains;
through his senses, he is the Supreme Lord who distinguishes this world from knowledge, from one another, and from the object of knowledge.
From him all bodies originate;
together with their root, he is eternal and constant. || 1.23.2 ||

He is skillful and wise, whose nature is consciousness (*citsvarūpa*). He is subtler (*aṇīyān*) than even a lotus fiber (*bisorṇā*), that is, more minute than a lotus stalk; he stands pervading everything, remaining as the all-encompassing substrate. And he is greater (*varṣīyān*) than the earth, being more vast because of his omnipresence; having begun with everything, he stands supporting it as its ultimate remainder. He is eternal (*dhruva*), of one uniform nature. From the knowledge of this world—which is born of the senses, being the cognition produced by the sense organs—[he is distinct]. What kind of knowledge? That which is "not other than the object of knowledge" (*jñeyāt*); here the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative. The meaning is: he is different from that objective knowledge which takes the forms of blue, yellow, and so forth, and which is non-different from those objects of knowledge such as blue and yellow. For it is heard in scripture: "Different indeed from this self consisting of consciousness is the inner self consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5).
In ultimate reality, he is the very nature of consciousness, absolutely pure;
yet, due to erroneous perception, he appears to exist in the form of the objects of experience.

Thus says the Purāṇa. The meaning is that the turbidity of blue, yellow, and other forms belonging to the Self—which is by nature pure and of the essence of consciousness—is an illusion caused by the coloring of the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) that takes on those forms. From the qualification "other than empirical knowledge," it is also established that the Self is of the nature of knowledge; for the Śruti declares: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1). Such is that Self, the Parameṣṭhin, who abides in the supreme state, his own essential nature (*svarūpa*). He is connected with the following term *vibhāja*. He is *vibhāj* because he divides himself through entry into various bodies in the form of gods, humans, and so forth; from him, as the cause, all bodies—the physical forms of gods, humans, and others—originate and arise. He is the root, the fundamental cause of the creation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by virtue of being its enjoyer; he is eternal, imperishable, constant, uniform, and changeless. (1.23.2)
In this life, the eradication of the humors (doṣas) is rooted in yoga;
having removed those that burn the elements, the wise man attains security. (1.23.3)

The eradication—the uprooting—of the defects (doṣas) such as anger and the rest, which will be described here in this life, has yoga as its root. The yogas to be described are non-anger and so forth; it has those as its root. And therefore, having cast out those defects such as anger that burn living beings, the wise man—one who has attained knowledge and realized the Self—attains security through the gateway of self-knowledge: security, which is fearlessness and liberation. "O Janaka, you indeed attain fearlessness," as stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (6.2.4). The verses are concluded. 1.13.3.
Now we shall set forth the defects that cause the burning of living beings. 1.23.4.
The burning of beings is *bhūtadāha*; those things conducive to that are *bhūtadāhīya*. The suffix *cha* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.5: "conducive to that. 1.13.4.
Anger, joy, wrath, greed, delusion, hypocrisy, malice, falsehood, gluttony, slander, envy, lust, resentment, lack of self-control, and lack of yoga— their destruction is rooted in yoga. 1.23.5.

Anger (*krodha*) is a disturbance of the internal organ caused by insults and the like, characterized by symptoms such as perspiration and trembling. Joy (*harṣa*) is an exaltation of the mind resulting from the attainment of what is desired, characterized by symptoms such as horripilation. Resentment (*roṣa*) is a slight variety of anger that merely causes mental opposition toward those who are hostile, such as friends. Greed (*lobha*) is attachment to material objects, which even obstructs the expenditure for dharma. Delusion (*moha*) is the lack of discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; although it is generally produced by anger and the other [faults], it is taught separately because it sometimes occurs even in their absence. Deceit (*dambha*) is the cheating of the world by manifesting a semblance of religious piety. Malice (*droha*) is the intent to harm. Falsehood (*mṛṣodya*) is untruthful speech. Gluttony (*atyāśa*) is excessive eating. Slander (*parīvāda*) is the proclaiming of the faults of others. Envy (*asūyā*) is intolerance toward the virtues of others. Desire (*kāma*) is sexual union with women. Resentment (*manyu*) is hidden hatred. Lack of self-control (*anātmya*) is the failure to master the senses, such as verbal fickleness and the like. Non-yoga (*ayoga*) is a distracted state of mind. These are the defects that burn living beings. Their suppression is rooted in yoga. (1.23.5)
What, then, are those disciplines (*yoga*)? He states them:

freedom from anger, freedom from elation, freedom from resentment, freedom from greed, freedom from delusion, freedom from hypocrisy, freedom from malice, truthful speech, moderation in eating, absence of backbiting, absence of envy, sharing with others, renunciation, uprightness, gentleness, tranquility, self-control, non-opposition toward all beings, discipline, nobility, compassion, and contentment—these are the rules of conduct for all stages of life (*āśrama*). By practicing these according to the prescribed rule, one becomes a traveler to all [auspicious] worlds. (1.23.6)

These qualities, beginning with non-anger (*akrodha*), are positive states of being (*bhāvarūpa*) and not merely the absence of anger and so forth, because they are taught as the causes for the eradication of anger and other vices. What, then, are they? Non-anger (*akrodha*) is the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) that "I shall not act" even when anger and the like arise. Non-exultation (*aharṣa*) is the uniformity of the mind (*aikarūpya*) in the gain or loss of desired objects. Non-wrath (*aroṣa*) is the absence of mental agitation even toward those who are hostile, such as friends and others. Non-greed (*alobha*) is contentment, the sense of having enough. Non-delusion (*amoha*) is attentiveness (*avadhāna*). Non-deceit (*adambha*) is the performance of actions for the sake of Dharma. Non-malice (*adroha*) is the absence of injury even toward others who have caused harm. Non-envy (*anasūyā*) is rejoicing in the virtues of others. Truthful speech (*satyavacana*) is speaking of things exactly as they have been perceived. Sharing (*saṃvibhāga*) is the giving of food and other things, even at the cost of restricting oneself. Renunciation (*tyāga*) is non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*). Uprightness (*ārjava*) is the uniformity of mind, speech, and body. Gentleness (*mārdava*) is ease of approachability. Tranquility (*śama*) is the abandonment of resentment (*manyu*). Self-control (*dama*) is the conquest of the senses. Since these two [tranquility and self-control] already encompass them, "absence of desire" (*akāma*), "absence of resentment" (*amanyu*), and "self-possession" (*ātmavattva*) were not taught separately in the previous sequence. Non-opposition to all beings (*sarvabhūtair avirodha*); the inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of ensuring non-opposition even toward the lowly. Yoga (*yoga*) is one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*). Nobility (*ārya*) is the state of the noble ones (*āryāṇāṃ bhāva*), which is the observance of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). Kindness (*ānṛśaṃsa*) is the avoidance of cruelty even when engaged in worldly dealings or speech. Contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is the absence of despondency. Convention (*samaya*) means established rule (*vyavasthā*); and from the context, this refers to the convention of those who know the Dharma. "Object" (*pada*) means the domain (*viṣaya*). The meaning of "the convention of those who know the Dharma" is that these qualities, beginning with non-anger, are to be practiced by members of all stages of life (*āśrama*), not only by yogis. For when these are cultivated, they strike down anger and the rest along with their very roots. Therefore, one who practices these—beginning with non-anger and ending with contentment—in accordance with the prescribed rule (*vidhi*) according to the scriptures, becomes "one who goes to the All" (*sārvagāmī*). This means he goes to and attains the "All," which is the Self (*ātman*), beneficial to all (*sārva*). By the use of the term "according to the rule," there is no fault even in speaking untruth and so forth in cases such as: "In a matter where the lives of living beings are at stake, one may speak an untruth as a witness. 1.23.6.1–6.105 (Note: The provided text corresponds to the commentary on verse 1.23.6).
Thus ends the twenty-third section;
thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Ujjvalā*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra*.
Having killed a Kṣatriya, one must give a thousand cows for the sake of expiating the enmity.
One should give. || 1.24.1 ||

Having killed a Kṣatriya, one should give a thousand cows to Brāhmaṇas. For what purpose? For the sake of expiating enmity (*vairayātanārtham*); *vaira* means sin; its *yātanā* is its removal—this is for that purpose. He will state later: “And in all cases, a bull is additionally required for the sake of expiation” (ĀpDh 1.24.4). Therefore, this gift is in the form of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). And expiation is for the purpose of destroying sin. Why then is it said here to be for the sake of expiating enmity? Some think: “Karma, whether meritorious or non-meritorious, is not destroyed without being experienced”; thus, expiation is merely another occasional rite (*naimittika-karmāntara*), like the *kṣāmavatī* offerings used when a house has caught fire. To refute them, this was stated. It is also stated in the Śrauta ritual: “They serve to destroy defects” (ĀpŚr 9.1.4). Another says: When someone is killed by another, he, while dying, harbors enmity toward him, thinking, “May I indeed kill him in another birth. This gift is for the sake of expiating that enmity. Furthermore, its nature as an expiation is established by what will be stated later. 1.24.1.
One hundred for a Vaiśya. || 1.24.2 ||
If a Vaiśya is killed, one should give a hundred cows.
Ten [times] for a Śūdra. || 1.24.3 ||
When a Śūdra is killed, one should give ten cows; by the context, it is understood that "gā" (cows) is intended. 1.24.3.
And here, the Ṛṣabha is added everywhere for the purpose of expiation. 1.24.4.

In all these cases, a bull must also be given as an additional gift; it is not only cows that are to be given. These three penances have the same scope as those prescribed in the *Mānava* (Manu-smṛti). As it says:
"But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born should give one thousand cows and a bull for the sake of his own purification."
Or, with his hair matted and remaining self-restrained, he shall perform for three years the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa,
dwelling far away from the village and making his abode at the foot of a tree.
The best of the twice-born should perform this very same penance for one year after killing a Vaiśya who is established in his proper conduct;
he should instead give one hundred and one cows.
A killer of a Śūdra shall perform this entire vow for six months,
or he shall give to a Brāhmaṇa ten cows and a bull as the eleventh.
And with regard to women, it is the same for these [cases]. 1.24.5.
In the case of the wives of these [classes], such as Kṣatriyas and others, when they have been killed, the penance is exactly the same as it is for men. 1.24.5.
Having killed one who has studied the Veda among the two higher castes, or one engaged in a Soma sacrifice, he becomes an outcast. || 1.24.6 ||

Among those mentioned, regarding the two preceding castes—the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya—one who has studied the Veda (*vedādhyāya*) is one who has completed his Vedic studies; having killed such a person, one becomes an *abhiśasta* (one accused of a heinous crime). *Abhiśasta* is a designation for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmaghna*). Or, "one engaged in a *savana*" refers to one of those same two castes who is engaged in a *savana*. By the word *savana*, the morning libations (*prātaḥsavana*) and so forth are not meant, nor merely a sacrifice in general. What then? It is the Soma sacrifice. One who is consecrated (*dīkṣita*) therein is "engaged in a *savana*," because of the scriptural observation: "He who is consecrated is indeed born as a Brāhmaṇa. Having killed him as well, one becomes an *abhiśasta*. Why specify "of the two preceding castes"? So that it should not apply to a Brāhmaṇa. However, it is intended to apply to a Brāhmaṇa, and the author will state later: "And even a mere Brāhmaṇa" [ĀpDh 1.24.7]. If that is so, then let it not apply to a Śūdra. A Śūdra is neither one who has studied the Veda nor one engaged in a *savana*. What then is the purpose? It is so that it may apply only to the two preceding castes, and not to their *anuloma* offspring, namely the Karaṇa and the Ambaṣṭha. Therefore, other duties pertaining to the castes (*varṇadharma*) also apply to the *anuloma* offspring. 1.24.6.
And [the term] "brāhmaṇa" alone [is used]. 1.24.7.
Having killed [her], he becomes one accused of a heinous crime; because of the mention of "mother," there is no requirement for consideration of lineage, learning, or refinement. 1.24.7.
And his conception was unknown. || 1.24.8 ||
Having killed the fetus of that mere Brahmin—without distinguishing whether it was female, male, or neuter—he becomes one who has committed a heinous crime.
And a woman of the Ātreya lineage. || 1.24.9 ||

"Those who have bathed after their menses are called *ātreyīs*," says Vasiṣṭha (VaDh 10.94). The word "of her" (*tasya*) carries over from the previous context. Having killed an *ātreyī*, that is, a Brāhmaṇa woman, one becomes accused; he becomes a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahā*), because a Brāhmaṇa embryo may be conceived in her. Others hold that an *ātreyī* is one born of the Atri lineage. 1.24.9.
His penance is as follows. 1.24.10.
The expiation, that is, the penance for one who has been accused in every possible way, will now be stated. 1.24.10.
Having built a hut in the forest, restrained in speech, and bearing a skull as his banner, he covered himself with a garment of half-wool from the navel down to the knees. || 1.24.11 ||

Because of the word *kṛ* (“having made”), a hut built by another is not to be accepted. One who restrains his speech is *vāgyata*, that is, one who controls his speech (*vācaṃyama*). The placement of the past participle at the end of the compound is seen in the group beginning with *āhitāgni*. He whose banner is a corpse’s head is *śavaśiradhvaja*; the elision of the *s* is Vedic. The meaning is: having fixed the head of a Brāhmaṇa killed by himself onto the tip of the flagpole. Others say it means the head of any corpse whatsoever. A garment made of hemp is *śāṇī*, a cloth; half of that is *ardhaśāṇī*; its fringe is *ardhaśāṇīpakṣa*, meaning half of both the length and the width. Having covered that much area so as to be below the navel and above the knees—that is, having covered that extent—and because it is dependent on what follows, it is connected with the upcoming statement, “he should settle in a village” (ĀpDh 1.24.14). This is an injunction for another action in the middle of the passage. 1.24.11.
His path lies between the two tracks. 1.24.12.

As he enters the village, the path should be understood as being between the tracks of carts and the like on the road. Another [teacher] says: where there are two tracks on both sides of a carriage way or similar thoroughfare, the meaning is that one should proceed through the middle of those two by the path used by pigs and other such animals. 1.24.12.
And having seen another [suitable person], he may depart. || 1.24.13 ||
