Upon seeing another noble person, one should step aside from the path. Regarding this, Kauṭilya states: "The path for chariots is five *aratnis* wide; that for elephants is four; and that for ordinary men is two. By this, among men, one should step aside by two cubits. 1.24.13.
With a broken, reddish bowl, he should settle in a village. || 1.24.14 ||
The refutation consists of mere phenomena. Taking an unbaked red earthen bowl as his alms-bowl, he should dwell in a village; that is, he should go to a village. 1.24.14.
Who would go for alms to seven houses for one who has been accused? 1.24.15.

Accused of being a slayer of a Brahmin, he should wander through seven houses while loudly proclaiming, "Who among the righteous will give alms to me? The mention of "seven" is for the purpose of precluding a greater number; if a sufficient amount is obtained in only two or three houses, then it should be done in just that many. (1.24.15)
That is the function. 1.24.16.
Whatever he obtains in seven houses, that alone is his livelihood, even if it is insufficient. 1.24.16.
One who has not yet received the vow of fasting. || 1.24.17 ||
If nothing at all is obtained in seven houses, then on that day there shall be a fast alone. 1.24.17.
And he should tend the cows. 1.24.18.
Performing penance in this manner, he shall protect cows day after day. || 1.24.18 ||
Regarding their going out and coming in, there is a second purpose in the village. 1.24.19.

The second purpose for entering the village is at the time of those cows' departure and their return. The first [purpose] was stated for the sake of alms; it is thus implied that one should not enter the village at any other time. || 1.24.19 ||
Having practiced for twelve years, he attained perfection through association with the virtuous. || 1.24.20 ||

Having thus performed this vow for twelve years, one should associate with the virtuous. One should practice that method by which association with the virtuous is established; and that is proven in the conduct of the learned and in other scriptures. It is stated as follows: having performed the penance, one should take fodder in one’s own hand and call the cow. If she comes and eats it with faith, then one should know that the vow has been properly performed by him; otherwise, it has not. 1.24.20.

Or, having built a hut on the path to battle, he may dwell there desiring to win back the cattle of the Brahmins; or, being thrice defeated, he may dwell there after having won them back and been released.

The *ājipatha* is the path by which bandits, having entered a village and carried off cattle and other property, flee; he should dwell there, having built a hut. Desiring what? Desiring to win back the cows of the Brāhmaṇas (*brāhmaṇagavyaḥ*)—the form *gavyaḥ* being derived from *gavī* with the suffix *śas*, where, according to Pāṇini 6.1.106 (*vā chandasi*), the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs instead of the *pūrvasavarṇa* vowel—meaning one who wishes to defeat the bandits and recover the cows of the Brāhmaṇas. Dwell­ing thus, engaging in battle with the bandits over the cattle and other goods they are carrying away, he becomes "thrice repulsed" (*triḥ pratirāddhaḥ*) by them after being defeated three times; or, having repeatedly defeated them and recovered the cattle and other goods, he is freed from that sin by giving them to the Brāhmaṇas. This applies to one who has already begun the twelve-year penance. The same applies to the subsequent cases as well.
Or, by knowing the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), one is liberated. || 1.24.22 ||
Alternatively, having bathed at the final purificatory bath of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, he is liberated.
When there is a conflict between the Dharma and worldly interest, this same rule applies to one who grasps at worldly interest. 1.24.23.

Where there is a simultaneous occurrence of *dharma*, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and *artha*, such as the construction of a wall, and where it is impossible to favor both, he who chooses *artha* at the expense of *dharma* must perform this very same penance. Alternatively, this refers to one who, abandoning *dharma* for the sake of *artha*, commits perjury and the like; regarding this, Gautama says: "Perjury, slander reaching the king, and making a false accusation against one's teacher are equal to mortal sins" (GDh 20.9). Manu also says: "Falsehood for the purpose of self-exaltation and slander reaching the king..."
"And persistent insistence on falsehood toward one's guru is equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
Having killed a Guru or a Śrotriya who has completed his ritual studies, one shall perform this same penance until the final exhalation of life.

The *guru* is the father, the teacher (*ācārya*), and so forth; the *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Veda. If he is one whose ritual duties are completed—that is, one for whom the rites ending with the *Soma* sacrifice have been finished—having killed both of them, one should perform [penance] according to this very rule just mentioned until the final breath. The "final breath" is the departure of life; one should perform it until that point. 1.24.24.
For him, there is no restoration in this world. || 1.24.25 ||

The meaning is that even though rites such as the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) following an *aśvamedha* sacrifice may be possible for him, there is no restoration or purification for him in this world or in this life. 1.24.25.
But the impurity is indeed cast out. || 1.24.26 ||

However, the impurity of one who has died is removed; therefore, the intention is that the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and other post-mortem ceremonies (*aurdhvadaihika*) must be performed by the son and others. Others, however, consider the preceding sūtra to be for the purpose of excluding that [impurity], interpreting "restoration" (*pratyāpatti*) as the re-establishment of the relationship with the status of father and so forth by means of the son and others. 1.2.26.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section.
One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall cut off his penis together with the testicles, place it in his joined palms, and walk toward the southern direction without returning. 1.25.1.

In this context, "guru" refers to the father, not the preceptor (*ācārya*) or others. By the word *talpa*, which denotes a bed, the wife is indicated; and she must be the mother herself, not her co-wife. Having approached her, one should cut off the penis along with the testicles using a razor or similar instrument, place it in his cupped hands (*añjali*), and set out toward the southern direction. Regarding "non-return" (*anāvṛtti*): he should go toward that direction from which there is no returning. Now, those who dwell on the shore of the southern ocean should also travel as far as possible and enter the ocean itself; for here, death is what is intended. On this point, Saṃvarta says:
"Having approached the wives of his father— excluding his mother— or his own sister,
or a maternal relative, or a sister born of another mother, that lowest of men,
having gone to these women out of delusion, shall perform the *taptakṛcchra* penances. Thus it is said.
Nārada, however, states: "The mother, the mother’s sister, the mother-in-law, the maternal uncle’s wife, the father’s sister,
the wife of a paternal uncle, the wife of a disciple, the sister, her female friend, and the daughter-in-law."
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, one who has gone forth, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
"Having approached any one of these [women], he is called a violator of the Guru's bed;
in that case, the cutting off of the penis is ordained as the punishment for him. (1.25.1)
Or, having embraced a glowing iron image, he would meet his end.

A female effigy made of iron or copper, hollow inside, is here called a *sūrmi*. Having embraced it while it is blazing in the fire—made red-hot—one would reach its completion; that is, one would die. 1.25.2.
A drinker of liquor shall drink liquor that has been touched by fire. || 1.25.3 ||
"Surā is to be known as threefold: that made from molasses (*gauḍī*), that which is pure (*sādhvī*), and that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*).

Just as even one of these must not be drunk, so all of them must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born. (MDh 11.95) One who drinks it is a *surāpa* (liquor-drinker). He shall drink surā that has been thoroughly heated until it reaches the touch of fire; having his body burnt by it, he becomes purified.

A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a club upon his shoulder, shall go to the king and confess his deed; the king shall strike him with that very club. Release from the penalty occurs only upon death. 1.25.4.

A thief who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa shall go to the king carrying an iron or Khadira-wood pestle upon his own shoulder, proclaiming his deed: "I have committed such an act; punish me. The king shall strike that thief with that pestle until he dies. By this execution, there is liberation from the theft. 1.25.4.
When permission has been granted, the sin touches the one who granted it. 1.25.5.
But if the king, out of compassion or other such motives, should grant him permission, saying, "Go," then that sin touches the king himself who gave the permission. || 1.25.5 ||
Or he may go straight to the north, or enter the fire. 1.25.6.
Or he should undertake severe austerity. || 1.25.7 ||
"Intense austerity" refers to the Mahāvrata and similar practices. One should indeed extend or repeat that. 1.25.7.
Or he may attain the Self through the diminution of his attachment. || 1.25.8 ||

"Bhaktam" means food. Its "apacaya" means reduction. On the second day, there should be one morsel fewer than the number of morsels consumed on the first day. In this manner, it continues through the third day and so forth, until only a single morsel remains. Even if completion is not reached at that point, then a reduction in the quantity of morsels must be made right there. Thus, by the reduction of food, he should bring himself to completion—that is, he should finish [the vow]. 1.25.8.
Or he shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
Alternatively, one may perform the *kṛcchra* penance continuously for one year; the rule is that these [penances] are heavy for grave sins and light for minor ones. 1.25.9.
Moreover, they also cite this: 1.25.10.
The meaning is that, regarding this very subject, they also cite a verse from the Purāṇas. 1.25.10.
Having committed theft, drunk liquor, or violated the teacher’s wife— even without having committed the murder of a Brahmin—
they should eat only a limited amount of food at every fourth mealtime.
They should descend into the waters according to the ritual sequence of the Soma-pressings;
by alternating between standing and sitting, they dispel evil through these three years. || 1.25.11 ||

Having committed theft and other such acts, excluding the killing of a Brahmin, those who eat at the fourth mealtime—meaning those whose time for eating is the fourth [period], such as eating today by day and tomorrow by night—are so described. Even then, they should eat sparingly and not consume delicacies. They should enter the waters; that is, they should bathe in water situated on the ground. This is "according to the ritual of the Soma-pressings" (*savanānukalpam*); the meaning is that they should follow the pattern of the pressings, such as the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) and so forth, namely, three times a day (*triṣavaṇam*). They should stand during the day and sit during the night; thus, passing their time by alternating between standing and sitting, they remove that sin in three years. (1.15.11)
Having abandoned the first caste and having destroyed the first caste, he should go and stand in battle; there they shall slay him. 1.25.12.

The first caste is the Brāhmaṇa; having killed him, one should go to battle and stand in the midst of the two armies. Does this apply to everyone? No, he says—excluding the first caste, meaning any other caste such as the Kṣatriya and so forth. If those soldiers kill him while he is standing there, they become guilty of sin if they do not kill him, just as [they would for failing to punish] a thief; he becomes pure when he is dead. 1.15.12
Or alternatively, having caused his hair, skin, and flesh to be offered as oblations, he may enter the fire.

Regarding the very subject just mentioned, there is another penance. The word *iti* is intended to include blood and the other parts as well. Having had the hair and other parts of his own body cut off and having caused the domestic priest (*purohita*) to perform the oblation (*homa*), he should afterwards enter that fire himself. When dead, he becomes purified. There, having kindled the fire, he should offer oblations with these mantras recited by Vasiṣṭha: “I sacrifice the hairs to Death; through the hairs I banish Death, svāhā! I sacrifice the skin to Death; through the skin I banish Death, svāhā! I sacrifice the blood to Death; through the blood I banish Death, svāhā! I sacrifice the sinews to Death; through the sinews I banish Death, svāhā! I sacrifice the flesh to Death; through the flesh I banish Death, svāhā! I sacrifice the bones to Death; through the bones I banish Death, svāhā! I sacrifice the marrow to Death; through the marrow I banish Death, svāhā! I sacrifice the fat to Death; through the fat I banish Death, svāhā! [VaDh 20.26] || 1.25.13 ||
For the killing of a crow, a peacock, a barhin, a cakravāka, a haṃsa, a bhāsa, a frog, a mongoose, a *ḍerikā*, or a horse, the penance is the same as that for a Śūdra. 1.25.14.

The *vāyasa* is the crow; the *pracalāka* is the chameleon, which can change its form at will; the *barhiṇa* is the peacock; the *cakravāka* is the ruddy goose, which moves about in pairs by day but is separated at night; the *haṃsa* is the swan that dwells on Lake Mānasa; the *bhāsa* is a particular kind of vulture; the horse, mongoose, and frog are well known; and the *ḍerikā* is the musk-rat. For the killing of all these together, the penance is the same as for a Śūdra. However, for killing each one individually, the penance must be determined accordingly. Some say that this very penance applies even to the killing of each one individually. (1.25.14)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section: [One should not eat] the milk of a cow or the meat of an ox without a specific reason. 1.26.1.

A *dhenu* is a milch cow; an *anaḍvān* is a bull fit for drawing a cart. If one causes injury to these two without a specific cause, an expiation must be performed as prescribed for a Śūdra. "Without a cause" means without anger or a desire for meat—that is, unintentionally. If the act is intentional, the rule for a Vaiśya and so forth should be consulted in other Smṛtis. || 1.26.1 ||
And when the draft animals are engaged in pulling [the load], so it is for other living beings. (1.26.2)

One who bears the yoke is a *dhurya*, namely a bull; those that can be drawn by such a one are *dhuryavāha*. When injury is committed against as many of these as there are, and regarding other living beings whose life consists solely of breath and who have no bones, the penance is the same as for a Śūdra. On this point, Gautama says: "Having killed a thousand vertebrate animals, or having killed boneless animals and a load-carrying ox" (GDh 22.20–21). 1.26.2.
Having reviled one who should not be reviled, or having spoken an untruth, one must eat food that is neither milk nor pungent or salty for three nights.

One who does not deserve to be reviled in any way—such as a father, a teacher, or others—is "unrevileable. Having reviled such a person—that is, having censured them or spoken falsehoods to them, excluding major or minor sins—one should avoid consuming milk and similar substances for three nights. By the mention of "milk," they say that its derivatives, such as curd and the like, are also included. 1.26.3.
For a Śūdra, there shall be a fast of seven nights.
But a Śūdra, in the case just mentioned, shall fast for seven nights. || 1.26.4 ||
And the same applies to women. 1.26.5.

The penances prescribed for the occasions beginning with "having killed a Kṣatriya" [ĀpDh 1.24.1] and ending with "false speech," must be performed by women in exactly the same manner. Although this is already established by the mention of the castes in the rule "the four castes" [ĀpDh 1.1.4], it is stated here as a restrictive rule (niyama) so that from this point forward, these apply only to men and not to women.

Another says: Since [the rule] is already established by the mention of "birth" (*jāti*) itself, this statement is for the purpose of extension (*atideśa*). And it is a traditional legal principle (*smārto nyāyaḥ*) that in cases of extension, only half [of the penalty] is obtained. Therefore, this statement is for the sake of women obtaining half [the penance]. And so says Bhārgava:
"One who is eighty years of age, or a child less than sixteen, as well as women and the sick, deserve only half the penance. (1.26.5)
In cases of false accusation against those [who have committed offenses], one limb shall be amputated; in the case of injury to living beings, [the same applies]. 1.26.6.

Regarding those for whose killing the state of being "accused" (abhiśasta) is declared by the rule, "Or one accused who has gone to a Soma-sacrifice," etc., one should cut off a single limb of theirs and perform penance like a Śūdra; provided that in the case of non-lethal injury, the capacity of that limb is destroyed by the cutting. 1.26.6.

Having committed acts such as un-Aryan behavior, calumny, or forbidden conduct; having consumed what is unfit to be eaten, drunk, or tasted; having discharged semen into a Śūdra woman or into a non-vaginal opening; or having performed a blameworthy act either intentionally or unintentionally—one should touch water with verses containing the word *ap*, or with those addressed to Varuṇa, or with other purificatory texts, according to the repetition of the act. 1.26.7.

The state of the noble ones (*ārya*) is *āryam*; that conduct (*ācāra*) which possesses this quality is *āryavat*, using the possessive suffix *-vat*. That which is other than this is *anāryavat*, such as speaking untruths and the like. Slander (*paiśuna*) is the reporting of another’s faults to the king. Prohibited conduct (*pratiṣiddhācāra*) is the performance of acts such as those prescribed in: "One should avoid the act of spitting and sexual intercourse in water" (ĀpDh 1.30.19). Unfit food (*abhakṣya*) is rice-porridge (*kṛsara*) prepared for no sacred purpose and the like. Unfit to be eaten (*abhojya*) is that which has been defiled by hair, insects, and so forth. Unfit to be drunk (*apeya*) is "the milk of a cow within ten days of calving," etc. (GDh 17.22). Upon consuming these, or having discharged semen into a Śūdra woman, such as a prostitute and the like, or having discharged semen into a non-vaginal place such as water, or having performed a faulty rite—whether a Vedic rite of sorcery (*ābhicārika*) or any other harmful act toward others—done either intentionally (*abhisaṃdhipūrva*) with full awareness or unintentionally, one should touch water while reciting the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed refreshing" (TS 5.6.1) and the four verses beginning with "Golden-hued, pure, purifying" (TS 5.6.1). Having first bathed silently, one should afterwards perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with these mantras. Or else, one may use the Varuṇa-verses: "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa," "That I implore of thee," "Do thou, O Agni, protect us," and "May he, O Agni, protect us"—or with other purificatory hymns (*pavitra*), such as the section beginning "Purifying, dwelling in light" (TaitBr 1.4.8), the *Śuddhavatī* verses (RV 8.95.7), and the *Taratsamandīya* hymn (RV 9.58.1). One should touch water as many times as the repetition of the act was performed. They say this is the secret expiation (*rahasyaprāyaścitta*). 1.26.7.
One who has committed the *avakīrṇa* offense should sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey using the *pākayajña* ritual.

A celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who approaches a woman becomes an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken his vow); he shall sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey, according to the procedure of a *pākayajña*, following the rules for a *sthālīpāka*. On this point, Manu says:
"But an *avakīrṇin* shall sacrifice to Nirṛti at night on a crossroads with a one-eyed donkey, according to the procedure of a *pākayajña*. (MDh 11.118)

Hārīta, however, states: “A *avakīrṇin* (one who has violated his vow of celibacy) with respect to women should sacrifice a donkey as an animal offering to Nirṛti at a crossroads according to the ritual procedure of a *pākayajña*. He should cook the sacrificial cake for the animal on the ground; having performed the rite with the portions [of the meat] in water, he offers oblations of clarified butter, saying: ‘I am overcome by desire, I am overcome; svāhā to the one who desires desire! I am afflicted by desire, I am afflicted; svāhā to the one who desires desire! || 1.26.8 ||
A Śūdra should eat from it. 1.26.9.

A Śūdra should eat the remnants of the sacrificial oblation mixed with clarified butter belonging to that donkey; this is an exception to the rule [ĀpGṛ 7.15]: "By that [remnant], he makes the Brāhmaṇa possessed of clarified butter. 1.26.9.
The expiation for improperly studied [Vedic texts]. 1.26.10.
That which is studied by transgressing the rules is wrongly studied; the expiation for that fault will now be stated. 1.26.10.

For one year, while remaining intent on the service of his teacher, he should restrain his speech, releasing it only for the purpose of Vedic study; likewise, the teacher [should restrain his speech] toward the teacher’s wife and when going out for alms. 1.26.11.

Remaining intent on the welfare of his teacher, he should remain restrained in speech for one year. The utterance of speech consists only of Vedic study, as well as in reporting matters to the teacher, and likewise regarding the teacher’s wife. "The practice of begging" means wandering for alms; in that context, he says, "Give me alms. From this very point it is known that this refers to one who has not yet returned home (an *asamāvṛtta*). 1.26.11.
In the same way, regarding other faulty offenses that do not cause loss of status (*apattaniya*), we shall explain the subsequent rules. 1.26.12.

Just as this expiation applies to what has been studied erroneously, so too do the subsequent expiations which we shall describe apply to these cases as well—by the use of the word "api" (also), it is meant that they apply even to what has been studied erroneously. They should be understood as pertaining to those blameworthy acts, other than those involving a loss of caste (*patanīya*), for which no specific expiation has been explicitly stated. 1.26.12.
Or he may offer oblations to Desire and Wrath with the formula: "Desire has done it; Wrath has done it. 1.26.13.
The oblation is performed with the two [formulas] ending in *svāhā*; the substance is clarified butter (*ājya*). 1.26.13.
Or he may mutter it. 1.26.14.

In this view, there is no utterance of *svāhā*. However, some desire the oblation with the formulas "To Desire, svāhā! and "To Wrath, svāhā!". But according to the view that it is a recitation (*japa*), the two mantras are those prescribed in the Sūtra. Furthermore, the repetition of both the recitation and the oblation is in accordance with the nature and frequency of the offense. 1.26.14.

On a festival day, he should either subsist on sesame seeds or fast; then, on the following day, having touched water, he should repeat the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times, either with each repetition accompanied by breath control (prāṇāyāma) or without breath control.

On the *parvan*—that is, on the full moon or the new moon day—one eats only sesame seeds and nothing else, such as cooked rice; this is "sesame-eating" (*tilabhakṣa*). Having touched water and bathed, one should repeat the *Sāvitrī* a thousand times by means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), that is, through successive acts of breath-control. In a single breath-control, one should repeat it as many times as is possible; thus there is a repetition of breath-controls until the thousand is completed. Or, one may do so without breath-control. (1.26.15)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section.

On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, having fasted while consuming sesame seeds, or on the following day, having touched the water of a great river, one should offer a thousand pieces of wood with the Sāvitrī mantra or recite it. 1.27.1.

A river originating from a mountain and flowing toward the ocean is a *mahānadī* (great river); that which arises therein is *mahānada*. Because of the statement, "One should place a thousand pieces of wood of a sacrificial tree," the ritual rule of the *svāhākāra* does not apply, since it has been stated: "That which is enjoined by the root *hu* involves the offering with the *svāhākāra*" [ĀpPar 3.4]. Or, one should simply recite [the mantra]. 1.127.1.
Or he may perform the *iṣṭi* sacrifices and *kratū*s for the purpose of purification. || 1.27.2 ||

The *pavitra* rites are for the purpose of purification. These include the *iṣṭis* such as the *mṛgāra*, the sacrificial rituals (*yajñakratu*), and the Soma sacrifices such as the *agniṣṭut* and others. These six are the expiations (*prāyaścitta*); they are heavy for heavy sins and light for light sins. 1.27.2.
Having eaten food that should not be eaten, one becomes void of excrement. 1.27.3.

In the case of eating the meat of forbidden animals such as cats and the like, one must achieve the state of being free from feces; one should fast for as long as it takes for the stomach to become free of feces. (1.27.3)
In what length of time is that attained? To this he says: "That is attained within seven nights. (1.27.4)

That state of being free from feces (*naiṣpurīṣya*) is attained within seven nights; the meaning is that one must fast for seven nights. Since the result is already established by the rule "one should fast for seven nights," the specific mention of "being free from feces" indicates that for those for whom this state is attained in merely three nights, purification occurs in that much time alone. And so says Gautama: "In the case of eating what should not be eaten, or consuming impure substances, the state of being free from feces [is the goal]; fasting for at least three nights, or for seven nights. (GDh 23.23–25) || 1.27.4 ||
Or he should touch water at both twilights during the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira. || 1.27.5 ||
At both twilights, evening and morning, he should touch water; his bath shall be performed in water that has reached the ground, or in cold water drawn out [of a well]. 1.27.5.
Or he should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights.
A specific type of vow to be accomplished over twelve nights is called the *kṛcchradvādaśarātra*.
He states the procedure for that:

"For three days one should eat only what is not prepared with oil and not eat during the day; then for three days each, one observes the vow of eating only what is unasked for; and for three days one eats nothing at all. This is the rule for the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance. 1.27.7.

At the beginning, for three days, he should not eat at night; he should eat only during the day. Then, for three days, he should not eat by day, but only at night. Then, for three days, he should eat only what is unasked for (*ayācita*); this is a prohibition against begging. By this, there is no prohibition against his own property. Thus says Gautama: "Then, for another three days, he should not ask anyone for anything" (GDh 26.4). Then, for three days, he does not eat anything at all—not even fruits and the like. This is the rule for the twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance. Here, according to other Smṛtis, it should be understood that he must consume sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and avoid conversation with women, Śūdras, and others. 1.27.7.
In this very manner he should practice for one year; that is the Kṛcchra-year penance.

One should practice this very rule continuously for one year; this is to be understood as the "year-long Kṛcchra," which was previously mentioned in the statement: "He shall perform the Kṛcchra for a year" (ĀpDh 1.25.8). 1.27.8.
Now, furthermore: even after committing many acts that cause loss of caste, one becomes purified by having performed the penance through three recitations of the Veda while fasting. 1.27.9.

Now, another expiation is stated: one must perform three recitations of the entire Veda (*pārāyaṇa*) while fasting continuously. *Pārāyaṇa* is the study of the Veda from the beginning until its completion. [The text says] "even many"; by the word "even," it is implied how much more so if there are only one or two. 1.27.9.
One who maintains an ignoble bed, who charges interest, and who drinks fermented liquors—
having been saluted like a non-Brahmin, he should sit upon blades of grass with his back scorched by the sun.

An *anāryā* is a Śūdra woman; "bearing her on his bed" means approaching her for sexual intercourse. "Giving interest" means giving wealth for the sake of interest; the meaning is that he lives by usury. "Kaṣāya" refers to intoxicants other than *surā*; a drinker of that is a *kaṣāyapa*. And whoever, like a non-Brāhmaṇa, praises all [others] while acting as a panegyrist (*vandī*), he too must sit upon grass, beginning from sunrise, until the sun heats his back—that is, until it heats his rear part. Because he acts in accordance with the sun's heat, he is said to be "behind" (*pṛṣṭhatas*) himself. In case of repetition, the penance is repeated, until he considers himself purified. 1.27.10.
Whatever black sin a Brahmin commits by serving a dark-skinned person for a single night, he may counteract it by eating only at every fourth mealtime while subsisting on water.
In three years, he destroys that evil. || 1.27.11 ||

The dark complexion is the Śūdra. Serving him for the sake of livelihood by becoming his obedient servant—this is the meaning. The rest is clear and has already been explained. Another says: "serving a Śūdra woman through sexual intercourse. In this view, this should be understood to apply to the procreation of offspring when approaching her during her fertile period (*ṛtu*). Manu says:

"For one who has drunk the saliva of a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*), for one who has been defiled by her breath, and for one who has begotten a child upon her, no atonement is prescribed. (MDh 3.19) [1.27.11]
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section;
thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Ujjvalā*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra*.
"In whatever way one covets the property of another, he becomes a thief"—so say Kautsa and Hārīta, as well as Kāṇva and Puṣkarasādi. 1.28.1.

Whether in times of distress or not, if one covets another's property or what belongs to another—be it much or little—with the thought "may this be mine," he is in every respect a thief; so hold Kautsa and others. 1.28.1.
"There are censures regarding possessions," says Vārṣyāyaṇi. 1.28.2.
Vārṣyāyaṇi, however, maintains that there are exceptions to theft regarding certain types of appropriation. 1.28.2.
He cites these very examples:
"Chaff and fodder for draft animals do not prevent their owners [from taking them]. (1.28.3)

*Śamī* refers to the seed-pod; those which grow within it, are burnt [by the sun], and ripen under the influence of time are *śamyoṣā*, namely the pod-grains such as mung beans, black gram, chickpeas, and so forth. A *yugya* is an ox that draws a yoke, that is, a draft animal pulling a cart; its fodder, its food consisting of grass and the like, is *yugyaghāsa*. These, when being taken, do not prohibit the owner—that is, they do not cause the owner to offer a prohibition. The meaning is that while these are being taken, the owners are not entitled to forbid it. The point is that even in taking them oneself, there is no fault of theft. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in another *smṛti*:
Those traveling on a journey may take a single handful of chickpeas, rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, or black gram, provided these items are not otherwise prohibited.
But Manu says:
"A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose means of subsistence are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane or two roots from another's field, does not deserve to be fined" (MDh 8.341). 1.28.3.
Excessive speech becomes unsuccessful. 1.28.4.

Even in the case of *śamyoṣa* and other such items, excessive taking—that is, taking beyond the limit—is considered unsuccessful and defective; the meaning is that in the case of taking in excess of the proper measure, the fault of theft (*steya*) arises. || 1.28.4 ||
"In all cases, it must be preceded by permission," says Hārīta. (1.28.5)
The teacher Hārīta maintains that the taking of all things in all circumstances must be preceded solely by the consent of the owner. 1.28.5.
One should not go to see a teacher or a kinsman who has fallen [from their status]. 1.28.6.
Although it has been stated that "no social interaction exists with those who have fallen," it is stated again: "I shall now declare the specific rules regarding teachers and others. 1.28.6.
And one should not make use of these enjoyments. || 1.28.7 ||

From this fallen teacher, or from a kinsman such as a father and so forth, one should not utilize nor accept enjoyments or the means of enjoyment, even if they have been obtained through inheritance. 1.28.7.
Having greeted him upon a chance encounter, one should pass by in silence. || 1.28.8 ||

If by chance one should encounter fallen teachers or others, one should approach them without following the prescribed ritual, remain silent, and pass by them without conversing at all; one must not stay with them for even a moment. || 1.28.8 ||
A mother performs many acts for the sake of her son; therefore, service toward her is perpetual, even if she has fallen from virtue. (1.28.9)

Regarding the state of being a son (*putratva*): the suffix *-tva* is used here in its own sense (*svārthika*), as in the expression "the body itself is something else" (*dehatvam evānyat*). For the sake of a son, a mother performs many actions with visible purposes, such as conceiving the fetus, carrying out the removal of impurities, giving breast milk, circumambulation, prostration, and so forth; therefore, even when she has fallen from her status, service toward her—such as anointing, bathing, and the like—must always be performed. (1.28.9)
But there should be no accumulation of [excessive] dharma. 1.28.10.

The inclusion (*anvaya*) within a single ritual act is the collective placement of ritual elements (*dharmasaṃnivāpa*). That [inclusion] must not be performed with a mother who has fallen [from her status]. For example, in the *Subrahmaṇyā* litany there is the mention of the mother’s name; likewise, in the *Varuṇapraghāsa* sacrifices, there is the rule: “As many as are the sacrificer’s dependents (*amātya*), including their wives, so many [cakes] plus one more,” and so forth. Now, in such cases, does the inclusion of the mother consist of service (*śuśrūṣā*)? He says: “Yes. For she is considered included when she is in accord (*saṃmata*), but when she is opposed (*vimata*), she is excluded. However, for the sake of the *Vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, she is not to be fed during the cooking. But when she has died, rites such as the funeral consecration (*saṃskāra*) must be performed; regarding this, however, there are conflicting views. (1.28.10)

Having renounced enjoyments acquired through unrighteous means, and having declared, "Neither we nor unrighteousness [shall remain]," covering the area from below the navel to above the knees, touching water at the three times of day, eating food that is neither milk nor pungent nor salty, he shall not enter a house for twelve years. 1.28.11.

The theft of a Brahmin’s gold; having approached, eaten with, or accepted gifts from Caṇḍālas or women of the lowest castes, a Brahmin falls through ignorance, but through knowledge he becomes equal to them. (MDh 11.176)

Such is the illustrative example. Regarding those enjoyments acquired through unrighteousness (*adharma*), having permitted them and then renounced them, he should utter the dismissal: "Neither we nor unrighteousness. Its meaning is: "We and unrighteousness shall not coexist. The passage beginning with *adhonābhi* has already been explained [cf. ĀpDh 1.24.11]. In this case, there is no option for wearing a garment of half-wool (*ardhaśāṇī*) or the practice of begging for alms (*bhikṣācaryā*). 1.28.11.
From that, success [is attained]. 1.28.12
And this [penance] lasts for twelve years; at its conclusion, perfection and purification come to pass. || 1.28.12 ||
Now, there would be association with the Noble Ones. (1.28.13)

Because of the instruction regarding expiation and the instruction regarding success, the repetition of "success" is for the purpose of providing an exception to the statement: "But through knowledge he attains equality" (MDh 11.176). || 1.28.13 ||
This same [rule] applies to other acts that cause loss of caste as well. 1.28.14.

Regarding those other offenses causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) mentioned previously that are distinct from those already discussed, for which no specific expiation has been explicitly stated, it should be understood that the very expiation just mentioned applies to them as well. Others hold that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the cases already discussed; in that regard, the option is determined by whether the act was committed intentionally or unintentionally. 1.28–14.
But he who has violated the bed of his guru shall enter a hollow metal image and, having set fire to both ends, burn himself.

But he who violates the teacher’s bed shall have a hollow iron image made capable of being entered within, and enter it; having entered, he shall kindle a fire on both sides and burn himself. There is only a slight difference here from the rule, "Or, having entered a blazing iron image, he may meet his end" (ĀpDh 1.25.2). This statement is intended to exclude the alternative mentioned immediately preceding it. 1.28.15.
"This is false," says Hārīta. (1.28.16)
But the sage Hārīta considers that this aforementioned penance ending in death must not be performed falsely.
Why is this so? He says:
for he who conceives of himself or another as a distinct entity is indeed one who is accursed. 1.28.17

The word *hi* indicates the reason. Because he who considers himself or another [to be an enemy] and kills them becomes indeed an accused person (*abhiśasta*) and is truly a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*). Since it is stated that one who desires to remove a sin causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) ought not to commit another such sin, and because of the mention of being "accused," there is a cessation of other death-penances (*maraṇāntika*) even in the case of Brahmins. (1.28.17)

What then is the expiation for that? He says: "By this very rule, one should perform [the penance] until the final exhalation. For him, there is no restoration in this world; however, his stain is removed. (1.28.18)

"Having covered the area from below the navel to above the knees"—by this very rule, which was stated immediately following [the previous sūtra], [the requirement is fulfilled]. The remainder has been explained. 1.28.18.

One who has violated the duty toward his wife shall put on a donkey skin with the hair turned outward and go for alms, saying, "Alms for one who has violated the duty toward his wife," to seven houses; that is his mode of subsistence for six months. 1.28.19.

But he who abandons his wife while she is still in her youth, even without a [valid] cause, is a transgressor against his wife (*dāravyatikramin*). Having put on and worn the skin of a donkey with the hair outside, he should beg for alms at seven houses, saying, "Give alms to the transgressor against his wife. Or, according to the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti*: "Give alms to the transgressor against his wife from her youth. That mode of life lasts for six months; after that, there is purification. (1.28.19)
But for a woman who has transgressed against her husband, there is the practice of the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights for that same duration of time. 1.28.20.

In the expression *bharturvyatikramaḥ*, the elision of the letter *r* is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). *Vyatikrama* means abandonment. For that woman who abandons her husband without a [valid] cause, the penance is the repeated performance of two *kṛcchra* and ten-night fasts for that duration, namely six months. (1.28.20)

Now, the killer of a learned Brahmin (bhrūṇahan), having put on the skin of a dog or the skin of a donkey with the hair turned outward, and having taken a human head for the purpose of facing [the enemy]... || 1.28.21 ||
Thus ends the twenty-eighth section.

Proclaiming that the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) is his name for the purpose of a mendicant’s staff, he should wander about, saying, "Who will give alms to a killer of an embryo? Having obtained sustenance for life in a village, he should take refuge in an empty house or at the root of a tree; for he has no association with the noble ones (*āryas*). By this very rule, he should live until his final breath. For him, there is no restoration to his former status in this world, but his stain is indeed removed. 1.29.1.

A Brāhmaṇa who has studied the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), who understands the meaning of the ritual manuals (*prayogaśāstra*) along with their commentaries, and who both performs and causes others to perform the sacred rites, is a *bhrūṇa*. Thus says Baudhāyana: “Having studied some portion of the Vedas, he is a Brāhmaṇa; having studied one recensional branch (*śākhā*), he is a *śrotriya*; one who studies the auxiliary limbs is an *anūcāna*; one who studies the *kalpas* is a *ṛṣikalpa*; and one who studies the Sūtras and the traditional expositions (*pravacana*) is a *bhrūṇa*” [BauGṛ 1.7.2–6]. He who kills such a person is a *bhrūṇahan* (feticide). He, having put on the hide of a dog or a donkey with the hair turned outward, shall take the head of any dead man for the purpose of drinking (*pratīpāna*). The prefix *prati-* here expresses the sense of the verbal root; the lengthening of the vowel is according to the rule *upasargasya ghañyamanuṣye bahulam* [Pāṇ 6.3.122], which allows for optional lengthening. “Drinking” (*pratīpāna*) is the literal term, but the mention of drinking is illustrative; eating is also included therein. Taking a part of a bedstead (*khaṭvāṅga*) for the purpose of a staff—*khaṭvāṅga* being a part of a bedstead, namely a pole—he shall wander here and there, proclaiming his own name based on his deed: “I am a *bhrūṇahan*. Or, he may take a *khaṭvāṅga* as it is well-known in the *Kāpālika* system. Even at the time of begging alms, he should wander saying, “Who will give alms to a feticide? Having wandered and obtained merely the means of subsistence (*prāṇavṛtti*) for his life’s journey in a village, he should resort to an empty house or the foot of a tree for shelter, thinking: “I have no association with noble men (*ārya*). As to how long he must wander, the text says: “By this very rule,” and so forth. This is understood. Regarding the passage, “Or a *śrotriya* who has completed his ritual duties” [ĀpDh 1.24.24], this refers to one who neither memorizes the texts nor knows their meaning, and who does not cause others to perform the rites. 1.28.21–1.29.1.
He who, being heedless, kills [a creature] when it has come into his grasp, reaps the fruit of that fault.

Regarding the subject matter introduced by the passage beginning with "Having killed a Kṣatriya" [ĀpDh 1.24.10], even for one who kills through negligence—that is, who kills unintentionally due to carelessness—the fruit of the fault is indeed incurred; it is not the case that there is an absence of fault simply because the act was committed through negligence. || 1.29.2 ||
Together with his resolve, once again. || 1.29.3 ||

When a killing is committed together with a prior intention (*saṃkalpa*), it becomes even more significant. Therefore, for an act committed through negligence (*pramāda*), the penance is light, whereas for an intentional act, it is heavy. As for what was stated previously—that "an action, whether performed intentionally or unintentionally, is accompanied by fault" (ĀpDh 1.26.7)—this was said because there is no distinction regarding the penance itself.
The same applies to other actions that are likewise defective. 1.29.4.
The same should be understood regarding other faulty actions as well, excluding killing: the fault is slight when unintentional, but great when intentional. 1.29.4
Likewise, [it is applied] to meritorious deeds. 1.29.5.

This same principle applies even to meritorious deeds (*puṇyakriyā*): when performed unintentionally, the fruit is small; when performed intentionally, it is great. For example—suppose thieves have stolen the property of a Brahmin and are fleeing, and by chance some hero arrives and slays them, or the thieves, seeing the hero themselves, abandon the stolen goods and flee; in that case, the hero’s merit is small. But when he intentionally recovers the property from the thieves himself and returns it to its owners, then it is great. Likewise, in approaching the wife of another with the thought that she is one's own wife, the demerit is small; otherwise, it is great. (1.29.5)
Even for the sake of examination, a Brahmin must not take up a weapon. || 1.29.6 ||

Examination (*parīkṣā*) is the knowledge of virtues and defects; that for which this is the purpose or motive is "one who possesses such [knowledge]. Even a Brahmin of this kind should not take up a weapon—how much less so for the sake of violence? This is the meaning of the word "even" (*api*). (1.29.6)
The counter-exception to this is stated in the Purāṇa: "He who kills one who has advanced for the purpose of violence, anger merely touches anger; there is no fault in him. (1.29.7)

It is heard in the Purāṇa: "There is no fault found in one who kills an assailant who has advanced or attacked for the purpose of violence or murder. The reason for the absence of fault is as follows: "For it is wrath alone that touches wrath; man does not touch man. On this point, Vasiṣṭha and Baudhāyana state: "He who kills an *ātatāyin* (an aggressor) born of a noble family and devoted to Vedic study does not thereby become a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*); wrath merely encounters wrath."
But Manu says:
"Weapons may be taken up by the twice-born when their duty is obstructed."
And when there is a disruption among the twice-born castes caused by the power of Time;
"One who kills in self-defense, in a conflict over sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), or in defense of women and Brahmins, does not incur sin if he acts according to dharma" (MDh 8.348–49).
Gautama states: "In a life-threatening situation, even a Brahmin may take up arms" (GDh 7.25). Vasiṣṭha says:
The incendiary, the poisoner, one with weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and those who seize land or wives— these six are assassins (ātatāyin).

"Even one who has mastered the Vedāntas, if he approaches as an assassin intent on killing, one may kill him in return; by doing so, one does not become a killer of an embryo. [VaDh 3.16–17] || 1.29.7 ||

To establish that even the sons born of those who have fallen from their status and have not performed penance are likewise subject to that fall, the author states the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*):

"Now, those accused [of sin], having come together, may practice what is righteous; thus they might deliberate, acting as sacrificers for one another, teachers to one another, and intermarrying with one another. (1.29.8)

The word *atha* indicates the introduction of a new subject. Those who have been accused or are outcastes (*patita*), having come together—*avasāna* meaning a house, and *sam* meaning in unity—they should live by building their dwellings in one place outside the village. They should practice the righteous conduct (*dhārmya*) that is about to be described. Having sharpened—that is, made firm and decided—their intellect (*saṃśitāṃ buddhim*), they should live by sacrificing for one another, teaching one another, and forming marriage alliances with one another; thus they should subsist. (1.29.8)
Having raised up sons, they should say, "Depart from us as brahmins; for thus, O noble ones, will you attain our own state. || 1.29.9 ||

Then, having assembled their sons, they would say: "O sons, depart from us—go forth in various ways, casting off affection, and go into the presence of the noble ones (āryas). For in this way, the noble and disciplined ones will show their approval toward us. The form *saṃpratyapatsyata* is in the future tense using the *luṅ* suffix according to Pāṇini 3.3.132 (*āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavac ca*), where the letter *y* following the *sakāra* is either a scribal error or a Vedic archaism. They will act with approval, thinking: "This will be intended even by the noble ones, because it was we ourselves who committed the act leading to downfall and performed the deed, not you. Furthermore, there is no loss of caste for one born of an outcaste, because he is a different person. (1.29.9)
He establishes this very point:
"Moreover, it does not fall while possessing the sense-faculties. (1.29.10)

For it is not the case that when the person falls, he falls together with the sense organ; rather, it is the person alone who falls, not the sense organ, just as one says "white" of the cloth and not of the whiteness. Furthermore, the two words *atha api* have the meaning of *api ca*. 1.29.10.

How is it that one who possesses sense-faculties does not fall? To this he says: "By this it should be understood that even one who is deficient in limbs produces [an offspring] with all limbs. (1.29.11)

The nature of the meaning just mentioned should be understood through this illustration that is about to be stated: even one who is deficient in limbs such as the eyes produces [an offspring] who possesses those limbs, such as the eyes; likewise, one who is devoid of qualification (adhikāra) produces one who possesses qualification, because a woman can also be a cause, and she is free from that defect. || 1.29.11 ||
Hārīta says that this is false. 1.29.12.
Hārīta maintains that this aforementioned nature of objects is not logically tenable as being false. 1.29.12.
Why is this so? He says:
"A woman is like a vessel for curd. (1.29.13)
That vessel in which curd is placed is a "curd-pot" (dadhidhānī); a woman who possesses the same qualities—that is, is similar—to it [becomes so]. 1.29.13.
What follows from this?

For when one churns impure milk that has been poured into a vessel for curd, no religious rite is performed by that means. Likewise, there can be no association with that which is produced as impure semen. || 1.29.14 ||

For when one curdles milk that has been defiled by a dog or other impure thing in a vessel containing curds, and having prepared it with the addition of buttermilk and so forth, churns it—no ritual act such as a sacrifice is performed with the ghee or other products derived from that. Likewise, regarding semen that is rendered impure through contact with an outcaste, which is discharged into a woman and mixed with her blood, and whatever form is produced thereby—the learned do not engage in sexual union with that [offspring]. Here, the phrase "impure semen" serves as a refutation of the argument that "one does not fall [from caste] unless accompanied by the organ. For logical arguments do not apply to matters based on scriptural injunction. Thus, even though the origin is the same, it is only the son who falls, not the daughter. As Vasiṣṭha says: "One born of an outcaste becomes an outcaste, except in the case of a woman; for she goes to another [man]. One may approach her, provided she is without inheritance" (VaDh 13.51–53). 1.29.14.
Malevolent incantations and curses cause impurity, yet they do not constitute a ground for expulsion from the caste. (1.29.15)

*Abhicāra* is indeed *abhīcāra*; the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to Pāṇini 6.3.122, which states that the vowel of a prefix is often lengthened before a word ending in the suffix *-dhañ* when it does not refer to a human being. *Abhīcāra* refers to rites such as the Śyena sacrifice. *Anuvyāhāra* refers to a curse. Even when these two are directed toward a Brāhmaṇa, they certainly cause impurity, yet they do not constitute grounds for loss of caste (*patanīya*). || 1.29.15 ||
"They are those who cause loss of caste," says Hārīta. (1.29.16)
Hārīta, however, considers even those two to be causes for falling [from caste]. (1.29.16)

But for one who commits an act leading to loss of caste, the penance consists of twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of seven days, twelve periods of three days, twelve periods of two days, twelve days, seven days, three days, two days, or one day. 1.29.17.

Even for those impure acts for which no specific expiation has been stated, the same expiation that applies to acts causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) shall serve as the expiation. For how long a time? From twelve months down to a single day. (1.29.17)
Is this distinction regarding time [for atonement] applicable without exception to all acts that cause impurity? No, he says:
"Thus, the expiation for acts causing impurity is according to the repetition of the act. (1.29.18)

Thus, this expiation for impurity should be understood according to the repetition of the act: in the case of intentional and continuous repetition, it lasts for a longer period; in the opposite case, the reverse applies. 1.29.18.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth section;
thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Ujjvalā*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra*.

In such passages as "They should not shave [their heads] after returning [from their teacher]" (ĀpDh 1.10.7) and "At the time for a *snātaka*" (ĀpDh 1.8.7), he states the time for the bath that has been occasioned:
"Some say one becomes a *snātaka* through learning. 1.30.1.
The knowledge of the Vedas is true knowledge; endowed with that, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), so some maintain. Manu also says:

"Having studied the Vedas—either all of them, two of them, or even one—in due order, and having remained steadfast in his vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he should enter the stage of the householder (*gṛhasthāśrama*). [MDh 3.2]
Likewise, by means of the vow consisting of forty-eight [units]. || 1.30.2 ||

*Parimāṇam* is simply *parīmāṇam*; the lengthening of the vowel is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). The mention of "forty-eight" is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the previously mentioned durations such as "less by one quarter" or "less by half" (ĀpDh 1.2.13–14). One should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) when endowed with a vow of forty-eight years or similar duration, even if not yet endowed with sacred knowledge (*vidyā*). || 1.30.2 ||
"And by means of knowledge and the vow," so say some. 1.3.3.0.3.

The elision of the third case singular ending in *vidyā* is according to Pāṇini 7.1.39, *supāṃ suluk*, etc. Some maintain that one should bathe when endowed with both knowledge (*vidyā*) and the vow (*vrata*). In this way, the phrase "having studied the Veda" in Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 12.1, *vedam adhītya snāsyan*, is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). On this point, Yājñavalkya says: "Having brought the Veda, or the vows, or indeed both, to completion, and having remained unbroken in his student discipline (*brahmacarya*), he should marry a woman possessed of auspicious marks. (YDh 1.52)
Thus [ends the section]. 1.30.3.
In all of these cases, the conduct is like that of a *snātaka*.

Three types of *snātakas* have been mentioned: the *vidyā-snātaka*, the *vratasnātaka*, and the *ubhayasnātaka*. In the case of all of them, the suffix *-vat* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.63, *tad arhati*, meaning "worthy of that. Thus, conduct and honor worthy of a *snātaka*—such as that prescribed in Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 13.2, beginning with *yatrāsmā apacitim*—must be performed. However, this conduct is not diminished for the *vratasnātaka*, nor is it increased for the *ubhayasnātaka*. 1.30.4.
Even if this is so, there is nevertheless a distinction in the fruit for the one who worships; thus he says:
"Due to the distinction in meditative absorption and the distinction in what is heard, there is a distinction in the fruit of worship. (1.30.5)
Concentration (*samādhi*) is the focused attention upon duties to be performed; *śruti* is what has been heard. 1.30.5.
Now, the observances of one who has completed his Vedic studies (snātaka). 1.30.6.

From this point forward, it should be understood that the observances of the *snātaka* are the subject under discussion. Although some of those about to be described are common to other stages of life as well, nevertheless, for the most part, the observances of the *snātaka* are what are being treated here. (1.30.6)
One should practice entering and leaving the village by the eastern gate, or by the northern one. 1.30.7.

When he goes out from a village or enters a village, he should do so by the eastern gate or the northern gate, and not by any other gate. Because of the injunction that "he should practice [this]," there is no penance even for entering or exiting by another gate if it occurs by chance. 1.30.7.
And during the two twilights, he should sit outside the village, remaining silent.

The junction of day and night is the *saṃdhi*; these two are the evening and the morning. Regarding this, Gautama states: "The two *saṃdhyās* last as long as the light is visible" (GDh 2.11). During those two *saṃdhyās*, one should sit outside the village and remain restrained in speech. Manu also says:

"One should stand reciting the *Sāvitrī* during the morning *saṃdhyā* until the appearance of the sun; but during the evening *saṃdhyā*, one should sit properly until the stars appear clearly" (MDh 2.101).

"One should stand during the morning [service] and sit during the afternoon," says Gautama (GDh 2.11). These two Smṛti rules refer to the student (*brahmacārin*), because here the injunction for sitting and the restraint of speech are prescribed for the *snātaka*. Others, however, explain that the mention of "sitting" is an elliptical indication of "standing," and that the restraint of speech refers to the cessation of worldly speech, not to the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* mantra. 1.30.8.
This is an exception concerning the case of one who has maintained the sacred fires:
"In a conflict between two rules, that which is based on direct Vedic revelation (śruti) is more authoritative. (1.3.9)

Contradiction (*virodha*) means opposition (*vipratiṣedha*). For one who maintains the *agnihotra* fire, sitting outside and performing the *agnihotra* oblation are contradictory. And thus it is heard in scripture: "This day-and-night is indeed the ocean; its two bathing-places (*tīrtha*) are the two junctions (*saṃdhi*); therefore, the oblation should be offered at the junction. In that case, only the *agnihotra* characterized by direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) must be performed, not the sitting outside prescribed by tradition (*smṛti*), because the latter has a root that must be inferred, whereas the former has a root that is already established. Jaimini also says: "But in case of contradiction, the Smṛti is to be disregarded, for there is no inference [of a Vedic basis] when such a contradiction exists" (PMS 1.3.3). || 1.20.9 ||
One should avoid all dyes on one's clothing. || 1.30.10 ||
All dyes, such as safflower and others, must be avoided on the garment; one should not wear a garment dyed by anyone. 1.30.10.
And the black [variety] is innate. || 1.30.11 ||
One should not wear anything that is black by its very nature, such as a woolen blanket or the like. 1.30.11.
He should wear a garment that does not shine brightly. 1.30.12.

It has the nature of shining; it shines intensely. Other than that, it does not shine. The lengthening [of the vowel] is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). One should wear—that is, cover oneself with—garment that is of such a kind. 1.30.12.
And [one should not neglect] what is within one's power to remedy. 1.30.13.
That which is repulsive, base, worn out, soiled, and coarse is "pratikṛṣṭa"; the opposite of that is "apratikṛṣṭa. He should wear such clothing when he has the means to do so. 1.30.13.
And during the day, he should avoid covering his head, except for the act of voiding urine or excrement. 1.30.14.

The word "ca" (and) serves to indicate a conjunction with what precedes. One should not cover one's head with a cloth or similar item even during the day. Is this rule without exception? No; it is with the exception of, that is, excluding, the act of voiding urine or excrement. 1.30.14.
But having covered his head, he should void urine and feces on the ground, having placed some covering over it.

While voiding urine or excrement, both by day and by night, one should do so with the head covered, having placed some grass or similar material upon the ground, and not directly upon the bare earth. Since the practice of acting according to one’s own will (*kāmacāra*) would otherwise apply here, it was stated that one should avoid covering the head during the day; this present rule constitutes an exception (*paryudāsa*) to that. Furthermore, since the rule “having avoided the act of voiding urine or excrement” [ĀpDh 1.30.14] was given, the state of acting according to one’s own will remains in force at the time of voiding urine or excrement. Therefore, the following is commenced: “but having covered the head. If that were the case, then let this alone suffice, and the previous exception need not exist. However, that exception must necessarily be maintained; otherwise, because the rule “but having covered the head” would find its application only at night, it would result in a prohibition for the daytime. Gautama, however, states that there is always covering at night: “One should not go about during the day with the head covered; but at night, and when voiding urine or excrement, one should go about with the head covered” [GDh 9.35–37]. 1.30.15.
One should avoid performing any ritual action in the shadow cast by urine or excrement.

Because of the observation in another Smṛti text stating, "and not on those that provide a livelihood," that [shadow] upon which travelers and others rest is what is intended; therefore, there is no prohibition against the shadow of an umbrella and the like, nor is there a prohibition against the shadow of clouds and so forth, because these cannot be avoided. 1.30.16.
But one should urinate so as not to miss one's own shadow.

The change to *tug* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Because of the explicit mention of the accusative case, the word "towards" (*prati*) must be supplied. Since urinating (*avamehana*)—meaning the act of voiding urine—is not something that can be subsisted upon, this does not fall under the scope of the previous prohibition; therefore, this is not a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). Consequently, when possible, one should urinate facing one's own shadow. 1.30.17.

One should not void urine or feces on a staircase, in a ploughed field, on a path, or in water. Likewise, one should avoid the acts of spitting and sexual intercourse in water. One should avoid performing the acts of voiding urine or feces while facing fire, the sun, water, a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, or a deity. 1.30.18.
The four [impure substances] are evident. Spitting is the discharge of saliva from the mouth and so forth. Deities are images of deities. 1.30.18.
One should avoid using stones, clods of earth, and fresh plants or trees broken off while upright for the purpose of cleansing oneself after voiding urine or excrement. 1.30.19.

Herbs (*oṣadhi*) are those whose life ends with the ripening of their fruit. Forest trees (*vanaspati*) are those that bear fruit without flowers. Because of the mention of "moist" (*ārdrān*), there is no fault in using dry [wood]. Because of the mention of "upright" (*ūrdhvān*), there is no fault in using wood broken by wind or other causes. One should not perform the purification of urine and feces with these materials, such as stones and the like. (1.30.19)
One should not, within the range of one's power, point out fire, water, a Brāhmaṇa, cattle, deities, a door, or a crosswind. 1.30.20.
When capable, one should not stretch out one's feet toward fire and other such things. || 1.30.20 ||
Moreover, they also cite this: 1.30.21.
Thus ends the thirtieth section:
One should eat food facing the east; one should speak facing the south;
one should void urine facing the north; and the washing of the feet should be done facing the west.
Thus [ends the section]. 1.31.1.

Uccāra refers to the act of voiding excrement. Pādāvanejana refers to the washing of the feet. Regarding eating and other such acts, the four directions are prescribed as follows. Manu also says: "One who eats facing east gains long life; one facing south gains fame; one facing west gains prosperity; and one facing north eats according to the cosmic order (ṛta). [MDh 2.52]

Yājñavalkya also says: "During the day and at the two twilights, one should void urine and feces with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) held around the neck and facing north; however, if it is at night, one should face south. [YDh 1.16]
One should void urine and feces far from one's dwelling, toward the southern direction or the south-western direction.

"Āvasatha" means a house; one should void urine and feces at a distance from it toward the southern direction. From the use of the accusative case, it is understood that one should go out [from the house]. "South-western" refers to the direction of Nirṛti. 1.31.2.
And when [the sun] has set, he should avoid the ritual acts of voiding urine and excrement outside the village or the dwelling. 1.31.3.

When the sun has set, one should not void urine or excrement outside the village; nor, even within the village, should one do so far from the house. This prohibition is for a visible purpose, due to the fear of thieves, tigers, and the like. In a place free from danger, there is no fault. || 1.31.3 ||
And one who is impure should not utter the names of the deities. || 1.31.4 ||
Being unpurified, one should avoid the mention of the deities, beginning with Agni. "Apidhānam" is a corrupt reading; the meaning is exactly this. 1.31.4
And he spoke harshly to both the deities and the king. || 1.31.5 ||
Regarding both the deities and the king, the dual number is used in view of the two groups [of objects]. One should avoid harshness, that is, censure. 1.31.5.
One should avoid touching the feet of a Brahmin with the word "cow."

"One should not touch a Brahmin or a cow with one's foot. The word "iti" indicates a category; by this, even non-Brahmins who are advanced in learning or age are to be excluded from such treatment. 1.31.6.
And because [the world] is grasped by the hand without a cause. 1.31.7.
The cause includes oil massage, scratching, and so forth; without these, one should avoid even touching with the hand those [objects] previously mentioned. 1.31.7.
One should avoid speaking ill of cows, sacrificial fees, and virgins. || 1.31.8 ||

One should not speak of the faults, even if they exist, of cows—even those that are not sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)—nor of sacrificial fees other than cows such as gold and the like, nor of a maiden or a young girl. While slander is prohibited as a limb of yoga in the section on the inner self (*adhyātma*), he will state immediately thereafter: "One should avoid anger and other faults that burn living beings" [ĀpDh 1.31.23]. This statement, however, is for the purpose of prescribing an additional expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the case of cows and the others. 1.31.8.
And one should not speak of a cow that is longing [for grass]. || 1.31.9 ||
One should not tell the owner that a cow, while longing for and eating crops, grain, and so forth, has done so. || 1.31.9 ||
And [the milk] mixed with the calf [is permissible] except on specific occasions. 1.31.10.

One should not say, even when there is no specific occasion, "This cow of yours is being sucked by her calf" regarding a cow that is actually joined with her calf. Because of the mention of "when there is no occasion," there is no fault for the speaker when a specific occasion exists, such as that stated in the rule: "If, after the calves have been driven away for the sake of the sacrificial oblation, they should suckle again" (ĀpŚr 9.1.23). 1.31.10.
One should not say of a non-cow, "It is a non-cow. One should rather say, "It is one that will become a cow. || 1.31.11 ||

And one should not call even that cow which is not a milch-cow "adhenus" (non-milch-cow). What then? One should say precisely "dhenubhavyā" (destined to become a milch-cow); for "dhenubhavyā" means "one who will be a milch-cow in the future. Regarding the rule "the suffix *mum* should be stated [after *dhenu*] when it is *bhavyā*," the *mum* does not occur here because, being formed with the suffix *cv*, it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). And since the rule must indeed be stated, this is a restriction of the word-form; it does not mean that one must speak in this way only upon seeing a non-milch-cow. 1.3.11.11.
One should not say "bhadra" when it is "bhadra"; one should say "puṇya" or "praśasta. || 1.31.12 ||

One should not say "what is auspicious" (*bhadram*) as "it is auspicious" (*bhadram*); rather, one should say it with either of the two terms "meritorious" (*puṇyam*) or "praiseworthy" (*praśastam*). *Praśastam* means "praised," [the lengthening of the vowel] being a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). 1.31.12.
And one should not walk over a calf’s tethering rope. || 1.31.13 ||

The "vatsatantrī" is the rope for tethering calves; one should not walk over it nor cross over it. The mention of "calves" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the bovine species in general. 1.31.13.
And one should not pass between two palanquins. || 1.31.14 ||

The *pleṅkha* are the two pillars of the swing; others say they are the two pillars of the archway (*toraṇa*). One should not pass between them; one should not go through the middle of those two. || 1.31.14 ||
He should not say, "This one is my rival. If he were to say, "This one is my rival," he would produce a hateful enemy. 1.31.15.

"One should not say in the assembly, 'This Devadatta is my rival. For what reason? If one were to say, 'He is my rival' (*sapatna*), it would mean 'one who hates'—this is a verbal derivative—and he would thereby create a hostile, envious, and competitive adversary. For when this is said, the other person thinks: 'He does not say this without cause; surely he harbors hatred toward me. Consequently, striving to counteract that [perceived hostility], the other person becomes a true rival. (1.31.15)
One should not say to another, "It is a rainbow. || 1.31.16 ||

Seeing a rainbow in the sky, one should not describe it to another by its name. If it must necessarily be mentioned, one should say "the jeweled bow" (maṇidhanuḥ), according to the teaching of Gautama (GDh 9.22). 1.31.16.
One should not look at [a bird] while it is falling. 1.31.17.

One should not look upon, nor count as "this many," the birds falling down while gathered together in a flock. Another says: one should not point out to another those virtuous ones falling from heaven due to the exhaustion of their merit, nor should one say, "The celestial lights are falling. (1.31.17)
One should avoid looking at the sun when it is rising or setting.
One should not look at the sun at the time of its rising or at the time of its setting. Manu, however, states: "One should never look at the sun when it is rising, nor when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky" (MDh 4.37).

During the day the sun protects living beings, and at night the moon. Therefore, on the night of the new moon, one should especially desire protection for oneself through conduct characterized by purity and celibacy. 1.31.19.

During the day, the sun protects beings—that is, it guards living creatures—by providing light. At night, it is the moon. Therefore, on the night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), one should desire protection for oneself more intensely. The word *svādhīyaḥ* contains the suffix *va*, which is Vedic; according to Pāṇini 5.3.63, "the forms *neda-* and *sādhu-* are used for *antika-* and *bāḍha-* respectively. Thus, it means "more intensely" or "more thoroughly. By what means? Through purity (*prāyatya*) and celibacy (*brahmacarya*), as well as by conduct at the proper time. This is the reading that accords with the sense. However, the reading currently being studied is either a scribal error or a Vedic archaism. Purity (*prāyatya*) is the state of being purified; through constant purity arising from bathing and other rites, through celibacy—which is the abandonment of sexual intercourse—and through conduct performed at the proper time, such as the worship of deities and the recitation of prayers (*japa*). (1.31.19)
But why does the moon not guard her on this night? He says:
for on this very night, both the sun and the moon dwell together. 1.31.20.
On this night—using the accusative case to denote duration—the sun and the moon dwell together for the entire night; yet there is no light from the moon while it dwells with the sun. (1.31.20)
One should not enter a village by a shortcut. If one should enter [by such a way], one should mutter this verse, "Homage to Rudra Vāstoṣpati," or another verse addressed to Rudra. 1.31.21.

A *kusṛti* is a wrong path. One should not enter a village by such a path. If, however, one must enter due to the absence of any other way, one should then mutter the verse beginning with “*namo rudrāya*” [TaitBr 3.7.9], or another verse dedicated to Rudra (*raudrī*), such as that beginning with “*imāṃ rudrāya tavase*” [TS 4.5.10]. Regarding this, the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of the Vājasaneyins states: “When about to enter a forest, he consecrates himself with the mantra: ‘*namo rudrāya vanasade svasti mā saṃpāraya*’ (Homage to Rudra who dwells in the forest; lead me safely across). When about to enter water, he consecrates himself with the mantra: ‘*namo rudrāyāpsuṣade svasti mā saṃpāraya*’ (Homage to Rudra who dwells in the waters; lead me safely across). Therefore, whatever action one may perform, one should do it all while saying ‘*namo rudrāya*’, for according to the Śruti, ‘this entire world is indeed Rudra. There is also a slight difference in this matter in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of Bharadvāja. 1.31.21.

One should not give the remains of food to one who is not a Brahmin. If one should give it, having scraped off some [of the food] with his teeth and placed it in that [person's hand], he may give it. 1.31.22.

A non-Brāhmaṇa is a Śūdra, according to the observation in the Vasiṣṭha Dharma Sūtra: "One should not give what is either leftover or not leftover to a Śūdra" (VaDh 18.14). Therefore, the rule "one should not give what is leftover" refers to one who is not dependent [on the giver]. If one should give it, this refers to one who is dependent. Having scraped the teeth with the fingernail—that is, having scraped them—and having placed that impurity into the leftover food, one should give it. In the form *skuptvā*, the change of *bh* to *c* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*) after the suffix *ktvā* from the root *skubhnāti*; or else, there is the addition of the letter *p* in the root *skunāti*. 1.31.22.
And one should avoid anger and other defects that burn living beings. || 1.31.23 ||

Anger and the other [passions] that burn the elements have been explained in the *Adhyātmapaṭala*. That statement refers to the domain of the yogin; however, this present statement is for the purpose of restraining anger and the like even in the case of a *snātaka* who is not a yogin. If it is argued that this very statement should serve both purposes—that of the yogin and that of the non-yogin—then, that being established, the statement is intended to demonstrate that the avoidance of anger and the rest is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of yoga. Consequently, if one fails to practice non-anger and so forth, the perfection of yoga simply does not occur; it does not, however, entail the penance required for the transgression of a *snātaka*'s vow. 1.31.23.
Thus ends the twenty-first section, which is consistent with the sacred teachings: one should avoid sexual intercourse during the rainy season and autumn. 1.32.1.
"Teaching" means instruction; one engaged in that should avoid sexual intercourse during the rainy season and autumn, even during the fertile period. 1.32.1.
And having united with her, he should not lie with her for the entire night. || 1.32.2 ||
Having coupled—that is, having engaged in sexual intercourse—he shall not lie down for that entire night together with his wife. || 1.32.2 ||
And while lying down, he should avoid teaching. || 1.32.3 ||
There is a prohibition against teaching while lying down, whether by day or by night; however, there is no fault for one who studies himself for the purpose of memorization. 1.32.3.
And he should not teach on that bed upon which he himself sleeps. 1.32.4.
On that bed upon which one lies with his wife at night, he shall not teach even while sitting on that same bed. 1.32.4.
He should not wear visible garlands or ointments. || 1.32.5 ||
If one were not such that garlands and ointments have appeared—that is, been manifested—for him; the change to *ṇ* is as before. 1.32.5.
One should always adorn one's wife during the night. || 1.32.6 ||

Because of the statement "with regard to his wife," the adornment is for the purpose of approaching her; therefore, this rule does not apply if she is unfit for approach due to physical incapacity or other such reasons. 1.32.6.
One should avoid diving into water with one's head submerged. || 1.32.7 ||

“Vamajjana” means immersion (*avamajjana*). The elision of the vowel *a* occurs according to the rule: “The grammarian Vāguri desires the elision of the *a* in the prefixes *ava* and *api*. “One should avoid together with the head” means one should not perform bathing with the head. All rules regarding immersion apply to those other than the *snātaka*, as well as to occasional (*naimittika*) rites. It is the teacher’s view that for a *snātaka*, the obligatory daily bath (*nityasnāna*) is not of the nature of immersion. 1.32.7.
And when [the sun] has set, there is bathing. || 1.32.8 ||
And when the sun has set, one should avoid bathing in every way. || 1.32.8 ||
One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, and the cleansing of the teeth [with a twig]. 1.32.9.

One should avoid items such as seats made of *pālāśa* wood. "Cleaning the teeth" refers to the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*). The word "iti" indicates a category; therefore, one should also avoid other household utensils made of *pālāśa* wood. (1.32.9)
And he offered praise to the Guru in his presence, saying, "You have bathed well," and so forth. (1.32.10)
And one should avoid reciting praises such as "well-bathed" and so forth in the presence of the guru.
Staying awake throughout the night. || 1.32.11 ||
