"Niśā" is the middle portion of the night; until that time, one should remain awake and not sleep. 1.32.11.
There is no suspension of study at night, except for the instruction of disciples in the Dharma. 1.32.12.
During the night there is a suspension of study; one should neither study nor teach. However, the instruction of dharma to disciples is permitted. 1.32.12
Or by himself with the mind. 1.32.13
An exception to the prohibition of study at night is as follows: "Or one may reflect upon it oneself by means of the mind. (1.32.13)
Teaching after midnight. 1.32.14.
This too is a counter-exception: teaching may take place even at night, beginning from the sixteenth *nāḍikā*. 1.32.14.
One should not go to bed thinking, "Having risen during the latter part of the night, there will be no time for study. 1.32.15.

The third part of the night is the *apararātra* (the latter part of the night). Having risen after midnight, one who teaches should not go to sleep nor lie down during the *apararātra*. Even if a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) such as that occurring on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight applies to that time, how much more so in regard to one's own private recitation (*svādhyāya*)? Thus says Manu: "Having studied the Veda, one should not sleep again at the end of the night when exhausted. (MDh 4.99) [1.32.15]
He may sleep at will. 1.32.16.

By this [verse], sleep is permitted for one who is seated while leaning against a pillar or similar support. The root *śri* means "to serve"; therein, the elision of the letter *r* is Vedic, as is the doubling of the letter *ś*. 1.32.16.
Or he may study it mentally. 1.32.17.

This [rule] also applies when one rises after midnight and finds that it is a time unfit for study (*anadhyāya*) while intending to teach; in such a case, it is said that he may study the portion already mastered in his mind, reflect upon it himself, or go to sleep after having taken refuge [in a place]. 1.32.17.
One should not frequent small, lowly regions inhabited by those of base conduct. || 1.32.18 ||
One should not associate with petty or lowly men, nor should one dwell in regions inhabited by low-caste people such as Niṣādas and others.
Assemblies and social gatherings. || 1.32.19 ||
Assemblies and social gatherings have been explained; one should not frequent them. 1.32.19.
If he should go to a social gathering, he should depart after having circumambulated it clockwise.
If he should go through a settlement for the sake of alms, he should then circumambulate it to the right and depart—that is, leave it. || 1.32.20 ||
And one should avoid entering cities. || 1.32.21 ||
Because of the use of the plural form, one must not enter the city many times; furthermore, there is an expiation for entering it occasionally or by chance. 1.32.21.
And he should not fail to answer a question. 1.32.22.

*Vivicya* means having analyzed the statement; *vivacanam* means a definitive conclusion. One should not speak regarding a matter that has been asked without having analyzed it, saying "it is thus. This refers to a subject matter that is difficult to determine. || 1.32.22 ||
Moreover, they also cite this: 1.32.23.
Moreover, regarding this matter, they cite this verse: || 1.32.23 ||
The root of one who speaks ill destroys his offspring,
cattle, and his dwelling; it is for the crushing of dharma and the destruction of the young.
Weeping, Death indeed answered the question. Thus [ends the section]. 1.32.24.

He who, having hastily determined a matter that is difficult to ascertain, speaks ill of it or describes it otherwise—that evil speaker tears away both the root and the tuft of that very evil speech. The "root" refers to his father and other elders; the "tuft" refers to future prosperity; he uproots and destroys both of these. The letter *va* is labio-dental. Is this all? No. He also destroys his offspring, such as sons and so forth, his cattle, such as cows and so forth, and his abode, such as his house and so forth. Therefore, because of the possibility of speaking ill, one should not even answer a question [with falsehood]. Here is an ancient legend: A certain sage had two disciples named Dharmaprahāda and Kumālana.

Once, having brought two large loads of sacrificial fuel from the forest, those two, out of exhaustion, threw them into the teacher’s house without having inspected the area. By one of them, the teacher’s infant son was stepped upon and killed. Then the teacher, having summoned his two disciples, asked: "By whom was this boy killed? Both of them said, "Not by me. Thereupon, unable to abandon the fallen child while accepting the innocent, the seer summoned Death and asked: "By whom was this one slain? Then, as he was caught in a dilemma of dharma, Death, weeping, answered the question after due deliberation. How so? "O Prahrāda of Dharma! For the sake of the child (*kumāranāya*). The fourth case ending is used in the sense of the sixth; thus, "this [act] is not for the sake of the child. While it should have been said, "O Prahrāda of Dharma, this was done by you," he said instead that it was not done by the other; yet, even so, it is understood by implication that it was done by the other—thus he spoke while weeping. The particle *ha* is for the purpose of indicating tradition (*aitihya*). In the word *Prahrāda*, the letter *ra* following the letter *ha* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). (1.32.24)
He should avoid mounting a donkey vehicle and ascending or descending uneven heights. 1.32.25.

One should avoid mounting a vehicle such as a cart yoked with donkeys; one should not mount it. Likewise, one should avoid ascending and descending uneven ground—ascending on high places and descending into low places. (1.32.25)
And one should cross a river with the arms. || 1.32.26 ||
*Taraṇa* means crossing. One should avoid crossing a river by means of one's arms. Because of the specific mention of "by means of the arms," there is no fault in using a boat or similar means.
And one should not board a boat that is in doubt [of its seaworthiness]. || 1.32.27 ||

One should avoid a boat that is "doubtful," meaning it has fallen into a state of uncertainty as to whether it will sink or not; such a worn-out boat should be shunned. In the reading where the word *nāvām* ends in the genitive case, the meaning is: "among boats, one should avoid the doubtful boat. (1.32.27)
And [he should avoid] cutting grass, trampling clods of earth, or spitting without a reason. 1.32.28.
One should not perform acts such as cutting grass without a specific reason. The reason for spitting is a condition such as a catarrh; in other cases, [the reason] must be sought.
And whatever else they proclaim, and whatever else they proclaim. || 1.32.29 ||

And whatever else is similarly proscribed by the teachers, that too—such as gambling with dice and so forth—one should avoid. The repetition [of the concluding phrase] is for the purpose of indicating the end of the inquiry. 1.32.29.
Thus ends the thirty-second section and the eleventh chapter in the *Ujjvalā*, a commentary on the Dharma composed by Haradatta Miśra.
And the first question concerns the vow of the two householders from the time of taking the hand in marriage. 2.1.1.

In the previous question (*praśna*), the duties (*dharma*) of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) were for the most part stated in the first two chapters; in the subsequent eight, those of all the stages of life (*āśrama*); and in the eleventh, those of the one who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*). Now, the rites to be performed beginning from the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) are declared—the day on which the hand is taken is "the taking of the hand. The prefix *adhi* is used in the sense of "above" or "after. Therefore, that vow which is to be performed by the two householders (*gṛhamedhin*), i.e., those belonging to the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*), is now stated; the singular number is used for the genus. The expression "from the taking of the hand onwards" is intended so that there may be no option as stated in another scripture, namely, "The fire begins with the wife, or with the inheritance" (GDh 5.7). The dual number in "of the two householders" is intended so that the rule does not cease upon the death of either one. However, even those who are bereft of a wife (*vidhura*) perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. 2.1.1.
Eating at the two [proper] times. 2.1.2.

Eating must be performed at both times: in the evening and in the morning; it is not to be restricted to one alone, because eating is already established by natural inclination (*rāga*). This is also made explicit in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]: "For the twice-born, eating in the evening and in the morning is enjoined by the Śruti.
One should not eat in between; this rule is equal to the Agnihotra sacrifice."

Others, however, consider this a restrictive rule (*niyama*): that when there is the capacity [to eat], one must necessarily consume [food] at both times so as not to interrupt the *prāṇāgnihotra*. And thus says Baudhāyana:

"Whether he be a student (*brahmacārī*) or a householder (*gṛhastha*), whoever practices austerity while fasting would become one who has broken his vow (*avakīrṇin*) due to the interruption of the *prāṇāgnihotra*. [BDh 2.7.9]
Except in the case of a penance; for regarding the penance, however, that very same rule applies. 2.1.2.
And there is no satiety with food. 2.1.3.

When used in connection with words having the sense of *suhita* (“satisfied”), the sixth case ending occurs for the instrumental; this is because of the rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārtha-* [Pāṇini 2.2.11], which indicates this. They should not attain satisfaction by means of food. One should not eat until satisfaction is reached. 2.1.3.
And on the festival days (parvan) of both [the lunar fortnights], there shall be fasting. 2.1.4.

The junction of the lunar fortnights is the *parvan*. Here, however, the day associated with that junction is intended. On those *parvan* days, both husband and wife must observe a fast; fasting consists in the omission of eating. (2.1.4)
Since it would otherwise follow that both times [for eating] apply without distinction, he says:
"In the other time, there is only the eating of the fast-food. (2.1.5)

That which is eating at one time during another period is also indeed *aupavasta*, that is, fasting itself; for the *Nighaṇṭu* states: “*Aupavasta* is fasting (*upavāsa*)”. That too is during the day and not at night, because it is seen so in the *Śrauta* texts: “He should not eat in the evening. Thus, the fasting mentioned here in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* in the passage beginning with “In this way, from now on” [ĀpGṛ 7.17] has been explained. 2.1.5.
And he should be satisfied with food. 2.1.6.
On the festival days, eating only once, they should eat as much as they require for satiety.
And whatever may be dear to these two, that they should eat on this day. 2.1.7.

It should not be said "on this day," because that is already established by context. Just as the rule "and [the eating] of food without satiety" (ĀpDh 2.1.3) applies to the *parvan* days, so too will this [present rule] apply there. Furthermore, it is not very appropriate for the singular term "on one day" (*ekasmin ahani*) to refer back to the plural term "on the *parvan* days" (*parvasu*) which is the subject under discussion. Therefore, even though it is separated in the text, the act of taking the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) is what is referred to by the word "day. For this very purpose, it is stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*: "One should recognize this day as the day on which he brought home his wife" (ĀpGṛ 8.7). On this day of the hand-taking, the couple should eat whatever is dear to them; however, this is not the scope of the prohibition: "one should not cook choice food for oneself alone" (ĀpDh 2.8.4). And this should be performed every year. For example, if one has performed the marriage under the asterism *Svāti* in the month of Caitra, then in the following year also, it should be done in that same month; for thus it becomes "that very same day. However, if it were performed every month upon the arrival of the same asterism, since the months differ—such as Caitra and others—it would not be recognized as "that very same [day]. Therefore, this should be performed every year under the asterism of the marriage. Just as there is an asterism for the consecration of kings, so there is an asterism for the marriage of householders. (2.1.7)
And they should sleep on the ground. 2.1.8.
On this very day, they two should sleep on the bare ground.
And the avoidance of sexual intercourse. 2.1.9.
And on this day, one must abstain from sexual intercourse. || 2.1.9 ||
On the following day, there is the preparation of a mess of cooked food (sthālīpāka).
And on the following day, a *sthālīpāka* (cooked offering) is to be performed. || 2.1.10 ||
The ritual procedure for that [offering] is explained by [the rules of] the Pārvaṇa [śrāddha]. 2.1.11.

The procedure for that *sthālīpāka*—the manner of its performance—is explained by reference to the *pārvaṇa* rite. This very statement indicates that the extension (*atideśa*) from the *pārvaṇa* does not apply to the *sāmayācārika* (customary) rites. However, some consider all of this to pertain specifically to the *parvan* (full-moon and new-moon) sacrifices; the fault in their view has already been stated. Furthermore, the expression "explained by the *pārvaṇa*" would be untenable, for a thing cannot be explained by itself. Moreover, the injunction "on the following day, the *sthālīpāka* [is performed]" [ĀpDh 2.1.10] would be redundant, since it has already been prescribed previously in the rule: "It should be performed on the *parvan* days by those who have fasted" [ĀpGṛ 7.17]. And the purpose of the rule "one should recognize this day" [ĀpGṛ 8.7] must be considered under that [other] view. 2.1.11.
People always teach this in the world. || 2.1.12 ||

In the world, regarding the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), it is established that this rite must be performed annually; thus the learned teach. Another says: the rite to be described hereafter is established by the conduct of the learned as a constant, universal duty; so the learned teach. (2.1.2)
Wherever they shall kindle the fire, there, having drawn three lines facing east and three facing north and having sprinkled them with water, they should kindle the fire. 2.1.13.

In connection with the *homa* (fire sacrifice), this is stated: whenever one is about to kindle or establish the fire in any domestic (*gārhya*) or conventional (*sāmayācārika*) rite—whether at home or in the forest—one should first draw three lines directed toward the east with their tips pointing eastward; then, having drawn three lines directed toward the north with their tips pointing northward, one should sprinkle them with water. Having sprinkled them and established the fire brought from the house of a learned *śrotriya*, one should kindle it—that is, one should set the fire ablaze with pieces of wood. Regarding this, it has been defined by the general rule: "The commencement is from the east or from the north, and the conclusion is likewise" (*ĀpGṛ* 1.5–6). Furthermore, according to the order of instruction, the eastern lines are to be drawn first, and then the northern ones.
One should first draw the eastern lines ending toward the south and beginning from the north;
likewise, one should draw the northern lines situated in front and beginning from the west.
Others, however, draw the boundary walls beginning from the south. || 2.1.13 ||
Having poured out this water, one should place another vessel to the north or to the east.
He should pour out this water remaining from the sprinkling to the north or the east of the fire. Having poured it out, he should place another vessel of water right there. 2.1.14.
Water-vessels should never be empty of water; this is the vow of the two householders. (2.1.15)

In the house, all water-receptacles—such as water-jars, small bowls, pots, and the like—should always remain unfilled with water. This too is a vow for the two householders. Furthermore, the dual number used for "the two householders" (*gṛhamedhinor*) in this ritual is intended to ensure that they themselves are the performers (*kartṛ*), so that they do not become mere instigators (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). Another teacher says: because of the repeated mention of "the two householders," the preceding rule applies to the student (*brahmacārin*) in cases such as "a thousand pieces of wood with the Sāvitrī verse" (ĀpDh 1.27.1); however, in the case of cooking, it does not apply to the woman because the gender in the word "about to kindle" (*upasamādhāsyan*) is intended to be significant, whereas in the rule "noble men, being purified" (ĀpDh 2.3.1), it does apply. 2.1.15.
He shall not sleep during the day. 2.1.16.
Copulation is sexual intercourse; that must not be performed during the day. 2.1.16.
And during the fertile period, he should unite with his wife according to the vow. (2.1.17)

The menstrual period (*ṛtu*) begins from the appearance of menses and lasts for sixteen days and nights. During that time, sexual union (*saṃnipāta*) with one's wife must be performed. The singular number here is Vedic; for the word *dāra* (wife) always ends in the plural. "In accordance with the vow" (*anuvratam*): a "vow" (*vrata*) is a restriction according to the scriptures, and [the act] is done in conformity with that. Regarding this, Manu says: "The natural menstrual period of women is recorded as sixteen nights, together with the other four days which are censured by the virtuous. (Manusmṛti 3.46)
Of these, the first four nights, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are to be censured; the remaining ten nights are praised.
[The nights of] the new moon, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth—
"A twice-born man who has completed his student-bath (snātaka) should always remain a celibate student (brahmacārī), even during the fertile period. [MDh 4.128] Yājñavalkya, however, says:
"Approaching his wife in this manner, he should avoid her when she is emaciated, as well as the *makhā* and *mūla* constellations. [YDh 1.80]

The Teacher (Ācārya), however, prescribes approaching [the wife] from the fourth night onwards: "They teach that from the fourth night until the sixteenth, one should approach her on each successive later night for procreation, as this leads to superior offspring during the fertile season" (ĀpGṛ 9.1). Thus, among these sixteen nights, the first three must be avoided under all circumstances. The fourth, eleventh, and thirteenth nights are permitted by the Teacher but prohibited by Manu. Among the remaining ten nights, sons are born on the even-numbered nights and daughters on the odd-numbered nights. Furthermore, because of the statement "on each successive later night" (ĀpGṛ 9.1), for one who approaches on the sixteenth night—provided there is no conjunction with the *Makhā* constellation or others—the son will be preeminent in every respect. On the fourth night, the offspring is inferior; in between, it is middling. Likewise, on the fifteenth night, a daughter is preeminent; on the fifth, she is inferior; in between, she is middling. Approaching on these sixteen nights alone is the cause of conception, and even then, primarily on the first [of those permitted]. This being the case, this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*): when capable, one must certainly unite during the fertile season; failing to do so, one would incur sin by obstructing the birth of a son. Accordingly, there is a traditional teaching regarding the fault [of not doing so].

"But if a man does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and he is present, his ancestors lie in her menstrual flow for that month" (BDh 4.1.18). There is no fault for one who avoids each preceding [wife] out of a desire for the specific qualities of a son. Others, however, consider this to be a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāna*), meaning: "One should unite only during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and not at other times. For them, since there would be no fault even in not approaching during the fertile period because there is no fixed rule regarding it, the traditional teaching on the fault would be untenable. In any case, this is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because the act of uniting is already prompted by natural passion (*rāga*). 2.1.17.
Even in the interval, it is indeed the wife alone. 2.1.18.

In the interval between the two seasons, even in the middle of that interval, there may be a union provided the wife is desirous. Even though, due to his own self-control, he lacks such subjection to passion, nevertheless, when the wife herself is desirous, he must certainly unite with her for the sake of protecting her. And the author will say: "Guard this thread with vigilance" (ĀpDh 2.13.6). Because of the continued application of the term "in accordance with the vow" (ĀpDh 2.1.17), this does not occur on days that are prohibited. 2.1.18.
And the sexual union [is permitted] according to the word of a Brāhmaṇa. 2.1.19.
Regarding this aforementioned act of lying together, the word of the Brāhmaṇa is the authority: "May we cohabit until the birth of a child" (TS 2.5.1). 2.1.19.
The union should take place while she is still wearing her woman's garment. 2.1.20.

The particle *eva* is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*). "Women's clothing" (*strīvāsa*) refers to clothing for the purpose of sexual enjoyment with women; by such [clothing], there can only be sexual union, and not the performance of rites such as the *brahmayajña*, even if it has been thoroughly washed. (2.1.20)
As well as communal gatherings and sleeping together. 2.1.21.
Up until their union, the husband and wife share a bed together. 2.1.21.
From that, diversity. 2.1.22.
Thereafter, they should sleep separately. 2.1.22.
Touching water. 2.1.23.
Then both of them must perform the ritual bathing by touching water; this applies during the period following menstruation. 2.1.23.
Thus ends the first section.
Alternatively, having washed off the smears, sipped water, and sprinkled the limbs, [one should proceed]. 2.2.1.

Alternatively, having washed with water and earth those stains of semen and dust, and having sipped water (ācamya), one should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the limbs beginning with the head; this [is the rule] for times other than the period of menstruation. 2.2.1.
For all social classes, there is supreme and immeasurable happiness in the performance of their own respective duties.

When all the specific duties (*svadharma*) of the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—whether those pertaining to caste, those pertaining to the stages of life (*āśrama*), or those pertaining to both—are performed without deficiency until their completion, there arises the supreme, most excellent, immeasurable, and imperishable happiness known as heaven. (2.2.2)
Therefore, it is not only this much. What then?

Following that, upon rebirth, by means of the remainder of the fruit of karma, one obtains birth, form, complexion, strength, intelligence, wisdom, wealth, and the practice of dharma. That proceeds happily in both worlds like a wheel. || 2.2.3 ||

Then, following the experience of happiness, there occurs a transition, which is birth in this world. And in that [birth], by means of whatever remainder of karma is yet to be experienced, one obtains a caste such as Brāhmaṇa and so forth, or birth in a distinguished family; a beautiful form, a complexion like gold and the like; strength capable of subduing adversaries; intelligence (*medhā*), the power to grasp texts; wisdom (*prajñā*), the power to grasp their meaning; wealth such as gold and other assets; and the performance of dharma. By the use of the particle *iti*, whatever else is likewise appropriate, all that is obtained. In every case, the remainder of dharma is the cause. Actions being experienced are experienced with a remainder, because even the taking up of a body in this life and so forth are the fruits of action. It has been stated: "one obtains the performance of dharma. When this is the case, the passage beginning with "In the performance of their own dharma for all castes" (ĀpDh 2.2.2) and ending with "obtains" is established even without being explicitly stated, as it occurs again [in each subsequent life]. Therefore, like a wheel, one revolves through both worlds—this one and the next—in nothing but happiness. The meaning is that one never experiences suffering; rather, the cycle of rebirth proceeds solely through a continuous succession of happiness. 2.2.3.
To show that the formative processes (saṃskāras) for the arising of the body are also necessarily required, he states an illustration:
"Just as there is an increase in the fruit of medicinal herbs and forest trees depending on the specific qualities of the seed, the field, and the cultivation, so it is [with the body]. (2.2.4)

A comparison should be understood here: just as in the case of medicinal herbs such as rice and the like, or forest trees such as the mango and the like, there is an increase in the fruit when the seed is sown in a particular field, with a particular treatment, and with a particular preparation; or rather, when the field itself undergoes a particular treatment such as plowing and so forth. Those same rice seeds, when sown in saline soil, do not sprout, but when sown in a field prepared by plowing and other means, they become stalk-bearing plants. In the same way, it should be understood regarding a person who has been perfected by the sacraments (saṃskāra) beginning with conception (garbhādhāna). 2.2.4.
By this, the increase of the fruit of the fault has been stated. || 2.2.5 ||

By this very same principle, the increase of the fruits of evil actions should also be understood as having been explained. Therein, by means of analogy (*ūha*), one should recite the opposite of "of all castes" (*sarvavarṇānām*) and so forth: "In the non-performance of their own duties (*svadharma*), there is supreme and immeasurable suffering for all castes" [cf. ĀpDh 2.2.2]. Consequently, through the remainder of the fruits of those actions, one obtains such defective substances as birth and so forth; thus, that performance of unrighteousness (*adharma*) revolves like a wheel, resulting in nothing but suffering in both worlds. It is just as there is a loss of fruit for seeds of medicinal herbs and trees when there is an absence of specific conditions regarding the field and the labor. 2.2.5.
He provides an illustration regarding the increase of the fruits of the faults:

"A Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya who has been accused of theft is born in the next world in an immeasurable hell; and upon returning to this world, he is born as a Caṇḍāla if he was a Brāhmaṇa, a Paulkasa if he was a Rājanya, or a Vaiṇa if he was a Vaiśya. (2.2.6)

A thief is one who steals gold; an accused person is a slayer of a Brahmin. Whether a thief or an accused person, a member of the [higher] castes such as a Brāhmaṇa, having experienced the fruit of his transgression in immeasurable hells in that other world, is born as a Caṇḍāla when that [state] has occurred and its effects are exhausted; a Rājanya (Kṣatriya) is born as a Paulkasa. A Pulkasa is one born from a Śūdra father and a Kṣatriya mother; he himself is a Paulkasa, the suffix *aṇ* being applied according to the rule for words beginning with *prajñā*. A Vaiśya is born as a Vaiṇa, a Vaiṇa being a bamboo-dancer. || 2.2.6 ||

By this same principle, others who have brought about the destruction of their own status through actions that result in defects are born in wombs characterized by such defects, just as in the case of the destruction of one's caste.

"Loss of caste" (*varṇaparidhvaṃsa*) means falling away from one's caste. In that loss of caste, just as Brāhmaṇas and others are born as Caṇḍālas and so forth, in this same manner, others besides thieves and those accused of crimes are also born in wombs such as those of pigs—which bear the fruits of their faulty actions—having become "ruined" (*paridhvaṃsa*), meaning they have fallen from their own caste; such persons are to be understood in that way. (2.2.7)
In the case of touching a Caṇḍāla, conversing with one, or seeing one, there is a fault; for that, there is an expiation. 2.2.8.

There is a fault in touching a Caṇḍāla; likewise in conversing with one, and in seeing one. The term "Caṇḍāla" is connected even with the preceding [terms]. In all those cases, the penance will be stated. (2.2.8)
Immersing oneself in water, touching it, conversing with a Brāhmaṇa during conversation, and seeing the luminaries when looking at them [purify]. (2.2.9)

When there is contact [with such a person], the expiation is simply immersion in water. The two following [verses] are straightforward. The mention of expiations in the section concerning the praise of one's own duties is for the purpose of censuring those who have fallen away from their own duties. Indeed, he is so called a despised Caṇḍāla for whom there is expiation upon being seen; for such a Brāhmaṇa is born who has fallen away from his own duty. (2.2.9)
Thus ends the second section;
thus ends the first chapter in the second book of the *Ujjvalā*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Noble and self-restrained persons should be the preparers of the food for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. 2.3.1.

The "noble ones" (*āryāḥ*) are those of the three [higher] castes, or Śūdras who have been consecrated by a noble person, as seen from the subsequent passage [ĀpDh 2.3.4]. They should be "careful," meaning purified by bathing and other means, in the cooking intended for the *vaiśvadeva* offering and for the meal of the householder; this is seen from the rule [ĀpDh 2.3.12]: "Of whatever food there is belonging to the householder... They should be the preparers of the food—food consisting of what is chewed, eaten, drunk, and so forth—and they should prepare that. Neither [the householder] himself nor women [should do so]. 2.3.1.
One should avoid food while facing someone who is speaking, coughing, or sneezing. 2.3.2.

Speech is the utterance of words; coughing is the rattling sound in the throat; sneezing is the act of blowing the nose. One should not perform these three while facing food. Although the plural number is used in the rule "they shall be the preparers" (ĀpDh 2.3.1), the singular form "one should avoid" is employed because the instruction applies to each individual act. 2.3.2.
Having touched his hair, his body, or his garment, he should touch water. || 2.3.3 ||

Having caught hold of, or touched, one's own hair or that of another, one should touch water. This is not a formal bath (*snāna*); what then? It is merely a touching. Although touching water was already prescribed previously upon touching hair, this statement is made so that the optional touching of cow-dung and other substances mentioned there shall not apply here. (2.3.3)
Or, Śūdras who have been consecrated by the noble ones may be the preparers. || 2.3.4 ||
Śūdras presided over by members of the three higher castes may be the preparers; this is understood from the context to refer to the food. (2.3.4)
For them, that same rule for sipping water applies. || 2.3.5 ||

For those Śūdras who are authorized to prepare food, that same rule for sipping water (ācamana) is to be understood as applicable which applies to the one whose food they cook: if it is for a Brāhmaṇa, with water reaching the heart; if for a Kṣatriya, with water reaching the throat; if for a Vaiśya, with water reaching the palate. And there is also the touching of the sense organs. 2.3.5.
Every day, he should shave his hair, beard, body hair, and nails.
Śūdras, while cooking, shall have their hair and so forth shaved every day; this is their additional [duty] compared to the Āryas. 2.3.6.
And he shall touch water along with his garment. || 2.3.7 ||

They should perform their bath together with their clothes. However, for the Āryas, having set aside the garment they were wearing, the bath may be performed even with only a loincloth (*kaupīna*) to cover them. This also applies to Śūdras, except when performing cooking. Thus says Manu:
"One should not constantly bathe with one's clothes, nor in an unknown body of water.
Or alternatively, they may sow [the seeds] only on the eighth days or on the festival days (parvan).

Or if they should have the hair and so forth shaved only on the eighth days, or only on the festival days (parvan), and not every day—"should shave" (*vapen*) here implies a causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*), meaning "they should cause [the barber] to shave. And thus, in the earlier rule "shaving of the body hair and nails" (*lomanakhavāpanam*, ĀpDh 2.3.6), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) was employed. 2.3.8.
When food has been prepared out of sight, one should place it over the fire and sprinkle it with water;
that they call the "purification for the gods. (2.3.9)

If Śūdras should prepare food out of sight while supervised by Āryas, then that food prepared out of sight, once brought forth, he himself should place upon the fire. Having placed it on the fire, he should sprinkle it with water. Such food as this they call "divine-purifying" (*devapavitra*); it is purifying even for the gods, how much more so for humans! 2.3.9.
When the food is prepared, standing [there], he should announce to the master, "It is ready. (2.3.10)

When the food has been prepared and cooked, one who is standing near or supervising the cooking should say, "It is ready" (*bhūtam*). To whom? To the owner for whose sake that food is intended. "Ready" (*bhūtam*) means "completed. (2.3.10)
"Subhūti, that is the Virāj, the food; let it not perish"—this is the reply. || 2.3.11 ||

The mantra beginning with “*tat subhūtam*” is the response. That food is *subhūta*, meaning well-prepared; it is the *virāj*, the food that is the means for shining forth (*virājanasādhana*). And the meaning is: “May that not be exhausted (*mā kṣāyi*), may it not be depleted. (2.3.11)
Whatever oblations and offerings of food a householder performs, they are connected with heaven and prosperity. (2.3.12)

Whatever food is available to a householder, whether cooked or uncooked, from a portion of that he should perform the oblations and offerings (bali) to be described hereafter; heaven and prosperity are their reward. 2.3.12.
During the employment of these mantras, for twelve days one should sleep on the ground, observe celibacy, and avoid alkaline substances and salt. (2.3.13)

Regarding the application of those mantras used for the *homās* and *balis*: "application" (*upayoga*) means the acquisition of knowledge according to prescribed rules. Thus says Baudhāyana: "In the case of their acquisition, there is a period of twelve nights," and so forth. During that time, one must sleep on the ground, sleep on the bare earth (*sthaṇḍila*), observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) by abstaining from sexual intercourse, and avoid alkaline and salty foods. This vow belongs specifically to the user (*upayoktṛ*), because it is an auxiliary to the study (*adhyayana*). Others, however, maintain that it applies to the wife as well, asserting that "application" refers to the first performance of the rite, and that the wife has a right to participate therein. (2.3.13)
For the highest [offense], there is a fast for one night. 2.3.14.

For the highest [rite], which will be described as "by the highest [rite] into the air" (ĀpDh 2.4.8), and for this [mantra] "those beings who roam" (BauGṛ 2.8.39), a fast of one night must be observed. || 2.3.14 ||
In the case of each of those offerings, the consecration consists of wiping with the hand,
sprinkling water, and placing them down, followed by the final sprinkling.

Among the offerings, the purification of each individual offering must be performed. What, then, is this? It is wiping with the hand and sprinkling with water. Having performed that, one pours out the offering. After having poured it out, the final sprinkling (pariṣecana) is to be performed. Although this is already established by the sequence of the instruction itself, they say that the specific mention of "afterwards" is for the purpose of allowing the giving of perfumes, garlands, and so forth in the middle. The expression "of each individual" is used so that—even though it is possible to do so—wiping and sprinkling are not done only once; rather, they should be performed separately even for those offerings gathered together in a single place. 2.3.15.
In the *aupāsana* or the cooking fire, he should offer oblations with his hand, using each of the first six mantras one by one. 2.3.16.

The fire on which the cooking is performed is the *pacanāgni*. For those who maintain the *aupāsana* fire, the offering is made in the *aupāsana* fire; for those such as widowers (*vidhura*) and others, it is in the *pacana* fire—thus there is a settled option. Others, however, consider this to be an optional choice. With the first six: “Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Svāhā to Dhruva Bhauma! Svāhā to Dhruvakṣiti! Svāhā to Acyutakṣiti! [cf. BauGṛ 2.8.9]. For these mantras are recited in the section of the mantra-text preceding the marriage mantras; because they require specific restrictive rules, they are included along with them. Some offer a seventh oblation to Sviṣṭakṛt as well, saying “Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt,” asserting that its application occurs everywhere in rites where medicinal herbs (*auṣadha*) serve as the sacrificial offering (*havis*). Others, however, do not recite “Svāhā to Soma,” but recite the Sviṣṭakṛt as the sixth. The mention of “taking by the hand” is intended to exclude other materials and the like. 2.3.16.
The sprinkling on both sides is as described previously. 2.3.17.

The sprinkling (pariṣecana) should be performed both before and after [the Vaiśvadeva offering]. How? Just as it was stated previously in the Gṛhya-sūtra: "O Aditi, give your consent" (ĀpGṛ 2.3.8). Since it has been made known that the extension (atideśa) from the Pārvaṇa does not apply to the rites based on customary practice (sāmayācārika), this is an injunction for what was not otherwise established (aprāptavidhi). Others, however, consider this to be a restrictive injunction (parisaṃkhyā), meaning that in the Vaiśvadeva there is only the sprinkling and no other ritual framework (tantra). 2.3.17.
Thus, for the offerings gathered in various places, there is a single sprinkling of water around them at the end.

Just as the sprinkling (pariṣecana) for the six oblations is performed once as a common procedure (*tantra*) because of their feasibility, so too regarding the offerings (*bali*) that are gathered in one place—such as those beginning with "with the following [verses] at the seat of Brahman" (ĀpDh 2.4.4)—the sprinkling which is obtained at the end, prescribed by the rule "sprinkling behind" (ĀpDh 2.3.15), should be performed once at the very end of all, not separately for each. If this sūtra did not exist, then because of the previous statement "for each of those" (ĀpDh 2.3.15), just as the wiping and the sprinkling with water are done separately for each, so too would the sprinkling be. However, here, precisely because of the specific instruction (*upadeśa*), the sprinkling is performed only once for those offerings situated in one place, and not in the case of a mere incidental gathering. Therefore, even though the north-eastern part of the house is the place for the bed, nevertheless, there is a separate sprinkling for the offering associated with desire (*kāma-liṅga*). 2.3.18.
When available, they should be performed with well-prepared [food]. || 2.3.19 ||

If there is soup, the offerings (balis) should be made mixed with it. Others, however, desire that they be mixed with other condiments as well. Thus says Baudhāyana: "At will, in the case of other receptacles" [BauGṛ 2.8.5]. For this is the preparation of the condiments. The meaning of the Sūtra is also: "The offerings should be made with food well-mixed with condiments, provided that it is available. (2.3.19)
To the west of the fire, he performs the rite with the seventh and eighth [verses], ending toward the north.

To the west of the fire, the offering of the bali should be performed with the seventh and eighth [formulas], namely, “To Dharma, svāhā! To Adharma, svāhā! (Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.8.11). This should be done ending toward the north, not ending toward the east. 2.3.20.
In the vicinity of a water reservoir, with the ninth [verse]. 2.3.21.
Where water is kept is the *udadhāna*, known as a *maṇika* (water-jar); in its vicinity, with the ninth [offering], namely "To the waters, svāhā" [Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.8.9]. 2.3.21.
In the middle of the house, with the tenth and eleventh [lines], ending toward the east.

With these two [formulas], “Svāhā to the herbs and forest trees! Svāhā to the Rākṣasas and the divine folk! [Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.8.17], one should perform [the rite] in the middle of the house, ending toward the east. 2.3.22.
In the north-eastern region of the house, with the four [bricks] to the north. || 2.3.23 ||

In the north-eastern part of the house, with the four following mantras—“Svāhā to the household deities, svāhā to the boundaries, svāhā to the lords of the boundaries, svāhā to all beings”—he offers oblations ending toward the east. 2.3.23.
Thus ends the third section:
[the ritual] at the place of the bed with the Kāmalinga mantra. 2.4.1.
At the place where he lies down, with the mantra: "To desire, svāhā" (Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.8.18). || 2.4.1 ||
On the threshold, by means of the mark of the intermediate space. || 2.4.2 ||

The *dehalī* is the wooden threshold at the bottom of the door; others say it is the lower ledge (*vedikā*) beneath that. And the intermediate door is also included there, by means of the characteristic mark of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), with the formula: "Svāhā to the intermediate space" (Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.8.26). 2.4.2.
With the northern [hand], he covers the lid.

That by which the door is closed is the *apidhānī*, the leaf of the door; others say it is the *argala* (bolt). Therein, with the subsequent mantra, "Whatever stirs and whatever moves in the world, that is a portion of Name; to Name, svāhā" [Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.8.29], he performs the rite. 2.4.3.
With the following [verses], [one should worship] in the abode of Brahmā. || 2.4.4 ||

Because the word "of the house" (*agārasya*) is understood from the preceding context, that place called the *brahmasadana* which is well-known in the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*) as being in the middle of the house—there, with the ten subsequent [offerings]: "To the earth, svāhā! To the atmosphere, svāhā! To the sky, svāhā! To the sun, svāhā! To the moon, svāhā! To the stars, svāhā! To Indra, svāhā! To Bṛhaspati, svāhā! To Prajāpati, svāhā! To Brahman, svāhā! [Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.8.33]—[he should offer] ending toward the east. Another says: since that place has already been utilized in the rule "in the middle of the house" [Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.3.22], the *brahmasadana* is where the Brahman priest sits to the south of the fire during domestic rites. 2.4.4.

To the south, with the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and the hand turned downwards, he should perform the rites for the ancestors using formulas containing ancestral signs. || 2.4.5 ||

To the south of the subsequent offerings, he should present an offering with the characteristic mark of the ancestors (pitṛliṅga), using the formula "Svadhā to the ancestors," while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), keeping the hand turned downwards, and raising the right hand so that it is palm upwards, offering between the thumb and the forefinger.
The *raudra* [offering] follows next, as in the case of the deities. 2.4.6.

To the north of the *pitṛbali* (ancestral offering), the *raudrabali* (offering to Rudra) is to be performed, just as for the other deities. The meaning is that the rule “wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) with the palm turned downwards (*avācīnapāṇiḥ*)” [ĀpDh 2.4.5] does not apply here. The mantra is: “*namo rudrāya paśupataye svāhā*. Although this mantra contains the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Paśupati as well, nevertheless, since it is an epithet of Rudra alone, the designation “*raudra*” (belonging to Rudra) is not untenable. They also perform the recollection of the deity using simply “to Rudra. Others say: “to Rudra, the Lord of Beasts (*paśupati*). Some, however, explain that the subsequent mantra belongs to Rudra and does not have Paśupati as its presiding deity; according to them, the location is either to the east or to the north of the ancestral offering (*pitrya*). 2.4.6.
The sprinkling for those two is separate, because of the difference in the *darbha* grass.

Even when those two oblations just mentioned are combined in one place, the sprinkling (pariṣecana) must be performed separately for each. Why? Because of the difference in their ritual characteristics (dharma). For the ancestral rite (pitrya), the sprinkling is counter-clockwise; for the other, because it belongs to the gods (daivata), it is clockwise.
At night, indeed, by means of the highest [concentration], one attains the power of moving through the air.

With the verse, “Those beings who roam at night, seeking the offering, the servants of Vitudas—to them I bring the offering, desiring prosperity; may the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity upon me, svāhā,” he should offer the *vaihāyasa* (aerial) oblation. And that indeed must be at night. Because of the word “aerial,” the offering is to be thrown into the open air itself, not in a place enclosed by a roof. Thus says Baudhāyana: “As he throws it into the open air with the words ‘those beings... Another says: the particle *eva* is out of its natural order, meaning that the oblation is offered at night with the *uttama* verse alone. In that case, there is a cessation of other offerings at night. Others, however, by means of an *ūha* (modification), offer the oblation even during the day, using the words “seeking the offering by day,” since such is seen in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra: “To those who roam by day, ‘by day’; to those who roam by night, ‘by night’. (2.4.8)
Added: "And one should cast the bali offering into the air for all the gods, as well as for the spirits that roam by day and those that roam by night.
He who performs these rites daily, undistracted and according to the instruction, attains heaven eternally.
And nourishment. 2.4.9.

He who, being undistracted and with a concentrated mind, performs these aforementioned offerings and oblations according to the instruction—that is, without deviating from the instruction—[as understood from the word "yaḥ" (who), it follows that it refers to] "him," for him there is eternal heaven and eternal prosperity. This repetition is intended so that there may be no suspicion that the previous statement, "connected with heaven and prosperity" [ĀpDh 2.3.12], was merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); rather, heaven and prosperity become truly eternal, and cannot be sublated even by other more powerful ritual acts.
And the best portion must be given. 2.4.10.
After the offering of the bali, a portion of the food should also be given to a mendicant.
One should feed the guests first. 2.4.11.

"He will speak of guests" [ĀpDh 2.6.5]. One should feed them first; one should not eat together with them, nor before them. In this same manner, one should feed all others who are to be fed only after the guests. 2.4.11.
Children, the elderly, those afflicted by disease, and women who are pregnant. || 2.4.12 ||

And those fools and others who live in the household, one should feed them as well immediately after her. Although the term "pregnant women" (*antarvatnī*) would have sufficed, the explicit mention of "women" (*strī*) is for the purpose of including sisters and others; the inclusion of the term "pregnant women" is for the sake of all those mentioned previously. (2.4.12)
At the proper time, the two masters shall not refuse one who comes seeking food. 2.4.13.
At the proper time, at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the two masters of the house should not refuse one who has arrived seeking food; something must certainly be given to him. (2.4.13)
"What should be done in the absence [of these]? To this he says: "In their absence, earth, water, grass, and kind words—these indeed are never exhausted in the house of a virtuous person. (2.4.14)

Ground suitable for sitting; water suitable for washing the feet and other purposes; grass suitable for bedding and seating; and auspicious speech, such as "Welcome, long-lived one! Please be seated. These things—ground and the rest—are never lacking, even in the house of a virtuous man who is destitute of wealth. The word *vai* indicates what is well-known. One should perform the hospitable reception (*upacāra*) with these. By the very use of the word *iti*, it is shown that those who know the Dharma teach in this manner. 2.4.14.
For one whose conduct is thus, there are endless worlds. || 2.4.15 ||

Those two householders who maintain such conduct from the beginning of their marriage until its end attain infinite worlds; for this prescribed mode of life is more difficult to perform than even the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, which are accomplished in only a few days. (2.4.15)
To a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied [the Veda], one should give a seat, water, and food; one should not rise to greet him. 2.4.16.

If a Brāhmaṇa who is not studying should arrive with the status of a guest, then a seat and other such things should be given to him, but one need not rise for him. From this very point it is understood that one should rise for a Brāhmaṇa who is studying. (2.4.16)
If one is to be saluted, one should rise up specifically for the purpose of saluting him. 2.4.17.

If, however, even one who has not studied becomes worthy of salutation by virtue of such rules as "one who has been a citizen for ten years," then he should rise specifically for the purpose of that salutation. 2.4.17.
And [the same applies to] a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya. 2.4.18.
Even if a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya are studying, a Brāhmaṇa need not rise to greet them; however, he should offer them a seat and other such courtesies. 2.4.18.
One should employ a Śūdra who has arrived as a guest in work; then one should give him food. 2.4.19.

If a Śūdra comes as a guest to a twice-born man, then he should employ him in tasks such as fetching water; indeed, he should so employ him. Then, when that work has been performed, he should give him food. 2.4.19.
Or, having brought a Śūdra from the royal household, they should honor him as a guest. 2.4.20.

Alternatively, those who are the household servants of this householder should fetch that Śūdra from the royal palace and honor him like a guest. For this very reason, it is known: “For the sake of honoring Śūdra guests, rice and other provisions must be established by the king in every village.
One must always wear an upper garment. 2.4.21.

By such rules as “during the attendance upon teachers” (ĀpDh 1.15.1), the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) is prescribed for certain occasions; however, here, by virtue of the context, it is stated that a householder must always wear an upper garment. 2.4.21.
Or rather, the sacred thread itself serves the purpose of the *upavīta*. 2.4.22.
Alternatively, it is the thread itself that serves for all the functions of the *upavīta*, and not the garment alone. On this point, Manu says:
"The *upavīta* of a Brahmin should be made of cotton, twisted upward, and triple-stranded" (MDh 2.44).
Bodhāyana, however, states: "The sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) is a cord made of *kūśa* grass, triple-stranded and twisted three times" (BDh 1.8.5).

Where it has been eaten, that place should be cleared away, carried out, and sprinkled with water; having scraped the residue from the vessels and mixing it with earth and other materials, one should pour it out to the north in a clean spot for Rudra. In this way, the dwelling becomes auspicious. 2.4.23.

In whatever place food has been eaten, one should collect the leftovers and such, heap them together, and remove them; having removed them elsewhere, one should sprinkle that spot with water. Then, from the vessels (*amatrāṇi*) in which the cooking was done—those very vessels—one should scrape off the remnants of the rice and the remnants of the condiments, remove them with wood or similar means, and mix them with water. Having mixed them, one should pour them out in a clean place to the north of the house, saying, "May this be for Rudra. When this is done, the dwelling becomes auspicious and prosperous. (2.4.23)
But the Brāhmaṇa is traditionally remembered as the teacher. 2.4.24.

The word *tu* has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and its position in the sentence is displaced. It is recorded in all the treatises that only a Brāhmaṇa may be the teacher of all [castes]. Here too, the author will state: "The duty of a Brāhmaṇa... (ĀpDh 2.10.4), and so forth. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to introduce an alternative rule for times of distress (*āpad*). 2.4.24.
Regarding this, it says:
"In times of distress, a Brāhmaṇa may study [the Veda] from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. (2.4.25)

The word "must be performed" (*kartavyam*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. "Distress" (*āpad*) refers to the absence of a Brāhmaṇa teacher. In that situation, study must be performed by means of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya; one must not remain without studying. Because of the specific mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," this alternative rule (*anukalpa*) does not apply to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. (2.4.25)
And following behind [is the rule] for the funeral procession. 2.4.26.

And following behind must be performed from the rear as long as the study lasts. The mention of "behind" is so that, due to shyness or other reasons, he might not walk at the side even slightly. This is a restrictive rule regarding the scope of all forms of service: for a Brāhmaṇa, service consists solely in following behind. And thus says Gautama: "Following behind is service" (GDh 7.2). 2.4.26.
Thereafter, the Brāhmaṇa alone should go first. 2.4.27.
Then, after the study [of the Veda] is completed and the study has been finished, the Brāhmaṇa alone should go in front. 2.4.27.
Thus ends the fourth section:
Having commenced the study of any of the sciences or even the Upaniṣads, there shall be no recitation on that day. 2.5.1.

The genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*). Having commenced the study—that is, having begun to recite—all the *vidyās*, including even the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgavidyā*), on that day there is no study; on that day, one must not perform recitation. The mention of the *upaniṣads* is for the purpose of indicating their preeminence, just as in the expression: "The Brāhmaṇas have arrived, and Vasiṣṭha has also arrived. (2.5.1)
And having studied [the Veda], one must not depart immediately. 2.5.2.

Regarding the occasion [expressed by the rule] "Having studied the Veda, being about to perform the ceremonial bath" (ĀpGṛ 12.1), one must not depart immediately from the presence of the teacher, nor should one go away. Generally, however, the vowel *i* is recited after the letter *m*. Even in that case, the meaning remains the same; the *i*, however, is either a Vedic archaism or a corruption of the text. 2.5.2.
If he should hasten to the presence of the teacher, he may go at his pleasure after having studied his own Vedic recitation; thus, welfare is secured for both. 2.5.3.

If, however, he should hasten to depart due to some business, then, having studied his lesson and the subsequent questions in the presence, sight, or shelter of his guru or teacher, he may go as he pleases. When this is done, welfare accrues to both the disciple and the teacher. || 2.5.3 ||

If the teacher should arrive after he has completed his studies, he should go out to meet him face-to-face, take hold of his feet, and, without feeling any disgust, touch water; having placed him in front and seated him, he should honor him according to the instructions. 2.5.4.

If the teacher should come to a student who has returned home and taken a wife, treating him as a guest, he should go out to meet him, and having approached him, clasp his feet—the use of the genitive case here being for the sake of denoting the object of the act of clasping. Even if it were possible that the teacher might have been touched by a *caṇḍāla* or another such person, he should nevertheless not touch water or bathe out of disgust. Or, regarding the clasping of the feet: even after touching the feet which may be covered in dust or smoke, he should not touch water out of disgust. Then, having placed him in front—that is, leading him into the house—and having set out the materials for worship, he should honor him with the *madhuparka* offering according to the instructions and the method prescribed in the *Gṛhyasūtras*. This restatement of the rules for worship, beginning with the seat and so forth, is intended to state specific details. (2.5.4)
He says this regarding him: "When a seat, a bed, food to be chewed, food to be eaten, or clothing is available, he should adopt a more humble manner of conduct. (2.5.5)

When the teacher is present, having entered that very house into a private room or similar space, he should adopt a more humble manner regarding his seat and so forth. Because of the use of the comparative suffix (*tara*), he should sit on a lower seat, one that is inferior even in quality. This should be understood to apply to his bed and other such things as well. (2.5.5)
Standing, and supporting the teacher with his left hand, he should cause him to sip water. 2.5.6.

"Standing" refers to one who is bent forward, because of the connection with the act of standing; for one who is actually standing upright is not able to cause [the guest] to sip water. Holding the water-pot or similar vessel with the left hand, supporting it from below, and wiping the door with the other hand—this is not explicitly stated, as its meaning is already established by implication. Having done this, the disciple himself should cause the teacher to sip water (*ācamayet*). For in this way he becomes approved. Although the teacher was already the subject under discussion, the mention of "teacher" again is to indicate that even when performing the *ācamana* for the teacher on occasions other than hospitality, one should cause him to sip water in exactly this manner.
Or another [deity] who has arisen. 2.5.7.
The word "vā" (or) is used for conjunction. One may likewise cause another to sip water [in his stead], provided that he is distinguished by his lineage, character, learning, conduct, and age. 2.5.7.
Desiring to emulate [the Buddha] in his standing, sitting, walking, and smiling. (2.5.8)

One expects that [the cause] might even be separated [from the effect]. By the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), the instrument (*karaṇa*) is indicated. In the case of the locations (*sthāna*) and so forth, it would exist posterior to the teacher (*ācārya*), not prior to him, nor simultaneous with him. (2.5.8)
When one is in the presence [of others], one should avoid passing urine or excrement, flatulence, speaking loudly, laughing, spitting, gnashing the teeth, yawning, frowning, clapping, and spitting.

The action of wind is the emission of flatus. Speaking loudly is conversing with anyone in a loud voice. Laughter is laughing. Spitting is the discharge of phlegm and the like. Cleaning the teeth is the removal of dental impurities; others say it refers to the clashing of teeth against one another. Sniffing is the discharge of nasal mucus. Furrowing the brows is the movement of the eyebrows; the short vowel is used according to Vedic (chāndasa) usage. Clapping is the striking of the hands together. Snapping is the cracking of the fingers. By the word "iti" (and so forth), other actions such as sitting at will are also included. One should avoid these; this is what is expected. These actions, beginning with the voiding of urine, one should not perform in the presence of the teacher.
Thus [ends the section]. 2.5.9.
One should avoid addressing one's wife or children with familiarity that implies intimacy, even when using terms of endearment. || 2.5.10 ||

"Touching" refers to embracing, smelling, and so forth; "speeches" refers to conversation, endearments, and the like. Even these he should not practice with confidence when his teacher is present, even regarding his wife or children. There is no fault, however, in examining him for fever or other ailments. (2.5.10)
One should avoid contradicting the teacher’s statement with one’s own statement. 2.5.11.
One should not offer opposition with one's own words—whether similar or otherwise—to the words of the teacher, whether they be correct or otherwise. (2.5.11)
And [the same applies] to those who are superior. 2.5.12.
One should not contradict with one's own speech the words of others who are even more praiseworthy. 2.5.12.
And [he should endure] all censures and insults from living beings. || 2.5.13 ||

One should avoid slandering, speaking of faults, reviling, and using vulgar language toward all living beings, even animals. The repetition of the term "slandering" (parīvāda) is for the purpose of emphasizing its avoidance to the utmost degree. (2.5.13)
And by means of knowledge, [he attains] the knowledges. 2.5.14.

And by means of knowledge, one should avoid disparaging or reviling other branches of knowledge. Disparagement (*parīvāda*) consists of saying, "Only the *Ṛgveda* has the ears as its mouth; the others are harsh to the ear. Reviling (*ākrośa*) consists of saying, "The *Taittirīya* is a branch of leftovers," or "The *Brāhmaṇas* of Yājñavalkya and others are merely modern compositions," and so forth.
If one does not shine through that knowledge, one should approach the teacher once again and accomplish it with disciplined observance. || 2.5.15 ||

The meaning is understood to be that one should again master that knowledge by which, having been studied or heard, one does not shine—that is, one would not become illustrious—and should act so that it becomes perfectly accomplished. How? Having approached and attended upon either that same teacher or another, according to the rule prescribed for the acquisition of new knowledge—namely, through service and other such duties.
In this regard, there is a rule for the teacher:

from the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) until the conclusion (*utsarjana*), the teacher must observe a restrictive discipline. He should avoid shaving the hair, meat, funeral feasts (*śrāddha*), and sexual intercourse. (2.5.16)

“Gathering the hair” means shaving the hair. This refers to one who has not maintained the sacred fires; however, for one who has maintained the sacred fires, the Vājasaneyaka school states: “One should have the hair shaved very sparingly” (ĀpŚr 4.1.5). 2.5.16.
Or [he may give] his wife for the sake of a ritual season. 2.5.17.

Or he may approach his wife during her season (*ṛtu*). This is the grammatical derivation of the form *ṛtvaḥ*: women have sixteen days of their menstrual cycle; the time occurring therein is *ṛtvaḥ*. By applying the suffix *yat* according to Pāṇini 4.4.110 (*bhave chandasi*), the substitution of *yaṇ* is prescribed by the rule 6.4.175 (*ṛtvyavāstvyavāstvamādhvīhiraṇyayāni chandasi*), and the elision of the *y* therein is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) feature. This is as in the passage used in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices: "For the sake of the season (*ṛtve*) he approaches his wife; do not sit upon him" (ĀpŚr 8.4.7–8), and so forth. 2.5.17.

He should be devoted to the transmission of knowledge and to the observances for his disciples in accordance with tradition. Acting thus, he secures the welfare of his predecessors and successors, as well as his own. 2.5.18.

In whatever manner and by whatever means the tradition (āgama) exists regarding both the meaning and the text, in that very same way knowledge should be imparted to disciples without envy. One should be diligent and attentive toward such a transmission of knowledge. Furthermore, one should be diligent in those rules pertaining to a householder that apply to teaching and other matters. Being thus engaged, he unites his ancestors—his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—and his descendants—his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons—with these being "connections" (saṃbandhān), a term formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of action; as well as his kinsmen and himself, he establishes them in security, in a state free from fear, upon the vault of heaven. || 2.5.18 ||
By renouncing the secretions originating from the mind, speech, breath, sight, hearing, skin, genitals, and stomach, one becomes fit for immortality. 2.5.19.

Those by which a person is caused to flow out or is drawn outward are the "outflows" (*āsrāva*), namely the objects such as sound and so forth. These are specified as "having their origin in the skin, the genitals, and the stomach. They are called "origins" (*ārambhaṇa*) because they are originated—that is, they are grasped or experienced. Among these, those originating in the skin are garlands, sandalwood paste, and the like; that originating in the genitals is the enjoyment of women; and those originating in the stomach are food, edibles, and so forth. The mention of the skin and the others is illustrative. One who completely avoids such outflows by means of the five senses beginning with the mind—eschewing them on all sides—is fit for immortality, that is, for liberation. In this context, "speech" refers to the sense of taste, and "breath" refers to the sense of smell. (2.5.19)
Thus ends the fifth section;
thus ends the second chapter in the second book of the Ujjvalā, a commentary on the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
When there is doubt regarding caste or conduct, one should kindle a fire for the sake of determining the dharma and, having approached it, inquire about the person's caste and conduct. 2.6.1.

If someone who has not previously been recognized should come for the purpose of studying the Dharma and approach him, saying, "I have approached you, O Blessed One; look upon me with a friendly eye, favor me with a gracious mind, be gracious to me, and teach me," then, in case there is doubt regarding his birth or conduct, he should kindle the fire and, having performed the rites beginning with "Wherever one places the fire" (ĀpDh 2.1.13) and ending with "he should place another [fuel-stick]" (ĀpDh 2.1.14), he should ask him in that presence about his birth and conduct: "Whose son are you, gentle sir, and what is your conduct? (2.6.1)

If he pledges his integrity, saying, "May Agni be the witness, Vāyu the hearer, and Āditya the observer; he pledges his integrity—may it be well with him; this man is free from guilt," then, having said this, one may proceed to instruct him. 2.6.2.

If he claims his own goodness, saying, "I am of a virtuous birth; I am the son of such-and-such, the grandson of such-and-such, and the great-grandson of such-and-such; I am of virtuous conduct and was brought up by my father; I have been trained in proper behavior, I have conducted myself correctly, yet by the force of destiny all [my kin] passed away while still children; for this reason alone I am unlearned in the Vedas," then—having recited the mantra beginning with "Agni is the witness"—he should proceed to instruct, to discipline, to teach, and to impart the teachings of the Dharma. 2.6.2.
Like a blazing fire, the guest approaches. 2.6.3.

At the conclusion of the five sacrifices, it has been stated: "One should feed the guests first" (ĀpDh 2.4.11). To explain the manner of doing so, he declares its necessity with this [verse]: A guest arriving at the house approaches like a blazing fire; therefore, he must certainly be gratified with food and other offerings. For if he departs disappointed, he would consume the house. (2.6.3)
Now, in order to describe the characteristics of a guest, he states the characteristics of a *śrotriya*, which are relevant to that:
"Having studied even a single branch of the Vedas in accordance with the law (*dharma*), one becomes a *śrotriya*. (2.6.4)

The discipline (*niyama*) pertaining to one who seeks knowledge (*vidyārtha*) is *dharma*. By means of that, having studied any branch whatsoever of the Vedas, one becomes a *śrotriya*. For each person has, with respect to each Veda, a single branch; that which was adopted by their ancestors through study and ritual practice is their own branch for each Veda. Having studied that, one becomes a *śrotriya*. It is not the case that one becomes a *śrotriya* by studying only one branch of each Veda, because that would contradict worldly convention. In the world, indeed, anyone who studies any branch whatsoever is well known as a *śrotriya*. (2.6.4)
He states the definition of a guest (*atithi*):
"One who approaches a householder engaged in his own duty, honoring dharma as his primary motive and having no other purpose, is a guest."
It comes to be. || 2.6.5 ||

The word *yaḥ* (who) is to be understood at the beginning, because the word *saḥ* (he) is seen at the end. Furthermore, since the characteristics of a *śrotriya* are taught in the middle, the Sūtra is to be construed by relying upon that [definition]. [The guest] is one who is a *śrotriya*, a householder (*kuṭumbin*) who dwells with his wife, who is endowed with his own duty (*svadharma-yukta*) and devoted to his own duty (*svadharma-nirata*). This is stated for the purpose of excluding other stages of life (*āśrama*); for they do not cook for themselves, as they are mendicants (*bhikṣu*). "He approaches" means he comes specifically for the purpose [of seeking alms]. "One who honors the Dharma" (*dharmapuraskāra*): the Dharma is the begging for alms for the sake of the teacher; he who places that Dharma foremost is "one who honors the Dharma. The suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of an action. He has the Dharma as his motive and no other motive. One who approaches such a person for such a purpose, and not by chance, is a "guest" (*atithi*). Bodhāyana, however, says: "One who is weary, previously known, who seeks only food and has no other purpose—he is a guest. Or rather, anyone from among all the social classes (*varṇa*) who arrives at the proper time is considered a guest; among all types of guests, such a person is the most excellent.
From worshipping him, there is peace, heaven, and prosperity. 2.6.6.
When hospitality has been rendered to such a guest, there is here the pacification of calamities, and after death, the attainment of heaven. 2.6.6.
Having approached him face-to-face and greeted him according to his age, he should offer him a seat. || 2.6.7 ||

He should go out to meet that guest; having approached him, he should greet him according to his age with rising from his seat, salutation, and so forth, and join him in welcome. Having welcomed him, he should have a seat brought for him by means of his disciples and others, or, in their absence, he should bring it himself. (2.6.7)
Some say that when there is sufficient space, the seat should not have many legs. 2.6.8.
Some maintain that when possible, a seat with few legs should not be given, but rather one with many legs, such as a stool; however, he himself permits even those with few legs. (2.6.8)
He should wash his feet; according to some, a Śūdra couple [should do so]. 2.6.9.
Some authorities maintain that two Śūdras should wash his feet; this [rule] is like that for a slave. 2.6.9.
In this regard, there is a distinction: one or the other [of the two] should be present at the consecration. 2.6.10.
Consecration (*abhiṣecana*) is the sprinkling of water with a water-pot (*karaka*) and so forth; one person should perform that, while another performs the washing. 2.6.10.
Some say that one should have water brought for him in an earthenware vessel. 2.6.11.
Some maintain that his water should be fetched in an earthen vessel; however, he himself [should fetch it] in a metallic one. 2.6.11.
One who has not yet returned home [from his teacher] should not fetch water. 2.6.12.

When an unmarried student (*brahmacārī*), sent by his teacher or having come on his own initiative as a guest, arrives, one should not fetch water for him, nor should one cause him to fetch water; one should think: "Water must not be brought for this man. (2.6.12)
And here, the non-returning of what has been studied is also an additional [ground for loss]. 2.6.13.

In this case, when an *atithi* (guest) has arrived who is not a fellow-student (*asamāvṛtta*), there is an additional requirement for the suspension of study (*adhyayana-saṃvṛtti*) compared to other types of guests. "Suspension of study" (*adhyayana-saṃvṛtti*) means the simultaneous completion of the study; that is, whatever portion [of the text] he arrives at, one must recite that together with him for a certain period of time. However, in the well-known reading, the final vowel of the preceding word is *samaḥ*, and the lengthening of the vowel *a* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) feature. (2.6.13)
Having consoled him, one should satisfy him with flavorful foods, edibles, and water, using at least the lowest quality of each. || 2.6.14 ||

Then, after washing the guest’s feet or after [the host] has completed his own study, he should comfort the guest with kind words. Having comforted him, he should satisfy him—even if only with water—at the very least, with juices such as those derived from cow products, and with edible foods such as fruits; he should make him content. The phrase "at the very least" (avarārdhyena) indicates the lowest possible standard. The word "even" (antaḥ) means "at the very end. From the word "iti," it is understood that he should also use other such things. 2.6.14.
One should provide a dwelling, a bed above, a mattress, a pillow, a coverlet, and an ointment. || 2.6.15 ||

A *āvasatha* is a place of rest. An *upariśayyā* is a bedstead. An *upastaraṇa* is a mattress. An *upadhāna* is a pillow; an *avastaraṇa* is an upper cloth, and together with that, it includes both the pillow and the mattress. An *abhyañjana* is oil or ghee for the feet. All of this one should give before the meal, or at the time previously requested. By the word "iti" (and so forth), other things also [requested] are included. 2.6.15.
Having summoned the preparer of food, he should pour out rice or barley for that purpose. || 2.6.16 ||

Having summoned the one who cooks—that preparer of food—one should set aside rice or barley intended for that purpose, namely for the sake of the guest, and give them separately, saying, "Cook this for such-and-such a person. The mention of rice and barley is illustrative. (2.6.16)

This [rule] is to be understood as applying when all have finished eating and a guest has arrived; however, at the time of eating, he says: "He should look at the food that has been served, saying, 'Is this more? or 'Is this less? (2.6.17)

One should take out as much food as there are eaters and place it in separate vessels; this is the distribution (*saṃvibhāga*). Having done that, one should look at those foods, considering whether "this is more" or "that is more. The protracted vowel (*pluta*) is used here because it is a deliberation (*vicāra*); the rule *pūrvaṃ tu bhāṣāyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.98), which restricts such usage to ordinary speech, is disregarded here, as this employment of the protracted vowel is purely Vedic (*chāndasa*). 2.6.17.
"Rather, one should say, 'Lift it up again. 2.6.18.
Having reflected thus, he should say, "Please take more out for the sake of guests. (2.6.18)
One should not eat the food of an enemy, nor of one who hates him; nor of one who suspects him of a fault, nor of one who has been found guilty of a fault. (2.6.19)

One should not eat the food of anyone who is himself an enemy as a guest, or who hates himself, or who suspects himself of a fault—imagining a fault such as theft within himself—or who is suspected of a fault by others, such that worldly people imagine a fault in him; one should not eat the food of any such person. (2.6.19)
The reason for this is that it is known from scripture: "For he consumes his evil. (2.6.20)
It is known from scripture that whoever eats the food of such a person as this, he consumes his very sin. 2.6.20.
Thus ends the sixth section.
This very sacrifice of the householder belongs to Prajāpati and is perpetually extended. 2.7.1.

This very sacrifice to men, seen by Prajāpati, is declared to be *prājāpatya*, or it has him as its deity. It is a sacrifice for a householder that must be performed constantly with diligence; it is not occasional, like the *agniṣṭoma* and other such rites. 2.7.1.
He procures the sacred fires for him:
that fire which belongs to guests is the Āhavanīya; that which is in the household is the Gārhapatya; and that upon which food is cooked is the Anvāhāryapacana. || 2.7.2 ||

The digestive fire within guests is the *āhavanīya* fire, for it is into that fire that offerings are poured. The fire in the household and the home is the *aupāsana*, which is the *gārhapatya* fire because it is to be maintained perpetually. The fire in the hearth where food is cooked is the *anvāhāryapacana*, the *dakṣiṇāgni*; for it is in that fire that food is cooked for the purpose of the *anvāhārya* feast. (2.7.2)
He who eats before his guest eats away the vigor, prosperity, offspring, cattle, and the merit of his sacrifices and charitable works belonging to the household. 2.7.3.

He who eats before the guest eats—that is, he consumes and destroys the vigor (*ūrj*) and other merits belonging to the household and the family. *Ūrj* means food; *iṣṭa* refers to rites such as the *agnihotra*; *pūrta* refers to Smṛti-based acts such as digging wells and the like; the others are well known. (2.7.3)

Rice with milk as a condiment is equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; with ghee it is equal to the Ukthya; with honey it is equal to the Atirātra; with meat it is equal to the Dvādaśāha; and with water there is an increase of progeny and longevity. 2.7.4.

Food with milk as its accompaniment is equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; from the context, it is understood that food sprinkled with clarified butter is equal to the Ukthya sacrifice; food sprinkled with honey is equal to the Atirātra sacrifice; food given together with meat is equal to the Dvādaśāha sacrifice. By giving water, there is an increase of progeny and of longevity; the word "increase" (*vṛddhi*) is connected even though it occurs later in the compound. (2.7.4)
It is known from scripture that both beloved and unloved guests lead one to the heavenly world. 2.7.5.
The unpleasant, the indifferent, and the hostile are excluded because they have been prohibited. || 2.7.5 ||
When he gives [gifts] in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, these become the very Soma-pressings (savana). || 2.7.6 ||
The foods given at the three times of day constitute the three pressings of this sacrifice, beginning with the morning pressing; therefore, one should give at all times. 2.7.6.
Whatever he performs, that indeed constitutes the *udavasanīya* sacrifice. || 2.7.7 ||
