"That he rises after the guest who is rising to depart—that indeed is his *udavasānīyā* (concluding offering) of this sacrifice. Generally, they do not recite the word *ut*, but recite only the word *anu*; even there, the meaning remains the same. 2.7.7.
That which consoles is *dakṣiṇā*, [which is] praise. 2.7.8.
That which consoles and praises is praise as a sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā). || 2.7.8 ||
That which he accomplishes, those are the Viṣṇu-strides. || 2.7.9 ||
Accompanying him on his journey is the means of accomplishment. || 2.7.9 ||
That which he turns back toward is the avabhṛtha bath. || 2.7.10 ||
Upāvartana is following [the teacher] and returning. 2.7.10.
Thus says the Brāhmaṇa. 2.7.11.
It has a connection with all of these. 2.7.11.
If a guest should approach the king, the king should cause him to receive a more distinguished honor than his own. || 2.7.12 ||
A consecrated Kṣatriya king should, through his domestic priest, cause even greater honor to be shown to a guest who has arrived than he would show to himself. 2.7.12.

If a guest should arrive at the house of one who maintains the sacred fires, the host should rise to meet him in person and say: "O Vrātya, where have you stayed? "O Vrātya, here is water. "O Vrātya, may you satisfy [yourself]. (2.7.13)

If a guest should arrive with reference to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), then he himself should go out to meet that guest. Here, because of the mention of "himself," one who has not maintained the sacred fires does not incur fault even if he causes another, such as a disciple, to perform this. Having approached him, he should say: "O *vrātya*, where have you stayed? This is a greeting of well-being. One who is established in his vow (*vrata*) is a *vratya*; he is the same as a *vrātya*—this is a rule for showing honor. "Where did you dwell during the previous night? "O *vrātya*, [here is] water"—with these words, he offers water. "O *vrātya*, satisfy yourself"—with this, he satisfies him with juices and other refreshments. The anusvāra and the letter *s* are Vedic (*chāndasa*). Because of the difference in the actions, the word *iti* is used with each mantra. All of this must be performed on all occasions. (2.7.13)

Before the offering of the Agnihotra, one should mutter softly: "O Vrātya, may it be as your mind desires"; "O Vrātya, may it be as your will ordains"; "O Vrātya, may it be as is dear to you"; "O Vrātya, may it be as is your longing. (2.7.14)

If he should sit down even before the time for the oblation, then, having placed [the vessel] on the *darbha* grass behind the fire before the oblation, he should mutter—or recite—the mantras beginning with "O Vrātya, as your mind... in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). In this regard, because of the use of the word "iti" after each mantra and because of the difference in their meaning, there is an option (*vikalpa*) among the four; others, however, maintain that there is a combination (*samuccaya*). And here, whether it be the Adhvaryu or the Sacrificer, whoever is the Hotṛ, he should mutter [the mantras] and then offer the oblation. 2.7.14.

If a guest should arrive when the fires have been taken out but not yet offered into, he himself should rise to meet him and say: "O Vratya, give me leave; I shall offer. Only when permitted thus should he offer. If he should offer without being permitted, the Brāhmaṇa declares that there is a fault. 2.7.15.

The plural number in the word *uddhṛteṣu* (“when [the fires] have been taken out”) refers to the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires. However, for one who maintains all three sacred fires (*tretāgni*), the oblation (*homa*) must be performed in all three, because of the grammatical coordination with the phrase *ahuteṣu* (“when they have not yet been offered”). Therefore, if a guest arrives immediately after an oblation has been made in the *āhavanīya* fire, the rule to be stated below still applies, since the offering has not yet been completed in all three fires. What, then, is that rule? One should go out to meet him personally and say, “O *vrātya*, grant me permission; I shall offer the oblation. Thereupon, he should grant permission by saying, “Offer it. The oblation must be performed by one who has been granted permission. If, however, one should offer it without being permitted—that is, without being authorized—the Vedic text states the fault involved in this. All of this is to be understood as recited in the *Atharvaveda*. According to this view, the performance of the oblation by oneself is mandatory. (2.7.15)

"If one should lodge guests for one night, he conquers the worlds of the earth; by a second night, those of the intermediate space; by a third, those of heaven; by a fourth, the distant worlds; and by an unlimited number of nights, he conquers unlimited worlds—so it is known. (2.7.16)

He who provides lodging for guests for one night conquers on earth those worlds that exist upon the earth; by a second night, those belonging to the intermediate space; by a third, those belonging to heaven; by a fourth, those worlds which constitute the supreme measure of happiness in the highest reaches. It is known from the Brāhmaṇa that "by means of unlimited nights, he conquers unlimited worlds. (2.7.16)

If a guest should arrive who does not declare his lineage, one should give him a seat, water, and food, saying simply, "I give this to a learned Brahmin. In this way, it becomes successful for him. 2.7.17.

One who is devoid of knowledge and so forth is "unaccomplished. If such a person should arrive claiming to be a guest, then one should give him a seat and other offerings while keeping in mind: "I am giving this to a *śrotriya*. For one who gives in this manner, that gift becomes successful; it is as if it were given to a *śrotriya* indeed. (2.7.17)
Thus ends the seventh section;
thus ends the third chapter in the second book of the *Ujjvalā*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra*.
One should not rise up or descend from one's seat for a guest who has already been accommodated by another; however, if he has been greeted first, one should do so. (2.8.1)

If a householder has provided lodging for a guest—that is, has granted him a place to stay—he should not rise up to greet him on the second day and subsequent days, nor should he descend from his seat to do so, provided that the guest was already greeted on the first day. However, if the guest was not greeted on the first day, he should rise up and descend from his seat to offer a greeting. (2.8.1)
The remainder of the food shall belong to the guests. 2.8.2.

Since this is already established by the rule, “One should feed the guests first” (ĀpDh 2.4.11), this statement is intended to mean that one should not eat food that was not given to a guest through negligence. 2.8.2.
One should not eat flavorful foods in the house without having given some to guests. 2.8.3.

One should not consume juices such as those derived from cow products in such a way that nothing remains in the house for future guests; this is because it is impossible to prepare such juices instantaneously. (2.8.3)
One should not cook choice food for one's own sake alone. 2.8.4.
One should not cook delicious food, such as sweet cakes and the like, for one's own sake. || 2.8.4 ||
One who has studied the Vedas is worthy of the cow-offering and the honey-mixture.
One who has studied the Veda together with its auxiliary sciences is a "Vedādhyāya. Such a guest is entitled to the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 2.8.5 ||
An Ācārya, an officiating priest (Ṛtvij), a Snātaka, or a righteous king [should be invited]. 2.8.6.

Even those who have not studied the Veda, such as teachers (ācāryas) and others, are worthy of the cow and the madhuparka offering. From this very fact, it is known that even those who have studied only a portion [of the Veda] may serve as officiating priests (ṛtvij) or teachers. The term "endowed with dharma" is an epithet for the king. The word "vā" is used in the sense of conjunction. 2.8.6.
To the teacher, the officiating priest, the father-in-law, and the king— these being present for less than a year— a cow and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) are offered.
This has been explained in the Gṛhya-sūtra [ĀpGṛ 3.9]. Here, the cow is prescribed as an additional item for the consecrated person. 2.8.7.
What is this *madhuparka*? To this he says:
*madhuparka* is curd mixed with honey, or milk mixed with honey. (2.8.8)
This is a restatement of what is prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, intended for what follows.
The absence [of water] is water. || 2.8.9 ||

In the absence of curd and milk, water may also be given; some say it should be mixed with honey, while others say no, because of the specific mention of "mixed with honey" [in the subsequent rule]. 2.8.9.
Regarding the phrase "the study of the Veda" [ĀpDh 2.8.5], he states what is intended by "Veda":
the Veda consists of six limbs. 2.8.10.
The Veda is understood as being endowed with six auxiliary limbs. || 2.8.10 ||
To the question "What are those auxiliary sciences?", he says: "Metre, ritual procedure, grammar, astronomy, phonetics, and prosody. (2.8.11)

*Chandas* is the Veda; it is called *chandaḥkalpa* because it "constructs" (*kalpayati*) the performance of rituals according to each specific recension (*śākhā*), by providing a systematic arrangement (*prayoga-kalpanā*) of the ritual acts along with their constituent parts (*aṅga-kalāpa*) as established by logic and studied in other recensions—this refers to the *Kalpasūtras*. *Vyākaraṇa* (Grammar) is a branch of knowledge that assists the Veda by explaining words and their meanings through the analysis of specific word-forms (*pada*) based on particular meanings. *Jyotiṣa* is the science concerned with the luminaries, such as the sun and others. One must make an effort regarding the absence of initial *vṛddhi* [in its formation]. It is also beneficial, as it explains specific times useful for study and for the performance of rites. *Nirukta* is essentially the completion of grammar itself. *Śīkṣā* teaches the points of articulation (*sthāna*) and efforts (*prayatna*) of the phonemes (*varṇa*), as well as the manner of pronouncing mantras during study and during ritual acts. The lengthening of the vowel [in *śīkṣā*] is due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group. *Chandoviciti* is that by which the meters (*chandas*), such as the *gāyatrī* and others, are "selected" (*vicīyante*) and understood through discrimination. These are the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). Their status as auxiliaries is established through the praise of the limbs (*aṅga-saṃstava*).
Grammar is said to be its mouth; astronomy is called its eye;
etymology is designated as its ear; and the analysis of meters is its feet.
"The Śikṣā is said to be the nose of the Veda, and the Kalpas its hands.
This is because they are beneficial. The benefit has already been explained. (2.8.11)
Here an objection is raised:

"But the word 'Veda' applies to those actions which have words as their means of accomplishment, upon the completion of the traditional collection [of texts]. In that case, the number [of Vedas] is contradictory. (2.8.12)

Those actions, such as the *agnihotra* and others, which are undertaken as the meaning of words and not as objects within the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), are "Vedic actions whose undertaking consists of the meaning of words. Their "recitation" (*samāmnāya*) is their instruction (*upadeśa*). Upon the completion of that—that is, when the collection of texts by which it is completed becomes exhaustive down to its practical performance—the word "Veda" applies there. This is because it "makes known" (*vedayati*) Dharma, or "by means of this, one knows" (*vidanti anena*) Dharma. Furthermore, the instruction does not become exhaustive down to practical performance through the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* portions alone; rather, it is also together with the *kalpasūtras*. Consequently, since these too are included within the very nature of the Veda, there are only five auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*). In that case, the number six is contradicted. (2.8.12)
He avoids [that objection],
for it is the established doctrine of those who know the principles of logic that the subsidiaries are not designated by the same terms as the primary acts.

The *Kalpasūtras* are indeed auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) [of the Veda], not the very nature of the Veda itself, because they are remembered as being of human origin. For among them, only a few are sentences from the *Brāhmaṇas*, while the majority are their own sentences. Furthermore, it is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of those who know the principles of logic that it is not proper to designate these auxiliary limbs by words denoting the primary [Veda] itself, such as "Chandas," "Veda," or "Brāhmaṇa. These two—the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion—should be seen more clearly in the section concerning the *Kalpasūtras*. As for what was said—that the instruction is not complete with only the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas—it is not the fault of the post (*sthāṇu*) that the blind man does not see it; rather, that is a fault of the person. But you must explain this: from where does this construction of ritual practice (*prayoga-kalpanā*) of the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* originate? One must say: "From the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas augmented by logical reasoning (*nyāya*). There is no other way. This being so, you too should strive [to understand], thinking, "May I become like that"; then one will understand the complete [instruction] through the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas alone. (2.8.13)
If, after having rejected a guest, one should remember him once the meal has been consumed, one must desist from eating and fast for that day.
Thus ends the eighth section.
On the following day, having gratified [the ancestors] according to his inclination, he should perform the concluding rites. 2.9.1.

If, having rejected a guest who has arrived in some manner, one proceeds to eat, then at whatever point during the meal one should remember—"Fie on me! He was rejected by me"—one should desist from eating right there, fast for that day, and on the following day, having sought him out and gratified him to his heart's content and according to his desire, one should fulfill one's duty; furthermore, one should follow him as he departs. (2.8.14–2.9.1)
To the question "From where?", he says: "As long as he possesses a vehicle, [he may go] with the vehicle. (2.9.2)
If the guest possesses a vehicle, he should follow him until he has mounted it. 2.9.2.
Until the other grants permission. 2.9.3.
The other, being without a vehicle, should follow him as long as he does not give permission, saying, "Go. || 2.9.3 ||
In the event of an inability to respond, one should desist at that boundary. || 2.9.4 ||

If, because his intention is directed toward something else, no such understanding or thought arises regarding the permission, then, having reached the boundary, he should turn back from there. The lengthening of the vowel in *prati* is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. The phrase "he should provide for" (*saṃsādhayet*) and so forth applies to all guests in general, not solely to those who have been refused entry. 2.9.4.
In the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one should make all beings, down to the dogs and the Caṇḍālas, sharers in the offering.

At the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should make all those who have arrived for the purpose of eating participants in the Vaiśvadeva offering, extending this even to the dogs and the Caṇḍālas—the letter *ā* here being used in the sense of inclusion. Something should be given even to them. And so Manu says: “For dogs, for outcasts, for dog-cookers, for those afflicted with loathsome diseases, for crows, and for worms, one should gently place food upon the ground” (MDh 3.92).
Some say that one should not give to those who are unworthy. 2.9.6.
Some maintain that one should not give to those unworthy, such as Caṇḍālas and others; in such a case, there is spiritual merit in giving, but no sin in not giving. (2.9.6)
One who has performed the purificatory rites should avoid the leavings of women, both those who have performed the rites and those who have not. || 2.9.7 ||

One who has been initiated (*upetaḥ*) but has not yet returned home after completing his studies (*asamāvṛttaḥ*) shall not eat the leavings (*ucchiṣṭaṃ*) of women, nor the leavings of one who has been initiated. If this were the case, there would be no fault in eating the leavings of one who has returned home (*samāvṛttaḥ*). If that is so, then let it be understood that one who has been initiated—whether he has taken a wife or not—should avoid the leavings of women and of those who have not been initiated. Even so, there would still be no fault in eating the leavings of anyone else for whom one has been initiated. The rule, "One may eat the leavings of one's father and of an elder brother" (ĀpDh 1.4.11), will serve as a restrictive injunction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that one may eat the leavings of the father *only* and of the elder brother *only*. If this is the case, then this very Sūtra is redundant, because by that very restriction, the possibility of eating the leavings of others is already excluded. In that case, the purpose is this: when the father has not been initiated, but the son has performed the penance and undergone initiation, then the eating of the leavings of that uninitiated father is prohibited with respect to him. The same should be understood regarding the elder brother. But even this is not a valid purpose, for it has already been stated: "When there is a lapse in dharma, [the food] is not to be eaten" (ĀpDh 1.4.12), and "One should avoid their arrival, eating together, and marriage" (ĀpDh 1.1.33). Furthermore, what is the purpose of the phrase "of women"? It is for the sake of prohibiting the leavings of one's mother. How could such a contingency arise? From the statement, "Service to the mother and the father is like service to the teacher" (ĀpDh 1.14.6), and from the praise of the teacher’s leavings as being "like the sacrificial oblation" (*havirucchiṣṭam eva tat*) (ĀpDh 1.4.1–2). Even this is not sound, because by the mention of the "father" in the rule "of the father and of the elder brother," the mother is already excluded. Therefore, in some regions, people practice eating together with their wives and with those who have not been initiated, as Baudhāyana says: "We shall explain those customs which are practiced in the south; such as eating together with one who has not been initiated, and eating together with a woman" (BDh 1.2.2–3). By this [Sūtra], the impropriety of such conduct is established. 2.9.7.
All gifts are preceded by water. 2.9.8.
Because of the word "all," even alms must be given preceded by water. 2.9.8.
In accordance with what has been heard regarding the monastery. || 2.9.9 ||

In a monastery or at a sacrificial rite, those gifts such as the priestly fee (dakṣiṇā) and others are to be given exactly according to the scriptural injunctions, not preceded by the offering of water.
For those who are constant devotees, a distribution of shares has been ordained without causing them any obstruction. || 2.9.10 ||

One should make a distribution of food to those who are permanent residents, devotees, those worthy of hospitality, servants, and so forth, at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, in such a way that no hardship befalls them. (2.9.10)
One may indeed cause hardship for oneself, one’s wife, or one’s son, but never for a slave or a laborer.

(2.9.11) [1] One who performs work having become a slave is a "slave-laborer" (*dāsakarmakara*). One should not cause him hardship even when there is hardship for oneself and others; how much less so should one cause hardship to him when he has come for the sake of his livelihood? (2.9.11)
And he should act so as not to obstruct his own self that he may become incapable of performing his duties. 2.9.12.

A householder should not deprive himself of the means to perform his duties, such as the Agnihotra sacrifice and other rites, nor of the means to acquire wealth, insofar as he is capable of doing so himself. 2.9.12.
Moreover, they cite this:
"Eight mouthfuls are the meal for a sage, sixteen for a forest-dweller,
thirty-two for a householder, and an unlimited amount for a student."

"The one who maintains the sacred fires, the ox, and the student of sacred knowledge—these three achieve perfection only while eating; for them there is no perfection for those who do not eat. (2.9.13)

Now, regarding the matter that one should not overstrain oneself, they cite two verses: "The sage who has renounced the world (saṃnyāsin) has eight mouthfuls as his food, measured by the non-distortion of the mouth. The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) has sixteen. 'Thirty-two'—the accusative case is used in the sense of the nominative—thirty-two mouthfuls are the food of the householder. But for the student (brahmacārin), whether seeking knowledge or lifelong (naiṣṭhika), there is no restriction on the number of mouthfuls. By the second verse, it is established that for the maintainer of the sacred fires (āhitāgni), even the rule 'eating at the two times' [ĀpDh 2.1.2] does not apply. The mention of the ox is for the sake of illustration; the mention of the student is for the sake of a visible purpose. They become successful, meaning they become capable of their respective duties. 2.9.13.
Thus ends the ninth section;
thus ends the fourth chapter in the second book of the Ujjvalā, a commentary on the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
The occasions for begging are: [the presence of] a teacher, a marriage, a sacrifice, the desire of one's parents to eat, and the breaking of a vow by an Arhat. 2.10.1.

"Bhikṣaṇa" means begging. In that context, the teacher and others are the cause [for such begging]. "Bubhūrṣā" is the desire to maintain oneself. For one who is worthy (*arhat*), that is, one possessing knowledge and so forth, there is an omission [of begging] because there is no need for it in observances such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice. (2.10.1)
In that case, having considered the merits [of the recipient], one should give according to one's ability. 2.10.2.

In such a case of begging, having examined the petitioner’s learning, conduct, and so forth, one must certainly give according to one's capacity, for there is sin in not giving. Gautama, however, mentions other occasions as well: “Outside the sacrificial altar, one should share one’s wealth with those who are the preceptor, those seeking a bride, those in need of medicine, those whose livelihood is exhausted, those about to sacrifice, those engaged in study, those on a journey, and the Vaiśvajit; among those begging, cooked food should be given to others. [GDh 5.21–22] The *vaiśvajit* is the performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice, and that sacrifice requires the giving away of all one’s possessions as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). 2.10.2.
But begging for the sake of gratifying the senses is without merit; one should not heed that. 2.10.3.

The pleasure of the self through the doors of the senses is "sensual pleasure" (*indriyaprīti*). One who begs for that—asking for garlands, sandalwood, and so forth, or their price—that begging does not necessarily constitute a cause for giving. Therefore, one should not pay heed to it; even if it is not given, there is no offense. Marriage, moreover, is not a secondary cause [for giving] when the first [wife] exists and is endowed with both virtue and offspring. This statement is made for that purpose, because [the obligation to give] would otherwise not apply in other cases. (2.10.3)
The specific duties of a Brāhmaṇa are: studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, receiving gifts, inheritance, and gleaning ears of grain. 2.10.4.

It has been stated [in ĀpDh 2.2.2]: “For all castes (*varṇa*), in the performance of their own duties (*svadharma*). Those very *svadharmas* are now being described. That which is given to sons and others is called *dāya* (inheritance); one who takes that is a *dāyāda* (heir); the state of being such is *dāyādya*, meaning the acceptance of inheritance. The term *sila* refers to grains that have fallen upon fields and the like, either still in clusters or having fallen from them. The gathering of these by means of fingers or fingernails is *siloñcha*. These eight—study and the rest—are the specific duties (*svakarma*) of a Brāhmaṇa. Among these, three—sacrifice (*yajña*), giving (*dāna*), and study (*adhyayana*)—are enjoined as obligations common to the twice-born (*dvijāti*). The others are taught as alternative means for one who, out of necessity, engages in the acquisition of wealth, intended to exclude other methods; that is, one should acquire wealth only through teaching and so forth, and not through theft and the like. (2.10.4)
And anything else that is not appropriated. 2.10.5.

And whatever else is unclaimed by anyone, such as forest roots and fruits, he may live upon that as well; this is understood from the context. By this, the rule regarding treasure-troves is explained. (2.10.5)

For a Kṣatriya, these same [duties] are prescribed, with the exception of teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts; to these are added the authority to wield punishment and to engage in combat. 2.10.6.

These same [occupations] are also the specific duties of a Kṣatriya, with the exception of the three beginning with teaching; however, he has two additional ones: that which is acquired through punishment and that which is acquired through battle. 2.10.6.
The duties of a Vaiśya are like those of a Kṣatriya, with the exception of the duty of fighting with weapons; they consist primarily of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. (2.10.7)

*Gorakṣyam* means the protection of cows; the suffix *ṇyat* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). *Vaṇijyam* is the business of merchants, consisting of the practice of buying and selling as well as usury; the suffix *ya* is applied according to the rule "after the words *dūta* and *vaṇij*. (2.10.7)
One does not choose as a sacrificial priest one who has not studied the Vedas, nor one who is haggling for a fee. || 2.10.8 ||

One who has studied and can expound the Veda together with its auxiliary branches is called *anūcāna*. One should not choose as a priest anyone other than such a person, nor one who stipulates that only this much should be given. (2.10.8)
One who is unworthy of sacrificing and unlearned [in the Vedas]. || 2.10.9 ||
One should not officiate at a sacrifice for one who has not studied the Vedas, while causing him to recite the required mantra according to his ability.
It has been stated that war is the specific duty (*svakarma*) of a Kṣatriya. To the question of how that is to be performed, he says:
one should act in accordance with the means taught for its application in battle. 2.10.10.

One should act in the matter of war in such a way that those who are experts in it teach the proper means. Those who apply themselves to that martial activity or to the science of war are the "experts" (tadyogāḥ). || 2.10.10 ||

The noble ones declare the slaughter of those who have laid down their weapons, whose hair is disheveled, who join their palms in supplication, or who have turned their backs in flight to be forbidden.

"Having laid down his weapons" means one who has abandoned his weapons. "With disheveled hair" means one incapable of restraining his hair. "With palms joined" means one who has made the *añjali* gesture. "Turning away" means one whose face is averted. All these are terrified; the virtuous censure their killing in battle. There is no fault in killing others not included in this enumeration. And thus says Gautama: "There is no fault in violence in combat" (GDh 10.17). Regarding the reading "nyastāyudhaḥ prakīrṇakeśaḥ," some say there is a *visarjanīya* [anusvāra], but that is a faulty recitation. In the word "parāṅāvṛttaḥ," the letter *ṅ* is a Vedic archaism. 2.10.11.

The teacher should prescribe atonement for those who, despite having understood the teachings through the scriptures, have fallen into error due to weakness of the senses, according to their specific actions as previously described. 2.10.12.

Those who have been purified by the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* according to the scriptures and have acquired knowledge through the treatises, yet—due to the weakness of their senses and lack of self-control—have fallen into error, fallen from their own duty, and engaged in prohibited acts, for them the teacher, the instructor, the preceptor, and so forth, shall prescribe an expiation (*nirveṣa*) or penance (*prāyaścitta*) according to the act, in accordance with the deeds, as stated in the treatises on Dharma. 2.10.12.
If they should transgress his command, he should cause them to be brought before the king. 2.10.13.

If men, having erred through lack of control over their senses, should transgress the scripture—the teaching—of that ruler and no longer abide by it, he should bring them before the king, saying, "He acts in this manner. || 2.10.13 ||
The king [addressed] the domestic priest, who was skilled in matters of dharma and artha.
That king should send for a domestic priest who is skilled in the treatises on dharma and the treatises on statecraft, saying, "Let this man be disciplined.
He should appoint the Brahmins. 2.10.15.
If those Brahmins who were the royal chaplain have committed transgressions, he should cause them to undergo, or they themselves should undergo, the appropriate penances. 2.10.15.
Now, if they should not remain there even then, he says what should be done:
"By means of specific force, one should cause them to wither through restrictive rules, excluding killing and slavery. (2.10.15)

Then he should emaciate them with restrictive practices such as bondage, fasting, and so forth, according to their specific strength—that is, in accordance with their capacity—excluding killing and slavery; that is, excluding beating and the like, as well as killing and servitude, he should cause them to perform all other forms of punishment, such as bondage, in accordance with their strength, until they think, "Let us perform penance. (2.10.15)
Thus ends the tenth section. Having thus spoken regarding the Brāhmaṇas, he now speaks concerning the others: for the other castes, having observed them until the separation from life-breath...
The king shall inflict punishment according to the actions [of the offenders]. 2.11.1.

For the other castes, excluding the Brāhmaṇas, the king himself shall personally impose the punishment prescribed by the domestic priest, having duly considered their actions and in accordance with them, even unto the loss of life; the vowel *ā* here indicates inclusion (*abhividhi*). (2.11.1)
And one should not inflict punishment when there is doubt. || 2.11.2 ||
In case of doubt regarding an offense, the king should not inflict punishment.
However,
having investigated thoroughly after considering the questions of the gods, the king should proceed to inflict punishment. || 2.11.3 ||

Having thoroughly investigated and ascertained the case through divine ordeals, such as questioning witnesses and so forth, ending with oaths, the king should proceed to inflict punishment; that is, he should take action. 2.11.3.
He states the fruit for one who acts in this way:
"One of such conduct conquers both worlds. (2.11.4)
"One whose conduct (*vṛtta*) is such is 'one of such conduct' (*evaṃvṛttaḥ*). Regarding this, Manu says:
"A king who punishes those who should not be punished, and fails to punish those who should be punished, incurs great infamy and is excluded from heaven after death. (MDh 8.128)
Regarding those traveling and those returning, when they meet on a path, by whom and to whom should the way be yielded? To this he says:
"The king's path [is yielded] when not meeting a Brāhmaṇa. (2.11.5)

A king who has been consecrated must be given the right of way here; if he is encountered by a Brahmin, then the path must be yielded to him even by unanointed Kṣatriyas, let alone by others. This statement is made for this very purpose, as the case would otherwise be already established by the rule to be stated later: "And [the path must be yielded] to those superior by caste" (ĀpDh 2.11.8). 2.11.5.
But when they have come together, the path belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone. || 2.11.6 ||

This refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa who has become a disciple during a time of distress. Even though he is a Brāhmaṇa who has become a disciple, when he encounters him, the path must be yielded to him alone, even by the king who is his teacher. (2.11.6)
It should be given by everyone to one oppressed by the burden of a vehicle, to the sick, and to a woman. 2.11.7.

A vehicle refers to a cart and the like. One oppressed by a burden means one overcome by a load. One who is afflicted means one who is diseased. A woman refers to any woman whatsoever. The path must be yielded to all of these by members of every social class (*varṇa*). By the use of the word "iti," [the list includes] the elderly, children, the emaciated, and so forth. (2.11.7)
And [the same applies] when those of a higher caste are approached by members of other castes. (2.11.8)
Those who are superior by caste and senior in caste must yield the path to others who are inferior in caste and to those who are outsiders.
It must be given by all for the sake of one's own well-being to those who are undisciplined, fallen, intoxicated, or insane. (2.11.9)

The *aśiṣṭa* is a fool; the others are well known. This [road] must be given by all these—whether of the same class (*sajātīya*), superior or inferior castes (*varṇa*), or outsiders (*bāhya*). "For the sake of one's own welfare" means for the purpose of self-protection; the meaning is that it is not for the sake of invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Regarding this, Kauṭilya has stated the measurement of the road to be given: "A chariot-road is five *aratnis* wide, an elephant-road four, and one for small animals and humans two" [KĀŚ 2.4.5]. || 2.11.9 ||
Through the practice of dharma, a low caste attains each preceding higher caste upon the transition of birth. 2.11.10.

By practicing the dharma—that is, by the performance of one's own duty—a person of a lower caste, such as a Śūdra, attains and reaches each preceding caste, beginning with the Vaiśya. Upon the revolution of birth, that is, through the transformation of birth, a Śūdra is born as a Vaiśya; there too, remaining steadfast in his own duty, he is born as a Kṣatriya; and there too, being devoted to his own duty, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa. This same principle is to be understood for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya as well. (2.11.10)
Through unrighteous conduct, a person of a higher caste falls to each successively lower caste upon the transition of birth. (2.11.11)

The preceding has already been explained. This refers to the performance of unrighteous acts other than the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), because regarding the great sins, the attainment of low birth has already been stated in the passage beginning with "the thief, the accused" (ĀpDh 2.2.6). || 2.11.11 ||
When one has a wife endowed with both virtue and offspring, one should not take another.

Faith and devotion toward the rites prescribed by revelation (*śrauta*), the domestic rites (*gārhya*), and the traditional law (*smārta*) constitute the perfection of *dharma*. The perfection of progeny consists in having sons. When such a wife exists, he should not take another. Although "wife" (*dāre*) is the subject under discussion, the use of the feminine form "another" (*anyām*) implies that she is his wife; thus, he should not take another wife, nor marry her. (2.11.12)
In the absence of either [of these], it should be performed before the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya). 2.11.13.

In the absence of either of the two—virtue (*dharma*) or offspring (*prajā*)—she should be superseded and taken away. Even in that case, it must be before the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), and not after the installation. This statement is made for this very purpose: since it has been stated that she is not to be superseded when both qualities are present, it follows by implication that she is to be superseded in the absence of either one; and if she is to be superseded even in the absence of only one, what doubt could there be regarding her being superseded when both are absent? (2.11.13)

The reason for [the statement] "prior to the establishment of the sacred fires" is as follows: for when the establishment (*ādhāna*) has taken place, he becomes connected with those rites of which this [fire] is a constituent part. 2.11.14.

For, because when the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires) exists—that is, when it is present—it is connected with and qualified by ritual acts (*karmabhiḥ*). By which acts? By those such as the *agnihotra* and others for which this *ādhāna* is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) and a benefactor (*upakāraka*). Here, because of the use of the word "existing" (*satī*), even if a son has been obtained, if the wife dies either before or after the *ādhāna*, the taking of another wife still occurs for the sake of fulfilling religious duty (*dharma*). Thus says Manu: "Having given the sacred fires to his wife who has died first during the funeral rites, he may again perform the act of taking a wife and likewise the *ādhāna* again. [MDh 5.168]

Yājñavalkya also says: "Having cremated his virtuous wife with the Agnihotra fire, the husband shall, without delay, take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule. (YDh 1.89)

Rational arguments do not apply to matters that are based solely on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). Therefore, this objection should not be raised: "The sacrificer has already been consecrated by the *anvārambhaṇīyā* [introductory] rite; this consecration cannot be produced in him again. Furthermore, the wife was previously unconsecrated and thus lacks eligibility for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices; how then can he be entitled to sacrifice with her? If the consecration produced by the *anvārambhaṇīyā* were, like a conjunction, inherent in both parties, then it would perish upon the death of the wife, and thus the man's need for a further consecration would not be untenable. Moreover, his eligibility for those domestic (*gārhya*) rites prescribed in the *smṛtis* which do not require the *anvārambhaṇīyā* remains uncontradicted even for her.

But surely, prior to the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna), one is connected with domestic (gārhya) and traditional (smārta) rites; why then is it said that "only when the establishment of the fires exists is one connected with [sacrificial] rites"?

True. From this very statement of the reason, it is understood that even if one possesses excellence in *dharma* and excellence in progeny prior to the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), there is no great fault in a man blinded by passion taking a wife at some point. Now, what is the case for one who has established the fires, whose wife—though faithful to the rites—is either incapable [of performing them], or whose sons have died or have not been born? In such a case, marriage must be performed, provided that the woman is suitable and that he is "endowed with *dharma* and progeny" and "connected with the rites. Nor does this contradict the rule "prior to the establishment of the fires," for that is a supplement specifically to the rule "it should be done in the absence of either one," and not to the rule "it should be done in the absence of both. In the *Bhāradvāja-sūtra*, although the performance of marriage is perceived as permitted for one who has established the fires without distinction—"Now, if one who has established the fires should take another wife, if he does not abandon the fires they would become worldly; for him, he should perform the re-establishment of the fires (*punar-agnyādheya*)," says Āśmarathya; "the re-kindling (*punar-ādhāna*)," says Ālekhana; "he should simply perform the re-establishment of the fires," says Auḍulomi—even so, this very same case [of the aforementioned deficiency] is its subject matter.
One should not give one's daughter to a man of the same lineage (sagotra). || 2.11.15 ||

A girl should not be given in marriage to one whose lineage (*gotra*) is the very same as that of the girl; for example, a Hārītā girl should not be given to a Hārīta, nor a Vātsyāyanī to a Vātsya, and so forth. (2.11.15)
And [one must not eat food] from those related to the mother by blood. 2.11.16.

Those related through the mother’s womb—such as the maternal uncle and others of the daughter—as well as those of the father (indicated by the word *ca*), to such persons, even if they are not of the same *gotra*, a girl should not be given in marriage. Regarding this, Manu says:
"A woman who is not a *sapinda* of the mother and not of the same *gotra* as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union" (MDh 3.5).
Vyāsa, however, says:
"Having bathed, one should carefully marry a maiden of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks, who is younger [than oneself], has brothers, and does not belong to the same *gotra*."
Some do not even permit marriage with a woman of the same lineage as one's mother;
however, if the [mother's] birth or name is unknown, one may marry her without hesitation.
"The sapinda relations of the mother must be avoided with effort by the twice-born. Thus [it is said].

Gautama: “Marriage is with those who do not share the same *pravara* (ancestral lineage). Beyond the seventh degree from paternal relatives and the progenitor, and beyond the fifth degree from maternal relatives. [GDh 4.2–5] Śaṅkha: “One should take a wife who is suitable, who does not share the same *ārṣeya* (Vedic lineage), who is not a blood relative, and who is within seven degrees of paternal kinship or five degrees of maternal kinship. Vasiṣṭha: “A householder, free from anger and joy, having been permitted by his teacher and having performed the ritual bath (*snāna*), shall take a wife who does not share the same *ārṣeya*, who has not had sexual intercourse, who is younger in age, and of equal status; she should be fifth in descent from maternal relatives and seventh from paternal relatives. [VaDh 18.1–2] Hārīta: “One who has leucoderma, one with leprosy, one with abdominal dropsy, one afflicted by consumption, one of short life, one without a *ārṣeya*, and one without a Vedic lineage (*abrahman*)—even if these families have not committed a formal loss of caste (*apatita*), they are to be avoided. For offspring conform to the family. Because of the absence of sacrificial rites from the beginning, one is ‘without an *ārṣeya*; because of the absence of Veda study, one is ‘without Vedic knowledge (*abrahman*); and because of belonging to a single family, one is ‘of the same *ārṣeya*. Therefore, having examined seven generations on the father’s side and five on the mother’s side, one should take as a wife a girl who is without a brother, of excellent character, and without a fire of her own. Paiṭhīnasi: “One should choose a maiden who does not share the same *ārṣeya*. One should avoid five on the mother’s side and seven on the father’s side; or three on the mother’s side and five on the father’s side. Yājñavalkya: [The text continues: “One should marry a woman who is not of the same *gotra* or *pravara* as oneself, and who is neither a paternal nor a maternal relative within seven and five degrees respectively. [YDh 1.53]

A man who has maintained his vow of celibacy should marry a woman who has belonged to no other man before, who is not a sapinda relative, who is younger than himself, and who possesses auspicious marks.

"One should marry a woman who is healthy, has brothers, and is not born of the same ṛṣi-lineage (ārṣa) or gotra, beyond the fifth on the mother’s side and the seventh on the father’s side. [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.52–53].
Viṣṇu says: "One should take as a wife a woman who is not of the same gotra and not of the same pravara, beyond the fifth on the mother’s side and the seventh on the father’s side. Nārada says:
"Up to the seventh [generation] on the father's side and the fifth on the mother's side,
those who share the same *gotra* as well as those who have the same *pravara* are ineligible for marriage. Thus says Śātātapa.
Having married a woman of the same *gotra* or likewise of the same *pravara*, one must perform her renunciation; the *atikṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.
"Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, or likewise one of the same maternal lineage (mātṛgotra),
or even one of the same *pravara*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance after abandoning her. Thus says Manu.
Having approached a daughter of one's father's sister, a daughter of one's own sister, a daughter of one's mother's sister,
or a daughter of one's mother's brother, one shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"A wise man should not take these four as wives; they are not to be approached as kin. By approaching them, he falls headlong into degradation. [MDh 11.172–73]

Bodhāyana: "If one should marry a woman of the same *gotra*, he should maintain her as he would his mother; having approached a woman of the same *gotra*, he should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Once the vow is completed, he must not abandon a Brahmin wife; he should treat her as a mother or a sister. It is known from the tradition of Kāśyapa that the fetus is not defiled. Now, if a marriage occurs through close consanguinity, one should avoid that section [of study]; for Bodhāyana holds that to be authoritative. It is known that progeny are indeed Mānavīs. There are thousands, millions, and billions of *gotras*."
There are exactly forty-nine of their ancestral lineages, according to the vision of the seers.
“As long as one *ṛṣi* is common among the *pravaras*, so long does the state of having a common *gotra* persist; this is the case for all groups except those of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras.

Thus [says] Sumantu: “All the wives of one’s father are mothers; their brothers are maternal uncles (*mātula*); their sons are the sons of a maternal uncle; and their sisters are the sisters of a mother. Therefore, they must not be married. (2.11.16)

In connection with the giving away of a daughter, he states the different types of marriage: "In the Brāhma marriage, having ascertained the family, character, learning, and health [of the groom], one should bestow the daughter, after adorning her according to one's ability, for the sake of procreation and joint performance of duties. (2.1.17)

That which is seen by Brahmā is the Brāhma [form of marriage]. In that marriage, having understood and examined the bridegroom’s kinsmen and others, he should bestow—that is, give—his daughter as a wife for the sake of "progeny and joint duties," meaning those duties which are to be performed together. The term *śaktiviṣayeṇa* is a particle resembling an inflected word; it should be understood in the sense of "according to one's ability" (*yathāśakti*). Thus, "having adorned her according to his ability, he should give her. This is the Brāhma marriage. In the reading *prajāsahatvakarmabhyaḥ*, the meaning is "for the sake of progeny and for the sake of joint duties. (2.11.17)
In the Ārṣa form of marriage, a pair of cattle must be given to the father of the daughter.
In a marriage witnessed by the seers, a pair of cattle—a cow and a bull—should be given to the father of the daughter; this is the Ārṣa rite. 2.11.18.
In the ritual procedure of a sacrifice to the gods, one should present [the offering] to the officiating priest.

When the gods have been invited and the sacrificial ritual has been spread out, while the officiating priest performs his duties, one should give away the maiden; this is the Daiva form of marriage. (2.11.19)
When two people unite out of mutual desire, that is the Gāndharva rite.

When a maiden and a suitor unite with one another in secret out of desire and become a couple, that is the Gāndharva marriage. The [metrical] feet are equal or long, as before. In this case, the rite of marriage must be performed after their union. (2.11.20)
Thus ends the eleventh section:
Having given wealth in exchange for the bride, they should take her away; that is the Āsura rite. 2.12.1.

That marriage in which one brings away a maiden after giving goods according to one's ability to a man who possesses a daughter is the Āsura rite; for Gautama says, "The Āsura is the bending down to women through wealth" (GDh 4.11). Therefore, a marriage by giving a house, land, ornaments, and so forth to the bride herself is not Āsura. 2.12.1.
Having caused those who have daughters to be proclaimed, they should carry her away; that is the Rākṣasa [form of marriage].

The *rākṣasa* marriage is that in which one carries off the girl after having provoked and overwhelmed her father or other relatives who possess daughters. Āśvalāyana states: “Having killed and split open the heads, one should carry off a weeping girl from those who are weeping; that is the *rākṣasa* [form]. Even in this case, the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) of marriage must be performed. Two other forms of marriage are mentioned in other scriptures. Regarding them, Āśvalāyana says: “‘Practice dharma together’—this is the *prājāpatya*. One should carry off a girl while she is asleep or intoxicated; that is the *paiśāca*. These two are not mentioned separately here because they are included within the *brāhma* and *rākṣasa* forms respectively. (2.12.2)
Of these, the first three are commended; among them, each preceding one is superior.
Among those forms of marriage, the first three—the Brāhma, Ārṣa, and Daiva—are commended; even among these, each preceding one is more highly commended than the following. (2.12.3)
As the marriage is conducted, so do the offspring become. || 2.12.4 ||
Offspring born of a praiseworthy marriage becomes praiseworthy; born of a censurable one, they become censurable. Regarding this, Manu says:
"In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, sons endowed with Vedic luster and esteemed by the learned are born in due order."
Endowed with beauty, virtue, and excellence, wealthy and renowned,
possessing abundant enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years.

"But in other [marriages], cruel and untruthful sons are born—sons who are despised by Brahman and Dharma due to improper marriages. [MDh 3.39–41] Thus, among the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, including the Prājāpatya, these are for the Brāhmaṇa; the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa are for the Kṣatriya; the Āsura is for the Vaiśya and Śūdra; and the Paiśāca is for no one at all. (2.12.4)
One should not step upon anything gathered by hand belonging to a Brāhmaṇa unless it has been sprinkled with water.

One should not step upon a spot of ground that has been leveled by the hand of a Brāhmaṇa, or smeared, or swept, unless it has been sprinkled with water; rather, one should step upon it only after having sprinkled it. 2.12.5.
One should not pass between the fire and a Brāhmaṇa.
One should not walk between the fire and a Brāhmaṇa. || 2.12.6 ||
And [he should honor] the Brahmins. 2.12.7.
He should not pass between [the teacher and others], nor should he walk among Brahmins. || 2.12.7 ||
Having obtained permission, he may pass beyond. || 2.12.8 ||
This is clear. 2.12.8
One should not carry fire and water simultaneously. || 2.12.9 ||
One should not hold fire and water simultaneously. || 2.12.9 ||
And one should avoid the simultaneous establishment of various sacred fires.
One should not perform the pouring together of fires that are situated separately. Others say that one should not throw fire into fire. 2.12.10.
When fire is being brought toward him face-to-face, he should not circumambulate it while it has not yet been established on the ground. || 2.12.11 ||

When fire is brought toward him as he is walking, he should not circumambulate it if it has not yet been established on the ground; however, when the fire is seen to be established, he should circumambulate it. 2.12.11.
And one should not let the hands touch each other behind one's back. || 2.12.12 ||
One should not join nor bind one's two hands together on one's own back. || 2.12.12 ||
Having fallen asleep while the sun was setting, or having failed to eat, he should remain seated in silence for the night;
when morning has dawned, having touched water, he may release his speech. 2.12.13.
When that [sun] is asleep, the sun sets; when that [sun] is asleep, the sun rises.
These two states—sunset and sunrise—occur respectively when the sun has set and when it has risen.

When both [the sun and moon] have set, he should remain silent for the entire night without drinking water or eating food, and he must not sleep. Then, on the following day, having bathed in the morning, he may release his speech. This is his atonement. 2.12.13.
Having slept, having risen, or having failed to urinate, he should remain standing during the day with his speech restrained. || 2.12.14 ||

The previous [section] has been explained. It is expected here that one should release speech after touching water. Since bathing is prohibited once the sun has set, one should bathe in the evening itself, release speech, and perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*). 2.12.14.
"Until one faints, one should restrain the breath," so say some. 2.12.15.

As long as there is exhaustion of the limbs, one should restrain the breath; having drawn in the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*), one should hold it. Some maintain that one should perform *prāṇāyāma*. This alternative depends on one's capacity. Regarding this, Manu says:
"One should recite the *Gāyatrī* together with the *Vyāhṛtis*, the *Praṇava*, and the *Śiras* three times while the breath is restrained; that is called *prāṇāyāma*. Thus it is said.
One should rotate this until exhaustion occurs. 2.12.15.
Or having seen an evil dream. || 2.12.16 ||
An evil dream is a bad dream, such as the leaping of a monkey and so forth; and having seen that... 2.12.16.
Or desiring to accomplish some purpose.
"Artha" means purpose; desiring to accomplish that, whether it be visible or invisible. 2.12.17.
And in the case of another transgression of the rules. 2.12.18.

The term "observance" (*niyama*) refers to the transgression of rules such as "one should void urine facing north" (ĀpDh 1.31.1) and so forth; in all such cases, the phrase "he shall restrain his breath until he is exhausted" (ĀpDh 2.12.15) is to be supplied as a supplement. 2.12.18.
When there is doubt regarding the consequences of a fault, that [action] should not be performed. || 2.12.19 ||
One should not perform that action in which a fault is expected as the result once it has been done, such as traveling alone in a dangerous place. (2.12.19)
Thus [it is] regarding study and non-study. 2.12.20.

The term "in doubt" (*saṃśaye*) is understood even when it is compounded; for instance, in the case of the doubt whether it is a day of study (*adhyāya*) or a non-day of study (*anadhyāya*), one should not perform that [recitation] even in such a doubt. An example is: "at the twilights, when there is thunder" (ĀpDh 1.9.20). This is an elaboration of the preceding rule. 2.12.20.
One should not speak as if it were a matter of direct perception regarding what is doubtful. 2.12.21.
One should not speak of a doubtful matter as if it were certain, like a direct perception, in order to avoid the fault of ignorance regarding one's own self. 2.12.21.

Among those who have committed the following offenses—those who eat at sunset or sunrise, those with deformed nails, those with black teeth, those who marry before their elder brothers, the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried, one who causes an elder brother to marry first, one who marries before his younger brother, one who causes a younger brother to marry first, and one who causes a younger brother’s wife to marry before he himself has married—the penance for each succeeding offense is more severe than that for the preceding one.

The first two have been explained. A *kunakhin* is one who has black nails. One whose teeth are dark is a *śyāvadan*, meaning one with black teeth; the substitution of *datr* [for *danta*] occurs by the rule "vibhāṣā śyāvārokābhyām" (Pāṇini 5.4.144), and the elision of its final syllable is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). One who marries a younger sister before the elder sister is married is an *agredidhiṣū*; one who subsequently marries the other [the elder] is a *didhiṣūpati*. When the elder brother has not performed the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) while the younger has done so, the younger is a *paryādhātṛ* and the elder is a *paryāhita*. When the elder brother has not performed the Soma sacrifice while the younger has done so, the younger is known as a *parivitta* and the elder is a *parivitti*. One who marries the wife of an elder brother is a *parivinna*; or, when the elder brother has not received his share [of inheritance] while the younger takes his share, that elder brother is a *parivinna* and the younger is a *parivividāna*. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the *paryādhātṛ* and the others. Among these, beginning with those who set out after sunset (*abhinimrukta*), for each subsequent one, the penance for causing impurity (*aśucikara-nirveṣa*)—which was previously mentioned as lasting twelve months and so forth—is more severe; whereas for each preceding one, it is lighter. However, in the case of the *abhinimrukta* and the *abhyudita*, both of the two penances just mentioned apply as alternatives. (2.12.22)
And some say that this mark should be removed after he has practiced [the penance]. 2.12.23.

Some maintain that after performing whatever penance has been prescribed for a particular bodily defect such as *kaunakhya* (scabies), one should remove that *kaunakhya* and other such defects; for another Smṛti states: "Except in the case of [the wife] and the sacred fires. (2.12.23)
Thus ends the twelfth section;
thus ends the fifth chapter in the second [book].
Sons [are born] to one who approaches a wife of the same caste, as prescribed by the ancient scriptures, according to the season.
They have a connection through their actions. 2.13.1.

The term *savarṇā* (of equal caste), *apūrvā* (not previously married), and *śāstravihitā* (prescribed by the scriptures) form a *karmadhāraya* compound. *Savarṇā* means of the same lineage; for a Brāhmaṇa, this refers to a Brāhmaṇī woman, and so forth. *Apūrvā* means not given to another; that is, she has no previous husband. *Śāstravihitā* means consecrated by the marriage sacrament (*saṃskāra*) prescribed in the scriptures, or one who conforms to the injunctions of the scriptures such as, “One should not give one’s daughter to a man of the same *gotra*” [ĀpDh 2.11.15]. When a son is born from such a wife to a man who approaches her according to the ritual for approaching during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) as taught in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, he becomes connected with the duties previously mentioned, beginning with, “The specific duty of a Brāhmaṇa... [ĀpDh 2.10.4]. The reading *gacchadhaḥ* contains a faulty *dhakāra*. 2.13.1.
And there is non-transgression by both through giving. (2.13.2)

They have a connection with the inheritance of both parents; and there is "non-transgression"—the word *ca* (and) being used in the sense of "if"—that is, if they do not transgress against their father and mother. But in the case of transgression, there is a loss of the inheritance. Another says: "In respect to the inheritance of both [parents], no transgression should be committed by them; the inheritance must necessarily be given. (2.13.2)
There is fault in sexual intercourse with a woman who has not been previously married, with one who is unconsecrated, or with one of a different caste. (2.13.3)

"Pūrvavatī" means one who has already had her hand taken by another; "asaṃskṭā" means one who lacks the sacramental rite of marriage; "varṇāntara" refers to someone of a different caste, such as a Kṣatriya or others, compared to a Brāhmaṇa or the like. When sexual union occurs with those women who have previously been married and so forth, a fault arises. Of whom? Of those very two who are engaging in sexual intercourse. (2.13.3)
Even in that case, it is the son alone who possesses the fault.

In this context, the suffix *tral* is used for the ablative case (*pañcamī*) according to Pāṇini 5.3.14: "It is also seen after other words. Furthermore, by both of these [rules], it is shown that the son alone is excessively full of faults. Regarding that, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are born from a woman who has a husband living (*pūrvavatī*): "He is a *kuṇḍa* while the husband lives; he is a *golaka* when the husband is dead" (MDh 3.174).

For one born of an *asaṃskṛtā* (uninitiated woman), there is no other name; rather, there is only the state of being *duṣṭa* (corrupt). But in the case of another caste (*varṇa*), there is a different birth-status (*jāti*). Regarding this, Gautama states: “Those born of women in the direct order (*anuloma*)—from those separated by zero, one, two, or three castes—are respectively known as Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, Niṣāda, Daupyantra, and Pāraśava. Those in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), however, are Sūta, Māgadha, Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, Vaidehaka, and Caṇḍāla” [GDh 4.16–17]. The word *eva* (only) is intended to exclude the daughter. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: “One born of an outcaste becomes an outcaste, except for the woman; for she belongs to another, he may approach her without inheriting property” [VaDh 13.51–53]. Furthermore, Manu says: “A jewel of a woman [may be taken] even from a low family” [MDh 2.238].

Now, about to describe the division of inheritance among sons, he states the decision regarding the inquiry: "Is a son begotten by one man on the wife of another the offspring of the begetter, or rather of the owner of the field? He says: "For the Brāhmaṇa text declares that the son belongs to the begetter. (2.13.5)
He says this because they cite not only the Brāhmaṇa, but also Vedic verses (gāthās) here:
"Furthermore, they cite:
'Only now, O Janaka, do I envy women; not so in the past.'"
When they spoke of the progenitor's son in the abode of Yama, [they said:]...
The progenitor of the seed leads his son away after death to the abode of Yama;
therefore, fearing the seed of another, men guard their wives.
Be vigilant and protect this lineage; let not others sow their seeds in your field.
In the life hereafter, a son belongs to the one who begot him.
"The weaver makes this web in vain. (2.13.6)

"The son belongs to the progenitor; the son belongs to the owner of the field"—this is the statement of the owner of the field who has been defeated in a legal dispute. "For all this time I considered myself the progenitor, but now for the first time I am jealous of women; I cannot endure their contact with another man. When will this end? Only when, in the abode of Yama in the world of the ancestors, he becomes the progenitor's son. The wise in Dharma have declared that the duty of a son belongs only to the progenitor who has departed to the other world, not to the owner of the field. This same point is stated with a slight distinction: "The depositor of seed (*retodhāḥ*), the giver of the seed, leads away the son—that is, he causes the offerings such as the *piṇḍa* given by the son to reach himself—having gone forth, having died, in the abode of Yama in the world of the ancestors. For that reason, they guard their wives, fearing the seed of others. [The form *bibhyantaḥ* is used with a Vedic *num* augment. Therefore, you too, being vigilant and not negligent, protect this "thread," the lineage of progeny. [The present tense is used in the sense of the imperative: "Protect! For what purpose? "Lest others should sow their seeds in your field. This is a case where the agent-suffix is used in the sense of the object by transposition (*vyatyaya*). [Alternatively: "Lest they should sow" means "let them not be sown. Another says: there is an elision of the *jas* ending after the word *para*. Thus: "Let other men not sow seeds in your field. Because in the hereafter, in the other world, the fruit of the son belongs only to the progenitor. "The taker" (*vettā*)—one who obtains the wife, the owner of the field—renders this thread useless for himself, making it his own. The word *iti* marks the end of the verse (*gāthā*). And this refers to the procreation of a son without the consent of the owner of the field. However, when the owner of the field is barren or diseased and requests, "Procreate a son in my field," or when, upon the extinction of the lineage, they appoint a widow—as Satyavatī was appointed to the field of Vicitravīrya by Vyāsa—then the son born belongs to both, the progenitor and the owner of the field. He is a "double-descended" (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*) son. Thus the Teacher himself says: "If he should have two fathers, one should designate two on each *piṇḍa*" [ĀpDh 1.9.7]. Yājñavalkya also says: [He provides the following verse: *Yad uktam—"janayituḥ putraḥ, kṣetriṇaḥ putraḥ" iti, tat parājitasya kṣetriṇo vacanam | etāvantaṃ kālam ahaṃ janako manyamāna idānīm eva strīṇām īrṣyāmi parapuruṣasaṃsargaṃ na sahe | kadā idānīm | yadā yamasya sādane pitṛloke janayituḥ putro bhavati, putrakṛtyaṃ paralokagatasya janayitur eva, na kṣetriṇa ity abruvan dharmajñāḥ | eṣa evārthaḥ kiṃcid viśeṣeṇocyate—retodhā bījapradaḥ putraṃ nayati putradattaṃ piṇḍādikam ātmānaṃ prāpayati paretya mṛtvā yamasya sādane pitṛloke | tasmāt kāraṇād bhāryāṃ rakṣanti pararetaso bibhyantaḥ | chāndaso num, bibhyataḥ | ato yūyam apy apramattā avihitā bhūtvā etaṃ tantuṃ prajāsantānaṃ rakṣatha | loḍarthe laṭ, rakṣata | kim artham | vaḥ yuṣmākaṃ kṣetre pareṣāṃ bījāni mā vāpsuḥ | vyatyayenāyaṃ karmaṇi kartṛpratyayaḥ | mā vāpsata, uptāni mā bhūvan | apara āha—paraśabdāj jaso luk | pare puruṣāḥ vaḥ kṣetre bījāni mā vāpsur iti | yasmāt sāṃparāye paraloke janayitur eva putraphalaṃ bhavati | vettā bhāryāyā labdhā kṣetrī vyartham eva tantum etaṃ kurute ātmasātkaroti | itiśabdo gādhāsamāptau | etac ca kṣetriṇo ‘nujñām antareṇa putrotpādanaviṣayam | yadā tu kṣetrī vandhyo rugṇo vā prārthayate mama kṣetre putram utpādayeti, yadā vā santānakṣaye vidhavāṃ niyuñjate, yathā vicitravīryasya kṣetraṃ satyavatī vyāsena, tadotpannaḥ putra ubhayor api putro bhavati bījinaḥ kṣetriṇaś ca | dvyāmuṣyāyaṇaś ca sa bhavati | tathācārya evāha—"yadi dvipitā syād ekaikasmin piṇḍe dvau dvau upalakṣayet" iti | yājñavalkyo ‘py āha |* [The verse follows: *Yad uktam—"janayituḥ putraḥ, kṣetriṇaḥ putraḥ" iti, tat parājitasya kṣetriṇo vacanam | etāvantaṃ kālam ahaṃ janako manyamāna idānīm eva strīṇām īrṣyāmi parapuruṣasaṃsargaṃ na sahe | kadā idānīm | yadā yamasya sādane pitṛloke janayituḥ putro bhavati, putrakṛtyaṃ paralokagatasya janayitur eva, na kṣetriṇa ity abruvan dharmajñāḥ | eṣa evārthaḥ kiṃcid viśeṣeṇocyate—retodhā bījapradaḥ putraṃ nayati putradattaṃ piṇḍādikam ātmānaṃ prāpayati paretya mṛtvā yamasya sādane pitṛloke | tasmāt kāraṇād bhāryāṃ rakṣanti pararetaso bibhyantaḥ | chāndaso num, bibhyataḥ | ato yūyam apy apramattā avihitā bhūtvā etaṃ tantuṃ prajāsantānaṃ rakṣatha | loḍarthe laṭ, rakṣata | kim artham | vaḥ yuṣmākaṃ kṣetre pareṣāṃ bījāni mā vāpsuḥ | vyatyayenāyaṃ karmaṇi kartṛpratyayaḥ | mā vāpsata, uptāni mā bhūvan | apara āha—paraśabdāj jaso luk | pare puruṣāḥ vaḥ kṣetre bījāni mā vāpsur iti | yasmāt sāṃparāye paraloke janayitur eva putraphalaṃ bhavati | vettā bhāryāyā labdhā k

"A son procreated through appointment (*niyoga*) in the field of another by one who is childless is, according to the law, the heir to the property and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 2.130]. Nārada also says:
"One born of two fathers (dvyāmuṣyāyaṇaka) should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and water separately to both;
likewise, he should take half of the inheritance from both the biological father (bījika) and the owner of the field (kṣetrika).

If there is a fault in sexual intercourse with women such as those who have a husband living (*pūrvavatī*), how then did Kataka and Bharadvāja (i.e., Ucathya and Bhāradvāja) exchange their wives, and how did Vasiṣṭha [approach] the Caṇḍālī Akṣamālā, and Prajāpati his own daughter? To this he replies:
"A transgression of dharma and an act of violence are seen among the ancients. (2.13.7)

"It is true that this practice has been observed; however, it is a transgression of dharma and not dharma itself, because its underlying cause is evident. Nor is this the only case; the violence of former times was also observed, such as when Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, cut off his mother’s head without deliberation at the command of his father. (2.13.7)
Is there, then, any fault even for them? No, he says:
"For them, due to the excellence of their vital energy (*tejas*), no transgression exists. (2.13.8)

For such is their splendor that they are not affected by such evils; and thus it is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so all his evils are consumed" (ChU 5.24.3).
Nor does this entail that the same [unreliability] follows for recent people as well; thus he says:
"The inferior person, employing [the Veda] after having investigated it, perishes. (2.1.9)

The word *tat* is a neuter dual formed by the rule *napuṃsakam anapuṃsakenaikavac ca* (Pāṇini 1.2.69), which prescribes a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) and a singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*). Having observed both that transgression and that act of rashness, the inferior person of the present day, employing such conduct himself, perishes and falls into ruin. For even though fire burns everything, we do not possess the same power. || 2.13.9 ||
In connection with the subject of offspring, he says: "Neither the gift nor the sale of a child is permitted. (2.13.10)

By the mention of "giving" (*dāna*), "selling" (*vikraya*) is included because of the commonality of relinquishment. And by the phrase "the law of buying" (*krayadharma*), "receiving as a gift" (*pratigraha*) is also included, due to the inclusion of the word "law" (*dharma*) and the commonality of acceptance. The giving, receiving, buying, or selling of one's offspring must not be performed. However, since Manu and others have enumerated both the "given" (*datta*) and "bought" (*krīta*) sons among the twelve types of sons, this prohibition is not a general one. What then? It concerns the eldest son, the only son, or a woman. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "One should neither give nor receive the eldest son; nor should one give away an only son, for he is for the continuation of the ancestors. A woman should neither give nor receive a son except with the permission of her husband. One intending to adopt a son, having summoned his kinsmen and informed the king, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* formulas in the middle of the house, should adopt a son who is not too distant in kinship and is closely related. [VaDh 15.3–6]. Furthermore, in the *Viśvajit* sacrifice where all one's possessions are given, offspring is not to be given, just like cattle and other property. But selling is prohibited in all cases. Regarding that, Yājñavalkya speaks among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
“Athiesty, the breaking of vows, and the sale of one’s sons.

[Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.236] This is also seen in the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* within the narrative of Śunaḥśepa: “He, seizing his eldest son, said,” and so forth [Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 7.3.15]. Furthermore, the employment of the word *apatya* (offspring) in the section concerning sons is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that it refers specifically to the eldest son; it does not derive from the etymology *apatyam* as that by which one does not fall (*na patanti anena*).
[As it is said: “In him he pays off the debt and attains immortality.”
"If a father should see the face of his son born alive" (AitBr 7.13).

In the case of marriage, it is heard in the sacred texts that the giving of a gift to one who has a daughter is optional and intended for spiritual merit; therefore, one should not treat as false the injunction that "one hundred [cows] plus an extra chariot (atiratha) should be given to one who has a daughter. In this context, the word "purchase" (kraya) is merely figurative praise, for the relationship [between husband and wife] arises from dharma.

In the *ārṣa* form of marriage, the giving of a gift to the father of the daughter is heard of in certain Vedic texts. Therefore, one hundred cows plus a chariot should be given to the father of the daughter; and the father of the daughter might treat this as a deception. This is seen in the text: “O gods, do not make our share deceptive” (*TS* 1.3.7). What is the meaning of “might treat as a deception”? It means that he might give it back to the groom again. Thus, this gift is optional (*kāmya*), being motivated by desire—namely, that the offspring may be as well-suited as the marriage itself, so that there may be sons equal to the *ṛṣis*. Consequently, it is for the sake of *dharma* and for the sake of progeny, not for the sake of sale. As for the word “purchase” (*kraya*) that is occasionally seen in a *smṛti* regarding that act of marriage, it is merely a figurative expression (*saṃstuti*) due to the similarity of the bestowal of wealth, not intended to establish an actual purchase. Why? Because the union of husband and wife arises solely from *dharma*. The same principle applies here to the rule: “In the *ārṣa*, two pairs of cattle (a male and female) should be given to the father of the daughter” (*ĀpDh* 2.11.18). On this point, Manu says:

"That for which the kinsmen do not take a bride-price is not a sale; that is merely an honoring of the maidens and an act of pure benevolence" (MDh 3.54). And all of this has been stated for the purpose of precluding any deviation from the rule: "There exists neither gift nor the law of purchase regarding offspring" (ĀpDh 2.13.10). 2.13.11.
Now, regarding the division of inheritance: having satisfied the eldest son with one special share of the property. 2.13.12.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.
A man who has sons shall divide his inheritance equally among them, excluding one who is impotent, insane, or an outcast. 2.14.1.

Having satisfied the eldest son with some preeminent wealth, such as cattle or the like, and having made him contented, he may divide the inheritance among his sons equally—both with himself and among themselves—even while still living. This includes property inherited through lineage as well as what was acquired by himself, as implied by the general statement. However, those who are impotent and so forth are excluded. The mention of the impotent and others is also indicative of those who are blind from birth and the like. As Manu says:
"Those who are impotent or outcastes, those who are blind from birth or deaf, as well as the insane, the idiotic, the mute, and anyone lacking sense-organs, are entitled to no share. (MDh 9.201)

In the case of those such as the blind, if a son exists, they too are entitled to a share. The same applies to the insane and the outcaste once the grounds for their status have ceased. However, the impotent and others must be maintained. The time for the division of the sons' inheritance is to be determined according to other Smṛti texts. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"When the mother’s menses have ceased, when the sisters have been given away in marriage, when sexual intercourse has ceased, and when the father has desisted from desire" (NSm 13.3).

And when the sons possess both the capacity and the faith for the performance of separate rites—that too is the time, because of the statement: "Therefore, there is a lawful separate performance" (MDh 9.111). The word "living" is used to establish that one must divide the sons while still living; this is the law. Otherwise, that term would be purposeless, as the case of one who is not living does not arise. In other Smṛtis, an unequal division by the father's own will regarding property acquired by himself is shown; the teacher’s position is that such is not the law. No share for the wife is explicitly mentioned; he considers her share to be part of his own. And he will say: "No division exists between husband and wife" (ĀpDh 2.14.16). Some, however, say that two-twentieths belong to the father.
The father, dividing his property, shall allot two-twentieths to each.

Because of this statement, this too is not the teacher’s (Ācārya’s) position: namely, that just as each son together with his wife receives one share, so it is for the father as well. Or rather—there is no fault—if the equality of shares applies only to the sons, while the self [the father] has a larger portion. On this point, Hārīta says: “The father is indeed the Āgrayaṇa vessel, and the other sons are the other cups; if the Āgrayaṇa should spill or be exhausted, one should take [the liquid] from the others. This means that after partition, in the event of the death of both parents, what is to be taken is from the shares of the sons. Thus ends the section on partition during the lifetime [of the parents]. (2.13.12–2.14.1)
Now, regarding the disposition of the wealth when the head of the household has died, he says: "In the absence of sons, it goes to the nearest *sapiṇḍa*. (2.14.2)

Because of the statement "in the absence of sons," when sons exist, they themselves shall take [the inheritance]; since there is no distinction specified, it is to be shared equally. Regarding this, there is a specific rule in the *Nāradasmṛti*: "Whatever remains after the father's debts have been paid from the paternal estate, that must be divided by the brothers; otherwise, the father would remain a debtor. (NSm 13.32)
But Kātyāyana says: "A debt contracted by a brother, a paternal uncle, or a maternal uncle for the sake of the family must be paid at the time of partition by the heirs equally."

In this regard, Yājñavalkya states: "When sons divide the inheritance after the father's death, the mother shall also receive an equal share" (YDh 2.126). This point was not explicitly stated here [in the preceding text], namely that her maintenance is to be provided by the sons alone. And so says Manu:

"The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth; and the son protects her in old age. A woman does not deserve independence. [MDh 9.3] Thus, in the absence of the mother as well, the sons and the unmarried daughters shall divide equally that property which was obtained from the husband's family or acquired by herself.
That woman’s property belongs to her children, and the daughter is entitled to a share thereof;
provided she is unmarried, but if she is married, she does not receive the mother’s property.

Thus says Bṛhaspati. Regarding property obtained from the father’s family, however, Manu states: "Daughters who have not yet been given in marriage shall indeed receive it; as for the mother’s separate property (yautaka), that is the share of the unmarried daughter alone" (MDh 9.131). Now, what is the case when there are daughters who have already been given in marriage, as well as sons?
