"When the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the maternal inheritance equally"— this is indeed the law of Manu. On this point, Vyāsa says:
"But those among them who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their elder brothers from that paternal wealth alone, as well as the unmarried girls, according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati speaks concerning marriage in successive order:
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are born from the Brāhmaṇa in due order;
they shall share [the inheritance] in portions of four, three, two, and one respectively.

"Those born of the Kṣatriya [caste] receive three, two, and one shares respectively; those born of the Vaiśya [caste], however, receive two and one shares. And it is clearly stated in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra]:
"Or rather, having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts..."
One who knows the Dharma should make a lawful partition according to this rule.
"A Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;
the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share" (MDh 9.152–53).

However, for one whose Brāhmaṇa wife is barren or deceased, the sons born of Kṣatriya and other wives shall take three, two, and one share respectively. But for one who has a son by only one wife, he shall take everything, with the exception of the son of a Śūdra woman. As Devala says:
An only son born in the direct order of castes shall indeed inherit the father's entire estate;
however, an only son who is a Niṣāda shall receive a third share of the Brāhmaṇa's property.
"Either a *sapiṇḍa* or a *sakulya*, being the giver of the *svadhā* offering, shall take [the property]. Thus it is said.

A *niṣāda* is a son born of a *paraśava* marriage. Regarding the case of sons born of *kṣatriya* women and others, Bṛhaspati states: "Land acquired through gift must not be given to a son of a *kṣatriya* woman or others."
Even if his father should give it away, the son born of a Brahmin woman shall take it when [the father] has died.
"One born to a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born classes does not deserve a share of land; he shall receive everything [only] from his own caste—thus the law is settled. Thus says Yājñavalkya.
"Even one born of a Śūdra woman by a Śūdra shall be an heir to a share by his own desire;

but when the father has died, the brothers shall make him a recipient of half a share. [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.136] Regarding wives, Viṣṇu states: "Mothers are entitled to shares following the shares of their sons. [Viṣṇu Dharmaśāstra 18.34] In this regard:

The legitimate son (aurasa), the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā), the son born of seed and field (kṣetraja), the son of an appointed daughter’s son (putrikāsuta), the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava), the maiden-born son (kānīna), the son received with a wife (sahoḍha), and the son of secret birth (gūḍhasambhava).
The son given, the son bought, the son self-given, the adopted son, the son cast off,
and the son begotten on any woman whatsoever— these are the fifteen known as sons.

"In this very order, in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one offers the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and takes the share; such is the general position in the Smṛtis. The *aurasa* (legitimate son) is born of a lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*). He was previously mentioned [in Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.13.1]: "Of a woman of the same caste who has been previously ordained by the scriptures... Gautama says: "A man without sons should, after performing sacrifices to Agni and Prajāpati, designate a daughter as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), having made the agreement: 'This offspring shall be for my sake. Bṛhaspati says:

"The biological son alone is declared the sole owner of the paternal wealth; appointed daughters are said to be equal to him, while all others are remembered as those who must be maintained. Thus says Manu.

"But if a son is born after a daughter has been appointed [as an heir], the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman. [MDh 9.134] Thus says Yājñavalkya.

"A son begotten by appointment (*niyoga*) in the field of another by a man who has no son is, according to the law, the heir to the estate and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both. This [son] is one and the same for the progenitor as a "seed-born" (*bījaja*) son, but for the owner of the field he is a "field-born" (*kṣetraja*) son. Thus says Bṛhaspati.

"Furthermore, both the grandson and the son of an appointed daughter bring about the attainment of heaven; they are proclaimed to be equal in regard to the inheritance, the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa), and the offering of water. Thus says Kāśyapa.
Seven types of girls who are reborn from marriage are to be avoided as the lowest of their families:
one promised by word, one promised in thought, and one for whom the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony has been performed.
She who has been touched by water, she who has been taken by the hand,
she who has circumambulated the fire, and she who is born of a remarried woman.
Kātyāyana says: "If a woman, having abandoned a eunuch or an outcast husband, takes another husband,
the son born of her is clearly the offspring of the biological father."
Manu:
"A son whom a maiden may secretly bear in her father's house, one should call him by the name Kānīna; he is born of the maiden and belongs to the man who marries her. [MDh 9.172]

Nārada says: "The son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna), the son born of a pregnant bride (sahoḍha), and he who is born of a concealed maiden (gūḍhaja)—the man who marries them is to be known as their father, and they are entitled to inherit from that father. [NSm 13.16]

Vasiṣṭha says: "If the unmarried daughter of a man should obtain a son through a husband of equal status, by that son the maternal grandfather becomes a grandfather-in-law (pautrī); he shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and inherit the wealth. [VaDh 17.23]
If she dies while still unmarried, the son belongs to the maternal grandfather; otherwise, he belongs to the husband. Manu says:
"If a woman who is already pregnant is married, whether her condition is known or unknown, the child belongs to the husband and is called *sahoḍha* (born of a pregnant bride). [MDh 9.173–74]

“He who is produced in a man’s house and whose father is not known is one born secretly in the house; he belongs to him by whose wife he was begotten. (MDh 9.169–70) Regarding the category of the *datta* (given son), when there are sons of brothers available, only one among them should be adopted. Among those, the *kṣetraja* (son of the wife) has already been discussed previously. Paiṭhīnasi states: “Now, those who are given, bought, made, or are the sons of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), having been born through the acceptance of another and through the lineage of the *ṛṣi*, they belong to two lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*) provided they are not born into a family that is not closely allied. Thus says Manu.

Manu has declared that among brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, they all become possessed of a son through that very son. But he who, for the sake of offspring, should purchase a son from his mother and father—
For he is a purchased son of that man, whether he be similar or dissimilar to him.
He who, being deprived of his mother and father, or abandoned by them without cause, offers himself to someone—that one is known as a self-given son. (Manu Dharma Śāstra 9.173–74, 177)

If one should adopt a son who is similar [in appearance], free from defects, and endowed with the qualities of a son, he is to be known as a *kṛtrima* (artificial) son. One who has been abandoned by both parents, or by either of them... [MDh 9.169–70]... [is to be known as a *kānīna*].
"The son whom one might adopt is called *apaviddha* (cast off).
[MDh 9.171] All of these belong to the same caste; this rule regarding sons among those of the same caste has been declared by me. [YDh 2.135]

Thus, from the statement of Yājñavalkya. Viṣṇu says: "In whatever place he may be born, he is the twelfth. [ViDh 15.27]. Yājñavalkya says: "The giver of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and the receiver of the inheritance among these is each subsequent one in the absence of each preceding one. [YDh 2.135]. Manu says:
"In the absence of each superior heir, the next inferior one is entitled to the inheritance.
[MDh 9.184] Nārada says: "These [heirs] succeed to the wealth in that order when the father has died."
"In the absence of each preceding one, the succeeding one shall obtain that [inheritance]. Thus [says Nārada, NSm 13.49].
Devala says:
"For all these sons of one who has no son of the body (aurasa) are declared to be heirs to the inheritance."
But when another is born from the same [father], seniority does not remain among them.
"Those sons of theirs who are of the same caste (savarṇa) shall receive a third part;
the rest shall live upon him, provided with food and clothing. Thus says Manu.

"But one should give a sixth share of the paternal wealth to the *kṣetraja* son; or the legitimate (*aurasa*) son may divide the paternal inheritance into five parts [and take four]. [MDh 9.146]. Thus says Bṛhaspati.
"But other sons, such as the son born of the wife (kṣetraja) and the rest, are entitled to five, six, or seven shares. Thus [it is said].

Hārīta states: “When about to divide the estate, one should give the twenty-first share to the son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the twentieth to the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the nineteenth to the son of two fathers (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), the eighteenth to the son begotten on the wife (*kṣetraja*), the seventeenth to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), and the remaining shares to the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*)”. Vasiṣṭha, beginning with the rule “one who intends to adopt a son,” says: “If a legitimate son (*aurasa*) should be born after he has been adopted, the adopted son is entitled to a fourth share” [VaDh 15.6, 9]. Since these scriptural texts exist, that which was previously stated by the Teacher—“their connection is through their respective duties, and there is no deviation regarding the inheritance” [ĀpDh 2.13.1]—must be understood as intended to prohibit the equal sharing of portions among the *kṣetraja* and other sons when a legitimate son born of a lawful wife exists.
Now, that which is not subject to partition. Regarding this, Manu says:
"What one may acquire by one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate—that which is obtained through one's own efforts—one need not give to others against one's will. (MDh 9.208)
Kātyāyana says: A learned man shall never give any portion of his wealth acquired through learning to those who are unlearned;
however, that wealth may be given by the learned man to those who are equal or superior in learning.
"When knowledge is obtained from another through the use of food provided by someone else,
that which is acquired by means of that [food] according to the prescribed rule is called 'obtained through knowledge' (vidyāprāpta)," so says Vyāsa.
"What has been given by the grandfather and the father, as well as what may have been given by the mother,
that must not be taken away from him; likewise [the property] acquired through valor and the wealth of a wife," so says Yājñavalkya.

If one recovers property that was taken away but had been acquired through inheritance, he need not give it to the co-heirs; the same applies to what is obtained through learning. Likewise, any ornament worn by women while their husband is still living [shall remain with them].
Heirs shall not divide that; those who do divide it fall [from their status].
Vyāsa says: Whatever vehicle or weapon is used in reliance upon common property...
If one acquires wealth through valor or other such means, his brothers are entitled to a share therein.
"Two shares should be given to him; the remainder shall be divided equally.

Thus ends the division among sons. In their absence, "he who is the nearest [relative] to the deceased shall take the inheritance"—this is the connection with what is to be stated hereafter. "The partakers of the lepa (the smearings) are those beginning with the fourth ancestor; the partakers of the piṇḍas (funerary cakes) are the ancestors beginning with the father."
The seventh among these is the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa); their sapinda-relationship extends through seven generations.

Thus ends the definition of *sapiṇḍas*. Among them, whoever is the nearest shall take [the inheritance]. However, the *sapiṇḍas* who have taken the estate should protect the wife; they do not, however, take her property—this is the view of the Teacher (*Ācārya*). For it is heard in scripture: "Therefore, women are devoid of sensory power and are non-inheritors" (*adāyādīḥ*). Manu also says: "Women are eternally devoid of sensory power and non-inheritors; such is the settled rule" (MDh 9.18). In this regard, regarding the absence of *sapiṇḍas* and others, Bṛhaspati states:
Except for a Brāhmaṇa, however, the king devoted to righteousness shall provide maintenance for their wives; this is remembered as the rule for inheritance.
For the sake of food, one *prastha* of rice with fuel should be given in the afternoon;
and one garment purchased for three *paṇas* should be provided every three months.
This alone is prescribed as the property of a widow for virtuous women:
clothing that is merely sufficient for wear, and likewise for the washerman.
Having set aside that wealth, he should allot what remains to the heirs;
the smoke-cessation offering (dhūmāvasānika) should be taken before the bath in the assembly hall.
"Having disregarded food, clothing, and garments when her husband has died," so says Vyāsa:
"A maximum inheritance of two thousand [coins] of wealth should be given to a woman."
"And whatever wealth has been given by her husband, she shall receive that according to her desire. Thus it is said.

"Two thousand *paṇas* is its measure; this is the maximum inheritance for a woman, not more. This applies when there is abundant wealth and a suspicion that kinsmen might not protect her. In the same way, those passages such as "the wife and the daughters" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.138), which concern the wife's acquisition of inheritance, should also be understood in this manner. Regarding this, some maintain that while the father, the brother, and the uterine brother are alive, the uterine brother alone should take the property. And so says Śaṅkha: "The property of one who has died without a son goes to his brothers; in their absence, the mother and father shall take it, or the eldest wife. Devala says:
Then the uterine brothers,
or the daughters who are equal [in status], or the father, if he is still living, shall divide the inheritance of one who dies without a son.
"Those of the same caste, brothers, the mother, and the wife, in that order. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"But a reunited coparcener [inherits from] a reunited coparcener, and a uterine brother [from] a uterine brother."
One should give a share to one who is born, and likewise take away a share from one who has died.
"But a uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall take the wealth, not a non-uterine brother;
nor shall one who is not a *saṃsṛṣṭin* take it, even if he is a *saṃsṛṣṭin*, if he is born of a different mother. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.141–42)

Here, because of the specific mention of "the uterine brother" (*sodara*), the inclusion of the term "brother" (*bhrātṛ*) in the verse "The wife, the daughters... (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.138) refers to one of a different womb (*bhinnodara*). Due to the greater degree of proximity, we hold that the father alone inherits; in his absence, the uterine brother; in his absence, his sons; in their absence, brothers of a different womb; and in their absence, the paternal uncle—this is how it should be understood. Furthermore, women such as the mother and others shall receive only enough for their subsistence. || 2.14.2 ||
In his absence, the teacher [should take it]; in the absence of the teacher, the pupil, having taken it, should employ it for those purposes or for religious duties. || 2.14.3 ||

In the absence of sapindas, the teacher shall take the inheritance; in his absence, the pupil shall take it. Having taken it, he should employ it for the sake of religious duties pertaining to the deceased, such as the digging of tanks and so forth; by the use of the word "or," it is implied that he may also use it for himself. 2.14.3.
Or a daughter. 2.14.4.
Or the daughter may take the inheritance; some say this is in the absence of sons, while others say it refers to the subject matter just mentioned. 2.14.4.
In the absence of all these, the king shall take the inheritance.
Because of the use of the word "all," this applies in the absence of kinsmen (bandhu) and those of the same lineage (sagotra). || 2.14.5 ||
"According to some, the eldest son is the heir. 2.14.6.

Some maintain that the eldest son alone is the heir to the inheritance; others, however, should live under him, and he too should protect them like a father. And thus says Gautama: "Or the eldest may take all, and support the others like a father" (GDh 28.3).
In a particular region, gold, black cows, and black land belong to the eldest son.

In some regions, they say that gold and the like are the share of the eldest son. "Bhauma" refers to what is produced from the earth, such as grain; specifically, "kṛṣṇabhauma" refers to black grains such as mung beans (*māṣa*). Others say it refers to black iron (*kṛṣṇāyasa*). (2.14.7)
The chariot and the household furnishings were in my father's house.
The chariot was his father’s share, as were whatever household utensils and implements there were, such as stools and the like. || 2.14.8 ||
Some say that the ornaments and the paternal wealth belong to the wife. 2.14.9.

Some, however, maintain that the portion consisting of the ornaments worn by the wife, as well as whatever wealth has been obtained from kinsmen such as her father and others, belongs to her. (2.14.9)
That is contradicted by the scriptures. 2.1.14.10
As for what was said—that the eldest is the heir—that contradicts the scriptures. || 2.14.10 ||
He shows what is contradictory [to that]:
"Manu divided his inheritance among his sons"—thus it is heard in the scripture without qualification. (2.14.11)
Because of the use of the plural number in the word "putrebhyaḥ" (to the sons), the hearing [of the Veda] applies without distinction. 2.1.14.11.
Here an objection is raised:
"Moreover, it is heard in a single [textual] passage that 'therefore, one should disinherit the eldest son with the wealth'. (2.14.12)

The meaning is "even so" (*athāpi nu*). It is heard in scripture that they "exclude the eldest son from his share," meaning they separate him [from the inheritance], even though it is stated as a singular entity. Just as there is only one eldest heir, it is likewise heard in scripture that [the exclusion] corresponds to that. (2.14.12)
He refutes this.

Furthermore, those learned in logic say that such statements are merely constant restatements (*nityānuvāda*) and not injunctions (*vidhi*), just as: "Therefore, goats and sheep move together among domestic animals"; "Therefore, the face of a graduate (*snātaka*) seems to quiver with the letter *r*"; and "Therefore, the goat and the Vedic scholar are most desirous of women. (2.14.13)

The phrase *athāpi* introduces an objection. Among animals, goats (*ajāḥ*) and sheep (*avayaḥ*) move together even though they belong to different species; this is their *repha*, or beauty. Here, however, there is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of the possessor with that quality, from which the suffix *kyaṣ* is derived. Thus, "the face of a graduate (*snātaka*) shines with earrings and so forth. The word *iva* is used as a poetic ornament for the sentence. A learned priest (*śrotriya*) possesses a great desire for women because of his long residence as a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) in the teacher’s household. Just as these sentences merely restate what is already observed and do not enjoin anything new, so too is the passage beginning with "therefore, the eldest son... [TS 2.5.2]; thus say those who know the principles of logic (*nyāyavidaḥ*). This alone is not the only restatement (*anuvāda*). What then? The passage "Manu [spoke] to his sons" [TS 3.1.9] is also indeed a restatement. (2.14.13)
For all those who are endowed with righteousness are entitled to a share.

The word *hi* indicates the reason: because these two are merely restaters (*anuvādaka*) and not enjoiners (*vidhāyaka*) of anything, therefore all those sons who are endowed with the [prescribed] qualities are entitled to a share. (2.14.14)
But even the eldest, if he acquires property through unrighteous means, one should exclude him from his share. || 2.14.15 ||

But if even the eldest son disposes of or employs property unrighteously, one should deprive him of his share. In the case of a partition during the father's lifetime, the father shall not give him a share; likewise, in the case of a partition after [the father's death], the brothers [shall not give it]. By the use of the word "likewise" (api), it is indicated that this applies all the more to anyone other than the eldest, thereby making known the preeminence of the eldest son. (2.14.15)
In the rule “while living, [the father shall divide] among his sons” (ĀpDh 2.14.1), no share for the wife has been shown. He states the reason for that:
“Between husband and wife, no division exists. (2.14.16)
Why?
Because from the taking of the hand, there is indeed jointness in ritual acts. (2.14.17)

Wealth is for the sake of ritual action, and a wife has no separate entitlement to perform rituals. What then? She has it by way of association, because of the scriptural statement: "Whatever duty must be performed by you, that is to be done together with her. In that case, what is the use of separate wealth? || 2.14.17 ||
Likewise regarding the fruits of merit. || 2.14.18 ||

Likewise, even regarding the fruits of merit such as heaven and so forth, there is indeed jointness; this is known from the indicative marks of mantras such as, "May they both attain undecaying light in heaven. (2.1.18)
And regarding the possession of material things. || 2.14.19 ||

Likewise, there is joint ownership even regarding the acquisition of property; for in that regard, the husband acquires wealth while the wife manages the household, and thus both security and prosperity depend upon both. Therefore, there is joint ownership in the possession of property. (2.14.19)
He establishes this very point: for they do not teach that there is theft when giving occurs on account of a specific occasion during the absence of the husband. 2.14.20.

For indeed, when the husband is away on a journey, the knowers of Dharma do not teach that there is theft on the part of the wife if she gives gifts for a specific occasion (naimittika), such as "one should give while cutting [the hair]," and so forth. If the property belonged to the husband alone, then there would certainly be theft [in such a case]. Because of the statement "in a gift for a specific occasion," however, there is indeed theft in other types of expenditure. This very point constitutes the disparity between husband and wife even though the property is common to both: namely, that the husband may employ it as he pleases, whereas the wife may only do so to this extent. Furthermore, the husband has no need for the wife’s consent regarding the employment of what he himself has acquired, because of his independence. For he is independent in the household, just as a king is in his kingdom. Therefore, the suspicion of theft applies to the wife, but not to the husband. (2.14.20)
Thus ends the fourteenth section.
By this, the duties of regions and families are explained. 2.15.1.

It has been stated that scriptural injunctions such as "the eldest is the heir" (ĀpDh 2.14.16) are not authoritative because they contradict [other] scriptures. By this, local customs (*deśadharma*) and family customs (*kuladharma*) are also explained. Those practices contrary to scripture—such as marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle (*mātulasutāpariṇayana*) and so forth—are not authoritative; those consistent with it are authoritative. Gautama also says: "The customs of regions, castes, and families are authoritative when they are not in conflict with the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*)" (GDh 11.20). || 2.15.1 ||

And for those related by birth on the mother’s side and on the father’s side up to the seventh person, or as far as the relationship is known—if they have died, one should touch water after excluding those who are still in the womb and those who have not yet completed a full year [since birth]. 2.15.2.

Those related through the mother’s womb are the maternal uncles and so forth. Those related through the father up to the seventh person are *sapiṇḍas*. Or, as long as a relationship is known or remembered—whether by birth, by name, or as "the descendant of such-and-such" (*āmuṣyāyaṇa*), "one of our lineage," or "a member of that family with such-and-such a name"—they are included. Thus says Manu: "But *sapiṇḍa* status ceases with the seventh person; the status of *samānodaka* (distant kinsmen) persists, however, as long as there is knowledge of birth and name. (MDh 5.60)

When they have died or passed away, the touching of water must be performed; a bath on account of death must be performed—excluding, that is, setting aside, fetuses and children who are less than a year old, whose full year has not been completed. Regarding children who have died, a bath need not be performed. 2.15.2.
Among them, [the first two] are indeed the mother and father. || 2.15.3 ||
When those children have died, the mother and father alone shall perform the ritual touching of water. || 2.15.3 ||
And those who take [them] away. 2.15.4.
And those who carry away and remove those dead children should also perform the ritual touching of water. 2.15.4.
And when his wife has been defiled by a paramour, he shall fast until the time [of her purification]. || 2.15.5 ||

A wife is a partner. The supreme gurus are the teacher, mother, and father. *Saṃsthā* means death. When a wife has died and when the supreme gurus have passed away, it is not merely a matter of touching water; rather, on the following day, until that time [the next day], there shall be fasting. 2.15.5.
Moreover: they should assume the appearance of those who are afflicted by disease. 2.15.6.
Those things by which the state of being afflicted is manifested should be performed upon the death of a wife or others.
What, then, are these?
Having disheveled their hair, scattered dust over themselves, and wearing a single garment, they face south, immerse themselves once, and having emerged, sit down. 2.15.7.

Having disheveled their hair, they scatter dust upon it. Having scattered it, wearing a single garment and without an upper cloth, facing south and gazing toward the southern direction, they dip once into the water, emerge, and sit down on the bank, still facing south. 2.15.7.
Thus three times. 2.15.8.
Having submerged themselves three times in this manner, they should sit down. 2.15.8.
Having poured out water with that as its cause, they return to the village without looking back and do whatever women say. || 2.15.9 ||

Then, based on that [instruction], they pour out water for those deceased relatives, such as wives and others, in such a way that the conviction arises in them: "This water has been offered to me. It is mixed with sesame seeds according to custom and because it pertains to the ancestors (*pitrya*). The formula is: "I give this water with sesame seeds to Bhāradvāja Yajñaśarman. Having poured out the water, they do not look back, but without looking behind them, they go to the village and enter their home. By this it is understood that this rite is performed outside. They perform whatever duties women prescribe, such as touching fire, touching a cow, and so forth. (2.15.9)
And regarding the others, some teachers teach this very same thing. 2.15.10.

Regarding what has been stated, such as “not eating at improper times” [ĀpDh 2.15.5], some teachers teach that this must also be performed when other sapindas—other than one’s wife and so forth—have died. 2.15.10.
One should feed those who are pure and learned in the mantras at all ritual performances. || 2.15.11 ||

Even when [the meal is] in private, one should feed those who follow the rules of injunctions and prohibitions, who are pure, who possess the mantras, and who have studied the Vedas—namely, at all rites, whether Vedic (śrauta), domestic (gārhya), or traditional (smārta), pertaining to the gods, the ancestors, or human beings; for it is seen in another Smṛti that "the feeding of Brāhmaṇas is infinite. (2.15.11)
He establishes the gifts according to place, time, purity, and the proper recipient. || 2.15.12 ||

The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the locative case (*saptamy-arthe*). A "place" (*deśa*) refers to Prayāga and the like; "time" (*kāla*) refers to solar eclipses and the like; "purity" (*śauca*) refers to the completion of penances such as the *kṛcchra*; and a "proper recipient" (*samīcīnaḥ pratigrahītā*) is one who is superior in age among those of equal qualities, according to the rule: "Among those of equal qualities, the elder in years is more excellent" (ĀpDh 2.17.10). The phrase "one should give" (*dadyāt*) indicates that gifts are to be bestowed upon these occasions. 2.15.12
That which is not offered into the fire and of which no portion is first given away must not be eaten. || 2.15.13 ||
That food of which a portion is not placed in the fire as an offering, or from which the first portion is not set aside and given away, must not be eaten. (2.15.13)
No oblation of alkaline salt is prescribed. 2.15.14.

That which, when seen being eaten, causes saliva to flow is "alkaline" (*kṣāra*), such as molasses, black pepper, *likuca* fruit, and so forth. One should not offer into the fire anything mixed with alkaline substances or salt. (2.15.14)
And likewise for one who has come into contact with inferior food. || 2.15.15 ||
Inferior food refers to horse-gram and the like; there is no rule for offering even food that has been mixed with such [inferior substances]. (2.15.15)

Now, for one to whom such food as this has been presented, how is his eating? Regarding that, it is said: For non-sacrificial food, there is an oblation; having removed warm ashes toward the north, one should offer it into those ashes. Thus it becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire. 2.15.16.

Having removed warm ashes from the *aupāsana* fire or the cooking fire toward the north, one should offer oblations upon those ashes with the *vaiśvadeva* mantras. This is the offering for non-sacrificial food (*ahaviṣya*). When performed in this manner, it becomes both an offering (*huta*) because the purpose of the action has been fulfilled, and yet it remains unoffered (*ahuta*) in the fire because it consists merely of ashes. Regarding this, Bodhāyana says: "Now, if this very thing should be so, having drawn out embers mixed with ashes to the north, one should offer upon them. Another says: "This is the consecration of those non-sacrificial side-dishes (*vyañjana*) which are eaten day by day; and the offering is performed once without mantras. (2.15.16)
The subsequent sūtra is clear in its meaning:
"A woman shall not offer the oblation. 2.15.17.
Nor one who has not entered [the order]. || 2.15.18 ||
Until the first feeding with solid food, fetuses do not become impure. 2.15.19.

Before the first feeding with solid food (*annaprāśana*), fetuses and infants do not become impure even upon contact with a woman in her menses or others; however, Gautama maintains that they require purification by wiping and so forth, as he says: "Except for wiping, washing, and sprinkling" (GDh 2.2). 2.15.19.
"Until one year has passed," say some. (2.15.20)
Some maintain that as long as a full year has not been completed, the embryos are not yet subject to the rules regarding ritual impurity. 2.15.20.
Or as far as they might not discern the directions. || 2.15.21 ||
As long as there is no knowledge of the divisions of the directions, they do not become effortless. 2.15.21.
"From the initiation ceremony onwards," says another [teacher]. 2.15.22.
"Before the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), they are not impure"—this is another view. (2.15.22)
The proof for this is as follows:
for in this case, authority is established by means of the treatises. 2.15.23.
For indeed, because when this initiation has taken place, one becomes eligible for the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions. || 2.15.23 ||
That is the final goal. 2.15.24

Even when referring to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the word "that" (*tat*) takes the feminine gender because it is in grammatical apposition with the word "end" (*niṣṭhā*). That end—that initiation—is the conclusion of the entitlement [to Vedic study]. (2.15.24)
And there is also the Smṛti. 2.1.25.

Regarding this matter, there is also a traditional teaching (smṛti): "Before the initiation ceremony (upanayana), one may act, speak, and eat according to one's desire," says Gautama [GDh 2.1]. 2.15.25.
Thus ends the fifteenth section;
thus ends the sixth chapter in the second book of the *Ujjvalā*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra*.

In ancient times, gods and humans existed together in this world. Then, by means of their actions, the gods went to heaven and the humans were left behind. Among them, those who undertake such actions come to exist in that other world together with the gods and Brahman; it was regarding this that Manu proclaimed the rite known by the word *śrāddha*. 2.16.1.

With the desire to explain the *śrāddha* rite, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is introduced for the purpose of generating interest: In ancient times, it is said, gods and humans existed together in this world. Then, unable to endure living with them, the gods went to heaven by means of their properly performed rites—those pertaining to the Vedas (*śrauta*), the household (*gārhya*), and the traditional codes (*smārta*). Humans, however, being incapable of acting in that manner, were left behind; they became inferior and remained in this very world. Since such is the power of ritual acts, therefore even now, among those humans, those who undertake and perform such rites just as the gods undertook them, they come to exist in that world together with the gods and Brahmā. Now, seeing humans thus falling away, Manu Vaivasvata, out of compassion, proclaimed this rite known by the term *śrāddha*.
For what purpose?
For the ultimate welfare of all beings. 2.16.2

The dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*). [It means] "for the sake of the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*) of all beings. In the reading *niḥśreyasā ca*, the letter *ca* is a Vedic substitute for the letter *ya*. Another says: there is a change of gender in the Veda; furthermore, the fruit of this ritual action is the ultimate good of all beings. (2.16.2)
In that [rite], the ancestors are the deities; however, the Brahmins serve the purpose of the Āhavanīya fire.

In that rite of the *śrāddha*, the ancestors—the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather—are the deities. However, the Brahmins while eating are to be understood as serving the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire, that is, for the ritual function of the *āhavanīya*. There are three acts in the *śrāddha*: the burnt offering (*homa*), the feeding of the Brahmins, and the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). Among these, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is intended to demonstrate that the feeding of the Brahmins is the most essential element. (2.16.3)
This should be performed month after month. 2.16.4.
This rite is to be performed month after month; because of the expression of repetition, it is a lifelong practice. (2.16.4)
The afternoon of the latter fortnight is superior. || 2.16.5 ||
Of the days belonging to the latter fortnight, the afternoon is more highly recommended. || 2.16.5 ||
Likewise, during the dark fortnight, the days are inferior. 2.16.6.
Of those very fifteen days of that fortnight, each succeeding one is more auspicious than the preceding.
When performed on any day of the dark fortnight, it gratifies the ancestors;
however, for the performer, there is a distinction in the fruit resulting from the restriction of time. || 2.16.7 ||

The satisfaction of the ancestors is equal on all days alike. However, for that performer who performs the *śrāddha* according to a fixed rule at times such as the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and so forth—meaning in every month on the first day alone, or on the second day alone, and so on—a specific excellence of fruit arises for that performer due to that restriction regarding the time. (2.16.7)
Who is this? To this he says:
"If it is performed on the first day, offspring consisting mostly of females is born. (2.16.8)

For one who regularly performs the *śrāddha* on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), his offspring—in the continuation of his progeny—will be predominantly female; generally, daughters are born. (2.16.8)
In the second [kalpa], there will be thieves. 2.16.9.
Sons are born. || 2.16.9 ||
The third [is for those] possessing spiritual luster. 2.16.10.
The perfection of conduct and Vedic study is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); those who possess it are "possessors of spiritual luster" (*brahmavarcasinaḥ*). 2.16.10.
In the fourth [case], he possesses small livestock. || 2.16.11 ||

Small animals are goats, sheep, and so forth; by means of them, the agent becomes possessed of that [quality]. In the subsequent singular forms as well, the designation of the agent should be understood. 2.1.6.11.
In the fifth [lunar mansion], males [are born]; one has many offspring and does not die childless.

They become males indeed, and they become many; moreover, one does not die childless, for the living soul itself dies while the sons are still present—not when they have died, nor when they have gone to another land, nor even when it has gone to another land itself. || 2.16.12 ||
In the sixth [chapter], the conduct regarding time and the conduct regarding the sense-faculties. 2.16.13.
One whose habit is traveling is a traveler; one whose habit is dice is a gambler. 2.16.13
Success is achieved on the seventh attempt. 2.16.14.
*Karṣaḥ* means cultivation; *rāddhiḥ* means accomplishment (*siddhiḥ*). || 2.16.14 ||
In the eighth [house], there is nourishment. 2.16.15.
The ninth [section] concerns animals with solid hooves. 2.16.16.
Horses and the like have single hooves. (2.16.16)
In the tenth legal proceeding, there is success. 2.16.17.
Trade is commerce, or the thorough mastery of the scriptures. 2.16.17.
In the eleventh [year], iron, tin, and lead. || 2.16.18 ||
*Kṛṣṇamaya* means made of black iron (*kṛṣṇāyasa*). Tin and lead are specific types of metal. 2.16.18.
In the twelfth [year], he possesses cattle. || 2.16.19 ||
On the twelfth day, many animals are present. 2.16.19.
In the thirteenth year, one has many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring; however, they die young. 2.16.20.
On the thirteenth day, one has many sons and friends; the offspring are handsome to behold. However, those sons die young; they perish while still in their youth. (2.16.20)
Success in weapons is attained on the fourteenth day. 2.16.21.
Victory in battle. 2.16.21.
In the fifteenth [day], there is nourishment. 2.16.22.
In that regard, the substances are sesame, beans, rice, barley, water, and roots and fruits. (2.16.23)
In that ancestral rite (śrāddha), substances such as sesame seeds and others must necessarily be employed according to their respective requirements. 2.16.23.
But when the food is oily, the satisfaction of the ancestors is more intense and lasts for a longer period. (2.16.24)

Whatever the food may be, if it is mixed with fats and sprinkled over with clarified butter and the like, the ancestors experience an exceedingly intense and superior satisfaction; and that satisfaction persists for a very long time. (2.16–24)
Likewise, by means of wealth acquired through righteous means and bestowed upon a worthy recipient. || 2.16.25 ||
Even by means of wealth acquired through righteous means and bestowed upon a worthy recipient, the ancestors experience such intense satisfaction for a much longer duration. || 2.16.25 ||
For one year, there is satisfaction with beef. 2.16.26.
Because meat is mentioned later on, it is also included here. With beef, the ancestors remain satisfied for one year. (2.16.26)
Thereafter, he performed an even more extensive sacrifice with the flesh of a buffalo.
Through buffalo meat, satisfaction lasts for a period longer than a year. || 2.16.27 ||
By this, it is explained that the meat of domestic and wild animals is pure for sacrificial purposes. 2.16.28.

By this [statement regarding] the meat of the buffalo, it is explained that the meat of other domestic animals such as goats and the like, as well as wild animals such as hares and the like, is also pure and pleasing to the ancestors. The inclusion of the term "pure" (medhya) is intended so that there may be no inclusion of those [animals] whose consumption is prohibited. 2.16.28.
Thus ends the sixteenth section:
on a bed of rhinoceros hide, [one enjoys] rhinoceros meat for an infinite time. 2.17.1.

When Brahmins are seated on seats covered with swords and shields, the ancestors remain satisfied for an infinite period of time by the gift of rhinoceros meat. In the reading "ānantyam," the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*). 2.17.1.
Likewise, [it is accomplished] with the meat of the fish Śatabali. || 2.17.2 ||
Śatabali, Bahuśakala, and the one named Rohita. || 2.17.2 ||
And of the vārdhāṇasa [sacrificial cake]. || 2.17.3 ||
The rhinoceros has been explained; through its meat, there is satisfaction for an infinite period of time. (2.17.3)
Being self-restrained and serene in mind, he should feed those Brahmins who know the Veda,
provided they are not related to him by birth, lineage, mantra, or being his pupil.

"Prayataḥ" means purified by bathing, sipping water (ācamana), and so forth. "Prasannamanāḥ" means one whose mind is tranquil and undisturbed. "Sṛṣṭaḥ" means full of enthusiasm; for it is seen in the rule: "If he is *sṛṣṭa* regarding the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, even though he has not killed him" (GDh 22.11). And in the rule "In the senses of livelihood (*vṛtti*), permission (*sarga*), and extension (*tāyana*), the root *kram* is used" (Pāṇini 1.3.38), *sarga* means enthusiasm. Being such as this, he should feed Brāhmaṇas. Of what sort? Those who know Brahman—that is, those who know the Self—and who are unconnected by birth and other ties. "Connection by birth" refers to maternal uncles and the like. "Connection by lineage" refers to those of the same *gotra*. "Connection by mantra" refers to officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and those for whom they sacrifice (*yājya*). "Connection by pupilage" refers to disciples and teachers. (2.17.4)
But when others have lost their virtues, even a uterine brother who has risen [to prominence] should be fed. || 2.17.5 ||

If others who are unrelated to the lineage and devoid of qualities such as conduct are found, then even a uterine brother endowed with conduct and other virtues should be fed; what need is there to mention sisters' sons and the like? This is the meaning of the word "api" (even). || 2.17.5 ||
By this, the resident pupils are explained. || 2.17.6 ||

By this [rule regarding] the uterine brother, the students (*antevāsinaḥ*)—as indicated by the use of the plural number—and indeed all those previously mentioned relations by birth and so forth, are explained; [the meaning is that] in the absence of others, these who have risen together [in the same Vedic school] should be fed. On this point, Manu says:
"This is indeed the primary rule (*kalpa*) for the offering of *havya* and *kavya*;
but this secondary rule (*anukalpa*), always practiced by the virtuous, should be known."

"One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the preceptor, the daughter’s son, the husband of a sister, a kinsman, the officiating priest, and the one for whom he performs sacrifices. (MDh 3.147–48) || 2.17.6 ||
Moreover, they also cite this: 2.17.7.
Regarding the matter that "relatives are not to be fed," those who know the Dharma cite this traditional statement: || 2.17.7 ||
The alms-food of the Piśācas called *saṃbhojinī* goes neither to the ancestors nor to the gods;
having its merit exhausted, it wanders only here in this world.
Like a cow that has lost her calf within the stall. || 2.17.8 ||

They eat together in this [place], hence it is called *saṃbhojinī*; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a location (*adhikaraṇe*). This is the name of this *piśācabhikṣā*. It goes neither to the ancestors nor to the gods; rather, having exhausted her merit and being devoid of any purpose for the next world, she wanders only in this very world, just as a cow whose calf has died wanders only within the house and does not go outside. (2.17.8)
He explains this:
"In this very world, as she enjoys herself, the family perishes from house to house. (2.17.9)

The meaning is that the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*), which serves as the cause for mutual enjoyment—that is, the act of giving at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*)—becomes fixed in this very world by going from house to house.
(2.17.9) Now, when many [suitors] of equal qualities have presented themselves, who is to be accepted?
Among those of equal qualities, one who is advanced in age is superior; and one who is destitute of wealth is preferable if he desires [the gift]. (2.17.10)

He who is advanced in age is to be accepted; even among such, he who is destitute of wealth and is desirous of obtaining it is to be accepted. Or rather—whether he be advanced in age or not, and whether he be destitute of wealth or not—he is to be accepted. But when two such persons meet, the choice depends on one's preference. 2.17.10.
The notification on the previous day. 2.17.11.
On the day before the *śrāddha*, one should inform the Brahmins: "Tomorrow there will be a *śrāddha*; on that occasion, you should grant the favor of serving as the *āhavanīya* fire. (2.17.11)
On the following day, the second [offering]. || 2.17.12 ||
On the following day, the day of the śrāddha, a second notification should be made: "The śrāddha is today. (2.17.12)
The third invitation. 2.17.13.
The invitation is the calling; at the time of eating, the third [form of address] is "Siddham, please come. || 2.17.13 ||
Some prescribe that the Śrāddha rite should be performed three times a day. 2.17.14.

It is not only the offering itself that occurs three times. What then? Some maintain that everything performed at the *śrāddha*, whatever it may be and however much, should be repeated three times. According to this view, there is a repetition of the fire-oblation (*homa*), the feeding, and the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) as well, all within that same afternoon. 2.17.14.
As with the first, so it is with the second and the third. 2.17.15.
In whatever manner the first *śrāddha* is performed, in that very same manner the second and the third should be performed. || 2.17.15 ||
Having gathered together portions from all the various foods, he should eat a single mouthful of the remainder, as previously prescribed. 2.17.16.

When all three *śrāddhas* have been performed and completed, one should take a portion from the remnants of the rice of all three *śrāddhas* and eat a mouthful that is at least half the size of a normal morsel. Thus it is stated in the *Gṛhyasūtra*: “With the following *yajus*, one should eat a mouthful that is at least half the size of a normal morsel from the remainder” [ĀpGṛ 21.9]. The sequence of the ritual procedure is as follows: on the previous day, there is the invitation to the nine or more [guests]; likewise on the following day in the morning; at the time of the meal, there is the formal address. Then, having concluded each [rite] individually starting from the *homa* up to the placing of the *piṇḍas*, one takes a portion from all [of them] and eats with the mantra: “Seated in the breath, [I consume] the nectar” [TS 2.20]. || 2.17.16 ||
But the practice of the northerners is that those seated on the mats bring water-jars to their hands. 2.17.17.
May that Śarāvatī protect us— she who, like a swan separating milk from water, divides [the speech] into eastern and northern [streams] for the sake of the grammatical perfection of the learned.

Thus says the grammarian. Those who dwell on the northern bank of that Śarāvatī river are the Northerners (Udīcyas); their practice (*vṛtti*) or custom is as follows: when the Brahmins are seated on their seats, water-vessels are brought to their hands, and from those water-vessels, the vessels for the *arghya* offering and so forth are taken to present the *arghya*. The mantras are: "O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*; O Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.7.10). Although it was stated that this is the practice of the Northerners, nevertheless, by virtue of its inclusion in the context of the ritual manual, it applies to all. (2.17.17)
"Let [the portion] be drawn out, and let it be offered in the fire," he addresses [the priests]. 2.17.18.

At the time of the *homakāla*, he addresses the Brahmins with this mantra: "Let [the fire] be taken up, and let [the oblation] be performed in the fire. In this mantra, the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) is used in the sense of a request (*adhīṣṭa*). (2.17.18)
"If you wish, let [the fire] be lifted; if you wish, let it be placed in the fire"—being thus permitted, he may lift it and offer oblations. 2.17.19.

Then, if the Brahmins should grant permission, saying, “Let it be taken up as you wish; let it be offered into the fire as you wish,” he, being thus permitted by them, may take it up and offer it. Taking up (uddharaṇa) means, for the sake of the Brahmins, setting aside a portion from the cooked food into another vessel. 2.17.19.
They declare that the sight of dogs and those excluded from the community (apapātra) at a śrāddha rite is censurable.

Those who are "apapātra" (excluded from the vessel) include the fallen (patita) and others, as well as those born of inverse unions (pratiloma). The learned (śiṣṭas) censure—that is, they condemn—the sight of such persons at a Śrāddha ceremony. Therefore, it should be performed in an enclosed space so that they do not see it. 2.17.20.

A leper, one who has been cursed, one who approaches the bed of another's wife, the son of a professional soldier born of a Śūdra woman to a Brāhmaṇa woman— these, when eating at a Śrāddha, become defilers of the row. 2.17.21.

*Śvitraḥ* means one afflicted with *śvitrī*, that is, white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭhī*). *Śipiviṣṭaḥ* refers to one who is bald; others say it means one whose penis is exposed. *Paratalpagāmī* refers to one who has gone to another's bed and has not performed the penance for it; this is the definition intended here. *Āyudhīyaputraḥ* is the son of a Brāhmaṇa who has adopted the livelihood of a Kṣatriya and subsists by means of weapons. As for the *caṇḍāla*, born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, he is not included here, because of the statement: "Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda" (ĀpDh 2.17.4). Therefore, it should be explained as follows: the son of one who, having produced a son through a Śūdra woman in an irregular marriage, subsequently produces a son through a Brāhmaṇī woman—that son is "born of a Śūdra in a Brāhmaṇī. For such a man has effectively become a Śūdra. Indeed, it is heard in scripture: "She becomes his wife (*jāyā*) when he is born again from her" (AitBr 7.3.13); and it is likewise recorded in the Smṛti.
"As for what is said regarding the taking of a wife from a Śūdra by those of the twice-born:

that is not my opinion, because in such a case, he himself is born as one of these. [YDh 1.57] These individuals, beginning with those afflicted by vitiligo (śvitra), become defilers of the row (*paṅktidūṣaṇa*) when eating at a *śrāddha*; they corrupt the row. Therefore, they are not to be fed.
Thus [ends the section]. 2.17.21.

One who has mastered the *trimadhu*, the *trisuparṇa*, and the *triṇāciketa*; one who knows the four *medhas*; one who maintains the five sacred fires; a singer of the *jyeṣṭhasāman*; one who has studied the Veda; the son of a learned man (*anūcāna*); and a *śrotriya*—these, when eating at a *śrāddha*, become purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). (2.17.22)

The triplet beginning with *madhu vātā ṛtāyate* (TS 4.2.9) is called *trimadhu*; for in it there are three occurrences of the word *madhu*, one in each verse. However, in this context, the person who studies that [text] is called *trimadhu*. The *trisuparṇa* is the triplet beginning with *catuṣkapardā yuvatiḥ supeśāḥ* (RV 10.114.3–6). Others, however, say it refers to the three *anuvākas* in the Taittirīyaka beginning with *brahmam etu mām* (TaitUp 4.38–40), for it is heard in scripture: "One should give the *trisuparṇa* unasked to a Brāhmaṇa," and "They purify the assembly up to a thousand [members]. As before, the term applies to the person. The *trināciketa*: the *Nāciketa* fire is studied in many branches, such as the Taittirīyaka, the *Kaṭhavallī*, and so on, as well as in the *Śatapatha*. He who knows that [fire] together with the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas is a *trināciketa*. Others say it is one who knows the three *cetās* of the *Nāciketa* fire. Others say it is one who studies the *virajā* *anuvāka*, beginning with *prāṇāpānavyānodāna* (TaitUp 4.64). The four *medhas* are the *Aśvamedha*, *Puruṣamedha*, *Sarvamedha*, and *Pitṛmedha*. One who studies them is *caturmedha*. Others say it is one who performs the four sacrifices. The *pañcāgni* is one who studies the five fires of the *Kāṭhaka* school, including the *Sabhya* and *Āvasathya* fires. The *Jyeṣṭhasāman* is well known among the Talavakāras as the song sung to the two verses *ud u tyam* and *citram* (TS 1.4.43.1–2). One who sings that is a *jyeṣṭhasāmaga*. In the reading *jyeṣṭhasāmikaḥ*, the suffix *ṭhan* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *vrīhi*. One who studies the Veda is devoted to his own recitation (*svādhyāya*). The son of an *anūcāna* is the son of one learned in the three Vedas (*traividya*). They also read *śrotriya* [in this list]; that should be understood as being for the sake of emphasis. These, while eating at a *śrāddha*, purify the assembly. Some read the word *iti* after "one who studies the Veda"; that is a faulty reading. By this, the reading "pañcāgni" without a case-ending is explained. 2.17.22
And one should not perform a Śrāddha at night. 2.17.23.

If, when the Śrāddha rite has begun, the sun should set due to a delay in the middle of the ceremony, then one should not perform the remainder of the Śrāddha at night; rather, one should perform it on the following day during the daytime itself. (2.17.23)
And once it has begun, there shall be no eating until its completion. || 2.17.24 ||

From the announcement on the previous day until the offering of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*), the performer is prohibited from eating in the interval. Immediately thereafter, they recite, "Except at the sight of Rāhu," which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "and not at night"; thus, one may perform [the rite] even at night during an eclipse of the moon. However, the northerners generally do not recite this. Furthermore, it has not been so explained by the ancients; rather, the phrase "and not at night" was explained as referring specifically to the occasion of a lunar eclipse. If it were to be recited, it would be more appropriate to place it immediately after the words "and not at night. (2.17.24)
Thus ends the seventeenth section;
thus ends the seventh chapter in the second book of the *Ujjvalā*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra*.
One should avoid melted butter, churned curd, oil-cake, honey, and meat. || 2.18.1 ||

*Vilayana* is pure butter (*navanīta*). That which is churned from curd by the hand or other means, but not mixed with water, is *mathita*. Thus say the lexicographers: "Buttermilk is *udaśvit*; *mathita* is buttermilk with one part water, *pādāmbu* with half water, and *nijala* with no water" (Amara 2.9.53). *Piṇyāka* is the cake of sesame seeds pressed in a machine. Honey and meat are well known; meat, even if not specifically prohibited, is included here. One should avoid these, beginning with *vilayana*. 2.18.1.
Black grain, the food of Śūdras, and whatever else is considered unfit to be eaten.

Black grain refers to black *kulattha* beans and the like, not black rice. One should avoid the food of a Śūdra, whether cooked or uncooked, as well as those others who are considered unfit for consumption or whose food is forbidden. 2.18.2.
One should avoid that which is unfit for sacrifice, untruth, and anger, as well as anything by which one might provoke anger.
Non-offerings include *kodrava* and similar grains. Falsehood is speaking untruth. Anger is wrath. Furthermore, one should avoid whatever action or speech would provoke anger in another. (2.18.3)
One who desires memory, fame, intelligence, heaven, and prosperity should avoid these twelve [things]. || 2.18.4 ||

*Smṛti* is the recollection of what has been learned. *Yaśas* is renown. *Medhā* is wisdom. *Svarga* (heaven) and *puṣṭi* (nourishment) are well-known. One who desires *smṛti* and the other benefits should avoid these twelve things, beginning with the dissolving of food (*vilayana*). The repetition of the word "should avoid" is a restatement for the sake of [emphasizing] the qualities, in order to enjoin *smṛti* and the others as the results. The mention of "twelve" is intended to include even the dissolving of food and so forth, lest only the subsequent items such as non-sacrificial food (*ahaviṣya*) be understood. 2.18.4.

Covering the area from below the navel to above the knees, touching water at the three times of the day, subsisting on food not cooked over fire, avoiding the shade, and remaining in a standing or sitting posture, he shall observe this vow for one year. (2.18.5)

“Covering [the body] below the navel and above the knees”—this has been explained [cf. ĀpDh 1.24.11]. *Triṣavaṇam* means bathing by touching water at the three *savanas*: in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. *Anagnipakvavṛttiḥ*: *vṛttiḥ* refers to the maintenance of the body; that [maintenance] must not be performed with food cooked on fire. Because of the mention of "fire," there is no fault in consuming mangoes and the like that have ripened naturally in their own time. *Acchāyopagaḥ*: not approaching shade. *Sthānāsanikaḥ*: one who lives by standing and sitting; by day he stands, and by night he sits, never lying down. He shall observe this vow for a year, beginning from the rule "melted [butter], churned [curd]," which was stated immediately after. This vow is equal to (*saṃmitam*), i.e., similar to, the vow of a student (*brahmacārin*) accomplished over forty-eight years. Those who know the Dharma declare that its fruit is exactly as great as that of the latter. It is not merely for the purpose of [fulfilling] the Smṛtis and so forth.

Another says: "The 'vilayana' (dissolving) and 'mathita' (churned milk)" [ĀpDh 2.18.1] and so forth constitute another vow for one who desires [the fruits mentioned in] the Smṛtis and other texts; however, that which begins with "below the navel" [ĀpDh 2.18.5] is the Saṃmita-vrata. And this applies to both the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*). Thus says Baudhāyana: "They call it the forty-eight-year vow; its summary is one year. We shall explain that year in detail. If he be a student, he should simply undertake the observances; but if he be not a student, having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, having gone to a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) and bathed," and so forth. [2.18.5]
The daily śrāddha. || 2.18.6 ||
Now, the daily Śrāddha that is to be performed day by day will be described; its name is the Nitya-Śrāddha. 2.18.6.
Outside the village, the pure ones prepare it in a pure place. || 2.18.7 ||

That daily *śrāddha* should be performed outside the village. Its preparation of food is as follows: "pure ones" prepare the food in a pure place. The mention of "pure ones" is for the sake of emphasis, since purity (*prāyatya*) has already been prescribed previously by the rule: "noble and restrained persons" [ĀpDh 2.3.1]. (2.18.7)
In that regard, there are nine substances. 2.18.8.
In that regard, for the perpetual śrāddha, only new substances are to be accepted. 2.18.8.
What, then, are they?
They are those by which food is prepared and those upon which it is eaten. (2.18.9)
Those vessels by which food is prepared, and those such as bronze bowls in which it is eaten, are called "new. (2.18.9)
And he should give those [remnants] to those who have already eaten. || 2.18.10 ||
One should give those vessels, such as those made of bell-metal and so forth, to the Brāhmaṇas who have eaten; thus every day. (2.18.10)
And he should feed those who have risen [to greet him]. || 2.18.11 ||
The expression "arisen together" (samudeta) is for the purpose of indicating an abundance of qualities. || 2.18.11 ||
And one should not give food-remnants to someone who does not possess those same qualities. 2.18.12.

That which remains in vessels after being eaten is here called *ucchiṣṭa* (leavings). One should not give even that to one who lacks those qualities which belong to those who have eaten; rather, one should give it only to one who possesses those very qualities. || 2.18.12 ||
In this manner, for one year. 2.18.13.
Thus, this perpetual śrāddha must be performed every single day for the duration of a year.
Of these, the best should be made with iron and goat-skin.

Of those days of the year, the final day—the day of completion—must be performed with a red goat, that is, one that is reddish-brown in color. Furthermore, the word *loha* is seen used in this sense elsewhere: “The goat is *loha*, whether it has horns or is hornless,” and “It is either black-spotted or *loha*-spotted. And in the *Camakas*, it occurs: “My dark one and my *loha* one. (2.18.4)
And he should cause a covered pavilion to be constructed.

The *māna* is the sacrificial shed (*dhiṣṇya*) and the altar (*vedikā*). Indeed, the use of the root *mā* (to measure) is seen in this sense [in the Vedic texts]: "In front of the *āgnīdhra* fire-shed, they construct a square, well-measured (*vimita*) hall, high in the east and low in the west. This is an instance of that very same root used without a prefix. One should have that measured out by laborers. And it should be covered with a curtain or the like. This too is to be situated outside the village. 2.18.15.
In its northern half, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas. || 2.18.16 ||
For that [gift] intended for a higher purpose, Brahmins should be fed. || 2.18.16 ||
"He sees both: the Brahmins eating and the ancestors in the honor," so they teach. (2.18.17)

By the power of this rite thus performed, he beholds both groups. Which ones? He sees the Brahmins eating at that very sacrifice, and likewise the ancestors assembled at the *māna* ceremony; the knowers of dharma teach that just as he sees the Brahmins eating with his own eyes, so too does he see the ancestors gathered at the *māna* as if by direct perception. (2.18.17)
From this point forward, [the rules concerning] what has been done and what has not been done. 2.18.18.
From this point forward, the *śrāddha* may be performed or not; if it is not performed, there is no transgression. (2.18.18)
For through the ancestral rite (śrāddha), the ancestors indeed experience satisfaction.

For because on the final day they come to see [the performer], through the *śrāddha* they experience satisfaction—that is, they make it known—to the one who performs the *śrāddha*. Therefore, it is said that [the rite] may be either performed or not performed. 2.18.19.
Now follows the ritual application for one desiring prosperity, beginning with "Under Tiṣya" and ending with "they should give the leavings"; this constitutes one [rite].
One desiring prosperity [should perform it] under the asterism Tiṣya. (2.18.20)
Thus ends the eighteenth section of the second chapter.

Having had white mustard seeds ground into powder, he should wash his hands and feet with them, rinse his mouth and ears, and then, sitting on a seat where the wind does not blow too strongly, being silent and facing south, he should eat; the skin of a goat is the first recommended seat.

A person desiring prosperity (*puṣṭikāma*) should perform the following procedure under the asterism Tiṣya (the *Tiṣyanakṣatra*). The instrumental case in *tiṣyeṇa* is used in the sense of location according to Pāṇini 2.3.45, *nakṣatre ca lupi*. Under the asterism Tiṣya, he should have servants prepare a powder made from white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*). Having had it prepared, he should wash his hands, feet, face, and ears with that powder. After washing, he should consume the remainder of the powder. If the reading is *prāsya*, it means he should scatter it. This specific ritual is to be performed every time the Tiṣya asterism occurs; however, thereafter it must be done daily. Having consumed it, he should eat while seated on such a seat as one where the wind does not blow excessively against him nor blows past him below—this is the connection with what follows. In this regard, the primary rule is that the seat should be the skin of a goat (*bastājina*). Restraining his speech and facing the southern direction, he should eat. (2.18.20–2.19.1)
They teach that food for a mother whose face is turned away in this manner is indeed detrimental to her longevity. 2.19.2.

Those who know the Dharma teach that food eaten by one facing thus toward the south is detrimental to the life-span and causes a loss of longevity for the mother of the eater. Therefore, one who has a mother should not observe this vow. 2.19.2.
The cup is made of udumbara wood, with a golden base; such is prescribed for the Praśāstṛ. || 2.19.3 ||

The root *cam* means "to eat"; that in which one eats is a *camasa*, a vessel for food. It is made of udumbara wood, meaning it is copper-colored; it has a golden navel, being adorned with gold in the middle. Such a vessel is praised (*praśasta*), meaning it is commended for eating. 2.19.3.
Nor should it be eaten by anyone else. 2.19.4.

Nor should anyone other than the performer—the father—even eat from that vessel. The particle *api* is a restatement of the verbal root’s meaning. Even if the reading were the masculine form *bhoktavyaḥ*, the meaning remains exactly the same. (2.19.4)
Taking his food in mouthfuls, he should not let it fall, nor should he open his mouth until the food is brought near; he should swallow the entire mouthful together with the thumb.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: taking only so much as can be swallowed at once—gathering it together, forming it into a mouthful (*piṇḍīkurvan*), not letting it fall in heaps on the ground, and not dropping fragments of food (*annalepa*)—one should swallow the entire morsel. When placing the morsel into the mouth, one should do so with the thumb, in such a way that the thumb also enters along with it; thus one should swallow all the morsels in the manner described. Regarding the act of swallowing, there is an injunction for another action in between: one should not lift the eating vessel from the left hand—that is, one should not release it; or rather, one may lift it or release it. Why is this stated, since no other method is possible? True; however, according to the maxim, “But it is restricted by the initial undertaking” (*prakramāt tu niyamyeta*, PMS 6.2.13), this is for the purpose of ensuring that whatever procedure was followed at the first meal must be performed in the same way until the end. 2.19.5.
And one should not make a sound with the mouth. 2.19.6.
This [is the rule] during the state of eating; the subsequent [rule] is likewise. 2.19.6.
And he should not shake his hand. || 2.19.7 ||
In this context, "hand" refers to the right hand. (2.19.7)
Having sipped water, he should hold his hands raised until they become wet.
Having eaten and sipped water, he should hold his hands upwards until they become dry and the water has completely departed from them. || 2.19.8 ||
Then he should touch fire. 2.19.9.
Having eaten, one must invariably touch water for ritual purification. 2.19.9.
And he should not eat anything else during the day except for roots and fruits.
Roots are bulbous roots; fruits are those such as mangoes and the like. One should not eat anything other than these during the day. There is no fault in eating them.
And one should avoid those things designated as *sthālīpāka* offerings. || 2.19.11 ||

In such injunctions as, "One should feed a Brahmin with that which is mixed with clarified butter" (ĀpDh 2.20.3), one should not eat having become a Brahmin. One should not eat those things designated for the ancestors and the deities, which have been set aside for them. 2.19.11.
And he should eat while wearing an upper garment and with the sacred thread over his left shoulder. || 2.19.12 ||

The upper garment is the upper cloth; having made that his sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), he should eat. Regarding his eating, some say that this alternative—“or else the cord itself serves the purpose of the sacrificial thread” (ĀpDh 2.4.22)—is applicable; others say there is a combination of both. 2.19.12.
But at the Naiyamika Śrāddha, one should offer only that which contains oil.
That monthly *śrāddha* which must be performed as a rule, one should offer that very thing accompanied by oily substances, and not dry food.
In this regard, the distinction is as follows: clarified butter and meat constitute the primary rule. 2.19.14.
This is clear. 2.19.14
In the absence [of these], oil is considered a vegetable. || 2.19.15 ||
In the absence of ghee, oil; in the absence of meat, vegetables. By the word "iti" (and so forth), whatever else is similarly appropriate [is included]. 2.19.15.
And under the Maghā asterisms, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with clarified butter according to the ritual for Śrāddha, in greater measure.
And during the bright fortnight of the month of Magha, by means of the prescribed rite for the śrāddha, one should feed Brāhmaṇas with food mixed with ghee.
Thus ends the nineteenth section.
At the monthly *śrāddha*, one should employ a *droṇa* of sesame seeds for each occasion by whatever means one is able. 2.20.1.

By whatever means one may be able to employ them—whether for anointing, rubbing the body, or as food and drink—one should, by that same means, employ a *droṇa* of sesame seeds at each monthly *śrāddha*. Since it is impossible to employ a *droṇa* for each individual Brahmin, one should employ them for the group collectively. Some maintain that the repetitive expression "a *droṇa*, a *droṇa*" is intended to indicate that this amount should be employed at every monthly *śrāddha*. Others, however, hold that such persons should be sought out with great effort and fed. (2.20.1)
One should feed those who have risen [from their seats], and they should not give the remnants of the meal to one who does not possess those same qualities. || 2.20.2 ||
This has been explained. The plural number in the word "dadyuḥ" (they should give) refers to the plurality of such agents; or it is a change in the grammatical voice. 2.20.2.

Now follows another procedure for one desiring prosperity, until the end of this chapter: During the northern course of the sun, in the fortnight of the waxing moon, having fasted for at least one night, one desiring prosperity should, under the asterism Tiṣya, cook a sacrificial mess of rice (sthālīpāka), sacrifice to Mahārāja, feed a Brāhmaṇa with that [food] mixed with ghee, and have him pronounce success for the sake of prosperity. 2.20.3.

A man desiring prosperity, having observed a fast for at least one night during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight of the bright half of the month, under the constellation Tiṣya, should cook a *sthālīpāka* (a mess of sacrificial food) and sacrifice it to the Great King Vaiśravaṇa. At the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the principal oblation is made with the formula: “To the Great King, Svāhā! This is followed by the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth, as well as the *jaya* and other rites. At the end of the sprinkling of water, he should feed a Brāhmaṇa with that *sthālīpāka* mixed with clarified butter. This statement is made with a view toward what follows. Having fed him, he should cause [the Brāhmaṇa] to pronounce the success of the rite, saying: “May there be prosperity! (2.20.3)
In this manner, day after day, until the final Tiṣya.

Thus, this [rite], beginning with the cooking of the *sthālīpāka* and ending with the recitation for success (*siddhivācana*), should be performed day after day until the next *tiṣya* [nakṣatra] arrives. 2.20.4.
Two [are taught] in the second [chapter]. 2.20.5.
When the second Tiṣya has arrived, one should feed two; the rest is the same. Thus up to the third. 2.20.5.
Thirty [verses] in the third [chapter]. || 2.20.6 ||
But during the third Tiṣya, he should feed three [brahmins], up until the fourth [Tiṣya]. 2.20.6.
In this manner, he continues for a year with increasing intensity.

In this manner, this rite is to be performed until the year is completed. Furthermore, there is an abundance of feeding for Brahmins: four starting from the fourth [month], five starting from the fifth, and so forth. 2.20.7.
Having stated this, he declares the fruit [of such action]:
"He nourishes great prosperity. (2.20.8)
He becomes endowed with great nourishment. || 2.20.8 ||
The fast begins from the very first day. 2.20.9.
The fast, however, begins at the very start of the Puṣya asterism, not of the Pratiṣṭhīya. 2.20.9.
One should avoid the food of those who have consumed their own vital energy (ātta-tejas).
One should not consume substances such as buttermilk or whey that have acquired a fiery potency. 2.20.10.
The locus of ashes and chaff. || 2.20.11 ||
One should simply avoid them. One should neither stand upon nor step over ashes or chaff. (2.20.11)
One should avoid washing one's feet or stepping upon them with the feet. || 2.20.12 ||
One should avoid washing one foot with the other, and likewise avoid placing one foot upon the other. || 2.20.12 ||
And the swaying of the feet. || 2.20.13 ||
Swinging is oscillation; it is moving back and forth. || 2.20.13 ||
And the final placement is upon the knee of the shank. 2.20.14.
One should avoid placing or resting the lower leg of one [foot] upon the knee of the other. || 2.20.14 ||
And scratching with the nails. || 2.20.15 ||
This is clear. 2.20.15
And cracking [of the joints] without cause. 2.20.16.

One should avoid cracking the joints of the limbs without cause; "cause" refers to fatigue, wind-disorders, and the like. This same meaning applies even when the reading is the compound *vādanasphoṭanāni*. (2.20.16)
And whatever else they proclaim. || 2.20.17 ||
Furthermore, he should avoid whatever else is censured and condemned by the learned, such as the cutting of grass and other acts distinct from those already mentioned.
And he was devoted to those things joined with righteousness and to the possession of material goods [only for their sake]. || 2.20.18 ||

One of the two *ca* particles is redundant; moreover, some do not read it at all. Regarding those acquisitions of material goods that are not contrary to the Dharma, he should be one who exerts effort toward them and brings them about; he should not be effortless. (2.20.18)
And one who bestows [gifts] at a sacred ford. || 2.20.19 ||
Whether it be a sacred ford, a virtuous recipient, or a sacrifice, he should be one who bestows thereon the wealth that has been acquired. || 2.20.19 ||
And let the driver go to a place that is not a ford, where there shall be no danger. || 2.20.20 ||

One should not give to a driver, a controller, or a non-giver, nor to one who does not give at a proper crossing (atīrtha), provided that there is no danger from such a person even if one does not give. However, if danger should arise, one must give even to slanderers and the like. 2.20–21.
And he was one who gathered men together. || 2.20.21 ||
He should be habituated to gathering people around him through the giving of wealth, pleasant speech, and similar means. 2.20.21.
And he shall enjoy pleasures that are not contrary to the Dharma. 2.20.22.
One should be habituated to the enjoyment of those pleasures that are not contrary to the Dharma, such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and the company of one's own wife.
In this way, one conquers both worlds. || 2.20.23 ||

Thus, endowed with great prosperity and practicing in the manner described, he conquers both worlds: this world through enjoyment, and the other world by bestowing [his wealth] upon worthy recipients. || 2.20.23 ||
Thus ends the twentieth section;
thus ends the eighth chapter in the second book of the Ujjvalā commentary on the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
"The rules common to all stages of life" (sarvāśramāṇāṃ samayapadāni) was stated previously. But what, then, are those stages of life? He says:
there are four stages of life: the householder's stage, the teacher's household, the life of a sage (mauna), and...
The stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprasthya). 2.21.1.

Those in whom persons seeking the highest good (śreyas) exert themselves are called *āśramas*. This is the general designation; the following are the specific designations. One who stays in a house (*gṛha*) and is intent on protecting his family is a *gṛhastha*; his state is *gārhasthya*, which is one *āśrama*. Dwelling in the teacher’s family (*ācāryakula*)—the term "teacher’s family" being used figuratively for the residence—is another; this is the second. The root *man* means "to understand"; one who understands is a *muni*, meaning one intent on knowledge; his state is *mauna*, which is another. One who goes forth to the forest is a *vanaprastha*, which is the same as *vānaprastha*; the suffix *aṇ* is applied here because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group; his state is *vānaprasthya*. The word *iti* indicates completion, signifying that there are only these many *āśramas*. Although only four are taught, the statement "there are four *āśramas*" is intended to prevent one from adopting the view stated in another Smṛti, namely: "The teachers maintain that there is only one *āśrama*, because the householder’s life is explicitly prescribed. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.36). 2.21.1.
Remaining undistracted in all of these according to the instruction, one attains security. 2.21.2.

He who conducts himself in all four of these stages of life (*āśrama*) according to the scriptures, remaining unperturbed and with a concentrated mind, attains the secure state that is free from fear.
