By this, the alternative regarding the stages of life should be understood as follows: one who seeks the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) must conduct himself with diligence in whichever stage of life he chooses, in accordance with the scriptures. And so says Gautama: "Some declare that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding his stages of life" (GDh 3.1). 2.21.2.
For all of them, from the initiation ceremony onwards, residence in the teacher's family is common. 2.21.3.
From the time of the initiation ceremony onwards, residence in the teacher’s household for forty-eight years or one of the other [periods] is common to all stages of life. 2.21.3.
There shall be no withholding of knowledge from anyone. 2.21.4.

"Non-abandonment" (*anūtsarga*); the lengthening [of the vowel] is Vedic. The non-abandonment of knowledge is common to all stages of life (*āśrama*). Therefore, residence in the teacher’s family is common [to all]. || 2.21.4 ||
Having understood [this], one should undertake whatever action one desires. || 2.21.5 ||

Having learned from his teacher that those duties which are prescribed for each stage of life (āśrama) must be performed by the householder, and that there is a transgression (pratyavāya) in their non-performance, as well as the specific fruit of these [duties], and having understood from the teacher that "these [duties] are capable of being performed, not those others," he should undertake whatever action or fruit he desires and enter that particular stage of life. || 2.21.5 ||
Since the state of the householder has already been explained in detail, [the author] now describes the nature of the teacher’s household, which is to be entered after the period of study:

"In this very manner, the student who seeks knowledge remains until the end under the teacher's authority; for the celibate student, the laying down of the body occurs in the teacher’s household. (2.21.6)

Just as for the student (*brahmacārin*) seeking knowledge who is still in the stage of learning, the rule for the life of a student (*brahmacarya-vidhi*) is set forth beginning with [Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.2.18], "Now follows the rule for the life of a student," wherein the regulations regarding the kindling of the fire and so forth are stated; by this very rule, for the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) who remains until the end—that is, until the fall of the body—performing the act of *upasadana* (sitting near the teacher), there occurs the laying down of the body, the abandonment of the body, within the teacher’s household. He should remain right there until death and not go to another stage of life (*āśrama*), provided he considers that very stage of life to be his own welfare. On this point, Manu says:
But when the teacher has indeed passed away, one should behave toward the teacher’s son who possesses good qualities,
or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a sapinda relative, just as toward the teacher himself.
But when these are unavailable, one who is capable of standing, sitting,
and moving about should perfect his own body by performing service to the sacred fire.
"The Brahmin who thus practices the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) without violation goes to the highest station and is not born here again. [MDh 2.247–49] || 2.21.6 ||
Now, concerning the wandering mendicants (parivrājas). 2.21.7.

Next, the duty of the wandering mendicant (parivrāja) is described: having renounced all undertakings, whether their results are seen or unseen, he wanders forth into the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsāśrama) for the sake of attaining the Self; thus he is a wandering mendicant, a renunciant (saṃnyāsī). 2.21.7.
For this very reason, one who observes celibacy goes forth into the religious life. 2.21.8.

For this very reason, one who possesses *brahmacarya*—that is, one whose *brahmacarya* has not been violated—may go forth from the stage of *brahmacarya* and undertake renunciation (*pravrajyā*), provided that at that very time his passions (*kaṣāya*) have ripened. Indeed, it is heard in scripture: "One may go forth from *brahmacarya* itself, or from the house, or from the forest" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4), and "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should go forth. From the expression "for this very reason," it appears that the teacher does not approve of one who has entered the householder stage attaining another stage by abandoning that [household life]. The intention there is as follows: since the taking of a wife contradicts the scriptural injunction, "One should perform the *agnihotra* for as long as one lives," how could such a person go forth? Therefore, even when dispassion exists, one is liberated while remaining a householder alone, by abandoning optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) and performing the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites while avoiding prohibited ones. As Yājñavalkya said: * *Brahmacaryād eva pravrajed gṛhād vā vanād vā* (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4) * *Yad ahar eva virajet tad ahar eva pravrajet* (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4) * *Yāvajjīvam agnihotraṃ juhuyāt* (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa) * *Tasmāt saty api vairāgye...* (Author's commentary) * *Gṛhastha eva mucyate* (Author's commentary) * *Yathāha yājñavalkyaḥ* (Author's commentary) (Quotation from Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.56–57): "One should practice *brahmacarya* until the end of one's life; or, having taken a wife, one should dwell in the house until old age; or, having performed sacrifices, one should enter the forest; or, having abandoned all attachment, one should go forth immediately.
