“Even a householder who has acquired wealth through righteous means, who is devoted to the knowledge of reality, who is fond of guests, who performs ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and who speaks the truth, is liberated. [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.205] Now, what contradiction is there in one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) entering the stage of a forest hermit (*muni-āśrama*) once he has become dispassionate? There is a contradiction with the scriptural injunction regarding debts (*ṛṇa-śruti*): “A Brāhmaṇa, at the very moment of birth, is born burdened with three debts: toward the sages by means of the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), toward the gods by means of sacrifice (*yajña*), and toward the ancestors by means of progeny (*prajā*). [Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10] Manu also says:

"Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation; but by pursuing liberation without having discharged them, one goes downward. (MDh 6.35) Here, "liberation" refers to the stage of life dedicated to liberation (*mokṣāśrama*). Now, if this were so, would it not follow that renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is not possible even after the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*)? To this we reply: in that case, renunciation is indeed appropriate according to the Vedic revelation (śruti), which states, "On whatever day one becomes dispassionate... (JābUp 4). This will likewise be appropriate for a householder who has become dispassionate, and it is also recorded in the Smṛti:

"Having performed the Prājāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee, and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa should renounce his home and go forth. [MD 6.38]

Likewise, for that householder who is old, whose wife has died, and who is incapable of taking a wife again, renunciation (pravrajyā) is also appropriate. Therefore, "on whatever day one becomes dispassionate" [Jābāla Upaniṣad 4]—this alone is the time for renunciation; everything else pertains to one who is not yet dispassionate; this is logical. As for the use of the restrictive particle *eva* in the Sūtra, it is employed in accordance with the Śruti, just as the Śruti, while saying "either from the house or from the forest," also says "one may renounce even from the stage of studentship (brahmacarya). Thus it is. 2.21.8 ||
They instruct him in that. || 2.21.9 ||
Those who know the Dharma instruct that wandering mendicant in what must be done.

Without fire, without a dwelling, without shelter, and without refuge, the sage should abandon all speech except for his sacred study; having obtained the means of subsistence in a village, he should wander without a home in this world and without expectation of reward in the next. 2.21.10

The *brahmacārin*’s fire-rite consists of the placing of fuel (*samid-ādhāna*). The householder’s consists of the *aupāsana* fire and the *agnihotra* oblation, etc. The forest-dweller’s (*vānaprastha*) consists of oblations, etc., in the fire prescribed by the rule: “Having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire” (GDh 3.27). But for him [the mendicant], there is no such fire-rite at all; thus he is *anagni* (without fire). His *niketa* is his natural dwelling place; because of the absence of that, he is *aniketa* (homeless). *Śarma* is happiness; because he has none, he is *aśarmā* (without happiness). He has not accepted anything as a refuge, nor is he a refuge for anyone; thus he is *aśaraṇa* (without refuge). *Svādhyāya* is the recitation of purifiers such as the *praṇava*. On this point Bodhāyana says: “The root of the tree is the Veda; the tree is the Veda, its root is the *praṇava*; the Veda consists of the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* leads to becoming Brahman—so said Prajāpati” (BDh 2.18.24–26). In that [state of the *praṇava*] alone he may release speech; elsewhere he should observe the vow of silence. Having obtained as much alms-food as is required to sustain life—that is, the maintenance of the vital breaths—this is the extent of his entry into a village; at other times he dwells outside. He is called *aniha* (without worldly aims) and *anamutra* (without aims for the next world) because he possesses neither worldly aims such as agriculture, etc., nor aims for the next world such as recitation and oblation, etc. Being such as this, he should wander. He should not stay in a single village for even two nights. On this point Gautama says: “He should not stay in a village for a second night except during the rainy season” (GDh 3.21), and “During the rains, he should be fixed in one place” (GDh 3.13). 2.21.10.
A garment was provided for him to wear. || 2.21.11 ||
That which has been released or abandoned by others due to its unsuitability is prescribed as his covering; he should cover himself with that. Gautama says: "Having washed it" (GDh 3.19). 2.21.11.
Some [teach] liberation from everything. 2.21.12

Some teachers instruct that there is liberation through the relinquishing of all clothes; one should not wear even a single garment, but should wander about quite naked. Another says: some declare his liberation from everything, both from injunctions and prohibitions, such that for him there is nothing to be done and nothing to be avoided. (2.21.12)
He elaborates upon this very point through examples:
"Having abandoned truth and falsehood, pleasure and pain, the Vedas, and both this world and the next, one should seek the Self. (2.21.13)

Having abandoned the rule that "truth must be spoken," as well as the rule that "in such cases untruth must be spoken—for that is superior to truth" (MDh 8.104) and so forth; having abandoned pleasure produced by the consumption of fine food and the like, suffering produced by cold, wind, and the like, the Vedas through the study of one's own recitation, this world consisting of worldly rites for desired fruits, and that other world consisting of transworldly rites for desired fruits—having abandoned all this, one should seek the Self, that is, one should meditate upon the realm of the inner self. 2.21.13.

Thus, the view of those perfected ones (siddhas) who, having destroyed injunctions and prohibitions by relying on the power of knowledge, act according to their own will, has been presented. Now, what is the protection for these very ones who act so freely? To that, he says:
"The bringing [of the disciple] to the Buddha. (2.21.14)

When the Self has been realized and understood, that very knowledge washes away all impurity and leads to security. For it is heard in scripture: "He does not increase by action, nor does he become smaller; having found the path of that very Self and known it, one is not smeared by evil action" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.23); and, "Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is consumed, even so are all his evils consumed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3). And it is also recorded in the Smṛti: "As a well-kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna... (Bhagavad Gītā 4.37).
"Even so, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes. [BhG 4.37] || 2.21.14 ||
This [view] he refutes:
"That is contradicted by the scriptures. (2.2.15)
That which is contradicted by those very scriptures that prescribe the duties to be performed by an ascetic is as follows. Regarding this, Manu says:
"One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter untruthful speech scattered through the seven gates."

"Neither by portents nor omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks, nor by instructions or discourses, should he ever seek alms. [MDh 6.48, 50] Therefore, those actions which are prescribed specifically with reference to the ascetic (*yatī*) alone must be performed. 2.21.15.
Regarding the statement, “In the Buddha there is the attainment of security” (ĀpDh 2.21.14), he says that this contradicts direct perception:
“If there were the attainment of security in the Buddha, one would not experience suffering even here in this world. (2.21.16)

If security were attained merely through the awakening to the Self, then the knower would not experience suffering even in this very body; but this is not the case. Furthermore, no one other than a consecrated king among the knowers is capable of enduring even the suffering of hunger for a mere moment. (2.21.16)
By this, the subsequent [case] is explained. 2.2.17.

The suffering of existence in the next world is explained by this very same principle; it does not cease for those who act according to their own whims. Therefore, one whose impurities have been ripened away by one’s own actions, who has realized the true nature of the Self through hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption, and who does not cast even a sidelong glance at prohibited things, becomes liberated by being devoted to the eightfold yoga. Regarding this, Bodhāyana says: “He may carry a single staff or three staffs” [BDh 2.18.1]. Gautama also says: “He may be shaven-headed or wear a top-knot” [GDh 3.22]. 2.21.17.
Now, the forest-dweller (vānaprastha). 2.21.18.
Next, the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is described. || 2.21.18 ||
For this very reason, one who is still a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) may go forth into homelessness. 2.21.19.

"He goes forth" (*pravrajati*) means he goes away definitively (*prakarṣeṇa vrajati*) so as not to enter again; that is, he establishes himself in the forest. And thus Gautama says: "And he should not enter a village" (GDh 3.33). The rest has been explained, as well as what follows. 2.21.19.
They teach it to him. 2.21.20.
He should maintain a single fire, have no fixed abode, and be without shelter or refuge as a sage, uttering speech only for the sake of his own Vedic recitation.

What, then, is his single fire? It cannot be the *aupāsana* (domestic) fire, because he is a student (*brahmacārin*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that he should place fuel sticks in the common (*laukika*) fire as before, both evening and morning. Another says: Gautama states, "Having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire" (GDh 3.27). The *śrāmaṇaka* is the name for the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra*; according to the method prescribed therein, a single fire is to be established, and in that fire, the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) is performed evening and morning. The rest has been explained. 2.21.21.
Thus ends the twenty-first section.
Wearing forest garments is prescribed for him. 2.22.1.
That which occurs in the forest is "araṇya," such as deerskin, bark garments, and so forth. 2.22.1.
Then he should wander about, subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses. 2.22.2.
Then, maintaining his livelihood by means of roots and other such things, and thus securing his subsistence, he should wander; he should be one whose nature is to roam. || 2.22.2 ||
They have proceeded from the end. || 2.22.3 ||

Having subsisted for some time on roots and other such things gathered by himself, at the very end—finally—they become active and fall away of their own accord. This is connected with what will be said later regarding "relying upon" (*abhiniśrayet*); having relied upon those [roots], one should subsist by means of them. (2.22.3)
Then one should rely [in turn] upon water, wind, and space. 2.22.4.
Then, for some time, he should subsist on water; then, he should subsist on air; then, he should resort to space and consume nothing at all. "Resorting" means practicing [that state]. 2.22.4.
Among these, each subsequent conjunction is superior to the preceding one in terms of its fruit. || 2.22.5 ||

It is called *saṃyoga* because it is joined (*saṃyujyate*) and adhered to (*saṃśrīyate*). Among those [substances] beginning with the root, each subsequent substance, as it is adhered to, is superior in terms of its result. || 2.22.5 ||
Alternatively, some teachers prescribe the sequence of stages beginning specifically with the forest-dweller. 2.22.6.

The word "atha" (now) introduces an alternative view. Previously, it was stated that one may enter the forest immediately after the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*); however, some teachers teach the successive stages of duties for that very same forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). 2.22.6.
How so?
Having completed his studies, taken a wife, and established the sacred fires, he undertakes those ritual acts which are prescribed as being no later than the Soma sacrifice. 2.22.7.

Having remained in the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), having completed his studies, and having become a householder, he should establish the sacred fires and perform the ritual acts. Which ones? Those for which the Soma sacrifice is the lower limit; "lower limit" (*avarārdha*) means the latter part, and that which occurs therein is "lower-limited" (*avarārdhya*). Those sacrifices for which the Soma is the lower limit are called "Haviryajñas," ending with the Soma sacrifice—meaning the Haviryajñas such as the Cāturmāsya and others, as well as the Soma sacrifice itself. These are those which are heard, those prescribed in the Śruti. (2.22.7)
Having built houses, he shall dwell outside the village together with his wife, his progeny, and the sacred fires.

Alternatively, having built houses in the forest outside the village, he may dwell outside the village together with his family and the sacred fires; in this case, the previously mentioned rule that "he maintains a single fire" (ĀpDh 2.21.21) does not apply. 2.22.8.
Or alone. 2.22.9.

Alternatively, having entrusted his wife to his sons, he may dwell alone by himself in the forest. In this case, according to the principle stated for the wandering mendicant (*parivrāja*)—namely, "having performed the *Prājāpatya* sacrifice" (MDh 6.38)—he should consign the Vedic fires into himself, establish the fire for the life-stage of the recluse (*śrāmaṇaka*), and become a possessor of a single fire. 2.22.9.
He should subsist by gleaning ears of grain. || 2.22.10 ||

The practice of *śiloñcha* has been explained. By means of that, he should maintain his livelihood; he should sustain his life. This applies equally to one who lives with a family and to one who is alone. Others, however, maintain that it applies only to one who is alone. 2.22.10.
And he should not accept anything beyond this. 2.22.11.
When he has become one who subsists by gleaning ears of corn and picking up single grains, from that time forward he shall not accept anything whatsoever as a gift. || 2.22.11 ||
And having been consecrated, he should perform the oblation. || 2.22.12 ||
When one should offer oblations, then one who has been consecrated and bathed should offer them; this is a restatement intended to prescribe a specific type of bathing. 2.22.12.
One should descend into the water slowly, striking the waves, and touch the water while facing the sun. 2.22.13.

One should enter the body of water slowly and without agitation. Having entered, one should touch the water by striking it with the hand and splashing it, and thus perform the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśet*) and bathe. 2.22.13.
Thus ends the rule for touching water everywhere. 2.22.14.
This is common to all castes and stages of life; accordingly, it will be mentioned later on. 2.22.14.
They teach that for those items used for cooking, eating, dwelling, axes, and sickles, a dual compound (dvandva) is formed when there is only one of each. 2.2.29.15.

Regarding those copper vessels and the like intended for cooking, and those made of bell-metal and the like intended for eating—as well as all four types of tools such as axes—one teacher instructs that two materials should be produced for each individual type. *Kāja* is also a specific kind of implement made of wood, similar to the axe and other tools. (2.22.15)
Taking one from each pair of opposites and giving up the others, he should dwell in the forest. || 2.22.16 ||

Taking each of those substances used for cooking and other purposes one by one for himself, and giving the others to his wife, he should dwell in the forest, attend upon [the sacred fires], and take refuge there. 2.22.16.
From this point forward, his fire-sacrifice, livelihood, attendance, and clothing shall be provided solely by means of the forest. 2.22.17.

For that forest-dweller, from the time of entering the wilderness onwards, the fire-oblation is performed with forest-grown grains such as *nīvāra* and the like; his livelihood is the maintenance of life; his hospitality consists of honoring guests; and his clothing is made of bark and similar materials. (2.22.17)
In those rites where there are *puroḍāśas*, *carus* should be prepared. 2.22.18.
In those rites, such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices, for which sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) are prescribed for a householder, he should perform oblations of cooked grains (caru) in their place.
And everything [is recited] in a whisper, together with the private study of the Veda. 2.22.19.

And the entire section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), including its subsidiaries and the principal rites, is to be performed in a low voice (upāṃśu), together with the study of the Veda for its own sake (pārāyaṇa) and the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña); that too must be performed in a low voice. 2.22.19.
One should not cause the forest to be proclaimed. 2.22.20.

Since the matter would have been established by the mere mention of "in a whisper," this specific statement is for the purpose of prohibiting directness; therefore, it means that one should speak in a whisper only so far as those staying in the forest cannot hear directly. 2.22.20.
A shelter for the sake of the sacred fire. 2.22.21.
That house, which serves as a refuge, must be constructed solely for the purpose of [protecting against] fire. || 2.22.21 ||
In the sky, by himself. 2.22.22.
And he himself should dwell in the open air alone. || 2.22.22 ||
On a bed or seat that is not spread with a cover. 2.22.23.
One should prepare one's bed and seat on a place that is not covered, but never after having spread anything over it. 2.22.23.
When new grain has been obtained, one may permit the consumption of old grain. || 2.22.24 ||
When new grain—such as *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, and the like—is obtained, one should permit the abandonment of the old grain previously stored. On this point, Manu says:
"In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard the forest-dweller’s food (muni-anna) previously accumulated, as well as worn-out garments, flowers, roots, and fruits. [MDh 6.15]
Thus ends the twenty-second section.
Or, desiring a more extensive rule, he should fetch the food every single day, morning and evening, with a vessel. 2.23.1.

This is for the forest-dweller living alone. Or, if he desires a more rigorous discipline, he should not store up grain. What then? He should fetch, day by day—that is, every single day—whatever food is necessary in the evening and in the morning, using whatever vessel is available, from those dwelling in the forest. (2.23.1)

Having lived in this manner for some time, he should then practice by subsisting on roots, fruits, leaves, and grasses; finally, he should resort to water, air, and space. Among these, each subsequent combination is superior in its result. (2.23.2)
Everything has been explained [ĀpDh 2.22.2–5]. 2.23.2.
The stages of life (āśramas) have been described. Now, their relative importance and lack of importance will be examined by way of opposing arguments and counter-arguments.
The eighty-eight thousand seers who desired offspring took the southern path of Aryaman and entered the cremation grounds. (2.23.4)

Eighty-eight thousand householder sages desired offspring; they rejoiced in offspring. Having reached the path of Aryaman—the southern road, the path of the sun’s southward course—and having traveled by the way beginning with smoke as described in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, they were born again and entered the cremation grounds; they met their death. Thus, throughout their lives, they attained the state of being born and dying, according to the injunction: “Be born, die” (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 5.10.8). This is a censure of householders. 2.23.4.
The eighty-eight thousand seers who led their progeny along the northern path of Aryaman indeed attain immortality. (2.23.5)

But those who did not desire offspring, having reached the path of the northern solstice and having traveled by the path beginning with light (*arcis*), attain immortality—there is a change of case [from singular to plural]—they "are fit for immortality," there is a change of verbal form [from third person singular to third person plural]—they "become capable," they "attain" [their goal].
Thus ends the praise of those who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas). 2.23.6.
The other three, distinct from the householder, are those whose vital seed is drawn upward; this is their praise. || 2.23.6 ||
Furthermore, there is praise for those very same [practices] by way of another method:
"Moreover, they become successful through mere resolve. (2.23.7)
Moreover, for those whose vital energy is drawn upward, their supernatural powers are accomplished by mere volition alone.
An illustration of this is as follows: "Granting offspring like rain, seeing from afar, possessing the speed of thought, and whatever else is similarly appropriate. (2.23.8)

If, during a great drought, they should desire, "May the god rain," the rain-cloud becomes one that rains according to their wish. Or, if they should show favor to someone who is childless, saying, "May a son be born to him," he indeed becomes possessed of a son. Likewise, even while staying among the Coḷas, if they should desire to see the Himavat mountains, it happens exactly so. Those whose speed is like that of the mind are "mind-swift" (*manojavāḥ*); the state of being such is "mind-swiftness" (*manojavatā*). If they should desire, "May we reach that place in just this much time," then in as much time as it takes to reach that place, they reach that place. And whatever else is similarly possible—such as the recovery of the sick from illness—that too occurs through their resolve. (2.23.8)
Since this is so,
therefore some declare these stages of life to be distinguished, both because they are based on scripture and because their fruit is directly perceptible. 2.23.9

Because they accord with such scriptural passages as, "On the very day one becomes dispassionate, on that very day one should renounce" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 4), and because their fruit is directly perceived in the manner described, some declare these stages of life for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*) to be distinguished—that is, superior to the state of the householder. || 2.23.9 ||
This [objection] he refutes by demonstrating the superiority of the householder’s life:

"The Vedas are the authority for those who are elders among the knowers of the three Vedas"—this is their settled conclusion. In that regard, those [rites] which are heard of as being connected with rice, barley, animals, clarified butter, milk, potsherds, and wives...
They consider that conduct which contradicts them—such as [the claim] that an action may be performed loudly or quietly—is not authoritative. 2.2.3.10.

The *traividya* are those who know the threefold knowledge—the three Vedas—both by recitation and by their meaning; among them, those whose knowledge is matured are the elders of the *traividya*. Their settled conclusion (*niṣṭhā*) is that the Vedas are the authoritative means of knowledge regarding objects beyond the senses. As the venerable Jaimini has stated: "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (PMS 1.1.2), and "Perception is not the cause [for knowing Dharma]" (PMS 1.1.4). Therefore, those who know [the truth] maintain that a practice contrary to the rituals heard in the Veda—which are characterized by being connected with rice and other materials, and which take such forms as "the *Ṛgveda* is recited aloud, the *Yajurveda* in a low voice"—is not an authoritative means of knowledge. This is what is meant: in all the Vedas and in all the branches (*śākhās*), it is precisely the ritual acts beginning with the *agnihotra* and ending with the "Path of the World-Creators" (*viśvasṛjām ayana*) that are enjoined as the primary intent. Consequently, the householder's stage alone is the best. If the Vedas are authoritative, then the stages of life for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*), which are contrary to that [householder's life], should certainly not be resorted to. And so says Gautama: "But the teachers [hold] to a single stage of life, because the householder's state is explicitly enjoined" (GDh 3.36).
Having praised the householder's life, he removes the censure expressed in the statement, "They resorted to cremation grounds" (ĀpDh 2.23.4),
by explaining that what is called a "cremation ground" is actually the rite of human purification prescribed at the conclusion of various rituals. (2.23.11)

As for the fact that a cremation ground is heard of in connection with householders, this is prescribed as a purificatory rite for the person called the Pitṛmedha, to be performed at the conclusion of various rites such as the Agnihotra; it does not mean that they become Piśācas and frequent the cremation ground itself. (2.23.11)
Why is that? He says: "Beyond that, an infinite fruit, designated by the word 'heaven,' is heard [in scripture]. (2.23.12)

After that, immediately following the rite of the cremation ground, the final, infinite fruit denoted by the word "heaven" (svarga) is heard: "This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world"—so it is known. In the phrase "anantyaṃ svargyam," the letter *y* is either a Vedic insertion (*upajana*) or a corruption (*apapāṭha*). 2.23.12.
Thus ends the twenty-third section.
Furthermore, he praises the householder's life itself by means of another method:
"Moreover, the sacred tradition declares his immortality through progeny: 'Through offspring you are born again; that, O mortal, is your immortality. (2.24.1)

Moreover, the sacred tradition, the Veda, declares that for this householder there is immortality—the state of being deathless—within his progeny, his lineage of offspring. O mortal one, subject to death, you are born again following after your offspring; you yourself are born in the form of your progeny. That indeed is the immortality, the state of being deathless, for you who are otherwise subject to death; for you do not die, since you persist in the form of your offspring. (2.24.1)
And this is indeed appropriate; thus he says:
"Moreover, this very [self] is perceived as established separately by direct perception, and its similarity is also seen; only the nature of the body is different. (2.24.2)

Moreover, this very same [tree] is perceived by direct perception as having grown separately; it appears as if it has become twofold. For the similarity between the two is indeed seen; only the bodies are distinct. The term *dehatva* contains the suffix *tva* used in its own sense (to denote the state of being). 2.24.2
"If he remains in the form of a son, what does that amount to? To this, he says:
"Abiding in the prescribed duties, they increase the fame and the heavenly realm of their ancestors in the life hereafter. (2.24.3)

Those sons, engaged in and established in the duties enjoined by the learned, increase the fame of their ancestors—the fathers, grandfathers, and others—who are connected with the *saṃparāya*, that is, the world beyond, saying: "This is his son, who performs such deeds; this is his grandson. And they increase heaven itself; for it is heard in scripture that those possessed of fame indeed dwell in heaven. (2.24.3)
In this way, there is a succession of lower and lower states for others. 2.24.4
In this manner, by such means, he increases the fame and the heavenly rebirth of others, one after another. || 2.24.4 ||
Until the dissolution of all beings, you shall be conquerors of heaven.
The dissolution of beings is the dissolution of the great elements; until that occurs, those who possess sons indeed live on in heaven. || 2.24.5 ||
"In the future Purāṇa it is said: 'At the time of renewed creation, they become the seeds. (2.24.6)

After the dissolution, there is creation again; this is "re-creation. In that regard, it is heard in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* that the Lords of Creatures (*prajāpati*) exist for the sake of the seed and for the sake of progeny within that cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). (2.24.6)
Moreover, there is also the word of Prajāpati: || 2.24.7 ||
Moreover, there is also a statement by Prajāpati on this point: "The householder's life alone is the most excellent. (2.24.7)

"The triple Veda, the life of celibate study, procreation, faith, austerity, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts—those who perform these [duties], with them we are; he who praises something else, having become dust, perishes. (2.24.8)

The threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) is the study of the three Vedas; *brahmacarya* is [the student’s life] lasting forty-eight years and so forth; *prajāti* is the procreation of offspring; *śraddhā* is faith and conviction in the scriptures; *tapas* is fasting and the like; *yajña* is the sacrifice beginning with the *agnihotra* and ending with the *somayāga*; and *anupradāna* is the giving of gifts both within and outside the sacrificial altar. We belong only with those who perform these [duties]; they alone are our companions. But anyone else who praises other stages of life (*āśrama*) such as that of the perpetual celibates (*ūrdhvaretas*), becomes like dust and perishes—he is destroyed. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the statement. (2.24.8)

Just as sons who behave according to the injunctions increase the fame and the heavenly merit of their ancestors, so too those who behave according to prohibitions would increase infamy and lead them to hell. To this he replies:
"In that regard, it is only those who commit sins who perish, like the leaf of a tree;
they do not harm others. (2.24.9)

In that regard, within the continuity of progeny, those who are the doers of evil are themselves destroyed and perish; they do not harm others such as their fathers and so forth. Just as, for example, whichever leaf of a tree is damaged by insects and the like falls off, yet it does not cause the tree or the branch to fall—so it is in this case. (2.24.9)
He establishes this very point:
"In this world, he has no connection with actions, nor, likewise, in the next world, with the fruits of actions. (2.24.10)

The singular number in the word *asya* is used with reference to the generality [of ancestors]. For this father or other predecessor, there exists no connection in this world with actions performed for the sake of a son. This is an illustration: just as the father or others have no agency in the actions performed for the sake of a son, so too in the next world there is no connection even with the fruits of those actions; such is the meaning. (2.24.10)
This should be understood by means of this [verse]. 2.24.11.

That which was stated—that [the fruits of] the evildoer alone perish and do not harm others—should be understood and ascertained as having that very meaning by means of the reason about to be explained hereafter. || 2.24.11 ||
This is the creation of Prajāpati and the sages. 2.24.12.

This creation, beginning with the gods and ending with the animals, belongs to Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha and to the sages such as Marīci and others. And they remain undestroyed, abiding each in their own station. For if those who perform meritorious deeds were themselves subject to destruction and would likewise destroy others, then it would not be possible that those who have performed merit still exist happily even today. (2.24.12)
Regarding this, he states an illustration:
"In that regard, the natures of those who have performed meritorious deeds are perceived as supremely radiant. (2.24.13)

In that creation, the bodies (*prakṛti*) of those merit-makers such as Vasiṣṭha and others are perceived in the sky as supreme, excellent, and blazingly radiant, just like the constellation of the Seven Sages (*Saptarṣimaṇḍala*). And it is heard in scripture: "These luminaries, namely the constellations, are indeed the fruits of meritorious deeds" (TS 5.4.1). This too is proof that the destruction of ancestors does not follow from the destruction of their sons.

It may be that someone, through a portion of their karma or through austerity, conquers a finite world while still embodied and attains the fulfillment of their will; yet that is not the preeminence of the stages of life.

It may well be that some *ūrdhvaretas* (one who has sublimated his vital energy) conquers the finite world with his very body—either by means of a portion of previously accumulated karma remaining after it has been partially exhausted, or through intense austerity (*tapas*)—and it may also be that perfection (*siddhi*) comes from mere volition (*saṃkalpa*). However, these are not the reasons for the superiority of the [other] stages of life (*āśrama*). Thus, the position that "the teachers maintain there is only one stage of life" (*aikāśramyaṃ tv ācāryāḥ*) is established. Others, however, think that all stages of life are both flawed and adorned; therefore, the conclusion remains: "In all of them, one who conducts himself according to the instructions without distraction attains security" (*teṣu sarveṣu yathopadeśam avyagro vartamānaḥ kṣemaṃ gacchati*). 2.24.14.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section;
thus ends the ninth chapter in the second book of the *Ujjvalā*, a commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra*.
The common and specific duties of all social classes have been explained.
Now we shall describe those of the king specifically. 2.25.1.

The mention of what has been said and what is yet to be said is for the purpose of concentrating the minds of the listeners. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and so forth are duties common to all social classes (*varṇas*). Study and so forth belong to the three [higher] classes; teaching and so forth belong to the Brāhmaṇa; fighting and so forth belong to the Kṣatriya; agriculture and so forth belong to the Vaiśya; and service belongs to the Śūdra. Here, the "king" intended is one who has been consecrated (*abhiṣikta*); for it is only for him that the collection of duties about to be described is possible. Because of his specific distinction, we shall state that which must be stated specifically. The reading with the accusative ending, *viśeṣān*, is indeed more appropriate. (2.25.1)
One should cause the house and the city to be measured out with the gate facing south.

"Veśma" means a house; "pura" means a city. Both of these should be measured out with their gates facing south; that is, one should have them constructed by architects and other craftsmen such that the door is on the southern side. (2.25.2)
In the inner city was his dwelling. 2.25.3.
In the middle of all the ramparts, within that innermost city, he should have a palace constructed for himself.
In front of that [fire] is the dwelling; they call that the invitation. 2.25.4.

In front of that house, a guest-house (āvasatha) should be constructed. It is called an *āvasatha* because people come and dwell (*vasanti*) in it; its specific designation is *āmantraṇa*, for it is there that guests are invited (*āmantryante*). 2.25.4.
To the south of the city is the assembly hall, with its door facing north, so that both the interior and the exterior may be visible. || 2.25.5 ||

The word *dakṣiṇena* ends in the suffix *-ena*. The word *puram* ends in the accusative case according to Pāṇini 2.3.31 (*enapā dvitīyā*). A hall (*sabhā*) should be constructed not far from the south of the city. It is described as having gates to the south and north—that is, one whose doors are in the southern and northern directions. If one asks why there are doors on both sides, it is for the purpose that both what occurs outside and what occurs inside may be clearly visible. This is the gambling hall; those seeking to gamble enter it, and it is the king’s place of revenue. (2.25.5)
In all these cases, the sacred fires should be maintained perpetually. 2.25.6.
In the dwelling, the private chamber, and the assembly hall—in all these places—the worldly fires shall be perpetual; they must be maintained without interruption. (2.25.6)
And the fire-sacrifice is to be performed daily, just as in the life of a householder.

And in those fires, the fire-worship must be performed constantly, just as in the domestic *aupāsana* rite; the meaning is that the evening and morning oblations (*sāyaṃprātarhoma*) are to be offered. The two mantras are also those same ones, and the sacrificial material is likewise that same one. (2.25.7)
In his residence, he should provide lodging for guests who are at least as learned as those well-versed in the Vedas. || 2.25.8 ||

One should lodge guests in the place called the guest-house (*āvasatha*). They are specified as "those for whom a *śrotriya* is the lowest limit. The word *avarārdhya* is a synonym for *avara*. [The meaning is: if one is unable to lodge all [guests], one should at least lodge those who are *śrotriyas*.
I shall provide them with dwellings, beds, food, and drink according to their respective merits. || 2.25.9 ||

To those guests, one should provide dwellings and other necessities according to their merit—that is, in accordance with their learning, conduct, and so forth—and especially so. "Dwellings" refers to inner apartments and the like; "beds" refers to couches and the like; "food" refers to rice and the like; and "drink" refers to buttermilk, soup, and the like. (2.25.9)
One should not live beyond the means of one's gurus and ministers. || 2.25.10 ||
The elders are the father and others; the ministers are the counselors. One should not live beyond them—that is, one should not surpass them in matters such as food, drink, and clothing. (2.25.10)
And in his realm no one shall perish from hunger, disease, cold, or heat, nor shall anyone do so intentionally.

In the realm and kingdom of this king, no one—not even a non-Brahmin—should perish or fall into distress through lack of food due to hunger, through disease or illness, through cold or frost (this also being indicative of rain and other such conditions), or through heat (the scorching rays of the sun). For it is the fault of the king if anyone should perish or fall into distress due to the absence of food and the like. Regarding the phrase "or intentionally," an illustration is given: when someone is to be made to pay a tax or a debt, he must not be exposed to cold or heat, nor should he be deprived of food; the king should punish anyone who acts in such a manner. (2.25.11)
In the middle of the assembly hall, having raised up the gaming-place and sprinkled it with water, he should cast down an even number of dice made of Vibhītaka wood, as many as required. 2.25.12.

In the middle of the assembly hall previously mentioned is the gambling-place (*adhidevana*). That spot where gamblers play with dice is the gambling-place; that he first digs up with wood or other tools. Having dug it up, he sprinkles it with water. Having sprinkled it, he scatters there an even number of dice made of *vibhītaka*—that is, products of the *vibhītaka* tree—as many as are required for the completion of the game. Who does this? He who is appointed there by the king, known as the master of the assembly (*sabhika*). 2.25.12.
The noble ones should be pure, truthful in character, and engaged in gambling. || 2.25.13 ||

The noble twice-born, pure and purified by dharma, possessing the habit of truth and speaking the truth—only such persons as these should be the gamblers (*dīvitāraḥ*) there; the meaning is that only they are permitted to play there. Having played there, they should depart after giving the stake (*paṇa*) to the master of the gaming house (*sabhika*) as agreed upon. He, in turn, should pay that revenue to the king daily, monthly, or annually. Furthermore, he alone shall punish those who gamble in other places, as well as those who cause quarrels in the gaming hall. On this point, Yājñavalkya says:
In a gambling match involving a hundred-fold interest,
the keeper of the gaming house shall take five percent from a rogue gambler and ten percent from any other.
"Having protected it properly, he should give the king the share as prescribed;
he should cause the victor to take what was won and give it to the winner; being patient, he should speak the truth. [YDh 2.199–200] || 2.25.13 ||
The taking up of weapons, dancing, singing, and instrumental music shall not exist except among those dependent upon the king. (2.25.14)

The taking up of weapons and other such acts should not be found, nor should they exist, among those persons who are dependent on the king or take refuge with the king, except [during] festivals and similar occasions; for such conduct occurs elsewhere as well. 2.25.14.
The king is a creator of security in whose realm, whether in village or forest, no fear of thieves exists. (2.25.15)

That king alone in whose realm—in village, forest, or city—there is no fear of thieves, is a maker of security, a bringer of safety; not so another, even if he were to give you a hundred [coins]. (2.25.15)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section:
By bestowing land and wealth upon Brahmins according to their merit, without causing hardship to his dependents, he conquers infinite worlds. 2.26.1.

Without causing hardship to his servants—that is, in such a way that no distress comes upon the group of dependents—he should give to the Brahmins land and wealth as is appropriate, according to their learning and conduct. By giving in this manner, he conquers infinite worlds.
When a king who seeks to conquer the property of Brahmins is slain, they call that sacrifice one where the self is the sacrificial post and the sacrificial fee is infinite. || 2.26.2 ||

When a king, desiring to recover the property of Brahmins stolen by thieves and others, defeats them with the intent of giving it back to the Brahmins, and is killed by those thieves in battle, those who know the Dharma say that for him this is a sacrifice in which his own self is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is infinite. Battle is the sacrifice; in it, his own self occupies the place of the sacrificial post. By "self," he means the body. The inner self (*antarātman*) occupies the place of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*). The wealth intended to be recovered is the sacrificial fee. However, in the Sūtra, the statement "they call it a sacrifice" is a figurative expression. (2.26.2)
By this, other heroes who cast off their bodies while fighting for a purpose are also explained.

The purpose [of this sacrifice] is the recovery of goods stolen by thieves and others that belong to Brāhmaṇas; those heroes who, for that purpose, fight and become "givers-up-of-the-body" (tanutyajaḥ), abandoning their bodies—they too are explained by this [sacrifice], wherein the king is the sacrificial post and the sacrifice has infinite sacrificial fees (anantadakṣiṇa). || 2.26.3 ||
In villages and cities, he should appoint noble, pure, and truthful men as overseers of the subjects. || 2.26.4 ||
"Noble, pure, and truthful in character"—this has been explained [ĀpDh 2.25.13]. He should appoint and employ such men in villages and cities for the purpose of protecting the subjects. 2.26.4.
The men among them would likewise possess those very same qualities. || 2.26.5 ||
Among those appointed, the men who are to be employed should possess such qualities as those of the noble ones and so forth. || 2.26.5 ||
The city, for a distance of one yojana on all sides, must be protected from thieves.
In every direction, for a distance of one *yojana* all around, the city must be protected from thieves. The reading "rakṣyan" (being protected) is a corruption.
A *krośa* [is the distance] from the villages. 2.2.6.7.

From the villages, however, a *krośa* must be guarded in all directions. Regarding the word "from the villages" (*grāmebhyaḥ*), the ablative case is used according to the rule: "The ablative should be stated when there is a measurement of distance. (Pāṇini 2.3.29). 2.26.7.
In that case, whatever has been stolen by them must be made good to him. 2.26.8.

In that case, whatever is stolen or robbed within a distance of one *yojana* or even one *krośa*, those appointed officials must restore it to the owners; it must be made good by them to the king, and the king shall cause it to be restored by them. Generally, they pronounce the letter *va* as a dental-labial.
He shall collect the lawful tax.

Regarding this, Gautama states: “The tax (*śulka*) on merchandise is one-twentieth. Whatever is sold by merchants, such as asafoetida and the like, the king shall take the twentieth part of that; this is designated as *śulka*. This is the righteous tax (*dhārmyaḥ śulkaḥ*); it should be collected and enforced by those appointed for the purpose. However, a specific rule concerning roots and other items has been stated by him alone: “For roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, and indigo, the tax is one-sixth. (GDh 10.26–27) 2.26.9.
One who is without property is a *śrotriya*. 2.26.10.
A learned Brahmin shall not be made to pay a tax; others may be made to pay. 2.26.10
And the women of all castes [are likewise]. 2.26.11.
Penalties: On account of the mention of "caste," women of inverse castes and the like are to be made to pay. || 2.26.11 ||
And the [stages of] youth precede the [appearance of the] secondary characteristics. 2.26.12.
The secondary characteristics are the beard and so forth; as long as these have not arisen, they are boys without marks (*akara*). 2.26.12.
And those who dwell there for the sake of knowledge. || 2.26.13 ||

Those who dwell with teachers for the sake of learning, even if they have acquired the outward marks [of a student], are non-payers of taxes as long as they have not completed their study of the Vedas. 2.26.13.
And those ascetics who are devoted to dharma. || 2.26.14 ||

Ascetics are those engaged in *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances; they are devoted to dharma and do not desire its fruits, being constantly intent upon obligatory and occasional duties. Why specify "devoted to dharma"? It is so that those who perform austerities for the sake of spells or the mastery of mantras—those who desire magical powers (*abhicāra*)—may not be included among the [true] performers of austerity. || 2.26.14 ||
And the Śūdra shall be the washer of feet. 2.26.15.
A Śūdra who washes the feet of members of the three higher castes and subsists on the water used for washing their feet is exempt from taxes.
And those afflicted by blindness, muteness, deafness, and disease. || 2.26.16 ||
And those such as the blind and so forth are non-factors, up to and including blindness and so forth. 2.26.16.
Those who are rendered useless by the possession of material wealth. || 2.26.17 ||

Furthermore, those such as wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) who are devoid of possessions and thus useless for worldly purposes, and whose holding of property is prohibited by the scriptures—they too are non-payers of taxes. And so says Vasiṣṭha: “A learned brahmin (*śrotriya*), a king’s servant, one without a protector, a wandering mendicant, a child, an elderly person, a youth, and those who are tranquil are exempt from tax” [VaDh 19.23]. || 2.26.17 ||
If a young man, though adorned, enters another's wife's quarters or a maiden's without prior intention, he shall be punished with a verbal reprimand. (2.26.18)

Where another’s wife, or a maiden choosing a husband, is seated, a young man entering there unadorned, unintentionally and out of ignorance, shall be rebuked with words: "She is sitting here; do not enter! (2.26.18)
But one who acts with malice intentionally should be punished. || 2.26.19 ||

But he who, knowing full well [the prohibition], enters with malicious intent and for the sake of seduction, shall be punished in proportion to the property and in proportion to the offense. The mention of "malicious intent" is so that there may be no punishment in the case of one entering having been sent by a teacher or others. 2.26.19.
When a sexual union has occurred, there shall be the excision of the penis together with the testicles.

Sexual intercourse is the act of union. When that has occurred, the punishment is the cutting off of the penis. The phrase "along with the testicles" is an adjective qualifying the penis even though it is a subordinate member; thus, it means the cutting off of the penis together with the testicles. (2.26.20)
But in the case of a maiden, having taken his own property, he should be banished. || 2.26.21 ||
But when sexual intercourse has occurred with a virgin, having confiscated all his property and banished him from the country, his penis shall not be cut off. (2.26.21)
Then [the king spoke] to his servant. 2.26.22.
From the time of their union onwards, the king must maintain the wife of another and the maiden by providing them with food and clothing for their servants.
And from this time forward, I shall refrain from sexual intercourse.
Therefore, from the first union onward, she must be protected from sexual intercourse; care must be taken so that they do not engage in sexual intercourse again. 2.26.23.
But when he has accepted the means of penance, he should release him from his obligations to his masters. || 2.26.24 ||

If they have thus been restrained and agree to undergo penance (*nirveṣa*), then, upon their undertaking of that penance, he shall release them to their masters—that is, he shall give them back: the wife of another to her husband or father-in-law, and a maiden to her father or brother. But if they do not agree to the penance, there shall be confinement for life. (2.26.24)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section.
For when conduct is as it was before, there is indeed a connection through righteousness. 2.27.1.

But when the penance has been performed, there is a connection with the Dharma as before—that is, as previously [stated]—wherein the ablative case is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus, "by means of the Dharma" [is established]. The word *hi* (for) indicates the reason. Since this is so, therefore a penance must necessarily be caused to be performed; consequently, there is no fault whatsoever in [participating in] sacrifices, marriages, and the like. 2.27.1
In connection with the subject of adultery with another's wife, it is said: "One should not disclose to others a woman who belongs to the same lineage. (2.27.2)

This refers to the case where a man who is childless, having determined his own lack of capacity, desires a son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and appoints his wife for another; or, when he has died, his father or other relatives desiring progeny. A woman who has entered from another family stands in the place of one belonging to the same lineage (*sagotra*). For she, having previously belonged to her father’s lineage, is now authorized by the duties of her husband’s lineage. Consequently, she becomes one who stands in the place of a *sagotra* relative to those on her husband’s side. Her husband, however, is directly a *sagotra*. She should not describe that woman, who stands in the place of a *sagotra*, to outsiders who are not of the same lineage, saying, "She is childless; offspring must be produced through her. Rather, he should describe her only to a *sagotra*, and among them, first to the husband's brother (*devara*), and in his absence, to a *sapiṇḍa*. (2.27.2)
What, then, is the distinction regarding one of the same lineage (*sagotra*)? He states this: for they teach that a woman is given in marriage to one of the same family (*kula*). 2.27.3.

For indeed, those who know the Dharma teach that when a maiden is being given away, she is given specifically for the sake of the family; therefore, one should declare her [as such] only to one of the same lineage. 2.27.3.
This [objection] undermines the aforementioned injunction;
it is a misconception arising from the weakness of the senses. 2.27.4.

Even if they acted thus in the past, nevertheless, that is contested and prohibited in the present day. Why? Because of the weakness of the senses; for men today have weak senses. Consequently, there would be an over-extension of the principle if one were to transgress against the husband even under the pretext of scriptural authority. (2.27.4)
And he says that even the distinction regarding one who belongs to the same lineage does not exist:
"For the 'otherness' of the hand is indeed undifferentiated. (2.27.5)

The hand by which the bride’s hand was previously taken with fire as witness becomes different from that very hand even for one of the same lineage (*sagotra*); because the state of being "other" (*paratva*) is undifferentiated and common [to all], there is thus no distinction. The reading "avaśiṣṭam" (remaining) is a corruption. 2.27.5.
Let there be another hand; what is the harm? But indeed, upon its transgression, both shall go to hell. (2.27.6)

If there is a transgression regarding that hand, both husband and wife shall go to hell. Indeed, the two particles *khalu* and *punar* serve to indicate what is well known. Therefore, the husband must not abandon that hand which was previously taken; nor must the wife abandon that hand by which her own hand was previously grasped. (2.27.6)
For the prosperity resulting from the undertaking of religious observances is greater than that resulting from the procreation of offspring. 2.27.7.

"Ārambhaṇa" means that by which something is commenced. That mutual agreement between husband and wife is the "commencement" (ārambhaṇa) of this [offspring]; thus, it is "one whose commencement is the agreement" (niyamārambhaṇa). Prosperity of such a kind is indeed more excellent—that is, more greatly increased. Therefore, because the offspring is commenced in the manner described, characterized by the appointment (niyoga), it is said to be "more excellent than that commenced offspring. Most read the word as "āpatyāt" [instead of "ārambhaṇāt"]. (2.27.7)
The offspring of an Ārya man from a Śūdra woman is an outcast (nāśya). || 2.27.8 ||
A nobleman of the three higher castes who is attached to a Śūdra woman who is the wife of another shall be expelled from the kingdom and banished by the king. (2.27.8)
A Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with an Ārya woman deserves death. 2.27.9.

However, a Śūdra who has sexual intercourse with an Ārya woman—that is, a woman of the three higher castes—is liable to corporal punishment. This applies specifically to one who, being an appointed guardian in charge of the inner apartments and the like, engages in such acts himself; for another, the previously mentioned excision of the penis alone applies. Thus, Gautama states in the section concerning Śūdras: "For approaching an Ārya woman, there shall be the extraction of the organ and the confiscation of all property; if she is of the same caste (gotrā), death is the additional penalty" [GDh 12.2–3]. Yājñavalkya, however, has prescribed the death penalty for any act of intercourse in the inverse order of castes (*prātilomya*). As it is said:
If [the offender] is of the same caste, the highest fine is prescribed; if [the victim] is of a lower caste, the middle fine;
but if [the victim] is of a higher caste, there shall be death for men and the cutting off of the nose and other [limbs] for women.

Thus, this [prohibition] should be understood as depending upon the circumstances and repeated practice. Likewise, the teacher’s statement, "An Ārya woman must not be given to a Śūdra" (ĀpDh 2.27.8), is also to be understood as depending upon the circumstances and repeated practice; or rather, it should be seen as referring to a Śūdra husband in the case of a sequential marriage for a Brāhmaṇa and others. || 2.27.9 ||
And he should cause his wife to fast. || 2.27.10 ||

If a woman of the three higher castes has been enjoyed by this Śūdra and has become his wife, he should cause her to emaciate herself through vows, restraints, and fasts. This applies specifically to those who have not borne children: "Women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have had sexual union with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not borne children, but not otherwise."
Because of this traditional teaching (smaraṇa). 2.27.10.
They teach that when one has sexual intercourse even once with a woman of the same caste who has previously belonged to another man, one-quarter of a *pātaka* falls upon him. 2.27.11.

A woman who has had another husband before is called *anyapūrvā*, meaning the wife of another; for having sexual intercourse once with such a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*), one falls [from his status]. For one who has fallen, the penance is twelve years; a fourth part of that—namely, three years of ordinary celibacy (*prākṛta-brahmacarya*)—is the penance for this offense. This applies to a Brāhmaṇa who, out of desire, is the first offender with the wife of a *Śrotriya* during her fertile period (*ṛtukāla*). Regarding this, Gautama says: “Two years for adultery with another’s wife, and three years for the wife of a *Śrotriya*” (GDh 22.29–30). 2.27.11.
Thus, in practice, there is a quarter [of the result] for each quarter. 2.27.12.
Thus, with each repetition in practice, a quarter [of the merit] falls away. 2.27.12.
Therefore: "In the fourth [case], everything. (2.27.13)

In the fourth offense, the entire penance falls; consequently, a full twelve-year penance must be performed, nine years for the third, and six for the second. This applies to the first offender according to each specific act and the particular type of woman involved. However, in the case of repetition with respect to the same woman, it should be calculated accordingly. In this regard, because of the traditional legal text (smṛti) stating: "Whatever [penalty] is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others, he should cause her to perform that same vow" (MDh 11.177), a quarter of the penance falls for each specific act even for a woman; the calculation should be made in accordance with that. 2.27.13.
The tongue of a Śūdra who reviles a righteous Ārya shall be cut out. || 2.27.14 ||

"If a Śūdra reviles, censures, or insults any one of the twice-born who is righteous and established in his own duty, then his tongue shall be cut off. Manu, however, has stated this as a general rule: "Whatever limb a person of a lower caste may use to offend a Brāhmaṇa, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the ordinance of Manu" (MDh 7.279).

Gautama, however, states: "A Śūdra who, having intended to harm or having struck twice-born men with verbal or physical violence, shall have that limb removed by which he caused the injury" (GDh 12.1). || 2.27.14 ||
Whether in speech, on the road, on a bed, or on a seat, striking with a staff against one who acts with equanimity [is a fault]. (2.27.15)

But if a Śūdra is equal to Āryas in speech and other respects, and does not remain in a subordinate position, he must be struck with a staff; he is to be beaten with a staff. This is his punishment. 2.27.15.
In the case of killing a human, theft, or seizing land, he shall be put to death after his own property has been confiscated. 2.27.16.

The seizure of land is the forcible appropriation of another's field. On account of such causes as the killing of a man and so forth, a Śūdra, after having his entire property confiscated, is subsequently to be put to death—that is, he is to be killed. || 2.27.16 ||
But for a Brahmin, there is the cessation of the eye regarding these things. || 2.27.17 ||

In the case of a Brāhmaṇa, however, upon these grounds, the eyes must be obstructed; the two eyes should be covered with a cloth or similar means so that he does not see for as long as he lives, but they are not to be plucked out, because of the traditional legal texts (smṛti) stating: "There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 12.46) and "A Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt" (MDh 8.124d). In the term "cakṣunirodhaḥ," the elision of the letter *r* is a Vedic archaism. 2.27.17.
One should cause him to violate his vows or bind him in secret. || 2.27.18 ||

He who transgresses the rules pertaining to the castes and stages of life—that violator of rules—or anyone else who commits forbidden acts, he shall bind in secret and confine him with fetters. || 2.27.18 ||
Up to the attainment [of meditative absorption]. 2.27.19.
He should continue until the boy declares, "I shall undertake the observances; I will refrain from what is forbidden. (2.27.19)
In the absence of formal attainment, it is to be abandoned. || 2.27.20 ||
If he does not enter [the meditative attainment] even after being restrained for a long time, then he is to be destroyed or expelled. || 2.27.20 ||
A teacher, an officiating priest, a graduate, and a king may provide protection, except in the case of one deserving death.

If the teacher should say to the king who has begun to inflict punishment, "I shall restrain him from this point forward; let him be released," then, having determined that where corporal punishment (*aṅgadaṇḍa*) was due there is a fine (*arthadaṇḍa*), where a fine was due there is beating (*tāḍana*), and where beating was due there is the "punishment of reproach" (*dhigdaṇḍa*), he should release him under the teacher's authority. The same applies to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). The priest and the teacher belong to the king as his own kin, not to the one being punished. A *snātaka* is protected by his learning and his vows. The king is the first among those [who protect]. All these are to be honored by the king; therefore, they may provide protection for one deserving of punishment, acting as guardians in the manner described, and no one else; yet even they [must not intervene] in the case of one who deserves death. For one whose offense merits execution, even teachers and the like cannot provide protection; he must simply be put to death. (2.27.20)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh section;
thus ends the tenth chapter in the second book of the Ujjvalā, a commentary on the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.
If one has acquired a field but, due to a lack of effort, there is no fruit, that which was prosperous shall be taken away from him when it comes into being. || 2.28.1 ||

A Vaiśya or one who follows the occupation of a Vaiśya, having taken possession of another’s field for the purpose of cultivation, if he does not apply effort or exertion toward the work of farming, and because of that lack, no fruit is produced, then on that account—if the cultivator is prosperous—he is to be made to forfeit whatever portion of the future fruit would have accrued; he must be made to pay it to the king, who shall cause it to be given to the owner of the field. (2.28.1)
For an uncontrolled laborer who abandons his work, there shall be punishment by flogging.

*Kīnāśa* means a farmer. If that *avaśin*—one who is not independent, lacking self-control, and destitute—a slave, should abandon his work, that is, should cease from the labor of cultivation, he must be punished with a beating; he is to be struck with a rod. Because he lacks wealth, there is no monetary fine. Another says: *avaśī* means one who is not subject to control, one who is disobedient. If, having taken possession of a field, he should abandon the farming work for a farmer (*kīnāśa*) who is not under his authority—that is, if he himself does not do it—then that person who took possession [of the field] is to be beaten with a rod. Or else, *avaśinaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: if a farmer who has no one under his own control, no independent person, nor a landowner, should abandon the farming work of a field previously ploughed, then a beating is the punishment for him; such is the instruction for the king’s officer. (2.28.2)
And likewise for the animal-sacrificer. 2.28.3.
A *paśupa* is a cowherd; even for him, in the event of the abandonment of his duty—that is, the failure to tend the cattle—there is punishment consisting of being struck with a staff. || 2.28.3 ||
And he shall provide an enclosure for his livestock. 2.28.4.
Furthermore, those cattle that have been entrusted to him for protection must be confined and seized, and he must be handed over to another cowherd. (2.28.4)
Having left the fold, he should not cause the cattle to suffer by driving them too early, nor should he exhaust them. || 2.28.5 ||

Those animals that are confined in a pen or a cow-pasture, having left that pen, become consumers of crops and other such things; he should emaciate them by means of confinement and other methods, making them lean. Who? One who possesses what has been consumed, or a royal officer. He should not cause excessive distress, nor should he obstruct them excessively, nor should he beat them. (2.28.5)
Having penned up animals for slaughter or destruction, one should release them back to their owners. (2.28.6)

If a man, having penned and taken cattle for protection, should release them into places of danger and, through negligence, kill or cause them to be lost—the loss consisting of their being carried off by thieves and the like—he must restore the cattle to their owners; in the absence of the cattle, he must pay their value. (2.28.6)
If, through negligence, he sees cattle released in the forest, he should bring them to the village and return them to their owners. (2.28.7)

If, through the negligence of their owners, they should release cattle into the forest without providing for their protection, then, having seen them, one should bring them back to the village and hand them over to the owners. Who? He who has been appointed there by the king as a protector. (2.28.7)
Furthermore, in the case of negligence, having restrained [the mind] even once. || 2.28.8 ||
If they are released again through negligence, one should confine them once more and return them to their owners. || 2.28.8 ||
Thereafter, one should not pay heed [to worldly affairs]. (2.28.9)

Thereafter, after the second application, one should not heed—that is, one should not pay attention to—what was said [previously], such as "having brought him to the village," and so forth; one should remain indifferent toward that matter. || 2.28.9 ||
One who, being ignorant, takes what belongs to another—whether firewood, water, roots, flowers, fruits, perfumes, food, or vegetables—is censured by mere word. 2.28.10

*Edhodakam* means fuel and water. *Grāsaḥ* refers to fodder and the like for the purpose of feeding cattle and other animals. In all these cases, the locative case is used in the sense of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*). He who, being ignorant—that is, taking without knowing that it is the property of another—takes or seizes fuel, water, and so forth, should be restrained by a royal official appointed to that matter with harsh words, having been forbidden from that object. (2.28.10)
The theft of the garment of one who knows [the truth]. || 2.28.11 ||
But for that learned man who takes it, the release—that is, the removal—of the garment must be performed. || 2.28.11 ||
One who takes food when his life is in danger is not to be punished, even if he did so out of desire. (2.28.12)

The word "likewise" (tathā) is connected with the word "eating. When there is a danger to life, one is not to be punished even if one takes firewood, water, or other such things intentionally; likewise, one who takes food when there is a danger to life is not to be punished. (2.28.12)
When the occasion for punishment has arisen, sin touches the king if he fails to act. || 2.28.13 ||

If, with regard to that person for whom a punishment has been incurred—meaning, in the non-infliction of the punishment—if one does not carry out the deserved punishment out of compassion or greed for wealth, then that sin touches the king. (2.28.13)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth section.

Now, it is a well-known principle that the fruit of an action belongs to the performer; how then can the sin committed by one person affect another? He says that this is because the status of being an agent is manifold:
"The instigator, the one who intends, and the doer [are all agents] with respect to actions whose fruits are heaven or hell."
The sharers [of the inheritance]. || 2.29.1 ||

One who prompts another to perform either dharma or adharma by saying, "Do it thus," is the prompter (*prayojayitā*). He is of many kinds: the commander (*ājñāpaka*), the requester (*abhyarthayitā*), and the benefactor (*anugrāhaka*). Commanding a subordinate, such as a servant, is "command" (*ājñā*). Prompting a venerable person, such as a teacher, is "request" (*abhyarthanā*). Benefaction is twofold: instruction and personal practice. Among these, he who instructs thus—"Kill this enemy; this is the means for you to acquire merit"—is the instructor (*upadeṣṭā*). Furthermore, when someone who intends to kill another stops one who is fleeing, and the one being stopped is killed, there the stopper is the benefactor (*anugrāhaka*). The consenter (*anumantā*) is one whose consent is required for an action to be accomplished; such a person, like a king, is the consenter regarding dharma and adharma. The doer (*kartā*) is the one who directly brings about the action. All three of these share in the results—both in actions leading to heaven or hell, and in both dharma and adharma—as partakers of a portion of the fruit. (2.29.1)
And although all [factors] are in some way or other the agent, nevertheless, whichever one initiates more [activity], there is a distinction in the fruit resulting from that. (2.29.2)

Among those [factors] such as the instigator and so forth, whichever one initiates more—whichever one's activity is more extensively utilized for the accomplishment of the purpose—in that one there occurs a specific result. (2.29.2)
The two householders are masters of the wealth. 2.29.3.

A married couple, as householders, are masters over the acquisition and expenditure of wealth. Even so, nevertheless, a woman is not empowered to expend it without the husband’s permission, whereas the husband is so empowered. This is to be understood from the following: "For they do not teach that there is theft when the husband is away on a journey or when giving for a specific religious occasion" (ĀpDh 2.14.20). 2.29.3.
With their approval, others as well may employ them in other taddhita suffixes. 2.2.29.4.

When the consent of that couple has been obtained, other sons and relatives may also act on their behalf regarding their worldly and otherworldly interests, even by means of the disposal of their property. (2.29.4)
In a dispute, those who are endowed with learning and noble birth, who are aged, wise, and undeluded regarding the principles of dharma [should be consulted]. || 2.29.5 ||

A *vivāda* (legal dispute) is a contradictory statement between the plaintiff and the defendant. In that regard, the ellipsis of the sentence is: "The adjudicators (*nirṇetāraḥ*) should be endowed with qualities such as learning and so forth. Learning (*vidyā*) is the perfection of study and knowledge. Noble birth (*abhijana*) is purity of lineage. "Elderly" (*vṛddhāḥ*) means those who have reached advanced age. "Intelligent" (*medhāvinaḥ*) means those skilled in reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*). Regarding "duties" (*dharmeṣu*), namely those pertaining to the castes and stages of life, they must be "unerring" (*avinipātinaḥ*); "error" (*vinipāta*) means negligence, and they must be free from that. (2.29.5)
Having deliberated upon the doubt as to whether it was by means of a sign or by fate... || 2.29.6 ||

And they, while deliberating upon points of doubt by means of indicative marks (*liṅga*), that is, through inference based on divine [evidence] such as the *taptamāṣa* ordeal and so forth—the word "iti" here denotes manner—and by whatever else is likewise appropriate, such as the contradiction of statements (*vacanavyāghāta*) and so on, having sifted through these and sought the established state of the matter, they should be the final determiners; thus the sentence is completed by supplying the verb "they should be. (2.29.6)

Now follows the procedure for witnesses. On an auspicious day, in the morning, when the fire has been kindled at the edge of water, having had both parties informed in the presence of the king, the principal witness, with the approval of all, shall [answer] the question regarding the truth.
He should say. 2.29.7.

It is an auspicious day and a favorable constellation; it is in the morning, not at midday or other such times. When the fire has been kindled, having lit the fire, and having placed water near it at its edge, in an assembly presided over by a king (*rājavati*), the witness proclaims himself before both parties—the plaintiff and the defendant—saying: "Am I an authoritative witness for you two? Or alternatively: "Regarding the future fruit that awaits witnesses in both cases—whether they speak the truth or speak falsehood—speak the truth, abandoning untruth; through truth you shall attain heaven."
Having spoken such a most terrible falsehood, you shall fall into hell.

Having been thus formally addressed, and having been questioned by the presiding judge and others—the ellipsis being "questioned"—when there is the consent of all, that is, the plaintiff, the defendant, and the members of the court, the primary witness, endowed with the qualities of a witness and free from defects, shall state the truth regarding the matter asked about, exactly as he himself knows it. (2.29.7)
The king shall inflict punishment for falsehood. 2.29.8.
The king, having determined that a witness has spoken falsely, shall inflict punishment. Regarding this, Manu says:
"If, within seven days of the witness having given his testimony, disease, fire, or the death of a kinsman should befall him, he shall be made to pay the debt and a fine. (MDh 8.108)
And one should not inflict punishment when there is doubt. || 2.29.8 ||
Not only is there royal punishment for speaking untruth, but furthermore—hell and so forth await one in the life hereafter. (2.29.9)
The "hereafter" (*sāṃparāya*) is the next world, and in that place there is hell. But it is not so:
"But men who have committed sins and been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed good deeds" (MDh 8.318).
Thus, this is its object. || 2.29.9 ||
Through truthfulness, there is heaven and the praise of all beings. 2.29.10.
When truth is spoken, heaven is attained; all beings praise him, even the gods. 2.29.10
That which is found among women and Śūdras is the ultimate limit of knowledge.

In women and among Śūdras, whatever knowledge exists is the culmination, the completion of knowledge; once that has been attained, the performance of ritual action is firmly established. || 2.29.11 ||
They teach that this is the supplement to the Atharvaṇa Veda. || 2.29.12 ||

Those who study what was proclaimed by Atharvan are called *ātharvaṇikas*. [The suffix] *ṭhak* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.63 (*vasantādibhyaṣ ṭhak*). Their sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is: "For the word *ātharvaṇika*, there is the elision of the syllable *i*" (Pāṇini 4.3.133), resulting in *ātharvaṇa*. This present work is a supplement to that Veda; thus those who know the Dharma teach: "Knowledge [should be imparted] among women and among Śūdras. (2.29.12)
The completion of dharma is difficult to achieve through mere traditional recitation; rather, it is accomplished through the performance of its defining characteristics. || 2.29.13 ||

*Samāmnāna* refers to the recitation word-for-word; by means of that *samāmnāna*, the completion of the Dharma cannot be achieved with difficulty, but rather it is completed through the act of defining (*lakṣaṇakarma*). That by which distinct things are understood is a "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*); it is completed by the performance—that is, the application—of that [definition]. The reading with two *t*s in the phrase *karmāt tu* is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*). Alternatively, there is the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the particle *āt*, and this should be understood in the sense of "immediately" (*sadyaḥ*). 2.29.13.
In this regard, the characteristic will be stated.

As for that characteristic: among all inhabited lands, one should adopt a conduct similar to that of the noble ones—those who are exclusively composed, perfectly disciplined, aged, self-possessed, free from greed, and devoid of hypocrisy. In this way, one conquers both worlds. 2.29.14
"Regarding 'all people' (sarvajana), this has been explained [in Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.20.8–9]. || 2.29.14 ||
"One should learn the remaining rules of dharma from women and from members of all social classes"—so say some authorities. 2.29.15.

Those dharmas which are distinct from those already mentioned are "residual dharmas" (*dharmaśeṣa*); some maintain that one should learn them even from sources such as women. These [residual dharmas] vary according to each country and each family, and must be understood accordingly. In this regard, there are examples such as the Dravidians performing a worship of the Sun when the sun is situated in Aries, having drawn a mandala on the ground, and so forth. The repetition [of the word *iti*] marks the conclusion of the chapter. 2.29.15.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth section;
thus ends the eleventh chapter in the second book of the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra;
thus ends the second book.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the second book of the *Ujjvalā*, the commentary on the *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra. And so, this *Āpastamba-dharmasūtra* is completed.
The second question is completed,
and this commentary on the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra, titled Ujjvalā, is also finished.
[1] I follow Bühler. The Mysore edition reads: *karmasu samarthaḥ*.
